# Writing social media posts with AI — what actually drives virality

*Deep research report — 36 items x 32 fields, generated 2026-09-11. 327 of 1152 field values (28.4%) came back marked uncertain and are omitted below rather than stated as fact.*

**Evidence discipline.** Most tactical numbers circulating about 2026 social media come from vendor blogs that cite each other, several of which are themselves AI-generated. Throughout this report, direction is treated as informative and magnitude as unverified unless the source is platform-official, primary source code, or peer-reviewed. Where credible sources disagree, both are recorded; the last source read does not silently win.

**Scope.** This report covers the writing craft and the science of what gets shared. Per-platform ranking mechanics are deliberately not re-derived here — see the companion note *Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026*, subject to the corrections listed immediately below.

## What did not hold up

18 claims that circulate as fact — several of them load-bearing in popular advice, and several that entered this research's own working notes before being caught — did not survive primary-source checking. This section exists so the reader can stop doing these things first.

**1. Claimed:** Each moral-emotional word gives ~+17% shares (IRR 1.17).

**Actually:** Best population estimate is **IRR 1.13, 95% CI [1.06, 1.20]** (inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis). 1.17 is one replication's *unweighted* mean, inflated by a single 1.66 outlier on the smallest dataset (6.3% of N). Median of the five datasets is **1.07**; four of five fall in 0.97-1.12. The honest practical magnitude is **+8% per SD** (dictionary) / +16% per SD (GPT). The paper is internally inconsistent: abstract says 1.17, Results says 1.15.

**2. Claimed:** A field experiment showed human-written Instagram posts beat AI-written ones (likes 42.6 vs 39.6, comments 5.3 vs 2.3, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%).

**Actually:** The means are right; **none of the differences is significant**. Mann-Whitney U: likes p=.91, comments p=.07, shares p=.17, saves p=.79, reach p=.89, impressions p=.51, ER p=.64. Flesheriu & Fron (2025) state 'H1 was not supported' and conclude **equivalence**. Dropping one launch-day outlier flips ER toward AI; readers significantly *preferred* AI captions (U=8.0, p=.045); 7 of the 12 top posts were AI. It is also an AI-*image*-plus-caption test in a culinary niche on one 770-follower account, with 64% of engagement attributed by the authors to the visual.

**3. Claimed:** X/Grok reads the tone of every post and throttles combative content even at high engagement.

**Actually:** The open-sourced live ranker (`github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm`, Apache-2.0) carries **no valence or tone score**. `Grox` runs spam/adult/violence classifiers plus text and image embeddings. The real mechanism is negative-action weighting in `home-mixer/params/param.rs`: `ReportWeight -234.0`, `MuteAuthorWeight -58.8`, `NotInterestedWeight -43.2`, `BlockAuthorWeight -31.2` against `FavoriteWeight 0.5` and `ShareViaCopyLinkWeight 20.0`; `Agatha` labels *accounts* by blocks/reports per favourite over 180 days. The vendors' conclusion is right and their mechanism is wrong — and the wrong mechanism yields the wrong tactic. The target is that nobody reaches for mute, not that you sound cheerful.

**4. Claimed:** Stats + quotes + cited sources lift generative-engine visibility up to 40%.

**Actually:** Three **separate** single interventions in Aggarwal et al. (KDD 2024, GEO-Bench, 10,000 queries): Quotation +41%, Statistics ~+31%, Cite Sources +28%, Keyword Stuffing -9%. A pair experiment does exist (§5.3) — best pair beats any single by >5.5% — but it ran on a **200-example subset**, 50x thinner than the headline table, and the two best singles do *not* form the best pair. GEO is also **redistributive, not expansive**: Cite Sources moves the rank-5 source +115.1% and the rank-1 source **-30.3%**.

**5. Claimed:** Localized content gets 3x the engagement of English-only.

**Actually:** Traces to a vendor claim of 3x **conversion** from cultural adaptation, which drifted into an engagement framing in circulation. Do not repeat it. Real anchor: CULTURE-MT (arXiv 2605.25626, N=1,002) — 90.80% culturally effective vs 50.40% for an 8B baseline, while BLEU/ChrF/COMET barely moved, meaning the standard quality gate is blind to the only failure that matters.

**6. Claimed:** Share-to-DM sends are weighted 3-5x likes on Instagram Reels.

**Actually:** No platform-published coefficient exists. Mosseri's own statement says sends are **'slightly' more important** than likes, and only for *unconnected* content — likes are slightly more important for connected content. The 3-5x traces to a vendor piece citing unnamed 'industry analysis' with no sample or method. The 84% dark-social figure is likewise unsourced.

**7. Claimed:** Aim for a hook rate above 30%; below 15% is weak.

**Actually:** 'Hook rate' is **not a Meta metric** — it is derived from two Ads Manager columns (3-second video plays / impressions), and Meta publishes no benchmark. Vendor bands contradict each other (one puts the platform median near 20%, another claims 28% average) and the <15% failure line is lower than any 2026 band found. Use a personal rolling median instead of any external band.

**8. Claimed:** LinkedIn penalizes you for posting twice within 4 hours.

**Actually:** **Negative result.** Untraceable to any primary source; the one targeted hit was a consultant newsletter where '4 hours' refers to tagging and ally reposts. 18-hour and 24-hour variants circulate alongside it — the signature of folklore. The real, documented spacing mechanism is X's author-diversity decay: `multiplier = (1 - floor) * decay^k + floor`, defaults decay 0.5 / floor 0.25, so consecutive same-author posts score 1.000, 0.625, 0.4375, floor 0.25. No timer involved.

**9. Claimed:** Creators with under 500 followers are cited by AI engines comparably to large accounts.

**Actually:** Semrush's actual finding is that **nearly half** of cited authors had **over 2,000 followers**. The follower-independence case is better supported by GEO's redistribution mechanism (rank-5 source +115.1%) than by the survey.

**10. Claimed:** EU AI Act Art. 50 exposes a solo creator to fines up to EUR 15M or 3% of turnover, with a grace period to 2026-12-02.

**Actually:** Art. 99(4) takes whichever is **higher**, but Art. 99(6) caps SMEs at whichever is **lower** — so for a Polish solo consultancy the binding figure is 3% of a small turnover, not EUR 15M. The grace period is **routinely misattributed**: Art. 111(4) is scoped to *providers*, to Art. 50(2) *marking*, and to *pre-existing systems only*. **Deployer duties have applied in full since 2026-08-02 with no transition.**

**11. Claimed:** Pangram found 30% of LinkedIn comments AI-generated across ~57,000 items.

**Actually:** The primary source (Spero & Aerts, 2026-07-09) reports **N=1,002,627 posts** from an opt-in Chrome-extension panel, Apr-Jun 2026: LinkedIn long-form **40.5%** fully AI, LinkedIn comments **23.7%** (n=12,447), X long-form 24.1% fully + 23.2% mixed, Reddit 4.4%, Medium 30.6%, Substack 10.0%. The ~57,000 / 30% version appears nowhere on Pangram's blog.

**12. Claimed:** LinkedIn's 360Brew paper documents its LLM ranking architecture.

**Actually:** **arXiv 2501.16450 was withdrawn by arXiv administrators in Aug 2025** over licensing. It was the load-bearing citation for LinkedIn's ranking architecture across this entire research set — treat every downstream claim resting on it as unsupported until re-sourced.

**13. Claimed:** Online diffusion splits into a bimodal pattern of broadcast versus viral spread.

**Actually:** The word **'bimodal' appears zero times** in Goel, Anderson, Hofman & Watts — the paper's own language is 'surprising structural diversity'. Do not put 'no bimodal split' in quotes either. Canonical citation is **Management Science 62(1):180-196, January 2016**, not 2015. Base rates worth carrying: average cascade size 1.3, ~99% terminate in one generation, only 0.025% (1 in 4,000) reach 100 nodes.

**14. Claimed:** STEPPS is the authoritative framework for what gets shared.

**Actually:** **'STEPPS' appears zero times** in Berger's own 2025 peer-reviewed synthesis (Annu. Rev. Psychol. 76:559-581); 'Contagious' appears once, in the reference list. The review organizes around six drivers (impression management, accessibility, emotion regulation, information acquisition, social bonding, persuasion) plus four moderators. STEPPS has no slot for four of them. The review is free under CC-BY — but only the `/doi/pdf/` path serves it; the HTML landing page 403s.

**15. Claimed:** Engagement pods now carry up to a 45% reach penalty, with ~97% detection accuracy.

**Actually:** Both magnitudes are untraceable vendor numbers. What is verifiable: LinkedIn's Professional Community Policies prohibit the **prior agreement** — *"don't agree with others ahead of time to like or re-share each other's content"* — which is exactly why a curated 30-50 account commenting routine is permitted at identical regularity. And X's own `param.rs` states engagement from group-chat coordination plus direct navigation *"has no ranking impact"*: on X, pods are **inert before they are penalised**.

**16. Claimed:** Make your writing more specific and concrete.

**Actually:** Wrong more often than right. A registered report over **8,977 Upworthy field A/B tests** (Aubin Le Quere & Matias, *Scientific Reports* 2025) found concreteness has an inverted-U effect: added concreteness helped **8.7%** of real headlines and **hurt 50.9%**.

**17. Claimed:** Storytelling persuades better than straight argument.

**Actually:** **77 experiments, N=24,380** (Rahmani et al. 2025, *Behavioural Public Policy*) found **no statistically significant difference** between narrative and non-narrative treatments. The honest case for storytelling is attention, not persuasion — which suits a dwell-ranked feed anyway.

**18. Claimed:** Use an LLM panel to pick which hook will perform best.

**Actually:** Generation and discrimination are separable, and models are near-chance at the second. A fine-tuned BERT scored **76.5% vs GPT-4o's 58.3%** against a 50.9% random baseline over 86,035 controlled pairs (arXiv 2505.03769). Independently, LOLA (arXiv 2406.02611, 17,681 Upworthy A/B tests) found prompt-based LLM approaches *'perform poorly'*. Use the panel to eliminate incomprehensible variants, never to pick the winner.

## Items

## B. AI tooling for the writing craft

### LLM ghostwriting with voice prompts

`llm-ghostwriting` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 9 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: LLM ghostwriting with voice prompts. Category: tooling. Definition: using a general-purpose chat model (ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini) as the drafting writer for social posts, steered by an explicit voice specification plus few-shot exemplars of your own past writing, with a human supplying the substance and the final edit. Maturity: established as a practice (near-universal among B2B creators by 2026) but entering a hostile phase — as of May 2026 LinkedIn actively suppresses text its classifier reads as generic AI output, so voice prompting has shifted from an offensive edge to a defensive minimum.

**as of date and volatility**

True as of 2026-09-11. Three different decay clocks apply. (1) STABLE: the peer-reviewed findings on LLM-induced homogenization of writing (Padmakumar & He, ICLR 2024) and on instruction drift within a dialog (arXiv 2402.10962) are not going to reverse. (2) 6-12 MONTHS: model behaviour — every major model upgrade re-tunes the default register, so a voice spec calibrated on one model version needs re-validation after an upgrade (documented behaviour drift in GPT-4 over time, arXiv 2307.09009). (3) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER: the enforcement layer. LinkedIn announced AI-slop suppression 2026-05-20 and changed comment ranking to per-viewer relevance on 2026-08-09; X open-sourced its Grok-based Phoenix ranker on 2026-01-11 and landed a 187-file, ~18k-line refresh on 2026-05-15, with xAI committing to public updates every four weeks. The banned-phrase list inside a voice spec is the fastest-rotting component — assume a one-quarter shelf life.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

Seven concrete steps, and the failure of the technique is almost always the omission of one of them. (1) CORPUS: collect 20-40 pieces of your own writing — past posts, vault notes, long Slack/email answers. Below ~20 there is not enough signal to extract a spec. (2) EXTRACTION: a separate model call reads the corpus and emits an explicit voice specification: 8-12 observable rules (sentence-length distribution, opening habits, how you handle hedging, punctuation you never use, formatting rhythm, point-of-view, what you refuse to say), each with three verbatim quotes from the corpus as proof. This is the artefact, not the chat. (3) BANNED LIST: the same call is asked what a generic model would default to that you never do — this becomes a hard negative-constraint list. (4) BRIEF: you write 3-5 rough lines yourself containing the non-substitutable substance (a number only you have, a first-hand scene with a time and place, a named person/client/tool, a stance you would defend). The model must never originate this. (5) GENERATION: spec + 3-5 full exemplar posts in-context + brief + 'add no facts I did not give you'. Both the spec and the exemplars are required: exemplars carry rhythm a spec cannot articulate, the spec carries the hard bans that exemplars underdetermine. (6) CRITIQUE: a second call in a FRESH context (not a continued thread) scores the draft against the spec and the banned list and returns only violations — a continued thread rationalises its own output. (7) HUMAN EDIT: you rewrite the first two lines and the last line by hand, every time. The mechanism is style transfer conditioned on an author corpus; the research analogue is few-shot authorship style transfer with authorship embeddings (TinyStyler, EMNLP Findings 2024), where a target-author sample set is what conditions the rewrite.

**ranking signal targeted**

Honest answer: this tactic moves no positive ranking signal directly. It is a throughput-and-defence tactic, not a distribution tactic. What it does move is a NEGATIVE gate that became real in 2026: the genericness classifier. LinkedIn's ranking now runs through a text-native decoder model (360Brew, 150B, Mixtral 8x22B base, >30 predictive tasks, arXiv 2501.16450), and its May 2026 policy explicitly demotes text that 'lacks any real unique perspective or substance'; X's Phoenix ranker is likewise a Grok-based transformer reading post text. So the signal is: pass/fail on 'is this generic', which gates whether the post reaches out-of-network recommendation at all. Secondary and weaker: dwell time / see-more expansion, via readability and rhythm that matched voice produces. Tertiary: nothing. Claims that voice prompting itself lifts comments, saves or sends are folklore.

**why it drives reach**

Causal chain, stated honestly. Voice prompting does not create reach; it removes the two things that cap it. First, cadence: drafting is the bottleneck for most working professionals, and a calibrated voice spec cuts per-post time roughly 2-3x, which buys more shots at the cold-start lottery (each post is an independent draw against a small test audience before out-of-network expansion — see [[Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026]]). Second, the suppression gate: since 2026-05-20 on LinkedIn, unedited generic output is not removed but confined to direct connections and followers, which zeroes out-of-network reach — the only reach that compounds. Voice matching plus a human-supplied specific is what keeps a post on the amplified side of that gate. The weak link in the chain is that nobody has measured reach-per-post as a function of voice-match quality; the cadence half is mechanical and the gate half is platform-stated, but the join is inferred.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Draft and vary — plus critique when you run a second pass. The model is a rewriter conditioned on your corpus, not an author. It does not retrieve (that is RAG-grounded post generation), does not score against engagement data (that is engagement prediction, covered in [[Marketing Agent Research]]), and must not originate the claim. The cleanest mental model: you supply the proposition and the evidence, the model supplies sentence-level execution in your register, and a second instance supplies adversarial review.

**automation level**

L1 (AI-assisted draft). It becomes L2 (autonomous with guardrails) only if you add a machine critique gate plus a hard human approval before publish — and L2 here means the draft is autonomous, never the publish. Nothing in this item sits at L3, and any tool marketing 'autonomous AI ghostwriting agents' in 2026 is an L1 drafter bolted to a scheduler. Note that L1 is not a limitation to be engineered away: the human step is exactly the input the 2026 platform classifiers are probing for.

**prompt patterns**

Concrete structures, not advice. (A) TWO-CALL VOICE EXTRACTION: call 1 — 'Here are 30 things I wrote. Emit a voice spec as 8-12 rules I could check a draft against mechanically. For each rule, quote three lines from the corpus as evidence. Then list 15 constructions a generic assistant would produce that appear nowhere in my corpus.' Call 2 uses that spec; never ask a single call to both infer and write. (B) NEGATIVE-CONSTRAINT BLOCK, verbatim in the prompt: ban 'it's not X, it's Y', 'Here's the thing', 'Let that sink in', 'The result?', 'In today's fast-paced world', rhetorical-question-then-one-word-paragraph, triadic lists, and em-dash-per-sentence rhythm. A vendor with its own detector (MagicPost, 2026) measured four of these as costing 4.3%-6.7% reach within-author — directionally useful, magnitude unverified. (C) REWRITE-NOT-GENERATE: paste your own rough 150 words and instruct 'restructure and tighten; you may cut, reorder and sharpen; you may not add a claim, an example or a number'. This is the single highest-yield pattern and the least used. (D) RUBRIC SELF-CRITIQUE in a fresh context: 'Score 1-5 and quote the offending line: (i) contains a number/name/date only the author could supply; (ii) zero banned constructions; (iii) sentence lengths vary — at least one line under 6 words and one over 25; (iv) the first line would stop a skim; (v) nothing asserted that was not in the brief. Return only failures.' (E) EXEMPLAR SELECTION RULE: pick exemplars for voice-representativeness, not for past performance — choosing your top-performing posts introduces survivorship and collapses every future draft into one format.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

moderate — split by sub-claim. STRONG/peer-reviewed: that LLM co-writing homogenizes text and raises inter-author similarity. MODERATE: that AI-drafted social posts can outperform human-written ones on engagement (one peer-reviewed multi-study paper, brand accounts on X). PLATFORM-OFFICIAL: that generic AI output is now demoted on LinkedIn. VENDOR-CLAIM/UNVERIFIED: every circulating percentage for how much reach AI-detected posts lose. ANECDOTAL: that a voice spec specifically (as opposed to any careful editing) is what recovers the loss.

**evidence provenance**

Mixed, and the mix matters more than any single number. Peer-reviewed: Padmakumar & He (ICLR 2024) on diversity loss; Huang & Zhou (Public Relations Review, 2025) on AI-vs-human engagement; Li et al. (arXiv 2402.10962) on instruction drift. Platform-official: LinkedIn's own May 2026 announcement by Laura Lorenzetti (VP & Executive Editor, LinkedIn Global Editorial), including its self-reported 94% flagging accuracy — a platform number about its own product, not independently verified. Platform-research: LinkedIn's 360Brew paper. Vendor-with-product-to-sell: MagicPost (sells a LinkedIn AI tool AND runs its own AI detector — both sides of the claim), SocialNexis, ViralBrain, plus a widely-recirculated 'Hootsuite analysed 10,000 pages' figure I could not trace to a primary Hootsuite publication. Single-creator anecdote: most 'my voice prompt tripled my reach' posts.

**conflicting evidence**

AI-VS-HUMAN PERFORMANCE (mandatory slot, and genuinely unresolved). Side A: Huang & Zhou (2025, Public Relations Review, peer-reviewed) find GPT-4-generated social posts outperform human-written ones on engagement across three studies, and that trained PR professionals given the same framework and paid incentives could not match the model. Side B: LinkedIn's own May 2026 policy demotes text its classifier reads as generic AI, and a cluster of vendor datasets report large negative deltas for AI-detected posts. These do not cancel out — they measure different things. Side A measured brand-account posts on X optimised for fluency/interactivity/information/tone, in a period with no provenance-based suppression; Side B measures personal-brand posts on LinkedIn under a classifier explicitly tuned against low-effort output, and is confounded because 'AI-detected' and 'low-effort' are the same population in observational data. Nobody has run the randomised test that would settle it: same author, same substance, voice-matched AI draft vs hand-written, randomised, on one platform. CADENCE: the main benefit of this tactic is throughput, which collides with the unresolved 2-4 vs 11+ posts/week dispute and with a vendor claim that three-to-four consecutive AI-heavy weeks produce compounding suppression that also hits later human posts — unverified, no primary source, but the direction is consistent with account-level quality scoring. LINK-IN-FIRST-COMMENT: not implicated by this tactic; no conflict to record here. THE DETECTOR LAYER also conflicts with itself: top detectors report 94-96% on unedited model output but independent testing puts real-world accuracy far lower once text is edited, and a 2023 Patterns study plus a 2026 follow-up found heavy false-positive bias against non-native English writers — so 'passes a detector' and 'is human' are not the same proposition in either direction.

#### fit

**scales with**

Caps on this tactic are personal, not structural. (1) Corpus size and honesty: below ~20 pieces of your own writing the extraction produces platitudes; the ceiling is how distinctive your writing actually is — a genuinely generic writer cannot be voice-matched into distinctiveness. (2) Your supply of substance: the tactic scales drafting, not having something to say, so it hits a wall at the rate you accumulate proprietary numbers and first-hand stories. (3) Review capacity: the critique + hand-edit step does not compress, so realistic ceiling is ~3-5 posts/day before the human step degrades. It does NOT scale with account size or network position — a 200-follower account gets the same drafting benefit. Objective-dependent ceiling worth noting: small accounts can be cited by AI answer engines comparably to large ones, but do not go viral comparably, so if citation is the goal the follower ceiling matters less than it looks.

**decay and saturation**

The core technique does not saturate — matching your own voice is by construction non-copyable, and unlike a hook template it cannot be arbitraged by everyone at once. What decays fast is every SHARED component: public voice-prompt packs, 'viral LinkedIn post' prompt templates, and the specific phrasings a model defaults to. Observed decay is 12-24 months for shared hook templates, and by mid-2026 four specific model-default constructions were already measurably penalised. Practical shelf life: voice spec ~2-4 quarters (re-validate after every model upgrade), banned-phrase list ~1 quarter, exemplar set ~2 quarters before it makes your output sound like last year's you. Structural risk rather than decay: as everyone adopts voice prompting, the differentiator migrates from HOW it is written to WHAT is in it — which is why this item is the weakest of the three tooling items on its own.

#### risk

**failure modes**

(1) DRIFT WITHIN THE SESSION: instruction stability degrades measurably within ~8 rounds of dialog (arXiv 2402.10962), so a long iterate-in-one-thread session ends in the model's default register no matter how good the opening spec was. Fix: fresh chat per post. (2) ABSTRACT SPEC: rules like 'be authentic, direct, human' have no effect; only mechanically checkable rules do. (3) SURVIVORSHIP EXEMPLARS: picking your best-performing posts as exemplars collapses every future draft into that one shape. (4) MODEL UPGRADE: the voice silently moves and you notice three weeks later from the comments. (5) SUBSTANCE HOLLOWING: the most common real-world failure — once drafting is cheap, you publish on days when you have nothing to say, and the voice is right while the post is empty. (6) SELF-CRITIQUE THEATRE: running the critique pass in the same thread produces a model grading its own output, which passes almost everything. (7) HOMOGENIZATION AGAINST YOURSELF: the diversity research says co-writing pulls different authors toward each other — over months, even a voice-matched corpus converges on a narrower band than you wrote unaided.

**ai slop risk**

HIGHEST of the three tooling items — this is the item that PRODUCES slop when done badly, and the other two exist largely to contain it. Specific tells, in order of diagnostic value: (a) no proper nouns, no numbers, no dates, no named tool or client anywhere in the post; (b) the antithesis construction 'it's not X, it's Y' and its cousins 'Stop X, start Y', 'The result?', 'Here's what nobody tells you'; (c) uniform paragraph lengths and an em-dash in every second sentence; (d) rhetorical question followed by a one-word paragraph; (e) hollow quantifiers — 'many leaders', 'most teams', 'in my experience' with no experience attached; (f) a closing engagement-bait question that does not follow from the post; (g) perfectly balanced triads. LinkedIn's own description of what it targets is the cleanest test to internalise: 'low-effort, AI-generated content that may sound polished on the surface but lacks any real unique perspective or substance' — note that polish is not the defence, it is the symptom.

**human input required**

The minimum non-substitutable contribution is ONE of the following per post, supplied before generation, never after: a proprietary number (your revenue, your error rate, your before/after, your client's result with permission); a first-hand scene with a time and a place ('Tuesday, third client call, they asked X'); a named artefact you can point to (a repo, a PR, a deck, a tool, a person, with attribution); or a judgment call you would defend in a room of peers who could push back. Plus one non-optional act: you rewrite the first two lines and the last line by hand. This is the gate that converts 'do not post slop' into something checkable, and it is precisely what the platform classifier is proxying for — LinkedIn's stated bar is that posts 'represent your voice and your perspectives' and that 'the ultimate value comes from the human behind the tool'.

**policy and legal**

ASSUMING A POLAND/EU-BASED CREATOR. EU AI Act Article 50(4), applicable from 2026-08-02, obliges DEPLOYERS of AI systems that generate or manipulate text 'published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest' to disclose that the text is artificially generated. Two carve-outs matter here. First, the human-review carve-out: the obligation does not apply where the content underwent human review or editorial control AND a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication — with the Commission's guidance making clear that review means a knowledgeable person deliberately examining the substance including fact-checking, and that a spelling or grammar pass does NOT qualify. Second, the 'matters of public interest' threshold: ordinary professional/personal-brand posting is not obviously within scope. A creator who writes their own brief, edits substantively, and publishes under their own name normally lands inside the carve-out on both counts — but 'normally' is not 'certainly', and a compliance-conservative reading (a standing 'drafted with AI, edited and verified by me' line in your profile or post footer) costs nothing. AI-assisted TEXT drafting does not trigger the deepfake/synthetic-media duties in Art. 50(2)/(4) first subparagraph, which target synthetic image, audio and video — an AI avatar would. PLATFORM ToS: LinkedIn permits AI assistance and demotes generic output; LinkedIn's Professional Community Policies require authentic identity and prohibit inauthentic engagement. GDPR does not bite on drafting per se, but does if your prompt corpus contains third parties' personal data. FTC endorsement/disclosure rules are a US regime and apply to material connections, not to drafting method.

**reversibility and blast radius**

LOW-TO-MODERATE, and the algorithmic risk is the smaller half. Algorithmic worst case on LinkedIn is documented and recoverable: flagged posts are suppressed from recommendations, not removed, and remain visible to direct connections and followers — change what you publish and distribution recovers, though a vendor claim that consecutive AI-heavy weeks cause compounding account-level suppression that also drags down later human posts is plausible-but-unverified. Account suspension is not on the table for AI-assisted text; it is on the table for automated mass-commenting, which the May 2026 policy names explicitly. The irreversible half is reputational: being publicly identified by peers as a slop account is not undone by an algorithm change, and in B2B the audience that matters is small and has a long memory. Blast radius is therefore capped at one identity, and the cheapest insurance is that the human-input gate is never skipped 'just this once'.

#### practice

**how to apply**

ONE-OFF SETUP (60-120 min). 1. Export 20-40 pieces of your own writing into one file — past posts, long vault notes, the best answers you have written to colleagues. In this vault, `content/` is already the corpus. 2. Run the extraction call: 'Emit a voice spec as 8-12 mechanically checkable rules, each with three verbatim quotes from this corpus as evidence. Then list 15 constructions a generic assistant would produce that appear nowhere here.' 3. Save the output as a versioned vault note (voice spec + banned list), with the model name and date in the frontmatter. This note — not the chat — is the artefact. 4. Load it into your platform container: Claude Styles ('Add a writing example') or a Claude Project / ChatGPT Project / Gemini Gem holding the spec plus 10-15 exemplars. 5. Pick 3-5 exemplar posts for voice-representativeness, explicitly NOT your best performers. PER POST (10-20 min). 6. Write a 3-5 line brief yourself, by hand, containing the non-substitutable asset. If you cannot write that brief, you do not have a post — stop here; this is the step that prevents the tactic from degenerating. 7. Generation call in a FRESH chat: spec + exemplars + brief + 'add no facts I did not give you; if something is missing, ask rather than invent'. 8. Critique call in a SECOND fresh chat holding only the rubric and the banned list: return violations only. Fix them yourself. 9. Hand-write the first two lines and the last line. 10. Run the checklist below as a hard gate. 11. Publish, and log which model version and spec version produced it. MAINTENANCE. 12. After every model upgrade, re-run five fixed briefs and diff against last month's outputs; if the register moved, re-extract the spec. 13. Every quarter, refresh the banned list against whatever the current model defaults have become and rotate two exemplars.

**checklist**

Hard pass/fail gate before publishing — any FAIL means do not post. 1. Contains at least one number, name, date or artefact that only I could supply. PASS/FAIL. 2. I wrote the brief before the model wrote anything. PASS/FAIL. 3. First two lines and last line rewritten by hand. PASS/FAIL. 4. Zero hits on the banned-construction list. PASS/FAIL. 5. No fact in the post originated with the model unverified by me. PASS/FAIL. 6. Sentence length varies — at least one line under 6 words and one over 25. PASS/FAIL. 7. I would defend the central claim in a room of peers who disagree. PASS/FAIL. 8. If the post were unsigned, someone who knows me could identify it as mine. PASS/FAIL. 9. The closing line follows from the post rather than being bolted-on engagement bait. PASS/FAIL. 10. Critique pass was run in a fresh context, not the drafting thread. PASS/FAIL.

**cost and time to execute**

SETUP (one-off): 60-120 minutes to assemble the corpus, extract and sanity-check the spec, and load it into a Style/Project/Gem. PER POST: 10-20 minutes — brief 5 min (the irreducible part), generation ~2 min, critique pass ~2 min, hand-edit 5-10 min. Compare against 30-60 minutes unaided for the same quality, so the saving is real but roughly 2-3x, not the 10x the tooling market implies. PER MONTH at 12 posts: ~3-4 hours of human time plus ~30-45 minutes of maintenance (banned-list refresh, post-upgrade re-validation). SUBSCRIPTIONS: $20/mo covers it entirely — ChatGPT Plus $20, Claude Pro $20 ($17 annual), Google AI Pro $19.99; heavier tiers ($100-200/mo) buy nothing this tactic needs. Optional LinkedIn ghostwriting SaaS adds $19-65/mo and mostly rebuys what a $20 plan plus a saved spec already gives you. TOTAL: roughly $20/mo + 4 hours/month for 12 posts.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

LEADING (move within days, fully under your control): (1) gate pass rate — share of drafts clearing the checklist without a rewrite; (2) EDIT DISTANCE between the model draft and what you published — the most informative single number here, and note that it should STABILISE, not fall to zero; an edit distance trending to zero means you have stopped supplying the human layer; (3) brief-failure rate — how often you abandon a post because you could not write a substantive brief (a healthy number is not zero); (4) time-to-publish. MIDDLE (days to a week): see-more expansion / dwell proxies, comment depth (replies per comment thread, not comment count), profile views per post. LAGGING (weeks): impressions relative to your own rolling 8-week median — never against absolute benchmarks, which are follower-tier dependent and vendor-sourced; follower growth; inbound DMs and opportunities. ORDER OF MOVEMENT: edit distance and gate pass rate first, comment quality second, impressions last and noisiest.

**measurement feasibility**

Mixed, and the honest split matters. FULLY OBSERVABLE, because you own it: gate pass rate, edit distance, brief-failure rate, time-to-publish — all computable locally with no platform access. Make these the primary KPIs precisely because they are the only clean ones. NOT NATIVELY OBSERVABLE: dwell time (LinkedIn creator analytics exposes impressions, reactions, comments, reposts and 'members reached', not per-post dwell); DM/dark-social sends, which are invisible everywhere and are a significant share of real distribution; and — critically — whether a given post was flagged by LinkedIn's genericness classifier, which is never surfaced. You only ever see the reach shortfall, never the cause, which makes attribution of any reach change to voice quality unreliable. USABLE PROXIES: impressions-per-follower ratio against your own median, comments-per-impression, save/repost rate where exposed, and 'how did you find this' asked in DMs. If you need a real read on the classifier, the only available experiment is within-author A/B over many posts, which needs more volume than most individual accounts have.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- audience fit
- detectability and disclosure
- effect size and n
- platform and format fit

### Multilingual localization pipelines

`multilingual-localization-pipelines` · automation L1 · evidence STRONG · 4 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Multilingual localization pipelines
- **category**: tooling
- **one line definition**: Using LLMs to re-author a social post for a second language and culture — adapting idiom, humour, register, cultural reference and platform norms rather than translating the words — so that one piece of thinking serves two audiences without reading as a translation in either.
- **maturity**: established as a corporate marketing practice (translation/localization platforms have existed for a decade); emerging and largely unvalidated as a solo-creator organic-social practice; the specific capability that makes it viable — LLM cultural adaptation rather than literal MT — only became measurable with 2026 benchmarks.
- **the distinction that matters**: Translation preserves meaning. Localization adapts references, units, examples and norms. TRANSCREATION re-authors to produce the same emotional effect, accepting that the words change completely. Social hooks live almost entirely in transcreation territory, which is exactly where machine translation metrics stop measuring anything useful.
- **pl en framing**: For a Poland-based creator this is not an expansion tactic, it is a structural decision: Polish reaches a dense, low-competition professional network where you have real standing; English reaches a vastly larger but saturated market where you are a stranger. These are different products, not one product in two wrappers.

**as of date and volatility**

- **as of**: 2026-09-11
- **volatility**: 6-12 months for the model-capability layer (which model transcreates Polish well changed measurably between 2025 and 2026); quarter-to-quarter for the vendor engagement-lift statistics; stable for the underlying linguistic and cultural facts (Polish register conventions, anglicism norms in Polish IT writing, what does not translate).
- **recent measurement points**: CULTURE-MT benchmark published 2026-05-25 — the first benchmark to measure cultural effectiveness in social-media UGC rather than semantic accuracy. Independent Polish content-generation ranking (Oxido / Jelesnianski) conducted 2026-02-24. Bielik v3 series tokenizer work published 2026-04.
- **what rots first**: Model recommendations. The Feb 2026 Polish test put Gemini 3.1 Pro first and European models last; a model release cycle later that ordering may invert. Re-test with your own three prompts rather than inheriting a ranking.
- **what is stable**: That LLMs routinely mistranslate idioms and puns even in high-resource languages, and that standard MT metrics (BLEU, ChrF, COMET) cannot detect cultural failure. Both are robust findings and both are structural, not fixable by scale.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **pipeline**:
  - 1. Decide the unit of reuse. Reuse the ARGUMENT and the EVIDENCE (the number, the incident, the client outcome), never the sentences. The moment you start from finished copy you have committed to translation.
  - 2. Write the primary-language version to completion, including the hook, in the language you think in. A post drafted in your second language and translated back is worse in both.
  - 3. Extract an abstract brief: the claim, the proof, the emotional beat, the intended reader action, the one line that must survive. Four bullets.
  - 4. Re-author from the brief in the target language, with explicit instruction to change examples, references, idioms and register to fit that audience. The hook is re-authored, not translated.
  - 5. Adapt the non-textual layer: platform norms (Polish LinkedIn is more formal and less confessional than US LinkedIn), units, currency, date format, name conventions, legal/market references, and which technical terms stay in English.
  - 6. Human pass by a native speaker — you, if this is your own language pair. Read the hook aloud. Anything you would not say out loud is a translation artefact.
  - 7. Publish on separate schedules, not simultaneously. Same-day duplicate posting is the observable pattern that makes both versions read as syndicated content.
  - 8. Measure per language separately. They are different audiences with different baselines; a pooled engagement rate is meaningless.
- **the technical core**: The measurable capability is cultural effectiveness, not translation quality. The 2026 CULTURE-MT benchmark separates these explicitly and finds that standard automatic metrics 'fail to capture pronounced differences among models' — BLEU, ChrF and COMET showed only minor variation across model scales while cultural-effectiveness scores diverged sharply (Gemini 3 at 90.80% effective / 38.30% highly effective vs a Qwen3-8B baseline at 50.40% / 28.24%). If your pipeline's quality gate is an MT metric, it is blind to the only failure that matters here.
- **what breaks first**: Humour, puns, and culture-loaded expressions — the CULTURE-MT domain breakdown shows culture-intensive domains (gaming, celebrity news) failing far more than descriptive ones (travel, home decoration). For a creator, that maps directly onto: hooks and jokes break, methodology sections survive.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **primary**: Semantic relevance matching to a language-and-interest-defined audience cluster. Platforms in 2026 distribute on interest-graph similarity; a post in Polish about Polish-market specifics is served to a far more tightly matched, far less contested audience segment than the same argument in English.
- **secondary**: Comment depth and reply quality. People argue, joke and ask follow-up questions more readily in their first language, and reply depth is a ranked signal — so language choice moves a ranking signal indirectly but genuinely.
- **competition effect not a signal**: The largest real mechanism is not a ranking signal at all: it is competitive density. Polish-language professional content competes against orders of magnitude less supply for the same attention. That is a market structure effect, not an algorithmic one, and it is probably the honest explanation for most published 'localization lift' numbers.
- **unknown**: Whether any major platform applies a language-consistency or topic-authority signal that penalises language-switching on a single account. Vendor commentary asserts topic-authority dilution; no platform has confirmed such a mechanism and no independent measurement was found. Treat as unknown — this is the single most decision-relevant unknown in this entry.

**why it drives reach**

- **causal story**: Three compounding effects. (a) Supply: far fewer people publish substantive professional content in Polish than in English, so the same quality clears a lower bar for distribution within that segment. (b) Response: readers engage more, and more deeply, in their first language — reported in the consumer-preference literature as 65% preferring native-language content even when it is lower quality than the English alternative, and 40% not engaging with brands that communicate in a language they do not speak. (c) Fit: a genuinely transcreated post carries local references and register that signal in-group membership, which drives the identity-signalling share behaviour the vault's narrowcast item covers.
- **the counterweight**: Total addressable audience. Polish gives you a higher share of a small pool; English a smaller share of a huge one. For a topic with a global technical audience (AI agents, JS/TS tooling) the English pool is where the ceiling is, and the Polish pool is where the floor is. Reach-maximisation and relationship-maximisation point different directions.
- **important scope warning**: Every published localization-lift figure comes from BRANDS entering new markets — multi-location retail, country pages, localized ad campaigns. None of it measures a single professional posting in two languages from one account. The mechanism is plausible; the transfer is not established.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **transcreate**: The primary role — re-author from a brief in the target language, changing examples and idioms. Not translate.
- **critique**: The highest-value and most reliable role: hand the model a draft and ask 'which phrases here read as translated?', 'which of these would a Polish developer never say?'. Models are markedly better at DETECTING translationese than at avoiding it.
- **register shift**: Adjust formality, directness and self-disclosure level to target-culture professional norms — the adaptation most creators skip and the one most visible to native readers.
- **terminology arbitration**: Decide which technical terms stay in English. In Polish IT writing, over-translating ('podpowiedź systemowa' for system prompt, 'wdrożenie' used where everyone says 'deploy') reads as more foreign than the anglicism does. A model prompted with a glossary handles this well; unprompted, it over-translates.
- **back translation check**: Translate the target version back to the source and compare to the brief — catches meaning drift cheaply.
- **what the model cannot do**: Judge whether a joke lands. The independent February 2026 Polish evaluation found humour the weakest category across all 12 models tested, with results described as simply weak. Anything comic must be human-authored in the target language.

**automation level**

- **level**: L1 AI-assisted draft. Parts reach L2 (glossary enforcement, back-translation QA, terminology consistency checks) behind fixed rules.
- **reasoning**: Cultural adaptation quality is not measurable by any automatic metric currently available — that is the central CULTURE-MT finding — so there is no automated gate that could make L2 safe for the creative layer. The consensus practical model across the 2026 localization tooling literature is explicitly 'AI plus human QA'.
- **vendor label warning**: Social tools advertising 'post in 30 languages automatically' are L2 translation schedulers. They produce translated posts, which is a different and much worse product than localized posts, and on a personal account the difference is immediately visible.
- **l3 status**: Nothing credible. An unreviewed auto-translated personal post is a reputational liability in the target language, and you will be the last to know.

**prompt patterns**

- **brief not text**: Do not paste the finished post. Paste the brief: 'Claim: X. Proof: Y (real number). Emotional beat: relief after frustration. Reader action: audit their own prompt. Must survive: the $340→$95 figure.' Then: 'Write this as a LinkedIn post for a Polish developer audience. Do not translate — write it as if this happened to you and you are telling Polish colleagues.'
- **explicit permission to diverge**: 'You may change the examples, the opening, the structure and the comparison entirely. The only things that must survive are the claim and the number.' Without this, models default to sentence-aligned translation even when asked to localize.
- **glossary pinning**: Supply a term list with the decision already made: 'Keep in English: prompt, deploy, agent, skill, token, pipeline. Translate: bill→rachunek, savings→oszczędności. Never use: podpowiedź systemowa, sztuczna inteligencja as a standalone noun where AI is meant.' This single block prevents the most common Polish failure mode.
- **register specification**: 'Polish LinkedIn register: direct but not confessional, no American-style vulnerability opener, no exclamation marks, second person plural avoided, form of address neutral. Assume the reader is a peer, not an audience.'
- **translationese detector**: Run as a separate pass on the finished target text: 'You are a Polish native speaker who has never read the English version. List every phrase that sounds like it was translated from English, and say why.' This catches calques, English word order, and over-long noun phrases. More reliable than asking the model to write natively in the first place.
- **read aloud test prompt**: 'Which sentences here would be awkward to say out loud in a conversation?' — a good proxy for the artificiality that native readers detect but cannot always name.
- **idiom handling**: 'If an idiom does not exist in Polish, do not explain it and do not calque it. Replace it with a Polish idiom that carries the same feeling, or drop the figure of speech entirely.' Models otherwise produce literal renderings of English idioms, which is the single loudest translation tell.
- **anti patterns**:
  - 'Translate this post to Polish' — produces grammatically correct text that no Polish person would write.
  - 'Translate this post to Polish, keeping the tone' — tone is the thing that does not survive; asking for it preserved guarantees a calque.
  - Translating the hook. The hook must be written, not converted; it is the most culture-bound sentence in the post.

**tool examples**

- **the actual recommendation**: General-purpose frontier LLMs, not translation tools. Translation platforms optimise for consistency and throughput across large corpora; social transcreation needs the opposite — deliberate divergence. For Polish specifically, the independent Feb 2026 test ranked Gemini 3.1 Pro first, Qwen 3.5 Plus second, Llama 4 third, with GPT-5.2, Grok 4.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 also strong; European models (EuroLLM, Mistral) underperformed. Verify with your own prompts — this is a 12-model, 240-response study, not a definitive ranking.
- **polish specific models**:
  - Bielik (SpeakLeash) — Bielik-11B-v3.0-Instruct scores 65.93 (5-shot average) on the Open PL LLM Leaderboard, beating several much larger models including Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct; Apache 2.0, so commercial use is permitted. Reported as handling marketing tasks better than PLLuM.
  - PLLuM — the Polish national LLM programme; best-trained variants carry CC-BY-NC-4.0, i.e. research-only, which rules them out for commercial content work.
  - Caveat: in the independent Oxido test both Bielik and PLLuM finished in the lower half of the field against frontier models. Polish-specific does not mean Polish-best.
- **translation and localization platforms**:
  - DeepL Pro — from ~$10.49/mo; still the strongest single-shot output quality for major business languages including Polish. Correct use here: a baseline draft or a back-translation check, not the final copy.
  - Smartling — enterprise, 50+ connectors, ~$2,000-10,000+/mo. Irrelevant at creator scale.
  - Lokalise — from ~$144/mo (Explorer), ~$499 (Growth) for AI-assisted translation. Built for software strings, not social copy.
  - Phrase, LILT, Smartcat — same enterprise lane.
- **polish evaluation resources**: Open PL LLM Leaderboard, PLCC (Polish Linguistic and Cultural Competency, 600 hand-written questions across six categories including grammar, vocabulary and culture), Polish MT-Bench, Polish EQ-Bench, KLEJ, PolEval. Useful for choosing a model; none measure social-copy naturalness.
- **platform native**: LinkedIn offers a reader-side 'See translation' button and multi-language targeting for COMPANY pages (by language and geography). For a PERSONAL profile there is no multi-language post variant — one post, one language, one audience.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

- **cultural adaptation is measurably hard for llms**: strong — peer-reviewed-track benchmark with a defined protocol and an evaluator validated at 86.03% agreement / Cohen's kappa 0.7205.
- **polish specific llm weakness on humour**: moderate — one independent, self-funded, multi-evaluator test (N=240 responses, 11 evaluators), not replicated.
- **native language preference drives engagement**: moderate — consistent across consumer-preference surveys over many years, but survey-stated preference, not observed behaviour.
- **the 3x engagement claim**: vendor-claim, and the framing in the research prompt does not survive checking — see conflicting_evidence.
- **solo creator pl en dual track**: unverified. No study, vendor or academic, measures an individual professional posting in two languages from one account.

**evidence provenance**

- **peer reviewed or preprint**: CULTURE-MT (arXiv:2605.25626, Wu, Zhang, Lyu, Guo, Zhang, Xu, Hu, Cao, Shen, Lu, 2026-05-25); Bielik 11B v2 technical report (arXiv:2505.02410); Bielik v3 tokenizer optimisation (arXiv:2604.10799); text-variation-and-engagement work (arXiv:2505.03769, Hu/Jin/Ye/Divakaran/Kumar, 2025-04-26).
- **independent industry**: Oxido / Marek Jelesnianski LLM ranking for Polish content generation — 12 models, 20 scenarios across 10 categories, 240 responses, 11 evaluators, 2026-02-24, explicitly self-funded and not vendor-sponsored. The single most useful Polish-specific source found, and still one small unreplicated study.
- **vendor with product to sell**: SOCi (12x engagement for localized posts; 11.5% vs 0.4% ER), BLEND (3X conversion), DeepL marketer survey (75% agree localization boosts engagement), Smartling/Lokalise tool comparisons and pricing, plus the entire 'localization lift' genre. Every multiplier in this entry originates here.
- **survey research**: CSA Research 'Can't Read, Won't Buy' line of work — 65% prefer native-language content even at lower quality, 40% will not engage across a language barrier. Widely cited, methodologically a stated-preference survey, frequently quoted with drifting numbers and dates.
- **verdict**: The linguistic claim (LLMs fail at cultural adaptation in specific, measurable ways) is well-evidenced. The commercial claim (localization multiplies engagement) is entirely vendor-sourced, measured on brands rather than individuals, and structurally confounded with effort and market entry.

**conflicting evidence**

- **the 3x claim does not check out as stated**: The research prompt records 'claimed 3x engagement for localized vs English-only'. What is actually findable is a vendor claim of 3X CONVERSION from cultural adaptation (BLEND) — a different metric — sitting inside a spread that runs from 86% (ad CTR/conversion) through 70-150% (eCommerce conversion) to 10-15x (brand country pages) and 12x (SOCi platform data, engagement). The spread across these claims is roughly 1.9x to 15x for overlapping constructs. No independent verification exists for any of them, and the '3x' figure specifically appears to be a conversion number that has drifted into engagement framing in circulation. Do not repeat '3x engagement' as a fact.
- **brand localization vs individual bilingual posting**: Directly conflicting implications. Brand localization evidence says localize everything — but it measures organisations entering markets where they previously had no local presence at all, which is a market-access effect, not a language effect. The applicable guidance for individuals, from the practitioner literature, is the opposite in spirit: pick one. 'If you are building a local business, write 100% in your local language; if you are targeting international clients, write 100% in English.' Both positions are defensible and they recommend different behaviour.
- **does language switching dilute reach**: Unresolved. One line of 2026 commentary says the algorithm does not penalise language choice and there is no confirmed mechanism; another says the 2026 LinkedIn algorithm rewards topic consistency, so rapid language switching dilutes topic authority without triggering an explicit penalty. Neither is platform-confirmed. The practical consequence is real: if dilution exists, the dual-track strategy costs reach in both languages, and you cannot currently find out except by measuring your own account.
- **bilingual post vs alternating vs separate accounts**: Three incompatible recommendations circulate for the same problem, all from practitioner sources, none measured: single post containing both languages (most common among international creators, but doubles length and halves hook impact for both audiences); alternating days by language (preserves hook quality, splits the feed experience); separate profiles (clean segmentation, duplicated effort, and LinkedIn's own structure discourages it). No comparative data exists.
- **ai translation quality vs ai translation sufficiency**: DeepL and frontier LLMs produce genuinely good Polish. The CULTURE-MT result is that good translation and culturally effective adaptation are measurably different things, and the metrics the industry uses to certify the first are blind to the second. A pipeline can be validated as high-quality translation and still produce posts no Polish reader would engage with.
