### Synthetic persona pre-testing

`synthetic-persona-pretesting` · automation L1 · evidence MODERATE · 2 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Synthetic persona pre-testing
- **category**: tooling
- **one line definition**: Screen a large batch of hook/post variants against an LLM-simulated audience panel ('synthetic respondents', 'silicon sample') to cut the field down to a shortlist before spending any real impressions, then confirm the shortlist with a real-traffic or real-human test.
- **maturity**: emerging — moving from experiment to standard practice in agency/insights workflows during 2025-2026, but with an unresolved validity base. Established for quantitative concept ranking and purchase intent; emerging-to-unvalidated for organic social hook selection specifically.
- **position in stack**: A pre-publish selection layer. It does not create reach; it changes which variant gets the one real shot. Pairs directly with the vault items 'Hook engineering' and 'Hook A/B testing loop'.

**as of date and volatility**

- **as of**: 2026-09-11
- **volatility**: 6-12 months for the tooling layer; quarter-to-quarter for vendor accuracy claims; stable-ish for the underlying academic validity picture, which has moved slowly and in both directions since 2023.
- **what rots first**: Vendor 'accuracy' percentages and tool line-ups (Minds, Synthetic Users, Evidenza, Aaru, Fairgen, Market Logic DeepSights) — these changed materially between 2025 and 2026. Model swaps (GPT-5.x, Claude Opus 4.x, Gemini 3.x) change panel behaviour without warning, so a calibrated panel silently decalibrates on model upgrade.
- **what is stable**: The core failure mode — persona-conditioned LLMs collapse onto a modal answer and amplify stereotypes — has been reported consistently from Bisbee et al. (2024) through the WWW 2026 companion paper. Treat that as durable.
- **notable dates**: Sarstedt et al., Psychology & Marketing 41(6), Jun 2024 (silicon-sample guidelines); arXiv:2510.08338 SSR paper, 9 Oct 2025; ICC/ESOMAR Code 2025 update adding synthetic-data disclosure duties; ACM WWW 2026 Companion reliability paper (DOI 10.1145/3774905.3795477), May 2026.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **pipeline**:
  - 1. Define the target audience as a structured persona spec — role, seniority, industry, platform habits, current pain, what they already believe, what would make them scroll past. Ground it in real artefacts you already own (your own follower export, past comment threads, sales-call transcripts, ICP docs) rather than inventing demographics.
  - 2. Instantiate a panel: typically 30-60 persona variants, systematically varied on 3-5 axes (seniority, scepticism level, familiarity with the topic, platform, time pressure). Vendor guidance cited in the 2026 marketing literature uses 40-60 personas per panel.
  - 3. Generate the variant set: ~15-25 hook/first-line variants (or full post variants) for the same underlying idea.
  - 4. Present variants to each persona ONE AT A TIME in randomised order — never as a ranked menu — and ask behavioural questions rather than preference questions: 'What do you think this post is about?', 'Would you keep reading or scroll? Why?', 'Would you send this to a specific colleague, and who?'.
  - 5. Score on comprehension (does the persona restate the promise correctly?), differentiation (do different personas read it differently?), and stated stop/scroll behaviour. Aggregate across the panel.
  - 6. Cut ~20 variants to ~3 survivors. Discard anything with comprehension failures or where personas cannot tell two variants apart.
  - 7. Run the 3 survivors as a real test — real-traffic A/B if you have paid distribution, or sequenced organic posts, or a small real-human panel (5-10 people from the actual audience in DMs/Slack) if you do not.
  - 8. Log real outcomes against the synthetic prediction to build a personal calibration record. Without step 8 the loop never learns whether your panel is any good.
- **key design choice**: Elicit text, not numbers. The core methodological finding of the strongest validation paper to date (Semantic Similarity Rating, arXiv:2510.08338) is that asking an LLM directly for a numeric rating produces unrealistic, degenerate distributions; asking for a free-text reaction and then mapping it to a scale via embedding similarity to reference statements recovers realistic distributions. Any panel that asks 'rate this hook 1-10' is using the method that is known not to work.
- **what it is not**: It is not a virality predictor. It is a variant-elimination filter. Its job is to remove the obviously confusing, ambiguous or undifferentiated variants — the bottom of the distribution — not to identify the winner at the top.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **direct**: None. Synthetic pre-testing moves no platform ranking signal by itself — it is a selection layer upstream of publication.
- **indirect**: Whatever signal the panel is instrumented to proxy. In practice: hook stop-rate / expansion rate (proxy for dwell time and 'see more' clicks), comprehension (proxy for completion rate), and 'would you send this to one specific person' (proxy for sends/DM shares, which Instagram weights heavily and which the outline records as 3-5x likes on Reels since Q1 2026).
- **honest note**: The 'would you DM this' question is the highest-value one to ask a synthetic panel precisely because dark-social sends are the signal you cannot observe natively afterwards. But there is no published validation that LLM personas predict real DM-send behaviour. Treat as unknown.

**why it drives reach**

- **causal story**: Organic social is a one-shot, high-variance channel: you typically get one publication per idea, the first 60-90 minutes determine whether the post is promoted, and a confusing first line kills the post before any other quality matters. Classic A/B testing cannot run here — you cannot serve two versions of an organic post to split audiences. Synthetic pre-testing restores a screening stage to a channel that structurally lacks one, so the single real shot is spent on a variant drawn from a pre-filtered pool rather than from the full, mostly-bad distribution.
- **expected value framing**: The gain is not 'picks the winner'. The gain is 'raises the floor of the sample you test'. Even a filter with modest discriminative power increases the expected quality of the 3 variants that reach real traffic — the vendor framing is 'testing the same number of real variants but from a much better starting pool'.
- **ceiling**: Bounded by the Goel/Anderson/Hofman/Watts (Management Science 2015) result that structural virality is a continuum with no bimodal split and no reliable tipping point — most virality is not predictable ex ante by anyone, human or model. Pre-testing can raise the mean; it cannot manufacture the tail.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **primary**: Simulate — the model role-plays audience members and emits reactions.
- **secondary**:
  - Vary — generate the 15-25 variant set in the first place
  - Score — map free-text reactions to a comparable scale (ideally via embedding similarity, not self-reported numbers)
  - Critique — surface the specific ambiguity that made a variant fail, which is often more useful than the score
  - Retrieve — ground personas in your own corpus (follower data, past comments, call transcripts) rather than in training-data stereotypes
- **what the model is bad at here**: Producing variance. LLM responses frequently lack the spread real panels have, and diversity does not appear on request — when explicitly asked to generate 'diverse personas' the output still collapses around a narrow stereotypical cluster.

**automation level**

- **level**: L1 AI-assisted draft, with parts of the scoring step reaching L2 autonomous-with-guardrails.
- **reasoning**: Persona spec, variant generation and the final cut are human judgment calls. The panel run and aggregation can be automated behind a fixed rubric (L2) once calibrated. Nothing here is L3: the decision of which variant to publish should not be delegated, because the failure mode (panel converges on the safest, most generic variant) is systematic rather than random and therefore not caught by sampling more.
- **vendor label warning**: Platforms marketed as 'AI focus groups' or 'AI research agents' are L1/L2 pipelines with a chat UI. None of them close the loop against real outcomes for you.

**prompt patterns**

- **panel instantiation**: Do NOT prompt 'act as a typical CTO'. Prompt a specific, grounded individual: role + tenure + what they shipped last quarter + what they are sceptical of + how they use the platform + what they were doing 10 seconds before they saw this. Generic persona prompts are the direct cause of modal collapse.
- **one at a time rule**: Present exactly one variant per turn, with the panel member having no knowledge of the other variants. Showing a ranked list invites the model to produce a plausible-looking ranking rather than a reaction.
- **behavioural not evaluative**: Ask 'what would you do' not 'how good is this'. Good question set: (a) 'In one sentence, what is this post about?' — comprehension; (b) 'Stop or scroll? What was the exact word or phrase that decided it?' — mechanism; (c) 'Is there one specific person you'd send this to? Who and why?' — send proxy; (d) 'What would make you distrust the author here?' — slop/credibility check.
- **ssr scoring**: Elicit free text, then map to the scale by embedding-similarity to a fixed set of anchor statements ('I would stop and read this', 'I would scroll past without noticing', …). This is the validated elicitation method; direct numeric self-rating is the known-broken one.
- **adversarial persona**: Always include 2-3 hostile personas: the 'I have seen 400 of these this week' sceptic, the domain expert who will catch the hand-wave, and the person who does not know you. These are the personas that catch slop, and they are also the ones the model will not generate unless you force them.
- **order and label randomisation**: Randomise variant order and never label variants with anything ordinal (A/B/C, v1/v2). LLM behaviour is sensitive to response order, labelling and framing, and these introduce systematic bias.
- **anti patterns**:
  - 'Rate these 20 hooks from 1-10 and rank them' — combines numeric self-rating, simultaneous presentation and ordinal labels; three known biases in one prompt.
  - 'Generate 50 diverse personas' — diversity does not survive the request; specify the axes yourself.
  - Asking the same model that wrote the hooks to also judge them without any persona grounding — you get self-preference, not audience simulation.

**tool examples**

- **dedicated synthetic research platforms**:
  - Synthetic Users (syntheticusers.com) — token-based; tiers from ~$12,500/year per 2026 vendor pricing page; ~$2-27 per synthetic interview equivalent
  - Minds (getminds.ai) — free tier, ~EUR 29/mo Premium, ~EUR 79/seat/mo Team (3-seat minimum); markets itself at marketing/agency teams and claims 80-95% accuracy [vendor claim]
  - Evidenza — enterprise B2B focus, staffed in part by the former LinkedIn B2B Institute team
  - Aaru — multi-agent behavioural simulation, positioned for higher-validation use cases
  - Fairgen / Fairboost — synthetic respondent boosting for niche or hard-to-reach populations; validated in third-party studies for augmentation rather than replacement
  - Market Logic DeepSights — grounds synthetic personas in an existing internal research repository
  - Personia, Persona Lab, blue-pill.ai — smaller vendors publishing the explicit 'screen 20, test 3' creative-pretesting playbook
- **diy stack**: For a solo creator this does not need a vendor: Claude Projects / Custom GPTs / Gemini Gems holding the persona specs, plus a small script for embedding-based SSR scoring (sentence-transformers or any embedding API). Marginal cost is effectively the existing $20-30/mo subscription.
- **validation reference implementation**: The SSR paper's ResponseRater class (semantic embeddings + PMF normalisation) is the reference for the scoring step.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

moderate for quantitative concept ranking and purchase-intent reproduction; anecdotal-to-vendor-claim for social hook selection specifically. No published study validates LLM persona panels against real organic social engagement outcomes.

**evidence provenance**

- **peer reviewed and preprint**: arXiv:2510.08338 (SSR, Oct 2025, industry-authored preprint with a real commercial dataset); Sarstedt et al., Psychology & Marketing 41(6), Jun 2024 (peer-reviewed review); ACM WWW 2026 Companion, DOI 10.1145/3774905.3795477 (peer-reviewed, negative result); Bisbee et al. 2024 (peer-reviewed, negative); arXiv:2512.00461 'Whose Personae?' (meta-review of 63 persona studies); arXiv:2509.26080 (review of LLMs as synthetic social agents); arXiv:2505.03769 (Hu, Jin, Ye, Divakaran, Kumar — cross-platform title-rewrite engagement, Apr 2025).
- **independent industry**: PyMC Labs practical guide (2026) — has a product but publishes methods and negative findings; five third-party validation studies cited for synthetic augmentation (Google, L'Oreal/IFOP, YouGov, GIM, Dig Insights).
- **vendor with product to sell**: Minds, Synthetic Users, Personia, blue-pill.ai, Situation Interactive, Delve.ai, Stravito. Every '80-95% accuracy', 'screen 20 to 3' and '40-60 persona panel' number in this entry originates here.
- **verdict**: The academic literature is net sceptical; the commercial literature is net enthusiastic; the two do not measure the same thing. Academia measures distributional fidelity to a human population. Vendors measure whether the output was useful for a decision. A panel can be badly calibrated as a population model and still usefully eliminate an incomprehensible hook.

**effect size and n**

- **best positive result**: Semantic Similarity Rating (arXiv:2510.08338): 57 personal-care product surveys, N=9,300 human responses; synthetic respondents reached 90% of human test-retest reliability with Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributional similarity > 0.85. Domain: purchase intent for physical products, not social copy.
- **best negative results**:
  - Literature review of 285 silicon-to-human sample comparisons (28 studies, 2022-2023): 24.9% similar, 9.8% partial, 65.3% diverged.
  - Later window (late 2023-early 2025, 14 studies): 50% strong similarity, 36% partial, 14% minimal — improving but far from settled.
  - ACM WWW 2026 Companion: LLM agents grounded on N=2,414 real World Values Survey respondents failed to reproduce the population distribution; responses collapsed onto a modal default at ~85% concentration.
  - Bisbee et al. 2024: GPT-3.5 silicon samples inflated partisan/racial affective polarization by roughly a factor of 7 vs human benchmarks.
  - Park et al. (2023) re-ran 14 Many Labs 2 studies with GPT-3.5 and replicated just over one third.
  - Silicon sampling on facial-recognition attitudes (AHFE): QWK 0.40-0.45 — captures general pattern, cannot replicate individual responses.
- **most relevant to hook selection**: arXiv:2505.03769 — a fine-tuned BERT classifier reached 74% accuracy at ranking which of two cross-posted titles would get more engagement, substantially beating GPT-4o and random baseline. Read this two ways: (a) title wording measurably moves engagement, so the thing being screened is real; (b) a frontier LLM was WORSE than a small fine-tuned discriminator at the pairwise ranking task — direct evidence against trusting an LLM panel's ranking of hooks. The ceiling for the best method was 74% on a 50%-baseline binary task.
- **vendor numbers flagged**: 'Screen 20 variants down to 3', '40-60 personas per panel', '80-95% accuracy' — all vendor-sourced (Personia, Minds), no independent replication found.
- **for social hooks specifically**: No effect size found. There is no published measurement of how much a synthetic-persona pre-test improves real organic social engagement.

**conflicting evidence**

- **core conflict**: Does LLM persona simulation reproduce human audience response? The 2022-2023 comparison base says mostly no (65.3% divergence across 285 comparisons); the 2025 SSR result says yes at 90% of human test-retest reliability given the right elicitation method. Both are credible. The reconciliation is probably that elicitation method, not model capability, drove most of the earlier failures — but that reconciliation is itself a hypothesis, and the May 2026 WWW paper (modal collapse at 85% concentration on WVS data) is a recent, peer-reviewed negative using grounded personas.
- **second conflict**: LLM-as-ranker vs specialised model. Vendors sell frontier-LLM panels as the ranking mechanism; arXiv:2505.03769 found a fine-tuned BERT beat GPT-4o at exactly this pairwise engagement-ranking task. If the goal is picking the more engaging of two headlines, the evidence favours a small supervised model trained on your own outcome data over a persona panel.
- **third conflict**: Direction of the whole item. This tactic is premised on AI being able to predict audience response to AI-written copy — but the vault's own 'AI vs human content performance' item records that whether AI-written social content outperforms human-written content is itself unresolved (UMinn/GPT-4 FIIT work says AI wins; a peer-reviewed within-subjects Instagram field experiment with 24 alternating posts says humans won on likes 42.6 vs 39.6, comments 5.3 vs 2.3, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%; a vendor study of 10,024 posts claims +31% for AI-assisted). A synthetic panel optimising toward what an LLM thinks people like may be optimising toward the losing side of that unresolved question.
- **fourth conflict**: Vendors frame synthetic panels as a replacement for human research; the five third-party validation studies (Google, L'Oreal/IFOP, YouGov, GIM, Dig Insights) validated synthetic data as AUGMENTATION of a real sample, not replacement. ESOMAR-adjacent guidance and the PyMC Labs guide both land on hybrid: synthetic in exploratory phases, smaller human validation rounds after.
- **do not resolve**: Leave all four open. The defensible position is narrow: use the panel to eliminate bad variants, do not use it to pick the winner.
- **correction 2026 09 11 instagram study is a null result**: CORRECTION (2026-09-11, verified against the full PDF): this file quotes raw means from Flesheriu & Fron (2025), Oeconomica Jadertina 2/2025, DOI 10.15291/oec.4845 (likes 42.58 vs 39.58, comments 5.33 vs 2.33, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%). The means are accurate but NONE of the differences is statistically significant: Mann-Whitney U gives likes p=.91, comments p=.07, shares p=.17, saves p=.79, reach p=.89, impressions p=.51, ER p=.64. The paper states 'H1 was not supported' and concludes EQUIVALENCE, not human superiority. Dropping one launch-day outlier flips ER in the AI direction (5.95% vs 5.79%); readers significantly PREFERRED the AI-written captions (U=8.0, p=.045); and 7 of the 12 top-performing posts were AI. Scope limits that further weaken it as evidence about AI TEXT: a single account with 770 followers, 24 alternating posts, a culinary niche, and AI-generated IMAGERY bundled with the caption - the authors attribute 64% of engagement to the visual. Do not cite this study as showing that human-written posts outperform AI-written posts.

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **works best**: Long-form text platforms where the first line is load-bearing and you get one shot: LinkedIn posts, X long posts, Threads, Substack subject lines, YouTube titles/thumbnails, and carousel slide 1. Also strong for paid creative, where the real A/B test afterwards is actually available.
- **works worst**: Short-form video. The panel can read a script but cannot evaluate pacing, face, audio hook, or the first 0.5 seconds of motion — which is where TikTok/Reels retention is actually decided. A synthetic panel scoring a Reels script is measuring the wrong object.
- **format notes**: Highest value on: hooks/first lines, carousel slide 1, headline/title, and the 'is this send-worthy' judgment. Lowest value on: overall post quality, humour, and anything depending on the reader knowing you — the model has no model of your existing audience relationship.
- **cross reference**: Which signal to instrument per platform: see the vault note 'Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026' (2026-07-06) rather than re-deriving ranking mechanics here.

**scales with**

- **caps**:
  - Quality and realism of your persona grounding — the single biggest lever. Personas derived from real follower exports, comment threads and call transcripts behave differently from invented ones.
  - Size of your own outcome corpus. The technique only compounds once you have enough published posts with real metrics to calibrate against; below ~50 logged posts you cannot tell a good panel from a bad one.
  - Whether you have real distribution to confirm with. With paid traffic the confirmation step is cheap and the loop closes fast; a purely organic creator confirms slowly and noisily.
  - Your own variant-generation ceiling — 20 bad variants filtered to 3 bad variants is still 3 bad variants. The filter cannot exceed the input distribution.
- **does not scale with**: Account size. Unlike most reach tactics, this one is fully available to a small account — and is arguably more valuable there, because a small account has fewer real impressions to waste.
- **objective dependence**: Note the vault's distinction: sub-500-follower accounts are cited by AI answer engines comparably to large ones but do not go viral comparably. If the objective is citability rather than virality, hook pre-testing matters much less.

**decay and saturation**

- **estimate**: The method itself should not decay — it is a private process, not a public pattern, so there is nothing for a platform classifier or an audience to become desensitised to.
- **what does decay**: Your specific calibration. Every frontier-model upgrade changes persona behaviour, so a panel validated on one model version is not validated on the next. Expect to re-calibrate on each major model change (roughly 2-4 times per year at 2025-2026 cadence).
- **saturation risk**: The real decay risk is second-order: if many creators screen hooks against similar LLM panels, the surviving hooks converge on what LLMs believe is compelling, which is measurably a narrow stereotypical cluster. That produces feed-level homogenisation and audience fatigue on the same handful of hook shapes — the same decay path that killed hook templates within 12-24 months. Guard by keeping at least one high-variance, panel-rejected variant in rotation.
- **shelf life**: Method: 3+ years. Any given calibration: 3-6 months.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- **modal collapse**: The panel converges on one answer. Symptom: 45 of 50 personas 'prefer' the same variant with near-identical reasoning. This is the documented default failure (85% modal concentration on grounded WVS personas) and it makes the panel look decisive exactly when it is least informative. Treat high agreement as a red flag, not a result.
- **stereotype amplification**: Persona conditioning exaggerates group differences rather than reproducing them (7x inflation on affective polarization). A panel will tell you a hook 'won't land with senior engineers' based on a caricature of senior engineers.
- **safe variant bias**: Models are trained toward helpfulness and inoffensiveness and systematically under-rate contrarian, blunt or uncomfortable hooks — the exact category the vault's 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes' item identifies as reach-productive. Left unchecked, the panel is a conformity filter.
- **prompt artifact sensitivity**: Response order, option labelling and framing measurably change output. A 'result' can be an artifact of presenting variant 3 third.
- **no relationship model**: The panel does not know your existing audience, your running jokes, your last post, or your credibility on the topic. It evaluates the hook as a stranger would — which is right for cold reach and wrong for follower reach.
- **loop never closes**: The most common practical failure: teams run the panel, publish, and never log the real outcome against the prediction. Without calibration data the panel is theatre. This is the failure to design against first.
- **wrong object**: Screening for 'which hook do people like' when the platform ranks on dwell, sends and reply depth. Liking is not the signal.

**ai slop risk**

- **level**: Moderate-to-high, and structurally sneaky — the risk is not that the panel writes slop, it is that the panel SELECTS for slop.
- **mechanism**: The model rewards clarity, symmetry and familiarity. Clean, familiar, frictionless copy is precisely the register that reads as AI-written. So a variant with an odd word, a specific ugly number, or an abrupt opening — the markers of a human who was actually there — tends to lose to a smoother variant that communicates the same thing more legibly.
- **specific tells the panel will promote**: Balanced triads, 'Here's what most people get wrong about X', colon-heavy openers, tidy parallel structure, hedged universals ('often', 'many teams'), and hooks that state the benefit instead of showing the evidence.
- **counter measure**: Add an explicit 'which of these could only have been written by someone who was in the room?' pass, separate from the preference pass, and never let a variant win on preference if it loses that pass. Also keep a rule that at least one shortlisted variant must be one the panel disliked.

**human input required**

- **minimum non substitutable**:
  - The underlying claim the post makes — a proprietary number, a first-hand incident, a named client, a decision you actually made. The panel tests packaging; it cannot supply substance.
  - The persona ground truth. Real follower data, real objections you have heard, real sales-call language. Invented personas are where the whole method goes wrong.
  - The final cut from 3 to 1, and the decision to override the panel when it rejects a variant for being uncomfortable.
  - The calibration judgment: deciding, after N posts, whether this panel has earned any trust at all.
- **gate wording**: A shortlisted variant may only be published if it contains at least one fact the model could not have produced — a number, a date, a name, or an event. If all 3 survivors are generic, the problem is upstream of the panel and no amount of screening fixes it.
- **why this matters mechanically**: Platform NLP classifiers and audiences are both probing for exactly this residue of first-hand experience; a well-screened but substance-free post is optimised on the wrong axis.

**detectability and disclosure**

- **is the output detectable**: No. Synthetic pre-testing leaves no trace in the published artefact. It is a research step, not a generation step; the published post is whatever you wrote and edited. No C2PA manifest, no SynthID watermark, no metadata.
- **the actual detectability question**: It shifts to whatever wrote the variants. If the 20 variants were LLM-generated and published with light editing, the detectability profile is that of LLM ghostwriting — NLP classifiers and reader pattern-recognition — not of the panel.
- **second order detectability**: Panel-selected copy may be MORE detectable than unscreened copy, because the filter rewards the smooth, canonical register that classifiers and readers associate with machine text. Worth monitoring.
- **disclosure triggered by the panel itself**: None for the published post. Disclosure duties attach if you present the panel's output as research — e.g. 'we asked 50 marketers and 80% said X' when the 50 marketers were synthetic. Under the ICC/ESOMAR 2025 Code, synthetic personas are explicitly distinguished from individuals and synthetic outputs must be labelled; publishing a synthetic panel result as human research would be a straightforward misrepresentation.
- **practical rule**: Never quote panel output publicly. It is an internal instrument.

**reversibility and blast radius**

- **worst case**: Low. The failure mode is a wasted post and a wasted afternoon, not an account action. Nothing in this workflow is visible to a platform.
- **recoverability**: Immediate — stop using the panel.
- **real risks ranked**:
  - Opportunity cost: hours spent on panel infrastructure that would have produced more value spent writing a post with a real number in it.
  - Systematic drift toward safe, generic copy across every post you publish — slow, compounding, and invisible without a calibration log.
  - False confidence: a decisive-looking panel result (modal collapse) read as a strong signal.
  - GDPR exposure if real audience data is pasted into a third-party model without a lawful basis — this is the only route to a genuinely expensive outcome.
- **blast radius**: Contained to your own content quality plus, in the GDPR case, a data-protection exposure. No shadowban, comment restriction or suspension pathway.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 1 ground the personas**: Export the last ~200 comments on your posts, plus 3-5 sales-call or discovery transcripts. Have a model cluster them into 5-8 recurring reader archetypes with verbatim quotes attached. Write those up as personas.yaml. Add for each: role, tenure, what they are currently frustrated by, what they are sceptical of, verbatim phrases they use. Budget: 2-3 hours, once.
- **step 2 add adversaries**: Hand-write 3 hostile personas the clustering will not produce: the saturated scroller, the domain expert who will check your number, the cold stranger with no context on you. Budget: 20 minutes, once.
- **step 3 write anchors**: For each panel question, write 5 anchor statements spanning the range ('I'd stop and read the whole thing' … 'I wouldn't register this existed'). These are your SSR reference points. Budget: 30 minutes, once.
- **step 4 generate variants**: For the post you are about to publish, generate 15-25 first-line variants spanning genuinely different strategies — not 20 rewrites of one strategy. Force coverage: a number-led one, a confession, a contrarian claim, a question, a named-name one, a blunt-ugly one. Budget: 10 minutes per post.
- **step 5 run the panel**: One variant per turn, randomised order, no ordinal labels, four questions: comprehension restatement / stop-or-scroll plus the deciding phrase / would-you-send-it-and-to-whom / what-would-make-you-distrust-the-author. Run across all personas. Budget: 10-20 minutes per post automated, longer by hand.
- **step 6 score and cut**: Eliminate first, rank second. Kill any variant with (a) comprehension failures in >20% of personas, (b) near-identical reactions across adversarial and friendly personas (undifferentiated), (c) 'what is this about' answers that do not match your intent. From what survives, take the top 2 by send-intent plus 1 high-variance variant the panel disliked. That third slot is mandatory — it is your hedge against conformity bias.
- **step 7 human confirmation**: Before publishing, send the 3 survivors to 3-5 real people from the actual audience — DM, Slack, a WhatsApp group — with one question: 'which of these would you actually stop on?'. This is the step the vendor playbooks skip and the validation literature insists on (hybrid: synthetic exploratory, human confirmation). Budget: 10 minutes, plus wait time.
- **step 8 publish and log**: Publish one. Log to calibration.csv: date, the 3 survivors, which was chosen, panel rank, real impressions, real expansion/dwell proxy, real sends if visible, real comments. Budget: 3 minutes.
- **step 9 calibrate after n**: After ~30 logged posts, check whether panel rank correlated with real outcome at all. If the correlation is indistinguishable from chance — which is a live possibility given the 74% ceiling that the best specialised model achieved on the pairwise task — demote the panel to a comprehension-and-slop filter only and stop using its rankings. Budget: 1 hour, quarterly.
- **minimum viable version**: If step 1-3 is too much: skip the panel entirely and run the two questions that carry most of the value — 'in one sentence, what is this post about?' and 'would you send this to one specific person, and who?' — against three hand-written personas in a single chat. 80% of the elimination benefit, 5% of the setup.

**checklist**

- **gate before publishing**:
  - PASS/FAIL — Personas are grounded in real audience artefacts, not invented demographics.
  - PASS/FAIL — At least 3 adversarial personas were in the panel.
  - PASS/FAIL — Variants were presented one at a time, in randomised order, with no ordinal labels.
  - PASS/FAIL — Panel was asked behavioural questions ('would you scroll'), not evaluative ones ('rate 1-10').
  - PASS/FAIL — Panel agreement is NOT suspiciously high (>80% converging on one variant = suspect modal collapse, do not treat as a result).
  - PASS/FAIL — Shortlist includes at least one variant the panel disliked.
  - PASS/FAIL — Every shortlisted variant contains at least one fact the model could not have invented (number, date, name, event).
  - PASS/FAIL — Shortlist was checked by at least 3 real humans from the target audience before publishing.
  - PASS/FAIL — No personal data from real followers or clients was pasted into a third-party model without a lawful basis and a DPA.
  - PASS/FAIL — Panel output is not being quoted publicly as if it were human research.
  - PASS/FAIL — The outcome will be logged against the panel prediction (calibration row created).
- **hard stop**: If the panel's top pick and your own instinct disagree, publish your own instinct and log both. Your instinct has information the panel provably does not have — your relationship with your audience.

**worked example**

- **documented industry case**: The clearest publicly documented version of this workflow is the vendor playbook: build a panel of 40-60 personas matching the target user, run each variant past them individually with comprehension questions, 'run 20 variants through a synthetic panel, identify the 3 that communicate most clearly and differentiate most sharply, then A/B test those 3 with real traffic — testing the same number of real variants but from a much better starting pool' (Personia, 2026). Flagged as vendor-sourced: no independent replication of the hit-rate exists.
- **constructed example marked as such**:
  - **note**: Illustrative, built for this entry — not a real published post. Included because no independently documented hook-level case with real outcome data was found.
  - **underlying substance**: A real migration: 3 weeks, an agent pipeline rewritten from a single 900-line prompt to 6 skills, token cost down from ~$340/mo to ~$95/mo.
  - **variant A number led**: We cut our agent's token bill from $340/month to $95 by deleting our best prompt.
  - **variant B confession**: Our 900-line system prompt was the most expensive thing we ever wrote.
  - **variant C contrarian**: Prompt engineering is why your agent costs too much.
  - **variant D generic control**: Here's what most teams get wrong about AI agent costs.
  - **typical panel outcome**: D scores highest on clarity with the friendly personas and near-zero on differentiation — every persona restates it identically and none can say what the post will actually claim. That combination is the slop signature and D is eliminated despite winning on preference. C is comprehension-ambiguous (personas split on whether 'prompt engineering' means the practice or the practitioner). A and B survive; A wins on send-intent ('I'd send this to our platform lead') because it carries a checkable number.
  - **what you do with it**: Publish A. Keep C in rotation as the panel-rejected hedge on a later post. Log the real expansion rate and sends for A against the panel's prediction.
- **why no better example exists**: No creator or platform has published a hook-level synthetic-pretest dataset with matched real engagement outcomes. That absence is itself the main finding about this tactic's evidence base.

**cost and time to execute**

- **setup one time**: 3-4 hours to build grounded personas, adversaries and SSR anchors. Optional: 2-4 hours to script the panel run and embedding scoring.
- **per post diy**: 20-35 minutes (10 min variant generation, 10-20 min panel run, 5 min cut) plus 10 minutes waiting on the human confirmation step. Compare: ~10 minutes for an unscreened repurpose, ~4 hours for an original-data post. The screening layer is cheap relative to producing the substance and expensive relative to just posting.
- **per post marginal api cost**: Roughly $0.10-1.00 in tokens for a 50-persona x 20-variant run on a mid-tier model, which is negligible; the binding constraint is your attention, not spend.
- **monthly diy**: $20-30 (existing Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini subscription), effectively $0 marginal. Add ~$5-20/mo if you use a separate embedding API for SSR scoring.
- **monthly vendor**: Minds from EUR 29/mo (Premium) / EUR 79 per seat/mo (Team, 3-seat minimum). Synthetic Users from ~$12,500/year, token-metered at roughly $2-27 per synthetic interview. For a solo creator the vendor tier is not justified — the DIY version captures nearly all the value.
- **verdict**: Worth it only if you post frequently enough for the calibration loop to accumulate data, and only if you are already producing substance worth screening. Below ~4 posts/month, skip the infrastructure and run the minimum viable version.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **primary kpi**: Calibration hit-rate: of the posts where the panel ranked the survivors, how often did the panel's top pick also win on the real metric? Baseline to beat is 33% (random among 3). Anything under ~50% sustained means the ranking is noise.
- **leading indicators**:
  - Expansion rate / 'see more' click rate on the published post — first proxy for whether the hook worked, moves within the first hour
  - Impressions-per-follower in hour 1 vs your own baseline — cold-start behaviour
  - Comment latency: time to first substantive (non-emoji) comment
  - Sends/DM shares where visible
- **process indicators**:
  - Panel disagreement rate — if it drops toward zero, your personas have collapsed and need re-grounding
  - Elimination rate — what fraction of 20 variants the panel kills for comprehension failure. Healthy: 40-70%. Near 0% means the panel is not discriminating; near 100% means your variants are bad.
  - Override rate — how often you publish against the panel. Consistently high means the panel is not earning its keep.
- **what moves first**: Expansion rate, within minutes. Everything else is downstream of whether the first line stopped the scroll.

**measurement feasibility**

- **observable natively**: Impressions, reactions, comments, reposts on all major platforms. LinkedIn creator analytics exposes impressions and, for some accounts, discovery source. Instagram exposes sends/shares per reach and saves. X exposes impressions and detail-expands.
- **not observable**: Dwell time (no platform exposes it to creators despite ranking on it), true 'see more' expansion rate on LinkedIn (not exposed; must be inferred), and the dark-social forwarding that the vault records as ~84% of B2B sharing. You are trying to calibrate a predictor against a partially hidden outcome.
- **best available proxies**:
  - LinkedIn: impressions-to-reaction ratio and comment depth as a joint dwell proxy; X: detail-expands / impressions
  - Instagram: sends per reach is exposed and is the closest thing to a real dark-social readout on any platform — use it as the calibration target if you are on IG
  - A trackable link with a per-variant UTM, where a link is natural to the post
- **honest constraint**: The measurement gap is the central practical problem with this tactic. You are screening for signals (dwell, sends) you mostly cannot see afterwards, which means the calibration loop is noisy and slow — on organic-only distribution, expect 30+ posts before the correlation is even estimable, and normal week-to-week reach variance will swamp small effects. Anyone claiming a clean read on synthetic-pretest lift from organic data is over-reading their numbers.

**ai search citability**

- **direct contribution**: None. Pre-testing selects a hook; hooks are not what AI answer engines cite.
- **possible negative**: Optimising the opening for scroll-stopping can pull it away from the answer-shaped, question-matching opening that generative engines retrieve well. Hook optimisation and citability optimisation can point in opposite directions — a curiosity-gap first line withholds exactly the proposition an answer engine wants to extract.
- **how to get both**: Treat them as two separate targets on the same post: an engineered hook for the feed, and an explicit, self-contained claim sentence with the number and the source within the first ~100 words for retrieval. The vault's own data anchor (Semrush, Jan-Feb 2026, 325K prompts / 89K LinkedIn URLs) shows top-cited posts carry only 15-25 reactions median — citability does not require virality, and the pre-test is optimising the other target entirely.
- **verdict**: Neutral-to-slightly-negative for citability. Do not run this tactic when the objective is LLM citation.

#### omitted as uncertain

- audience fit
- prompt artifact link

### Visual and carousel generation

`visual-carousel-generation` · automation L1 · evidence MODERATE · 4 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Visual and carousel generation
- **category**: tooling
- **one line definition**: Using AI image models and AI-assisted design tools (Canva Magic Studio, Ideogram, Nano Banana Pro / Gemini image, GPT Image, Flux, Seedream) plus carousel builders (Contentdrips, AuthoredUp, Taplio, Canva) to produce the visual layer of a social post — single images, text-in-image graphics, and multi-slide carousels exported as PDF document posts.
- **maturity**: established for template-driven carousels and layout automation (Canva Magic Design has been in market since late 2023); established-but-churning for text-in-image generation, where the model line-up changed materially three times between Nov 2025 and Jun 2026; emerging and contested for fully AI-generated photographic imagery in a personal-brand context, where the audience penalty is real and the provenance-labelling regime only came into force in Aug 2026.
- **two distinct things**: This item covers two mechanisms that are usually conflated and behave very differently. (a) CAROUSEL ARCHITECTURE — a format that buys dwell time through forced sequential interaction; the AI contribution is layout, resizing and slide-splitting, and the risk is low. (b) GENERATED IMAGERY — synthetic pixels in the frame; the AI contribution is the artwork itself, and this is where detectability, disclosure and audience backlash all live. Do not let (b)'s risk profile be laundered by (a)'s performance numbers.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **carousel path**:
  - 1. Take one argument with a real payload — a number, a process you ran, a before/after. A carousel amplifies structure; it cannot manufacture substance.
  - 2. Split into 6-12 slides, one idea per slide, each slide ending in an unresolved beat so the swipe is motivated. Slide 1 is a hook slide, not a title slide: it must state the promise and imply that the payoff is further in.
  - 3. Generate or adapt the layout. Canva Magic Design / Magic Switch produce and resize a deck from a prompt or a pasted text block; Contentdrips, Taplio and similar auto-split a blog post or an existing LinkedIn post into slides and apply a branded template.
  - 4. Export as a multi-page PDF. On LinkedIn in 2026 there is no separate 'carousel' object for personal profiles — the only route to a swipeable in-feed carousel is uploading a multi-page PDF as a document post, so every 'carousel maker' is really a slide designer with a clean PDF export.
  - 5. Publish with real body copy. The document is the dwell engine; the text post above it is still what the ranking model reads for topical relevance and what appears in search and in AI-engine retrieval.
  - 6. On Instagram the equivalent is a native multi-image carousel (up to 20 frames), not a PDF.
- **generated imagery path**:
  - 1. Decide the job of the image: stop the scroll (editorial/illustrative), carry text (quote card, stat card, slide background), show evidence (screenshot, chart, photo of the actual thing), or establish identity (recurring visual signature).
  - 2. Only the first two are safe jobs for a generative model. 'Show evidence' must be a real artefact — a generated screenshot of your own dashboard is fabrication, not illustration.
  - 3. For text-in-image, use a model with a dedicated typography path (Ideogram line) or a strong copy-fidelity model (Nano Banana Pro reportedly preserves exact casing and URLs better; Ideogram reportedly leads on standalone English typography). Verify the rendered characters by reading them, every time.
  - 4. Everything from a Google image model ships with a SynthID pixel watermark plus a C2PA manifest by default; other major providers attach C2PA Content Credentials. This happens whether or not you want it.
  - 5. Human pass: correct the text, fix the hands/logos/charts, and — critically — decide whether a generated image is the right answer at all versus a screenshot of the real thing.
- **the mechanism that actually matters**: Both paths are competing for the same thing: the first ~0.3 seconds of visual attention that decides whether the text gets read at all, and then dwell. A carousel earns dwell structurally (the reader must act 8 times); a single generated image earns only the stop. That asymmetry is why carousels show up in every 2026 format ranking and generated hero images do not.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **carousels**: Dwell time and, on LinkedIn, document-specific engagement depth — swipe-through is the mechanism, dwell is the signal. Secondarily saves (carousels are the most-saved format on Instagram, reportedly 3-4x Reels) and sends. On Instagram, Mosseri has publicly named watch time, sends per reach and likes per reach as the three dominant Feed signals; carousels are structurally good at the first two.
- **generated single images**: Stop-rate only — an upstream attention signal, not a ranked one. No platform ranks on 'has an image'. The image buys the chance for the copy to earn dwell.
- **text in image**: Indirectly targets dwell (reading takes time) and saves (a reference graphic is savable). Note the counterweight: text locked inside an image is invisible to the platform's NLP topic classifier and to AI answer engines, so a stat rendered only as pixels is withheld from both the relevance model and the retrieval layer.
- **unknown**: Whether platforms down-rank detected-AI imagery as a ranking input, as opposed to labelling it. Current reporting says labelling, not demotion — but Instagram/TikTok/YouTube all deprioritise 'unoriginal' content, and heavily templated AI visuals plausibly fall into that bucket. Treat as unresolved.

**why it drives reach**

- **carousel causal chain**: Swipe requires a deliberate physical action per slide → time-on-post rises far above a text post's → dwell is a primary ranking input on LinkedIn and Instagram in 2026 → the post is shown to a wider second-wave audience → the wider audience produces more saves and sends → sends are the strongest cross-audience distribution signal on Instagram. The format converts reader effort into algorithmic evidence of quality. Nothing about it requires AI; AI only lowers the production cost from ~90 minutes to ~15.
- **visual causal chain**: Image occupies more feed real estate and is processed pre-attentively → higher stop-rate → more of the audience reaches the first line of copy → the hook gets its chance. This is a funnel-widening effect at the very top, not a ranking effect.
- **the honest caveat**: Every published multiplier for carousel performance comes from tool vendors analysing their own users' posts, and they disagree with each other by an order of magnitude (see conflicting_evidence). The direction — carousels over-perform text on engagement rate — is consistent across every source and is mechanically plausible via dwell. The magnitude is not knowable from available evidence.
- **cross reference**: Per-platform ranking mechanics: see the vault note 'Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026' (2026-07-06, 17 platforms) rather than re-deriving them here.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **draft**: Generate slide copy splits from a long text; generate first-pass layouts (Canva Magic Design); generate illustrative imagery and backgrounds.
- **vary**: Produce N visual treatments of the same slide deck for pre-testing; auto-resize one design across LinkedIn 1200x1500, Instagram 1080x1350, X 1600x900 (Canva Magic Switch / auto-resize).
- **edit**: Inpaint, remove backgrounds, replace objects while respecting original lighting (Magic Edit / Magic Eraser); upscale; extend canvas.
- **render text**: The one genuinely hard capability — legible, correctly-spelled, correctly-cased typography inside a generated image. This is what separates Ideogram-class models from general image models and it is the capability that matters most for social graphics.
- **critique underused**: The highest-leverage and least-used role: hand the finished carousel back to a multimodal model and ask 'read slide 1 as a stranger scrolling — what do you think this is about, and would you swipe?'. Cheap, and it catches the dead title slide that kills most carousels.
- **what ai does not do**: It does not produce the evidence. Screenshots, real dashboards, real charts of your own numbers, photos of the actual workshop — these are the images that carry proof, and they are exactly the ones a model must not generate.

**automation level**

- **level**: L1 AI-assisted draft for imagery and slide copy; L2 autonomous-with-guardrails for the mechanical steps — template application, auto-resize, PDF export, background removal.
- **reasoning**: Text rendering still fails in ways only a human reading the pixels will catch (dropped letters, changed casing, invented words), and the decision of whether to use a generated image at all is a brand/credibility judgment. The layout-and-export half is genuinely safe to automate.
- **vendor label warning**: Tools marketed as 'AI carousel agents' that take a URL and post a finished PDF are L2 pipelines with no editorial gate. Running one unattended is the single fastest route to publishing a graphic with a misspelled word in 48pt type.
- **l3 status**: Nothing credible. An unattended generate-and-publish visual pipeline is a brand-damage generator, not a growth system.

**prompt patterns**

- **text in image**: State the exact string in quotes, the casing, and the position, then the style — in that order. 'Render exactly this text, preserving capitalisation: "$340 → $95". Large, top-third, left-aligned. Everything else: flat editorial illustration, single accent colour.' Models drop or 'improve' text that is described rather than quoted, and casing is the most commonly silently altered property.
- **negative space for copy**: Always reserve the caption area: 'leave the lower 35% visually quiet — flat background, no detail — for overlaid text.' Otherwise you get a beautiful image with nowhere to put the words.
- **aspect and safe area**: Specify the target ratio AND a safe margin: 'vertical 4:5, keep all text and the subject inside a 10% margin' — feed crops and thumbnail crops eat edges differently per platform.
- **series consistency**: Lock a style token and reuse it verbatim across every image for months: one sentence naming palette in hex, line weight, texture, lighting, and framing. Consistency is what turns generated images into a recognisable visual identity instead of stock noise; a rotating style reads as 'whatever the model gave me that day'.
- **carousel slide split**: Prompt the split by function, not by length: 'Split this into 8 slides. Slide 1 = the promise plus the number. Slides 2-7 = one move each, each ending mid-thought. Slide 8 = the one thing to do tomorrow. Max 18 words per slide. No slide may be a summary of the others.' Word limits are the difference between a carousel and a PDF of paragraphs.
- **anti slop for visuals**: Explicitly ban the house style of 2024-2026 AI illustration: 'no glowing neural-network motifs, no blue-orange gradient, no abstract floating cubes, no hexagon grid, no isometric robot, no lens flare.' These are the visual equivalent of 'delve' and readers now pattern-match them in under a second.
- **the critique prompt**: Attach the exported PDF or image and ask: 'You are scrolling LinkedIn at speed. Look at slide 1 only for one second. What is this about, and is there any reason to swipe?' Then: 'Read every character of text in this image and list anything misspelled, mis-cased, or cut off.' The second one catches what your eyes skip on a graphic you have stared at for twenty minutes.
- **anti pattern**: 'Make me a professional LinkedIn carousel about AI agents' — produces the exact templated artefact the platforms deprioritise as unoriginal and readers scroll past.

**tool examples**

- **text in image and graphics models**:
  - Ideogram (3.0 / 4.0 line) — built around a dedicated typography system; widely cited as the reference for text-in-image. A vendor comparison puts Ideogram 3.0 at '90-95% text rendering accuracy' [vendor blog, unverified]. Ideogram 4.0 reportedly launched ~2026-06-03.
  - Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image, ~2025-11-20) and Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, ~2026-02-26, per Google Workspace Updates) — strong conversational editing and, in head-to-head reports, better strict copy fidelity (preserves ALL-CAPS headlines and lowercase URLs where Ideogram altered casing).
  - GPT Image 2 (~2026-04-21) — reported LM Arena leader at the time of release [secondary source, unverified].
  - Flux 2 Pro (Black Forest Labs) — ~$0.055/image API, strong general quality.
  - Seedream 4.0 — ~$0.03/image, noted specifically for bilingual CJK+Latin typography.
  - Google Imagen 4 tiers — Fast ~$0.02, Standard ~$0.04, Ultra ~$0.06 per image.
- **design and layout**:
  - Canva Magic Studio — Magic Design (decks and social carousels from a prompt), Dream Lab (text-to-image, powered by Leonardo.ai), Magic Edit / Magic Eraser, background removal, auto-resize across platform ratios, Magic Charts, Canva Code. Canva Pro ~$12.99/mo. The pragmatic default for a non-designer.
  - Adobe Express + Firefly — deeper photo editing and Adobe ecosystem integration; Firefly's commercially-safe training provenance is the differentiator if that matters to you or a client.
- **carousel builders linkedin**:
  - Contentdrips — ~$19/mo, cheapest text-first carousel-to-PDF option
  - AuthoredUp — from ~$19.95/mo, LinkedIn-specific writing, formatting and preview; free tier with limited features
  - Taplio — Starter ~$39/mo, Growth ~$69/mo (AI features gated to Growth); can auto-generate carousels from a blog post, an existing LinkedIn post, or a URL
  - Canva — no AI carousel generation, manual design, but the best template and brand-kit control at the lowest price
- **format constraint to remember**: For a LinkedIn personal profile in 2026 the deliverable is always a multi-page PDF uploaded as a document post. Every tool in that list is, functionally, a PDF exporter.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

- **carousel format advantage**: moderate — direction consistent across many independent-ish datasets and mechanically explained by dwell; magnitude unverified and wildly inconsistent between sources.
- **ai generated imagery benefit**: unverified — no credible study shows AI-generated imagery outperforms human-made or real-photo imagery on social engagement.
- **ai generated imagery penalty**: anecdotal-to-vendor-claim for magnitude, moderate for direction — the audience trust penalty is reported consistently but every percentage is vendor- or survey-sourced.
- **tool capability claims**: vendor-claim throughout. Every text-rendering accuracy percentage found traces to a tool-vendor blog or an API-reseller comparison post.

**evidence provenance**

- **platform official**: Adam Mosseri's public statements on Instagram Feed signals (watch time, sends per reach, likes per reach); Google Workspace Updates blog for the Nano Banana 2 release; European Commission digital-strategy pages for the Article 50 Code of Practice; TikTok's own C2PA adoption announcements.
- **peer reviewed**: None found specifically on AI-generated visuals and social engagement. The nearest academic work is on AI image abuse patterns (arXiv:2403.12838, spammers/scammers using AI images for Facebook audience growth) — adjacent, not a performance study.
- **independent survey**: Hootsuite 2024 consumer survey (62% would trust or engage less with a post known to be AI-generated); NIM 'Transparency without trust' work on consumer attitudes to AI-generated marketing content.
- **vendor with product to sell**: Every carousel performance multiplier in this entry (6.60% document-post ER, 596%, 125%, 3.7x, 3:1, 2-3x impressions, +14% YoY), every text-rendering accuracy figure, and the 20-35% AI-content engagement penalty. These come from social-media SaaS blogs, carousel-tool blogs and AI-API resellers — commercially motivated, often citing each other, and several plausibly AI-written.
- **verdict**: Treat the carousel format advantage as real and the numbers as decoration. Treat the AI-imagery penalty as real in direction and unquantified in size. Treat every model benchmark as a marketing artefact with a shelf life of one quarter.

**effect size and n**

- **carousel vs text**: Reported figures, all vendor-sourced and mutually inconsistent: LinkedIn document posts at 6.60% engagement rate vs text posts 'struggling to break 2%'; '596% more engagement than text-only' attributed to an analysis of 1 million social posts; '125% more engagement'; '3.7x more engagement'; '3:1'; '2-3x further on raw impressions'; 'document performance up 14% YoY into Q1 2026'. Spread across these claims is roughly 1.25x to 6.96x for the same comparison — which is itself the most useful number here, because it tells you the measurement is not trustworthy.
- **instagram carousel vs reels**: Reels reported at 2-3x absolute reach; carousels reported at higher engagement per person reached for accounts over 50K followers (0.52% vs 0.50% — a difference small enough to be noise) and 3-4x more saves. Sends reportedly weighted 3-5x likes for Reels distribution since Q1 2026. All vendor-sourced.
- **ai content trust penalty**: 20-35% lower engagement for content perceived as AI-generated [vendor synthesis, no methodology published]; 62% of consumers would trust or engage less if they knew a post was AI-generated (Hootsuite 2024 survey); 39% say heavy AI use in a brand's marketing reduces trust; consumer enthusiasm for AI reported at 19% in 2026 vs 50% two years earlier. Direction robust across sources; magnitudes not independently verified.
- **text rendering accuracy**: '90-95%' for Ideogram 3.0 [vendor blog]. No standardised benchmark, no defined error metric, no sample size given. Effectively meaningless as a number; useful only as a ranking hint.
- **api cost per image**: $0.005-$0.20 across the 2026 market; a 33x spread between mini and flagship tiers. Concrete anchors: GPT Image mini ~$0.005, Imagen 4 Fast ~$0.02, Seedream 4.0 ~$0.03, Imagen 4 Standard / GPT Image ~$0.04, Flux 2 Pro ~$0.055, Imagen 4 Ultra ~$0.06. Batch APIs roughly halve this.
- **ai generated imagery lift**: No effect size found. There is no study measuring whether AI-generated imagery increases or decreases social engagement versus human-made imagery at equal design quality.

**conflicting evidence**

- **carousel magnitude**: The central conflict. '596% more engagement than text-only' (attributed to 1M posts) versus '125% more' versus '3.7x' versus '3:1' — all describing the same comparison, all published in 2026, all from tools that sell carousel creation. They cannot all be right and the selection effects are obvious: people who make carousels are people who invest more effort per post, so the format is confounded with effort. Record the direction; discard the multipliers.
- **carousel vs video**: Vendors selling carousel tools rank carousels first; vendors selling video tools rank video first. On Instagram the reconciliation in the data is that they optimise different objectives — Reels win reach (2-3x), carousels win saves and per-reach engagement. 'Reels are the discovery engine, carousels are the conversion engine' is the honest framing, and it means the format choice is an objective choice, not a quality ranking.
- **does ai content get algorithmically penalised**: Directly conflicting. One line of 2026 commentary asserts 'no platform penalizes AI posts in 2026 — Instagram, YouTube and TikTok deprioritize unoriginal, templated content, and the AI label carries a trust cost' (i.e. the penalty is audience-side, not algorithmic). Another line asserts platforms actively suppress AI content. The reconciliation that fits the platform statements: platforms demote UNORIGINAL content and LABEL AI content; AI-generated visuals are demoted only insofar as they are also templated and unoriginal. Unverified either way.
- **does disclosure help or hurt**: Conflicting and important. Labelled AI ads score measurably lower on favourability than unlabelled equivalents in blind tests even when creative quality is rated equal — i.e. disclosure has a direct cost. But non-disclosure risks a larger backlash on discovery, and from 2026-08-02 disclosure of AI-generated or AI-manipulated visuals is a legal obligation for EU deployers, not a choice. See the vault's 'AI disclosure paradox' item — rich, process-level disclosure mitigates the penalty where a bare label does not.
- **model leaderboards**: Ideogram is claimed as the text-rendering leader by one comparison and as having lost its clear lead to Nano Banana Pro by another, in the same quarter, with opposite results on the same property (casing fidelity). Both are API-reseller blogs. Do not pick a model from a blog — run your own three-prompt test.
