- PASS/FAIL: Can I state the post's single payoff in one sentence?
- PASS/FAIL: Does the fold (~140 chars, checked in a real mobile preview) cut mid-tension rather than after the payoff?
- PASS/FAIL: Does the first line after expansion immediately pay something, so the click is rewarded?
- PASS/FAIL: Does every beat open the next one, or does any beat close the post early?
- PASS/FAIL: No paragraph over three sentences; one idea per line?
- PASS/FAIL: Rhythm deliberately broken at least once so it does not read as machine-formatted?
- PASS/FAIL: Stop-reading audit run, and the first STOP falls after the main payoff?
- PASS/FAIL: Skim test (first four words per line) still carries the claim?
- PASS/FAIL: Length justified by content, not by a target character count - would I defend every sentence to a hostile reader?
- PASS/FAIL: The post does not repeat a payoff it already delivered?
- PASS/FAIL: Logged (characters, beats, fold text, first-90-min ER) for the personal benchmark?

**worked example**

- **real documented structure**: The clearest real, quotable artefact is the measured fold itself. On LinkedIn, text is truncated at roughly 140 characters on mobile and roughly 210 on desktop (AuthoredUp, from a 372,126-post dataset covering Sep 2025 - Feb 2026). That means for the ~57% of engagement that happens on mobile, the post most people read is 140 characters long. Everything in this entry follows from that single observable fact.
- **real measured finding**: From the same dataset: posts of 1,301-2,000 characters showed a 2.61% median engagement rate against 2.10% for posts under 400 characters, with median impressions of 1,106 and a median of 5 comments - roughly a 27% gap. The honest read is not 'write 1,300 characters' but 'posts with enough substance to justify 1,300 characters do better', which is a statement about substance wearing the costume of a statement about length.
- **constructed illustration**: CONSTRUCTED, not a real post. WEAK (inverted pyramid, payoff first): 'Here is how we cut onboarding from 14 days to 3: we deleted the setup wizard, moved credentials to a single env file, and pre-seeded the demo database. Below, the details of each step.' The reader has the answer at line one; everything after it is optional, so measured dwell is short even for readers who expand. STRONG (payoff late, fold mid-tension): line 1 - 'We cut developer onboarding from 14 days to 3.' / line 2 - 'The change that did it was the one we almost cancelled.' [fold falls here at ~99 characters, mid-tension] / then three beats, each a failed attempt with its own small payoff / then the actual change and why it was nearly cancelled. Same content, same length; the second one has a reason to reach the end.
- **why the example is honest**: Note what is NOT claimed: that the strong version measurably lifts dwell. Nobody can measure that from outside. What is claimed is that the weak version gives the reader an explicit stopping point at line one, and the strong version does not.

**cost and time to execute**

- **per post**: 15-30 minutes of structural work on top of writing - beat map ~5 min, ordering ~5 min, fold surgery ~5 min, stop-reading audit ~5-10 min, rhythm pass ~5 min. Roughly doubles the polish time of a 30-minute draft.
- **per month**: At 12 posts/month: ~4-6 hours. Tooling: LLM ~$20/mo (does most of the audit work), AuthoredUp ~$12.46-19.99/mo for the fold preview. Realistic floor: $20/mo with a free fold previewer and a spreadsheet.
- **setup cost once**: ~2-3 hours to write the structural prompts into a skill reference and build the logging sheet. Because dwell is invisible, the log is the only thing that turns this from folklore into practice - it is not optional overhead.
- **comparison**: Versus a 4-hour original-data post, structural work is cheap and multiplicative: it is 25-30 minutes that determines whether the 4 hours are read. Versus a 10-minute repurpose, it roughly triples the time cost and is usually not worth it - repurposes rarely have a 45-second payoff to architect.
- **hidden cost**: The discipline of cutting. The stop-reading audit routinely tells you to delete a third of a post you liked, and that is the actual price of this tactic.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **what you actually want**: Dwell time and completion. Neither is observable on text surfaces.
- **leading indicators you can see**:
  - Engagement rate per impression in the first 60-90 minutes - the best available expansion proxy
  - Comment substance: multi-sentence comments that quote or extend the body prove people reached the end; 'Great post!' proves they did not
  - Saves/bookmarks - only fully-read reference-grade posts get saved, and saves are among the heaviest 2026 LinkedIn signals
  - Ratio of comments to reactions - rising ratio suggests deeper reading
  - For video posts, view duration, which is the one directly-reported dwell analogue
- **lagging**: Impressions, reach, follower growth - all downstream and heavily confounded.
- **what moves first**: Comment substance, within the first hour. It is qualitative, but it is the earliest honest read on whether anyone finished the post.
- **personal benchmark**: Segment your own posts by structural shape (fold type, beat count, character band) and compare your own medians over 30+ posts. Given the measurement gap, this is not merely better than external benchmarks - it is the only real evidence available to you.

**measurement feasibility**

- **verdict**: This is the worst-measured tactic in the entire research set, and that should be stated plainly before any of its advice is adopted.
- **not observable**: LinkedIn exposes no dwell time and no 'see more' expansion rate to creators - dwell is explicitly an internal ranking signal only. X, Threads and Reddit likewise expose no read-depth for text posts. There is no API for any of it.
- **observable**: Video view duration (LinkedIn, Meta, TikTok, YouTube) and native retention curves on short-video surfaces. Carousel/document completion is partially visible on LinkedIn.
- **usable proxies**: (1) First-90-minute ER per impression; (2) comment substance, read manually; (3) save rate; (4) self-run structural A/B across your own posts, comparing your own medians; (5) a newsletter mirror of the same content, where read-depth is genuinely measurable - with the caveat that a subscriber base is a more committed population than a feed, so the numbers transfer directionally at best.
- **honest limit**: Every dwell number in public circulation - the 1.2%/15.6% bands, the ~40% reach bonus, the 60-70% never-expand figure - originates from practitioner reports whose underlying data cannot be audited, and the peer-reviewed literature warns that even genuine time measures cannot distinguish engaged reading from passive exposure. Treat all of it as direction, never as target. If a tool claims to score your post's dwell time, it is scoring readability.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- as of date and volatility
- audience fit
- conflicting evidence
- effect size and n
- how it works
- sources
- why it drives reach

### Hook engineering

`hook-engineering` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 7 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Hook engineering
- **category**: copy
- **definition**: Deliberate construction of the opening unit of a post - the first 1-3 text lines above the 'see more' fold, or the first ~3 seconds of video - so that the scroll stops and the post earns the attention the ranker needs in order to measure anything else.
- **maturity**: established as a discipline, decaying as a template practice - the taxonomy is durable, the specific templates saturate within 6-12 months
- **one line**: The gate every other tactic sits behind: no hook, no dwell, no completion, no distribution.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **two different objects share the name**:
  - **video hook**: The first ~3 seconds. Measured as hook rate = 3-second video plays / impressions x 100. 'Hook rate' is NOT a native Ads Manager column - it is derived from two official columns. Meta's own definition of the numerator: '3-second video plays' counts the number of times a video played for at least 3 seconds, or for ~97% of its length if shorter than 3 seconds, counted per impression and excluding replays (Meta Business Help Centre). The official completion-side metric is ThruPlay (played to completion or >=15s).
  - **text hook**: The lines visible before truncation. LinkedIn truncates at roughly 140 characters on mobile and roughly 210 on desktop; Threads caps a post at 500 characters and Bluesky at 300, so on those surfaces the hook and the post are nearly the same object; on X the first line doubles as the primary in-app search keyword slot.
- **taxonomy of first lines**:
  - **type**: Number / specific-figure lead | **shape**: Open with a concrete quantity you own ('We cut onboarding from 14 days to 3.') | **evidence**: First lines containing a number: 35 median likes vs 26 without, N=278,996 number-led posts inside a 1,179,958-post corpus (MagicPost, vendor, correlational).
  - **type**: Contrarian / myth-bust | **shape**: 'Everyone says X. Our data says the opposite.' | **evidence**: No clean effect size found. The vault note reports unique/contrarian angles associated with up to ~165% more organic reach on LinkedIn - vendor-claim, unverified.
  - **type**: Confession / failure admission | **shape**: 'I lost a 40k contract because of one line in a proposal.' | **evidence**: Story-first post types show 0.80-1.03% median engagement rate vs a 0.39% platform median across 1,141,932 posts (MagicPost, vendor, correlational).
  - **type**: Result reveal (outcome first) | **shape**: Put the payoff at the top and the method below the fold.
  - **type**: Tension / stakes statement | **shape**: Name what is at risk, specifically. Bluesky and Threads practitioners report specific tension-creating first lines beat vague curiosity gaps.
  - **type**: Named-entity / proprietary-data lead | **shape**: 'After 61 client audits, the same three things broke.' Hardest to imitate, and the most defensible against the AI-slop classifier.
  - **type**: Definition or reframe | **shape**: 'X is not a Y problem. It is a Z problem.' Heavily saturated in 2026 - one of the canonical LLM cadences.
  - **type**: Question opener | **shape**: 'What if your onboarding is the reason you churn?' | **evidence**: UNDERPERFORMS in the largest corpus available: 19 median likes and 4 comments vs 29 likes and 6 comments for non-question openers - a 34% gap that holds across all three follower bands (<5k: 10 vs 13; 5k-50k: 26 vs 34; 50k+: 129 vs 187), N=143,789 question openers (MagicPost, vendor, correlational).
  - **type**: Listicle promise | **shape**: '5 things I learned...' The single most published type and the most saturated: 0.44% median ER on N=142,301, barely above the 0.39% platform median.
  - **type**: Pure curiosity gap / withheld payoff | **shape**: 'Nobody told me this about pricing.' Highest policy risk band - Meta's Transparency Center explicitly lists clickbait and engagement bait among content whose Feed distribution is reduced, and demotes accounts that repeatedly post it.
- **first line length**: Punchy beats paragraph, but the curve is shallow and non-monotonic: 1-5 words = 30 median likes (N=144,760); 6-10 words = 29 (N=436,663); 11-15 words = 25 (N=280,014); 16+ words = 28 (N=318,523). Read the 11-15 word dip as noise-prone, not as a law.
- **the concreteness rule**: The one peer-reviewed mechanism here. Aubin Le Quere and Matias (Scientific Reports, 2025) meta-analysed 8,977 valid A/B headline tests (35,910 headline instances) from the Upworthy Research Archive. Finding: the effect of concreteness depends on the baseline. 'When the baseline headline is too vague, higher headline concreteness increases clickthrough rates. When headlines are too concrete, higher headline concreteness decreases clickthrough rates.' Interaction coefficient -0.058, p<0.001. At low test concreteness (2.06) the difference was +0.05 log-odds (~5.5% practical increase); at high test concreteness (4.41) it was -0.08 log-odds (~9.9% practical decrease). Only 8.7% of Upworthy headlines benefited from more concreteness while 50.9% were hurt by it. Practical translation: aim for middling concreteness - specific enough to be believable, vague enough to leave a gap.
- **execution loop**: Write the body first. Extract the single most surprising true fact from it. Generate 10-20 first-line variants across at least four taxonomy types. Score them against a rubric (specificity, gap size, does the body pay the promise, no template cadence). Preview against the real 140-character mobile fold. Ship one; log which taxonomy type it was; compare against your own last 20 posts, not against a vendor benchmark.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **primary**: The earliest retention threshold on the surface - the one that gates every later signal. Video: the 3-second play, which feeds watch-time and completion prediction. Text: the 'see more' expansion, which feeds dwell time (an officially confirmed LinkedIn ranking signal, and an explicit 2026 personalization input on Reddit's Home feed).
- **secondary**: First-hour / first-90-minute engagement velocity, because a post nobody opens cannot be commented on inside the test window.
- **explicitly not targeted**: Saves, sends/DM shares, reply depth and semantic relevance. A hook does not move any of these directly - it only buys the post the chance to move them. Treating hook rate as a proxy for reach is the most common measurement error in this area.
- **honest answer**: On text surfaces the causal chain hook -> expansion -> dwell -> reach is inferred, not observed. Nobody outside LinkedIn has seen the expansion-to-reach coefficient. Call it a plausible mechanism, not a measured one.

**why it drives reach**

Every 2026 feed ranker is a cold-start experiment: the post goes to a small test pool (roughly 2-5% of network on LinkedIn, a seed pool on TikTok/Reels) and is judged on quality-per-impression, not on totals. The hook is the only part of the post the test pool is guaranteed to see. If the hook fails, the denominator (impressions) fills up while the numerator (expansion, watch, dwell, comment) stays near zero, so the ranker reads low quality-per-impression and closes the gate - not because the content was bad, but because it was never sampled. Because signals are normalized per impression and dwell-weighted, a weak hook does not merely fail to help, it actively supplies negative evidence. This is also why hook work has asymmetric returns: it cannot make a thin post valuable, but a weak hook can make a valuable post unmeasurable.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **does well**:
  - Variant generation - 10-30 first lines from one body, forced across taxonomy types so you are not choosing among 20 samples of the same shape.
  - Critique and scoring against an explicit rubric (does the body pay this promise? is there exactly one gap? is there a fact only the author could supply?).
  - Classification - tag your own last 50 posts by hook type and join to your own engagement data, which converts folklore into a private benchmark.
  - Compression - cutting a 34-word opener to 9 words without losing the specific number.
  - Retrieval - surfacing the author's own past winning hooks as few-shot examples instead of generic templates.
- **does badly**:
  - Supplying the substance. The model has no proprietary number, no client, no failure.
  - Judging novelty. It cannot see your feed, so it cannot tell you a template is saturated - it will happily regenerate the most common 2025 shapes because they dominate its training distribution.
- **best configuration**: Human supplies the fact; model supplies the permutations; human picks. Inverting that order is exactly what produces slop.

**automation level**

L1 AI-assisted draft is the honest level for organic. L2 (autonomous with guardrails) is reachable only in PAID video, where hook rate gives a real automated fitness function - generate variants, run them, kill anything under the account's own rolling median, human approves the survivors. Nothing credible sits at L3. Note that tools marketed as 'AI hook generators' (Taplio, Reepl, the various hook-generator sites) are L1 template engines with a scheduler attached, regardless of 'AI agent' framing.

**prompt patterns**

- **pattern 1 extract then vary**: Two-call structure. Call 1: 'Here is my post body. List the 5 most surprising, verifiable, specific facts in it - facts a stranger could not have guessed. Quote them verbatim. If there are fewer than 3, say so and stop.' Call 2: 'Using fact #2 only, write 12 opening lines: 3 number-led, 3 confession/failure, 3 contrarian, 3 result-reveal. Max 12 words each. No question openers. No colon-then-payoff constructions. Every line must contain the number or the proper noun.' The stop condition in call 1 is the important half - it fails loudly when the post has no substance to hook.
- **pattern 2 concreteness ladder**: 'Rewrite this hook at five levels of concreteness, from 1 (pure gap, no specifics) to 5 (every detail named). Label each.' Then pick level 3. This operationalises the Scientific Reports inverted-U instead of defaulting to 'be more specific', which the data says hurts roughly half the time.
- **pattern 3 adversarial gate**: 'You are a skeptical reader who sees 300 posts a day. For each hook: (a) name the template it is copying, or say ORIGINAL; (b) state what you would expect the post to say, then read the body and say whether the promise is paid; (c) give it a stop-scroll score 1-10 and say what you would have to cut to earn a 9.' Reject anything that gets a template name in (a).
- **pattern 4 fold fit**: 'Cut this to fit 140 characters so the truncation lands mid-tension, not mid-word and not after the payoff. Show me what the reader sees before and after the cut.' Fold position is a craft variable most generators ignore.
- **pattern 5 personal corpus fewshot**: 'Here are my 15 highest-dwell posts from the last year with their first lines. Infer my hook grammar - sentence length, punctuation habits, how I use numbers. Now write 10 hooks for today's post in that grammar.' Few-shotting on your own winners is the single highest-leverage change and the main defence against generic cadence.
- **anti pattern**: 'Write me 10 viral LinkedIn hooks about [topic]' with no body, no fact and no corpus. This is the prompt that produces the feed's sameness.

**tool examples**

- Meta Ads Manager (native) - '3-second video plays' and 'Impressions' columns; hook rate must be computed from them. ThruPlay is the official completion metric.
- Motion - creative analytics; source of the most-quoted 2026 Meta hook-rate dataset (578,750 creatives across 6,015 accounts, ~$1.29B spend).
- AuthoredUp (2026 pricing ~$12.46-19.99/mo) - 200+ hook and CTA templates, readability scoring, and a mobile preview showing the exact 'see more' cut-off. No AI generation, which makes it the honest fold-testing tool.
- Taplio (2026 pricing ~$39-52/mo) - AI drafting trained on a claimed 500M+ LinkedIn posts; L1 generator plus scheduler.
- MagicPost - publishes the 1.18M-post first-line analysis quoted throughout this entry; useful as a corpus, sells a product.
- Claude / GPT-class models - the variant-generation and critique engine in the prompt patterns above; ~$20/mo.
- LinkedIn Post Preview (linkedinpreview.com) and similar free fold-preview tools - an adequate substitute for AuthoredUp's preview alone.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

Split, and the split matters more than any single label. (a) That the hook gates distribution: moderate-to-strong - it follows from platform-official cold-start descriptions and from Meta's and LinkedIn's own metric design, and it is consistent across every surface. (b) That specific first-line types outperform: moderate at best - one large-N vendor corpus, correlational, one platform. (c) Every hook-rate benchmark band: vendor-claim. (d) The concreteness inverted-U: strong - peer-reviewed registered report over 8,977 field A/B tests.

**evidence provenance**

- **peer reviewed**: Aubin Le Quere and Matias, Scientific Reports (2025) on headline concreteness; Loewenstein, Psychological Bulletin 116:75-98 (1994) on the information gap; eye-tracking work on feed attention (Sulflow et al. 2019; Mayer et al. 2024) establishing that feed scanning is 1-2 automatic fixations unless something holds the eye.
- **platform official**: Meta Business Help Centre definitions of '3-second video plays' and ThruPlay; Meta Transparency Center on engagement bait and clickbait demotion; LinkedIn Engineering on dwell time as a ranking signal.
- **independent large n**: None found for hook rate. The Upworthy Research Archive is the only genuinely independent large-N field dataset in this entry, and it is news headlines from 2013-2015, not 2026 social posts.
- **vendor with product to sell**: Every hook-rate band (Motion/Taylor Sicard, Benly, Skaler, sepia-lab, rule1, AdMake, Coinis, Hawky, Reloop, adlibrary); every LinkedIn first-line median (MagicPost, which sells a LinkedIn writing tool); AuthoredUp's length data.
- **warning**: The first page of results for 'hook rate benchmark 2026' is dominated by near-identical vendor pages with no shared primary source, several of which read as machine-generated SEO pages citing each other. Treat convergence among them as evidence of copying, not of replication. One of the more careful ones (Taylor Sicard) states it outright: 'Meta publishes no official hook-rate benchmark, which is exactly why the public numbers vary, so treat any band as directional.'

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **works best**:
  - **LinkedIn**: Highest leverage of any surface, because the fold is hard (~140 chars mobile) and dwell time is a confirmed ranking signal. See the vault note's LinkedIn section: a strong hook line before the 'see more' fold is named as the first lever for dwell.
  - **TikTok / Reels / Shorts**: The 3-second hook is the gating metric by design; the vault note puts first-3-5-second retention directly under completion rate among TikTok's top weighted signals.
  - **X**: First line is both hook and the primary in-app search keyword slot - one line has to do two jobs.
  - **Threads / Bluesky**: 500 and 300 character caps mean the hook is most of the post. Both reward specific, tension-creating first lines over generic curiosity gaps; Bluesky explicitly does not optimise for dwell, so hook value there is reply-velocity, not read-depth.
- **backfires**:
  - **Facebook / Instagram feed**: Withheld-payoff hooks collide directly with Meta's published clickbait and engagement-bait demotions, and repeat offenders are demoted account-wide.
  - **Reddit**: A hooky title reads as marketing and gets downvoted; the title should describe, not tease.
  - **Newsletters / owned surfaces**: No ranker to game; a curiosity-gap subject line that under-delivers costs unsubscribes, which are permanent in a way a bad post is not.
  - **Carousels / documents**: Slide 1 is the hook, but LinkedIn now penalises low carousel completion, so a hook that oversells a padded deck is worse than no hook.
- **format note**: Hook rate as a computable number exists only for paid video. On organic text there is no hook metric at all - which is why the discipline drifts toward folklore.

**scales with**

- **what it needs**: A supply of genuinely surprising, first-hand facts. That is the binding constraint, not writing skill - you can only write a number-led hook if you have a number.
- **follower band**: Roughly neutral. The question-opener penalty and the number-led lift both persist across <5k, 5k-50k and 50k+ bands, so hook craft is one of the few tactics not gated by account size.
- **what caps it**: Body quality. The ceiling on hook work is the promise the body can pay; past that, better hooks make the gap more visible, not less. It also caps at feed saturation - in a niche where everyone uses the same five templates, hook lift converges to zero.
- **objective dependence**: For viral reach, hook work is necessary and insufficient. For AI-engine citation it is close to irrelevant - LLM retrieval does not read your first line as a hook.
- **paid vs organic**: In paid, hook work scales linearly with creative production budget (more variants, more tests). In organic it scales with how many genuinely different things you have actually done.

**decay and saturation**

- **taxonomy**: Durable - 5+ years. The categories are grounded in curiosity psychology, not in platform mechanics.
- **specific templates**: 6-12 months, and shortening. Once a template is in an AI writing tool's default output it is in tens of thousands of posts within a quarter. The 2026 casualties are visible in the feed: 'Unpopular opinion:', 'Let that sink in.', 'It's not X. It's Y.', 'Here's the thing:'.
- **benchmark numbers**: 3-6 months. Hook-rate bands move with Meta creative-ranking changes and with whichever vendor dataset gets quoted next.
- **structural pressure**: Saturation is now accelerated from both sides - AI generation on supply, classifier detection on demand. LinkedIn's slop-report button turns template reuse into a reader-reported signal, a decay mechanism that did not exist before July 2026.
- **what does not decay**: A hook built on a fact only you hold. It cannot be copied, so it cannot saturate.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- Promise gap - the hook writes a cheque the body does not cash. Reader expands, bounces in 2 seconds, and the post now has a worse dwell profile than if nobody had expanded it. On LinkedIn this is strictly worse than a weak hook.
- Engagement-bait drift - the hook slides from curiosity into 'Comment YES if you agree', which Meta and LinkedIn both actively demote, with account-level consequences for repetition.
- Template collapse - the hook is recognisably the same shape as 40 other posts that week, so it reads as noise regardless of the content behind it.
- Optimising the proxy - chasing hook rate until hold rate and conversion fall. A shock opener can raise 3-second plays and lower everything downstream.
- Fold mismatch - the hook is tested on desktop (~210 chars) and truncates wrong on mobile (~140), cutting after the payoff instead of before it, which removes the reason to expand.
- Wrong surface - importing LinkedIn hook grammar to Reddit or a technical forum, where it reads as marketing.
- Substance vacuum - hook work used as a substitute for having something to say. The most common failure, and the one hook engineering is most often used to hide.

**ai slop risk**

- **level**: High - the highest of any copy tactic in this research, because hook generation is the most automated step in social writing and the output space is small.
- **why**: Models are trained on the feed, so they regress to the feed's most common shapes. Ask for 'viral hooks' and you get the 2024-2025 template set back, polished.
- **specific tells**:
  - Colon-then-payoff at a fixed rhythm: 'The truth: ...', 'Here's the thing: ...', 'The result: ...'
  - Negation-reframe triad: 'It's not X. It's not Y. It's Z.'
  - Round or suspiciously clean numbers ('10x', '3 lessons', '90 days') with no provenance
  - Universal-quantifier openers: 'Most people get this wrong', 'Nobody talks about this', 'Everyone is doing X'
  - Symmetrical sentence lengths across a whole variant set - a human writes uneven lines
  - Em-dash cadence and tricolon in a short opener
  - Stakes with no subject: 'This changes everything' with no named this
  - A hook that could be prefixed to any post in the niche - the strongest single test
- **mitigation**: Require a proper noun, a date, or a number the model could not have invented inside the first line. Few-shot on your own past winners rather than on templates. Generate 20 and reject 19 - the slop is in accepting the first plausible output, not in generating variants.

**human input required**

- **minimum non substitutable contribution**: One verifiable, first-hand specific inside the visible hook: a number you measured, a client or tool you named, a date, a failure you owned, or a judgment only someone with your track record could make.
- **checkable gate**: Delete every word the model wrote and ask: is there still a fact left that only I could have supplied? If no, the hook is slop regardless of how it reads.
- **why this is the right gate**: It is what the classifiers are effectively probing for. LinkedIn's stated detection target is not 'was a machine involved' but low-effort signals - recycled structure, restated ideas, absence of first-hand perspective. An AI-assisted post carrying your own numbers and opinions is treated as normal content; a human-typed post with no first-hand content is not protected by having been typed.
- **time cost**: The fact-extraction step, not the writing step. Budget 5 minutes finding the number, 5 minutes generating 20 hooks, 5 minutes choosing.

**detectability and disclosure**

- **machine detectable**: Not reliably. Text detectors have a documented and severe false-positive problem - seven detectors flagged non-native English writing as AI-generated 61% of the time, unanimously on ~20% of papers, while almost never misfiring on native writing (Liang et al.). Directly relevant here: a Polish author writing in English sits in the population these detectors handle worst.
- **provenance standards**: C2PA Content Credentials are an ISO-adopted standard for media provenance but are not solved for plain text and break on a screenshot. SynthID watermarking applies to Google-generated media, not to arbitrary text pasted into a feed. No major feed auto-labels AI-assisted text in 2026.
- **what actually flags you**: Humans. Since 2026-07-30 any LinkedIn reader can hit 'Seems like AI slop' from the three-dot menu on a post or comment; reports are private, feed moderation, and train LinkedIn's classifiers. LinkedIn also privately flags to authors in their own dashboard when readers find their content inauthentic. This is a reader vote, not a detector - a careful AI-assisted post may never be flagged and a human-written post may be.
- **disclosure triggered**: None for AI-assisted hook drafting on any major platform in 2026. No platform requires disclosure of AI assistance in text composition, as distinct from synthetic media and AI avatars, which do trigger labelling.

**policy and legal**

- **eu ai act art 50**: Applicable since 2026-08-02. The text-specific duty covers AI-generated or AI-manipulated text 'published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest'. Two reasons it rarely bites for a hook: (1) an ordinary professional or promotional post is generally not public-interest information; (2) the Article carries an explicit exemption where the content 'has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility'. Caveat from practitioner commentary: the review must be substantive, not cursory approval, and the exemption effectively expects a documented editorial workflow with an identified responsible person. For a Poland/EU-based solo creator writing hooks with AI and editing them: keep a light record of the editorial step; do not lean on the exemption for public-interest commentary you did not actually review.
- **platform rules**: Meta's Transparency Center reduces Feed distribution of clickbait and engagement bait and demotes accounts that repeatedly post it; engagement bait is defined as posts explicitly soliciting votes/shares/comments/tags/likes outside a genuine call to action (missing persons, fundraising, petitions are carved out). LinkedIn suppresses low-effort AI content and, since 2026-07-30, collects reader slop reports. Neither prohibits AI-assisted drafting.
- **advertising law**: If the hook makes a performance or outcome claim in a commercial context, EU/PL consumer-protection and unfair-commercial-practices rules apply to the claim itself regardless of who wrote it. A hook is an advertising claim the moment it promises a result.
- **practical position**: AI-assisted hook drafting with genuine human editorial review is compliant in the EU today. The exposure is in what the hook claims, not in how it was drafted.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 1**: Write the body first. Always. A hook written before the body is a hook the body cannot pay.
- **step 2**: Extract facts. Ask the model for the 5 most surprising verifiable specifics in the body, quoted verbatim, with an instruction to stop if there are fewer than 3. If it stops, the post is not ready - go get a number, not a better hook.
- **step 3**: Pick the one fact a stranger could not have guessed.
- **step 4**: Generate 12-20 first lines across at least 4 taxonomy types from that single fact. Exclude question openers on LinkedIn; include them on Threads/Bluesky/X where reply velocity is the target.
- **step 5**: Apply the concreteness ladder - rewrite the leading candidate at 5 concreteness levels and take level 3. Resist the reflex to take level 5.
- **step 6**: Run the adversarial gate: name the template each hook copies, predict what the body will say, then check whether the body pays it. Kill anything that gets a template name.
- **step 7**: Fold-test on mobile at ~140 characters (AuthoredUp preview or any free fold previewer). Make the cut land mid-tension - after the setup, before the payoff. Rewrite the break point, not just the words.
- **step 8**: Sanity-check against your own last 20 posts, not a vendor benchmark: is this shape one you have already used twice this month?
- **step 9**: Publish, then log hook type + first line + fold position alongside the post's results in a sheet. After ~30 posts you have a private benchmark that beats every number in this document.
- **step 10 paid only**: For video ads: ship 3-5 hook variants of the same body, compute hook rate = 3-second video plays / impressions per variant, kill anything below your account's rolling median, and always read hold rate alongside it so you do not buy 3-second plays with a shock opener.

**checklist**

- PASS/FAIL: Does the visible-before-the-fold text contain at least one number, proper noun, or date that only I could supply? (fail = rewrite, not regenerate)
- PASS/FAIL: Does the body pay the exact promise the hook makes? Read the hook, write down what you expect, then read the body.
- PASS/FAIL: Fold-tested at ~140 characters on mobile, with the cut landing mid-tension?
- PASS/FAIL: Free of explicit engagement solicitation ('comment X', 'tag someone', 'like if')?
- PASS/FAIL: Would this first line be wrong on any other post in my niche? (if it would fit anywhere, it is slop)
- PASS/FAIL: Not the same taxonomy type as my last two posts?
- PASS/FAIL: No colon-payoff, no negation-triad, no universal-quantifier opener?
- PASS/FAIL: Concreteness at level 3 of 5, not level 5?
- PASS/FAIL: On LinkedIn - not a question opener; on X - target keyword present in line 1?
- PASS/FAIL: Logged (hook type, first line, fold position) for the personal benchmark?

**worked example**

- **real documented case**: The Upworthy Research Archive provides the only genuinely clean public evidence. Upworthy ran 27,616 field A/B tests on live headlines; Aubin Le Quere and Matias analysed 8,977 valid tests (35,910 headline variants). Their published result, quoted: 'When the baseline headline is too vague, higher headline concreteness increases clickthrough rates. When headlines are too concrete, higher headline concreteness decreases clickthrough rates.' The distributional finding is the useful one: of the real headlines tested, 8.7% were improved by added concreteness and 50.9% were made worse. That is a large, adversarially-collected field dataset saying the most common piece of hook advice is wrong more than half the time.
- **real corpus case**: MagicPost's 1,179,958-post LinkedIn corpus, June 2025 - June 2026: first lines opening with a question (N=143,789) earned a median of 19 likes and 4 comments; non-question openers earned 29 and 6. The gap survives follower-band controls (10 vs 13 likes under 5k; 26 vs 34 at 5k-50k; 129 vs 187 at 50k+). The authors state the caveat themselves: 'the why is interpretation, so read these as hypotheses, not measured facts.'
- **constructed illustration**: CONSTRUCTED, not a real post - included to make the fold concrete. Weak: 'I've been thinking a lot about developer onboarding lately, and I wanted to share some lessons that I think could help teams who are struggling with the same thing.' (fold cuts at ~140 chars mid-throat-clearing; no fact; fits any post). Strong: 'We cut developer onboarding from 14 days to 3. The change that did it was the one we almost cancelled.' (99 chars, fits the mobile fold whole, carries two owned numbers, leaves exactly one gap, and the body can pay it). Note the strong version sits at concreteness level ~3: it names the numbers but withholds the change.

**cost and time to execute**

- **per post organic**: 10-20 minutes on top of the body: ~5 min extracting the fact, ~3 min generating 20 variants, ~5 min the adversarial gate, ~3 min fold-testing. Zero marginal cash cost if you already pay for an LLM.
- **per month organic**: At 12 posts/month: ~3-4 hours. Tooling: LLM ~$20/mo; AuthoredUp ~$12.46-19.99/mo for the fold preview and hook library; Taplio ~$39-52/mo only if you also want generation and scheduling. A free fold previewer plus a spreadsheet gets ~80% of this at $20/mo total.
- **per post paid video**: Materially higher - 3-5 hook variants means 3-5 edits (0.5-2h each, or $50-200 each outsourced) plus test budget. Creative-analytics tooling (Motion and peers) typically runs several hundred USD/mo and only pays back above meaningful spend.
- **setup cost once**: ~2 hours to build the hook rubric and the logging sheet. This is the highest-ROI two hours in the whole area, because it converts every future post into evidence.
- **comparison**: Against a 4-hour original-data post, hook work is the cheapest multiplier available - but only on a post that already has the data. On a thin post it is 20 minutes spent making nothing more visible.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **leading paid video**: Hook rate (3-second video plays / impressions), read alongside hold rate. Moves within hours.
- **leading organic video**: 3-second retention and the first drop-off point on the retention curve, available natively on TikTok, Reels and Shorts.
- **leading organic text**: Engagement rate per impression in the first 60-90 minutes. This is the only observable proxy for 'did anyone expand it'.
- **lagging**: Impressions, reach, follower growth - all downstream of the hook and confounded by everything else.
- **the metric that would settle it**: 'See more' expansion rate. Not exposed by any platform.
- **personal benchmark**: Rolling 90-day median of your own hook rate (paid) or first-90-minute ER (organic), segmented by hook taxonomy type. After ~30 logged posts this outranks every external band in this document.

**measurement feasibility**

- **fully observable**: Paid Meta/TikTok video - both hook-rate inputs are native columns. Organic short video - native retention graphs.
- **not observable**: LinkedIn text. There is no dwell-time metric and no 'see more' expansion metric in creator analytics; LinkedIn treats dwell as an internal ranking signal only. The same is true on X and Threads for read-depth.
- **proxies to use**: (1) First-90-minute engagement-rate-per-impression as an expansion proxy; (2) for video posts, view duration as a directly-measured stand-in; (3) self-run A/B - post structurally similar content with deliberately different hook types and compare your own medians; (4) comment content as a qualitative read - comments quoting the body prove expansion, comments reacting only to the hook prove the opposite.
- **honest limit**: On text surfaces you are inferring the hook's effect from a metric three steps downstream. Any single-post read is noise; only the 30-post median is informative. Anyone quoting a precise organic text hook-rate is quoting something that does not exist.

### Listicle formats

`listicle-formats` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 7 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Listicle formats ("N lessons / N mistakes / N tools")
- **category**: copy
- **definition**: A post organised as an explicitly enumerated set of discrete, self-contained items announced by a count in the first line — '7 mistakes I made scaling X', '5 lessons from Y', '12 tools that replaced Z'. The number is both the promise and the navigation.
- **maturity**: SPLIT, and this split is the single most important finding. DECAYING as a human-engagement play on professional feeds (saturated, parodied, cheap to mass-produce with an LLM). SIMULTANEOUSLY ASCENDANT as the dominant AI-citation format — vendor analysis of ~400M citations puts 63% of LLM citations on listicle pages. The same structure is dying on one surface and winning on another.
- **one line verdict**: Stop writing listicles for the feed and start writing them for retrieval; if the items are not independently valuable, the count is padding and the format punishes you twice.

**as of date and volatility**

- **as of**: 2026-09-11
- **stable layer**: Processing fluency and the enumeration effect are stable: numerals in headlines act as visual anchors and promise bounded, structured effort, and this is measured in the Upworthy field-experiment literature (Banerjee & Urminsky). Decade-scale, not going away.
- **volatile layer**: Quarter-to-quarter on two independent fronts. (1) FEED: LinkedIn's 360Brew ranker (confirmed Mar 2026) reweighted toward dwell time and substantive comments; comment ranking became per-viewer in Aug 2026; polls collapsed after the reported Mar 2026 authenticity update. (2) RETRIEVAL: the AI-citation advantage of listicles is a 2026 observation from a fast-moving measurement field — Evertune's figures cover March-April 2026 and were updated May 2026. Retrieval behaviour changes with every model and every AI-search UI revision.
- **rot rate**: Feed-side claims: 6-12 months. AI-citation claims: quarter-to-quarter, and the incentive for everyone to publish listicles means the citation advantage is itself a saturating edge. Re-verify the Evertune-class numbers before building on them.
- **asymmetry warning**: The two layers are decaying in opposite directions right now. Any advice that treats 'listicles' as one thing is already wrong.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **the mechanism**: Enumeration does three things at once. (1) It PRICES the post: '7 mistakes' tells the reader exactly how much attention they are committing, which lowers the bar to starting. (2) It CHUNKS the post: each item is independently comprehensible, so the reader can abandon at item 4 and still feel they got value — this raises completion-equivalent behaviour and, on LinkedIn, sustains scroll depth. (3) It PROMISES completeness: a count implies the author surveyed a space and selected, which is a cheap authority signal.
- **processing fluency**: The numeral is the active ingredient in the first line. Banerjee & Urminsky's analysis of thousands of Upworthy headline field experiments found that the presence of numbers in headlines raised click-through, consistent with the processing-fluency literature — while most OTHER fluency cues they tested did not produce significant effects. Numbers are one of the few textual cues with a replicated direction.
- **the open loop variant**: 'N mistakes' outperforms 'N lessons' on engagement for a specific reason: a mistake list is an implicit accusation-or-absolution test. The reader scans to find out whether they are making mistake 3. That is a self-relevance mechanism, not a curiosity mechanism, and it is why mistake-framed lists generate more 'I'm guilty of #4' comments — which happen to be exactly the substantive comments LinkedIn's ranker rewards.
- **why the format is structurally different from a persuasion arc**: A listicle has NO required reading order and NO single thesis. This is its strength for retrieval (any item can be lifted intact) and its weakness for persuasion (nothing accumulates; the post makes ten small points instead of one large one). Choosing a listicle is choosing breadth over depth, and the choice should be deliberate.
- **where the count becomes the problem**: The number is a commitment made before the content exists. If you have five real items and announce ten, items 6-10 are padding, and padding is precisely what both readers and citation engines punish — an LLM citing your item 8 and finding it vacuous is the failure mode that stops it citing item 1 next time. The widely-repeated craft rule holds: five strong entries beat ten weak ones.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **primary feed signal**: Scroll depth and dwell time. A listicle is the most reliable structure for keeping a reader inside the post body, because each item resets the decision to continue. On LinkedIn — where dwell is the dominant practitioner-observed 2026 signal and 'see more' expansion is the gate — an enumerated body is a direct dwell instrument.
- **secondary**: SAVES. Listicles are the highest-save-rate text format because they are reference material: the reader saves item 6 for later even if they read all ten now. Saves drive content longevity and resurfacing on both LinkedIn and Instagram.
- **tertiary**: Self-relevant comments ('#4 hit me'). Cheap to elicit, and on LinkedIn's per-impression, NLP-filtered comment weighting, these clear the substantive threshold more often than reaction-bait does — but only barely.
- **on x specifically**: Listicles map to threads, which target ShareViaCopyLinkWeight (+20.0, the highest positive weight in X's published scorer), ShareViaDmWeight (+5.0) and bookmark/save behaviour. A numbered thread is the most copy-link-shared text shape on the platform.
- **explicitly NOT targeted**: Reply depth as CONVERSATION. A listicle answers rather than asks; it closes ten loops instead of opening one. If the objective is a comment thread with actual back-and-forth (ReplyWeight +5.0, and bidirectional-follow reply boost +15.0 on X), the listicle is the wrong shape — a single contested claim beats ten uncontested ones.
- **honest note**: No platform exposes a 'format = list' feature. This is inference from reader behaviour to ranker inputs, not a measured signal.

**why it drives reach**

- **feed causal chain**: Numeral in the first line -> lowered commitment cost -> expansion past the fold -> per-item re-decision keeps the reader scrolling -> dwell time and scroll depth accumulate -> 360Brew / Phoenix escalate distribution. The chain is short and each link is plausible, which is why the format worked for a decade.
- **the broken link in 2026**: Step 1 no longer clears. The numeral has lost its attention advantage on professional feeds through sheer base rate: content saturation on LinkedIn is reported at roughly three times the posts-per-connection of 2022, and enumerated posts are over-represented in that growth because they are the cheapest shape for an LLM to emit. A cue only works while it is diagnostic; when every third post opens with a number, the number stops signalling anything.
- **retrieval causal chain**: This one is intact and is where the format's value moved. Numbered self-contained items -> clean chunk boundaries -> each item retrievable and quotable without surrounding context -> LLM cites the item -> the author's name and claim appear inside an AI answer. Evertune's May 2026 analysis found 63% of ~400M citations pointed to listicle pages, with ranked lists 71-86% of those depending on the model. The mechanism is transparent: retrieval systems reward extractability, and enumeration IS extractability.
- **the reconciliation**: Listicles did not stop working. Their payoff moved from the feed to the index. Judged on impressions they look dead; judged on being cited six months later by an assistant answering a buyer's question, they are the strongest format available.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **what the model is genuinely good at**:
  - EXTRACTION, not invention: 'read these three post-mortems, this transcript and these 40 notes, and pull every distinct failure I actually described — quote the source line for each.' The model finds your items; it must not author them.
  - DEDUPLICATION: listicles fail by containing the same item three times in different words. 'Which of these 11 items are restatements of each other? Merge and show me the true count.' This is the single highest-value AI pass on this format.
  - PADDING DETECTION: 'which of these items would still be true and useful if deleted entirely? Rank by how much the post loses.' Then cut the bottom.
  - CHUNK REWRITING FOR RETRIEVAL: rewriting each item as a self-contained 40-60 word unit that makes sense lifted out of context — the specific craft that converts a feed listicle into a citable one.
  - ORDERING: 'order these by how surprising each is to a senior practitioner, most surprising first' — the strongest item must not be item 7.
- **what it must not do**: Generate the items. 'Give me 10 mistakes people make with X' returns the ten most common statements about X in the training corpus — by construction, the ten things your audience has already read. This is the purest form of slop available and the format most vulnerable to it.
- **the asymmetry**: Listicles are the format where AI adds the most value (extraction, dedup, chunking over YOUR corpus) and does the most damage (item invention). The difference is entirely whether the model is pointed at your material or at its own weights.

**automation level**

- **level**: L1 (AI-assisted draft) for the whole pipeline. The extraction and dedup passes are the closest thing in this research to a genuinely valuable L1 use.
- **where L2 is defensible**: Two narrow gates can run unattended because their failure mode is rejection, not publication: (a) a padding detector that flags any item with no proper noun and no number; (b) a chunk-length linter enforcing the 40-60 word self-contained form on each item. Both reject drafts, never ship them.
- **why not L3**: Item selection is a judgement about what YOUR audience does not already know, informed by what you actually did. No model has either input. An L3 listicle pipeline is a slop generator with a scheduler attached — and this format is where such pipelines are most commonly deployed, precisely because it is the easiest to fake.
- **vendor labelling caveat**: Tools marketed as 'AI content agents' that produce '10 tips' posts on a schedule are L1 schedulers with a template. Nothing credible sits at L3 in 2026.

**prompt patterns**

- **pattern 1 corpus extraction**: SYSTEM: You are an extraction tool. You may only output claims that appear in the supplied material. Inventing an item is a failure. USER: Here are my notes, post-mortems and client transcripts from the last 18 months. Extract every DISTINCT mistake I explicitly describe having made or observed. For each, output: (a) the mistake in one sentence, (b) the verbatim source line, (c) the file it came from. If you cannot supply (b) and (c), do not output the item.
- **pattern 2 true count**: Here are 14 candidate items. Identify which are restatements of the same underlying point at different levels of abstraction. Merge them. Then tell me the TRUE count of distinct items. I will use that number in the headline even if it is 4. Do not pad to reach a round number.
- **pattern 3 padding audit**: For each item, answer in a table: does it contain a proper noun? a number? a condition under which it does NOT hold? Then rank all items by how much the post would lose if that item were deleted. Show me the bottom third — those are candidates for cutting, not rewriting.
- **pattern 4 chunk for retrieval**: Rewrite each item so it is self-contained: comprehensible to someone who has read none of the other items and does not know who wrote it. Target 40-60 words. Each must open with the claim stated as a fact, then the evidence, then the boundary condition. Do not use 'this', 'that' or 'the above' to refer to anything outside the item.
- **pattern 5 surprise ordering**: Score each item 1-10 on how surprising it would be to someone with ten years in this field. Reorder most-surprising first. Tell me which items score below 4 — those are table stakes and should be cut, not demoted.
- **pattern 6 anti template**: This reads like every LLM listicle. Rewrite to remove the signature without changing any claim: vary item lengths (some one line, some five), delete every parallel-construction opening (each item currently starts the same grammatical way), remove the tidy summary paragraph at the end, and make at least two items admit a limitation. Return a diff.
- **anti pattern**: 'Write me 10 lessons about X.' This is the single most common prompt in social-media AI use and it returns the corpus median every time.

**tool examples**

- **drafting and extraction**: Claude (Opus/Sonnet 2026) and ChatGPT (GPT-5.x) for the extraction/dedup/chunking passes. Long-context models matter here specifically — the extraction pass is only useful if the whole corpus fits.
- **carousel production**: Canva (Magic Design / bulk-create for numbered slide decks), Ideogram (reliable text rendering inside images — the binding constraint for numbered slides), Figma + a slide template. LinkedIn document posts are the highest-engagement format on the platform, and a listicle is the native content for them.
- **linkedin suites**: Taplio (Starter $39 / Growth $69 / Pro $199 per month, 2026; AI drafting from Growth, ~25% off annual), Hypefury (~$6/month per channel), Supergrow, Contentin. All ship listicle templates — useful for layout, dangerous for content.
- **retrieval and grounding**: The vault itself plus brain-mcp for corpus search; any RAG setup over your own notes. This is the anti-slop mechanism for this format, not an optional extra.
- **linting**: Vale for prose rules (enforce 'no parallel item openings'), plus any AI-text classifier as a risk check rather than a gate.
- **measurement**: Native LinkedIn analytics (saves are visible; dwell is not), Shield/Taplio for per-post history, X native analytics for bookmarks on threads.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

SPLIT BY CLAIM, and conflating them is the main error in circulating advice. MODERATE for 'numerals in headlines raise click-through' (large-N field experiments, but the key paper is a preliminary working paper). VENDOR-CLAIM for '63% of AI citations go to listicles' — large, mechanistically plausible, but produced by a GEO platform selling optimisation. ANECDOTAL for 'listicles are saturated and decaying on LinkedIn' — this is real practitioner consensus plus visible parody, with no measurement behind it. UNVERIFIED for every specific 2026 LinkedIn penalty percentage in circulation. NO DIRECT EVIDENCE AT ALL for the most useful question: whether an 'N mistakes' post outperforms a non-enumerated post of equal substance on the same account.

**evidence provenance**

- **large n field experiments working paper**: Banerjee & Urminsky, 'The Language That Drives Engagement: A Systematic Large-scale Analysis of Headline Experiments' (SSRN 3770366, Chicago Booth). Thousands of Upworthy A/B experiments, NLP-coded textual cues. CAUTION: the circulating version is stamped 'PRELIMINARY RESULTS FROM AN EXPLORATORY DATASET' with an explicit warning that confirmatory results are likely to differ. Direction only.
- **peer reviewed adjacent**: Robertson et al. (2023) Nature Human Behaviour — same Upworthy corpus (N=22,743 RCTs, ~105,000 headline variations, ~5.7M clicks, ~370M impressions), establishing what a well-powered headline effect actually looks like (~2.3% per negative word). Useful as a magnitude calibrator: real textual-cue effects are small.
- **vendor with product to sell**: Evertune (GEO measurement platform) — ~25,000 top-cited URLs, ~400M citations across ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Google AI Overviews and Perplexity; top 6,000 cited URLs per model for March-April 2026, published via Search Engine Land May 2026. Semrush (SEO platform) — 325,000 prompts, 89,000 LinkedIn URLs, Jan-Feb 2026. Socialinsider — 1.3M LinkedIn business posts. Buffer — 52M+ posts. Each has a product that the finding supports.
- **trade press amplification**: The Evertune result reached most readers through Search Engine Land rather than the vendor directly, which adds editorial filtering but not independent verification.
- **circular and likely ai generated**: The bulk of 'LinkedIn algorithm 2026' blog content asserting specific listicle penalties, '60% engagement-bait penalties', '97% detection accuracy' and 'polls now 0.07% engagement' cites other blogs of the same kind. Several read as AI-generated. Direction may be informative; treat every magnitude as unverified.
- **absent entirely**: No platform-official statement about enumerated-post treatment exists on any platform. X's open-sourced ranker (github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm) contains no format-level feature for lists — confirming that any 'the algorithm likes listicles' claim is inference, not mechanism.
