#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **cross reference**: Per-platform ranking mechanics are not re-derived here — see [[Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026]] (17 platforms, 2026-07-06).
- **linkedin text post**: SATURATED. Works only when the items are proprietary. The count in the first line no longer buys attention on its own; the specificity of item 1, placed above the fold, does.
- **linkedin document carousel**: BEST FEED FIT BY A DISTANCE. One item per slide is the format's native home: documents are the highest-engagement LinkedIn format, drive saves, and get repeated ranking chances. Optimal ~8-10 slides. CRITICAL 2026 caveat: carousels now penalise low COMPLETION, which converts padding from a soft sin into a ranking penalty — a 10-slide deck where slides 7-10 are filler will underperform a tight 6-slide deck.
- **linkedin newsletter article**: THE HIGHEST-VALUE PLACEMENT and the one almost everyone skips. Newsletters/articles are evergreen, searchable, and the strongest AI-citation surface on LinkedIn. If the Evertune finding holds, the listicle belongs here first and in the feed second.
- **x**: Thread format. Numbered threads are the most copy-link-shared text shape on X, targeting the +20.0 weight. But X's author-diversity multiplier decays consecutive posts from the same author, and the out-of-network discount (~0.75) applies — a long thread is not free.
- **instagram carousel**: Strong fit. Multi-slide re-serving gives unseen slides fresh ranking chances, and saves (weighted ~3x a like) are the listicle's natural currency.
- **tiktok shorts**: WEAK. '5 things' videos exist but the enumeration fights retention — announcing five items tells the viewer they can leave after two. Better to withhold the count.
- **where it backfires hardest**: Any context where depth signals competence: technical audiences, senior practitioners, and anything adjacent to a hiring or buying decision. A list of ten shallow items reads as a survey of the surface.

**audience fit**

- **b2b**: Mixed and increasingly negative at the top of the seniority range. Junior and mid-level professional audiences still engage; senior practitioners and buyers read enumerated posts as content marketing. The exception that always works: a list of specific, named, checkable things (tools with versions, failure modes with error messages, clauses with numbers).
- **b2c**: More durable. Consumer audiences have lower template fatigue and the reference/save use-case is stronger.
- **technical audiences**: HOSTILE to generic lists, RECEPTIVE to enumerated specifics. '7 lessons from scaling' fails; '7 things that broke when we moved from X 4.2 to 5.0, with the error each threw' succeeds. The enumeration is not the problem — the abstraction is.
- **en vs pl**: EN professional feeds are the most saturated; the count in the first line is close to fully discounted. PL-language professional feeds are meaningfully behind on saturation, so the format still earns attention — but localisation matters more here than in any other format, because list items are where idiom and cultural reference break under translation. A directly translated EN listicle reads as imported marketing.
- **general vs specialist**: Inverse relationship between audience breadth and viable list length. Broad audience tolerates 10 shallow items; specialist audience wants 3 deep ones. Choosing the count is really choosing the audience.

**scales with**

- **the binding constraint is corpus size**: This is the format whose ceiling is set almost entirely by how much you have written down. A genuine 'N mistakes' list requires N distinct documented mistakes. Without a corpus — notes, post-mortems, transcripts, past posts — the extraction pass has nothing to extract and the model falls back to its weights, which is exactly the failure mode. A vault like this one is the enabling asset.
- **experience inventory**: Secondary ceiling. Even with perfect notes, most practitioners have on the order of 20-50 genuinely non-obvious items across their whole career, not hundreds. Sustainable listicle output is therefore low-frequency — which is the opposite of how the format is typically used.
- **not capped by account size**: Format is size-neutral for feed reach, and for AI citation the ceiling is markedly flatter: sub-500-follower accounts are cited by AI engines comparably to large ones. Citability is the objective where a small account competes on equal terms.
- **team size**: Scales well with a team — a listicle can aggregate items from multiple people's experience, which is one of the few legitimate ways to raise the true count without padding.
- **objective dependent ceiling**: For FEED reach the ceiling is low and falling (saturation). For AI-CITATION visibility the ceiling is high and the binding constraint is publishing on a durable, indexable surface rather than in an ephemeral feed post. Same content, different placement, different ceiling.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- PADDING TO A ROUND NUMBER. The defining failure. Announcing 10 when you have 5 means half the post is filler, and on LinkedIn carousels — where low completion is now penalised — padding is a direct ranking cost, not just a reader cost.
- CORPUS-FREE GENERATION. Asking a model for the items returns the training-corpus median: the things your audience has already read, phrased in the way they have already seen. Highest-frequency slop failure of any format in this research.
- ABSTRACTION DRIFT. Items degrade from 'the retry logic double-counted, which cost us 340 duplicate invoices' to 'be careful with retry logic'. Once every item is a maxim, the list is indistinguishable from every other list.
- COVERT DUPLICATION. Items 2, 6 and 9 are the same point at different altitudes. Readers feel it as thinness without being able to name it. This is what the dedup pass exists to catch.
- SATURATION DISCOUNT. The numeral no longer earns attention because the base rate of enumerated posts is too high for the cue to be diagnostic.
- NO CONVERSATION. The format closes loops rather than opening one, so it generates self-relevant reactions ('#4!') rather than the reply threads LinkedIn's ranker rewards most and X weights at +5.0.
- STRONGEST ITEM BURIED. Ordering by narrative or chronology rather than by surprise puts the best item where most readers never reach it.
- CITATION POISONING. On the retrieval side: an engine that lifts your weak item 8 and finds it vacuous has been given evidence about the quality of your source. Padding has a cost that persists beyond the post.
- CADENCE COLLAPSE. Because the format is cheap, it invites volume; volume drops engagement-per-impression; per-impression-normalised rankers then depress subsequent posts.

**ai slop risk**

- **risk level**: VERY HIGH — second only to persuasion formulas, and arguably worse in practice because listicles are the shape most people actually ask models to produce. 'Give me 10 tips about X' is the single most common social-content prompt in existence.
- **specific tells**:
  - PARALLEL CONSTRUCTION: every item opening with the same grammatical shape (imperative verb, or gerund, or 'Don't...'). Human lists are grammatically ragged; model lists are not.
  - UNIFORM ITEM LENGTH: ten items each 1-2 lines. Real experience does not distribute evenly — some lessons take a sentence, some take a paragraph.
  - ROUND NUMBERS: 5, 7, 10. A list of 4 or 9 signals the count came from the content; a list of 10 signals the content came from the count.
  - NO PROPER NOUNS AND NO NUMERALS INSIDE THE ITEMS — the headline has a number, the body has none. A reliable diagnostic.
  - NO ITEM ADMITS A LIMIT. Every item asserted unconditionally, none saying 'except when...'. Boundary conditions are the clearest evidence of first-hand experience.
  - TIDY SUMMARY PARAGRAPH at the end restating the list's theme — a model habit, rarely a human one.
  - Cadence uniformity across the whole post (runs of 18-24 word sentences) — reported in 2026 as the most reliable general AI marker.
  - NOT a tell in 2026: em dashes. GPT-5.1 suppresses them by default and human professional usage is comparable. Do not gate on this.
- **the compounding problem**: This format is where slop is most visible AND most consequential, because a generic listicle is simultaneously ignorable in the feed and worthless-to-harmful in the index. A padded list teaches a retrieval system that your source is thin.
- **mitigation**: Hard rule: no item ships unless it traces to a line in your own corpus. The extraction prompt should REFUSE to output items it cannot source-quote. This single constraint eliminates most of the risk.

**human input required**

- **minimum non substitutable contribution**: EVERY item must trace to something you did, measured, or witnessed — not the post as a whole, every item. This is the format where the usual 'add one personal touch' advice fails, because a single authentic item surrounded by nine generic ones reads worse than nine generic ones alone: the contrast makes the padding obvious.
- **the per item gate**: Each item must carry at least one of: a number you measured, a named artefact (tool + version, vendor, document), a dated incident, or a boundary condition you discovered the hard way ('this stops working above ~50 concurrent users').
- **the hardest and most valuable input**: The BOUNDARY CONDITION. Models produce confident universal advice; practitioners know where advice stops applying. 'Do X — except when Y, where it made things worse for us' is the sentence a model cannot write about your work, and it is the sentence that makes the item both credible and citable.
- **the count itself is a human judgement**: Deciding to publish 4 items instead of padding to 7 is an editorial act with a real cost (worse headline) and a real payoff (no filler). No automated pipeline makes that trade honestly, because the count is the thing the template wants filled.
- **the gate**: If a competent competitor in your niche could have written every item, the human contribution is zero. FAIL.
- **time cost**: 15-45 minutes of retrieval per post. As with persuasion formulas, the cost is in having kept the record, not in writing.

**policy and legal**

- **jurisdiction assumed**: Poland / EU-based creator.
- **eu ai act article 50**: In force since 2026-08-02. Two distinct duties: deepfake disclosure for synthetic media depicting real people or events (not triggered by a text listicle, but potentially triggered by AI-generated imagery on slides if it depicts identifiable people), and disclosure of AI-generated TEXT published to inform the public on matters of public interest — with an express exemption where the content underwent human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person bears editorial responsibility. Penalties up to EUR 15M or 3% of worldwide turnover; grace period to 2026-12-02 for pre-existing systems.
- **why listicles carry above average exposure**: Enumerated formats gravitate toward public-interest subject matter — '7 things the new AI Act requires', '5 changes to employment law', '10 health metrics to track'. That is precisely the Art. 50(4) territory. A listicle is also a series of DISCRETE FACTUAL ASSERTIONS, each independently checkable, which raises the substantiation burden relative to a narrative post making one hedged claim. Ten items is ten claims.
- **the mitigation is the quality workflow**: Genuine human editorial review satisfies the exemption and is already required by the per-item gate above. The compliance answer and the craft answer are the same answer.
- **advertising and consumer law**: Listicles that rank or recommend products — the exact sub-genre that dominates AI citations — engage EU/PL unfair-commercial-practice rules. Undisclosed paid placements in a ranked list, or rankings presented as neutral that are not, are a live exposure. Disclose commercial relationships inside the item, not in a footer.
- **third party content**: Tool and resource lists name other people's products. Factual, non-disparaging listing is fine; comparative claims about competitors must be substantiable.
- **platform tos**: AI-assisted text is permitted everywhere. The relevant prohibitions are mass-produced/templated content (YouTube's Inauthentic Content Policy, 2026, enforced at channel level) and engagement bait. A listicle pipeline running at volume is the workflow most likely to drift into 'mass-produced'.

**reversibility and blast radius**

- **typical worst case**: LOW and reversible on the feed side. A padded listicle underperforms and disappears within the platform's half-life (LinkedIn ~24-72h). No enforcement attaches to publishing a list.
- **the non obvious persistent risk**: The RETRIEVAL side is not reversible on the same timescale. Content published to durable surfaces (newsletters, articles) is indexed and can be cited for months or years. A list with a wrong or vacuous item can be surfaced by an assistant to a prospective client long after you would have forgotten the post, and you cannot recall a citation. Feed mistakes decay; indexed mistakes persist.
- **account level risk**: Moderate and cumulative. High-volume templated listicle output is the behaviour pattern most likely to attract mass-produced-content treatment (YouTube enforces this at channel level; LinkedIn's per-impression normalisation applies a softer version). Recovery is weeks of better posting, not a deletion.
- **brand damage**: Being quoted as an example of LinkedIn slop. Realistic, spreads faster than the original, not deletable.
- **enforcement risk**: Near zero for the format. Non-zero if the post ends in engagement bait ('comment LIST and I'll send it') — a pattern the format invites and classifiers flag.
- **recovery playbook**: Correct indexed items at the source (edit the article/newsletter — this is why durable surfaces are preferable to feed-only posts: they are editable). Reduce list frequency, publish 3-5 posts carrying proprietary specifics, and let per-impression averages recover.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 0 precondition**: Confirm you have a CORPUS to extract from — notes, post-mortems, transcripts, past posts. If the items would have to come out of a model's weights, do not write a listicle; write the one thing you actually know instead. This gate rejects most listicle ideas and should.
- **step 1 extract before you count**: Run prompt_pattern_1 against your own material with the source-quote requirement enforced. Never decide the number first. The single most damaging move in this format is choosing '10' and then hunting for content.
- **step 2 find the true count**: Run prompt_pattern_2 (dedup). Expect 14 candidates to collapse to 6. Publish the collapsed number. '6 mistakes' is a better headline than '10 mistakes' with four repeats, and it is the honest count.
- **step 3 audit for padding**: Run prompt_pattern_3. Cut the bottom third rather than rewriting it — a weak item improved is still a weak item, and on carousels it now costs completion.
- **step 4 order by surprise**: Run prompt_pattern_5. Most surprising first. Item 1 must be above the fold and must be the one that makes a senior person stop. Cut anything scoring below 4 on surprise: table stakes are what makes a list generic.
- **step 5 make each item self contained**: Run prompt_pattern_4 (40-60 words, claim then evidence then boundary condition, no cross-references). This is the step that converts a feed post into a citable asset, and it costs nothing on the feed side.
- **step 6 add the boundary conditions by hand**: At least two items must state where the advice stops applying. The model cannot supply these. This is the highest-value ten minutes in the whole process.
- **step 7 destroy the template signature**: Run prompt_pattern_6. Vary item lengths deliberately. Delete the parallel openings. Delete the summary paragraph. Apply as a diff, by hand.
- **step 8 choose the surface deliberately**: Feed post for reach, carousel for saves and depth (8-10 tight slides, no padding — completion is penalised), newsletter/article for citation and durability. For anything you want cited by an assistant in six months, the newsletter version is the primary artefact and the feed post is the trailer.
- **step 9 gate and publish**: Run the checklist. Any FAIL returns to step 2.
- **step 10 ration the format**: No more than one listicle per five posts, and never two consecutive. Decay is driven by your own repetition as much as by the platform's.
- **total time**: 45-90 minutes for a corpus-grounded list, most of it retrieval and boundary-condition writing. A padded one takes 6 minutes and should not exist.

**checklist**

- **gate type**: pass/fail — any FAIL blocks publication
- **items**:
  - SOURCING: every single item traces to a specific line in my own notes, work, or measured experience. One unsourced item = FAIL for the whole post.
  - TRUE COUNT: the number in the headline equals the number of genuinely distinct items after deduplication. If I padded to reach a rounder number, FAIL.
  - NO COVERT DUPLICATES: no two items are the same point at different levels of abstraction. FAIL if any pair merges.
  - SPECIFICITY PER ITEM: every item contains a number, a proper noun, a version, a date, or a named artefact. Any purely abstract item = FAIL (cut it, do not rewrite it).
  - BOUNDARY CONDITIONS: at least two items state where the advice stops applying. Zero = FAIL.
  - SURPRISE FLOOR: no item is table stakes for someone with ten years in this field. FAIL — cut it.
  - ORDERING: the most surprising item is item 1 and appears above the fold. FAIL otherwise.
  - SELF-CONTAINMENT: each item is comprehensible lifted out of context, with no 'this', 'that', or 'as above' pointing outside itself. FAIL otherwise (and it is uncitable).
  - RAGGEDNESS: item lengths vary; items do not all open with the same grammatical construction; there is no tidy summary paragraph. Uniformity = FAIL.
  - CAROUSEL COMPLETION: if this is a document post, is every slide worth swiping to? Any slide that exists to reach a slide count = FAIL (low completion is penalised).
  - COMPETITOR TEST: could a competent rival in my niche have written this identical list? If yes, FAIL.
  - NO ENGAGEMENT BAIT: no 'comment LIST and I'll DM it', no 'tag someone who needs this'. FAIL if present.
  - COMMERCIAL DISCLOSURE: if any ranked item involves a paid relationship, it is disclosed inside that item. FAIL otherwise.
  - PUBLIC-INTEREST REVIEW: if the list informs the public on a matter of public interest (law, health, elections, AI policy, safety), have I genuinely reviewed and can I evidence editorial control? FAIL if I skimmed model output.
  - SUBSTANTIATION: every one of the N claims is individually defensible if challenged. Ten items is ten claims — FAIL if any is not.

**cost and time to execute**

- **per post time grounded**: 45-90 minutes. Breakdown: 20-40 min corpus extraction and verification (the real cost), 10 min dedup and padding audit, 10 min writing boundary conditions by hand, 10 min self-containment rewrite, 5 min anti-template diff, 5 min checklist.
- **per post time if carousel**: Add 30-60 minutes for slide design, or 15 minutes with a fixed template. Carousels are the highest-return placement for this format but carry a real production cost.
- **per post time ungrounded**: 6 minutes. This is exactly why the format is saturated, and why the 6-minute version should never ship.
- **per month time**: At one listicle per five posts and 3 posts/week — roughly 2-3 listicles/month — about 3-5 hours/month, plus carousel production if used. Plus a one-off 2-4 hours to build the extraction prompt chain against your corpus.
- **tool subscriptions**: Minimum viable: one long-context frontier model, ~USD 20-30/month (Claude Pro / ChatGPT Plus). Long context matters more here than for any other format, because extraction quality scales with how much corpus fits in one pass. Optional: Canva Pro ~USD 12-15/month for carousel production; Ideogram for text-in-image; Taplio Starter $39 / Growth $69 / Pro $199 per month (2026); Hypefury ~$6/month per channel. Vale free.
- **total monthly**: USD 20-30 model-only; USD 35-50 with carousel tooling; USD 60-120 with a LinkedIn-native suite.
- **comparison anchor**: A grounded listicle sits in the middle of the cost spectrum — well above a 10-minute repurpose, well below a 4-hour original-data post. Its distinguishing property is DURABILITY: the retrieval-side payoff accrues over months, which changes the return calculation versus a feed-only post of the same cost.
- **hidden cost**: The corpus. Everything above assumes notes exist. If they do not, the real cost of this format is the habit of writing things down, which is months, not minutes — and is the reason a maintained knowledge vault is the enabling asset for it.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **leading first 60 90 minutes**:
  - SAVES/BOOKMARKS per impression — the earliest and most diagnostic signal for this format specifically. A listicle that is read but not saved had no item worth keeping, which is the format's defining failure.
  - Comments that name a specific item ('#3 is what got us') rather than generic praise — direct evidence the body was read, not just the hook.
  - Impressions still climbing after 30 minutes rather than flattening, as a dwell proxy.
  - On X threads: bookmarks and quote-posts in the first 30-60 minutes (QuoteWeight +5.0) rather than likes (+0.5).
- **lagging 24 72h and beyond**:
  - Saves-per-impression versus your trailing median for the same format — the only comparison that means anything.
  - Carousel COMPLETION rate if available (slide-through depth) — with low completion now penalised, this is the metric that tells you whether you padded.
  - Long-tail impressions past 72h, indicating the resurfacing that evergreen educational content earns under 360Brew.
  - Follower conversion, which for this format indicates the list demonstrated a reference-grade knowledge base.
- **the slow kpi that actually matters**: AI-citation appearance. Periodically ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode the question your list answers, and check whether you appear. This is a months-scale metric, is the format's real payoff, and is invisible in every social analytics product.
- **format specific diagnostic**: Track saves-per-impression against TRUE ITEM COUNT across your own posts. If your 4-item lists out-save your 10-item lists, you have measured your own padding — the most useful private finding available in this format.
- **negative indicators**: Comments shifting from item-specific to generic; saves-per-impression falling while impressions hold; your own reluctance to reread the post a week later.
- **what not to track**: Likes, and any industry ER benchmark — Socialinsider's ~5.20% LinkedIn average and Buffer's 21.77% carousel median use incompatible denominators, so neither is a target you can meaningfully hit.

**measurement feasibility**

- **directly observable**: Impressions/members reached, reactions, comments (with text, so item-specificity can be judged by hand), reposts, and — crucially for this format — SAVES, which LinkedIn and Instagram both expose. The listicle is unusual in that its primary value signal is natively visible.
- **partially observable**: Carousel slide-through/completion is available on Instagram and partially on LinkedIn document posts. Since completion is now the penalty axis for padded carousels, this is worth checking even where the data is coarse.
- **NOT observable**: Dwell time on both LinkedIn and X (X's own scorer uses dwell, click-dwell time and active seconds; none are exposed to authors). 'See more' expansion rate. Share-via-DM (X ShareViaDmWeight +5.0) and copy-link shares (+20.0 — the highest positive weight in X's published scorer, and entirely invisible to you). Roughly 84% of B2B sharing is reported to happen in untrackable private channels, and listicles are precisely the content people forward privately, so this format's real circulation is systematically under-measured.
- **the citation metric is manual**: AI-citation visibility has no creator-facing analytics. Options: manual spot-checks against a fixed prompt set on a monthly cadence (free, crude, sufficient), or paid GEO-tracking platforms (Semrush, Evertune and similar) which are priced for brands rather than individuals. Manual is the realistic answer for one creator: keep a list of 10 questions your content should answer and check them monthly.
- **best available proxies**:
  - Saves-per-impression as the quality proxy — the closest thing to a direct read on item value.
  - Item-specific comments as the read-depth proxy.
  - Unexplained profile views and inbound DMs referencing a specific item as the dark-social proxy. Asking 'which one hit?' in DM replies is crude and is the only instrument available.
- **measurement honesty**: You cannot A/B test list length or item count at individual-creator volume — the variance between posts swamps the effect. Track the saves-per-impression-versus-true-count relationship over 20+ posts as a descriptive pattern, not as a causal test.

### Narrowcast / share-to-DM trigger design

`narrowcast-dm-trigger-design` · automation L1 · evidence STRONG · 12 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Narrowcast / share-to-DM trigger design
- **category**: copy
- **definition**: Writing a post so that one reader forwards it privately to one specific other person — optimising for the private send (DM/Slack/WhatsApp/email forward) rather than the public like — by making the content useful to a nameable recipient rather than flattering to the sharer.
- **maturity**: established as psychology (peer-reviewed since 2014), emerging as an explicit copy discipline, and currently the highest-leverage under-exploited signal on the feed platforms

#### mechanism

**how it works**

The mechanism is a deliberate switch of the reader's attentional frame from 'how will I look if I post this' to 'who specifically needs this'.

THE SCIENCE. Barasch & Berger (Journal of Marketing Research 51(3), 2014, 286-299, six studies) show that audience size changes WHAT people share. Broadcasting to many makes communicators self-focused, so they avoid content that makes them look bad and favour self-presentational content. Narrowcasting to one person makes them other-focused, so they favour content that is USEFUL TO THE RECIPIENT. The mediator is focus of attention, not privacy per se — which is the executable part: you can induce other-focus with copy, inside a public post, without the reader being in a private channel yet.

THE FOUR TRIGGERS, in descending reliability:
1) SPECIFIC UTILITY TO A NAMEABLE ROLE. The content solves a problem that belongs to a job title, not to everyone. 'If you run a 2-person agency that bills hourly' beats 'if you're a founder'. The narrower the role, the faster the reader retrieves a specific person.
2) IDENTITY SIGNALLING ('this is so you'). The content is a recognisable portrait of a type of person the reader knows. The send is an act of affection or teasing — the forwarded message is effectively 'I thought of you'. This is the most emotionally reliable trigger and the hardest to fake.
3) ARGUMENT-SETTLING. The content resolves a disagreement the reader has already had. It gets forwarded into the thread where the argument happened. Requires a stated, falsifiable position — hedged content settles nothing.
4) COMPLETENESS / REFERENCE VALUE. The content is the whole answer, so forwarding it discharges an obligation ('you asked me about X — here'). This overlaps with saves and is the variant that also builds AI citability.

THE DESIGN MOVE. Most posts are written to be agreed with. A narrowcast post is written to be FORWARDED, which means: no dependency on the surrounding context (it must survive being pasted into Slack with no caption), no in-joke that requires following the author, a self-contained payload, and an explicit or implicit recipient. The single highest-yield edit is replacing a broad 'you' with a specific role descriptor early in the post.

THE PLATFORM PAYOFF. Instagram's sends-per-reach, TikTok's share-to-DM, and LinkedIn's Sends all read a private forward as the strongest available endorsement — it costs the sharer social capital with a named individual, which is far more expensive to fake than a tap. Note the trap: the SEND is countable, the downstream reading, forwarding and conversion are NOT (see measurement_feasibility).

**why it drives reach**

Three compounding effects. (1) RANKING: a send is the least-fakeable engagement available — it has a named recipient and a reputational cost to the sender — so rankers weight it heavily for deciding whether to push content to people who do not follow you. (2) AUDIENCE TRANSPLANT: unlike a like, a send delivers the content to a person selected by a human who knows both the content and the recipient. The targeting is better than the algorithm's, and it lands in a channel with near-100% open rates and no ranking layer. (3) DARK COMPOUNDING IN B2B: a forward into a Slack channel or a WhatsApp group reaches a buying committee the platform could never target and cannot see, which is why the private path is claimed to convert far better than the public one — and also why almost none of it appears in your analytics. The causal chain is therefore: other-focused copy → private send → both a strong ranking signal AND an untracked high-trust distribution path, running in parallel.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Retrieve and critique, with one genuinely novel role. (1) RECIPIENT SIMULATION — the core use: give the model the draft plus 4-6 real roles from your network and ask it to name, for each, who they would forward it to and what they would type above it. If the model cannot produce a plausible covering message, the post has no send trigger. (2) OTHER-FOCUS AUDIT — have the model classify every sentence as SELF-PRESENTING (makes the author look good) or RECIPIENT-USEFUL (helps the reader's reader), then report the ratio; Barasch & Berger's mechanism makes that ratio the operative variable, and most drafts come back 70%+ self-presenting. (3) SPECIFICITY TIGHTENING — rewrite the audience descriptor from a category to a role with a constraint. (4) STANDALONE TEST — strip all context and ask whether the excerpt still makes sense pasted into Slack. What AI must NOT do: invent the useful payload. The forwardable substance is a number, a template, a decision rule or a warning from your own work; a model can only sharpen how it is framed.

**automation level**

L1 (AI-assisted draft) for framing and recipient simulation; L2 (autonomous with guardrails) is defensible for the other-focus audit and the standalone test, both of which are mechanical pass/fail checks that can run pre-publish without judgement. L3 does not exist here and is structurally impossible: the forwardable payload is by definition proprietary knowledge the model does not have. Beware the vendor framing — tools marketed as 'AI share optimisation' or 'virality agents' are L1 schedulers with a rewrite step; none of them can manufacture the utility that causes a send.

**prompt patterns**

1) RECIPIENT SIMULATION (the primary gate): 'Here is a draft post: <draft>. Here are six real people in my network: <role + one-line context each>. For each: would they forward this privately to one specific person? If yes, name the recipient's ROLE and write the exact message they would type above the forward. If no, say no and give the reason in one clause. Then tell me how many of the six said yes.' A draft that scores under 2/6 is not forwardable; iterate on the payload, not the wording.

2) OTHER-FOCUS AUDIT (operationalises Barasch & Berger): 'Classify each sentence of this draft as SELF-PRESENTING (its main function is to make me look competent, successful, or insightful) or RECIPIENT-USEFUL (its main function is to help the reader's reader do something). Return the ratio and rewrite the three most self-presenting sentences to be recipient-useful without removing the underlying fact.'

3) THE NAMEABLE-ROLE TIGHTENER: 'My draft addresses "<current audience descriptor>". Rewrite that descriptor five ways, each narrower than the last, until it names a role plus a constraint that makes exactly one kind of person recognise themselves — e.g. not "founders" but "solo consultants who bill hourly and have just hired their first employee". Then tell me which version makes it fastest for a READER to think of someone else who fits.'

4) STANDALONE / SLACK-PASTE TEST: 'Take this post out of its feed context. Imagine it pasted into a Slack channel with no caption and no author name. Does it still make sense and still deliver its payload? Identify every dependency on context, on my identity, or on the reader having seen my previous posts — those are the things that kill forwards.'

5) IDENTITY-SIGNAL FINDER: 'What kind of person is this post a recognisable portrait of? Write the one-sentence description someone would send with it: "this is so you because ___". If you cannot complete that sentence without generic flattery, the identity trigger is missing.'

**tool examples**

Drafting/critique: Claude (Opus 5 / Sonnet 4.x, 2026) or ChatGPT — the recipient-simulation prompt is the whole tool, model choice is secondary. Native analytics for the signal itself: Instagram Insights (sends and sends-per-reach, since 2024-2025), TikTok analytics (shares, with share-destination breakdown), LinkedIn post analytics (Saves and Sends, added late 2025 — this was the enabling change that made the tactic measurable on LinkedIn at all). Third-party: AuthoredUp and Shield Analytics for LinkedIn post-level history; Metricool or Later for cross-platform send tracking. For the dark-social portion that analytics cannot see: self-reported attribution on inbound forms ('how did you hear about this?') and UTM-tagged links you place in the forwardable asset itself — imperfect, and the only options available.

#### evidence

**evidence provenance**

PEER-REVIEWED: Barasch & Berger, Journal of Marketing Research 51(3):286-299 (2014), six studies — the narrowcasting/broadcasting mechanism. Berger, Annual Review of Psychology 76:559-581 (2025), 'What Gets Shared, and Why?' — a review that explicitly treats audience, modality, channel and device as moderators of what gets shared, i.e. the 2025 restatement of the same result. PLATFORM-OFFICIAL: Adam Mosseri's January 2025 explainer naming watch time, likes-per-reach and sends-per-reach as the three signals that matter most, with sends slightly more important for unconnected content. PLATFORM FEATURE (verifiable): LinkedIn adding Saves and Sends to post analytics, late 2025. VENDOR-WITH-PRODUCT-TO-SELL / UNSOURCED: the '3-5x likes' weighting — traced to 'industry analysis, July 2026' with no named analyst, no sample size and no methodology; the derived 'one send = 15 likes'; and the '84% of B2B sharing happens in untrackable private channels' figure, which circulates across a dozen agency blogs with no primary study attached (it echoes mid-2010s dark-social research from ad-tech vendors). VENDOR LARGE-N: AuthoredUp's 600,000+ LinkedIn posts, giving a save ≈ 5x a like and ≈ 2x a meaningful comment.

#### fit

**audience fit**

B2B: the strongest fit by a wide margin — private forwarding into Slack, Teams, WhatsApp and email forwards is the dominant B2B sharing mode, buying committees are multi-person, and 'useful to a colleague' is the native currency. Technical audiences: strong — engineers forward specifics (a config, a benchmark, a gotcha) and almost never forward opinion. B2C: works, but shifts from utility to identity signalling ('this is so you'), which is harder to engineer and easier to get wrong. EN: default assumption for all cited data. PL: the psychology transfers without question (it is attentional, not cultural-specific), and the platform signal is language-agnostic; the practical difference is that a Polish-language post has a smaller forwarding graph, so a send is worth proportionally more and easier to trace back. For a Poland-based B2B/technical creator writing in English, this is the single best-fitting tactic in the whole table.

**scales with**

Caps on NICHE DENSITY and on the specificity of your payload, not on account size — which is what makes it unusually attractive for small accounts. A post is forwarded because one reader can name one recipient; that requires the reader's network to contain people with the problem, so a dense professional niche outperforms a large diffuse following. Second cap: the supply of genuinely forwardable material. Every send-worthy post costs a real artefact (a number, a template, a decision rule, a warning), and you cannot produce those faster than you produce experience — this, not distribution, is the true ceiling. Third: corpus size does NOT help here (unlike AI citability, which compounds with volume). Team size helps only if the team has its own first-hand material. Note the objective-dependent ceiling: a small account can earn an excellent sends-per-reach RATIO while producing a trivial absolute number of sends, and the ratio is what the ranker reads for cold-start — so the tactic works at small scale in a way that broadcast-virality tactics do not.

#### risk

**failure modes**

1) SELF-PRESENTING DRAFT. The most common failure by far: the post is written to make the author look good, which by Barasch & Berger's mechanism is exactly what broadcasting produces and exactly what does not get forwarded. It will collect likes and zero sends, and the analytics will read as 'decent post'.
2) AUDIENCE TOO BROAD. 'For founders' does not let a reader retrieve a specific person; 'for solo consultants who just hired their first employee' does. Breadth feels safer and kills the trigger.
3) CONTEXT DEPENDENCE. The post references your previous post, your ongoing series, or an in-joke. Pasted into Slack it is unintelligible, so it does not get pasted.
4) NO PAYLOAD. The post is insight-shaped but contains nothing the recipient can USE. Forwarding it would make the sender look like they wasted the recipient's time — the exact reputational cost that makes sends valuable now works against you.
5) THE EXPLICIT ASK BACKFIRES. 'Send this to someone who needs it' reads as bait, risks classifier demotion, and (worse) shifts the reader back into self-focus by making the share about compliance rather than about the recipient.
6) INVISIBLE SUCCESS MISREAD AS FAILURE. The post gets forwarded 40 times into private channels, shows modest public engagement, and you conclude it flopped — then stop doing the thing that was working. This is the failure mode that actually ends most narrowcast strategies.
7) IN-NETWORK UNDERPERFORMANCE. On Instagram, likes matter slightly more for connected reach; a send-optimised post can look weak to your own followers while doing its job with strangers.

**ai slop risk**

MODERATE — lower than for hooks or CTAs, because the payload has to be real, but with two specific slop signatures. TELL 1: THE FAKE SPECIFIC. A model asked to 'make this more specific' invents plausible-sounding numbers and roles ('I worked with a 12-person SaaS team and we cut onboarding by 40%'). It reads forwardable and is fabricated; the recipient's first follow-up question exposes it. TELL 2: THE UNIVERSAL-RECIPIENT PARADOX. AI-written 'narrowcast' copy addresses an audience narrow in TONE but broad in FACT — 'if you're a founder who's ever felt overwhelmed' — which sounds targeted while excluding nobody, and therefore triggers nobody to name a recipient. TELL 3: the explicit 'Send this to the one person who needs to read it today 💌' closer, which is the single most model-default narrowcast line in existence and now reads as bait to humans and classifiers alike. CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR: if the post contains no fact that would be wrong if applied to a different company, it has no payload and will not be forwarded. A genuine narrowcast post is falsifiable — it says something specific enough to be wrong.

**human input required**

The forwardable payload itself, which is definitionally non-substitutable. At least one of: (a) a number from your own work with its context ('we ran 40 client onboardings; the drop-off was at step 3, not step 1, and here is the step 3 fix'); (b) a template, checklist, config or decision rule you actually use, reproduced in full so the forward is self-contained; (c) a first-hand warning — the specific way a named approach failed for you, dated; (d) a named client or project you can reference; (e) a judgement call with your reasoning shown, stated firmly enough that someone could forward it to settle an argument. Secondary but nearly as important: YOU must be able to name, before publishing, at least two real people in your own network who would forward this and who they would forward it to. If you cannot do that from memory, no prompt will fix it. This requirement is also precisely what platform NLP classifiers are probing for — the presence of specifics a model could not have produced.

**detectability and disclosure**

The output of this tactic is plain text, so: no C2PA, no SynthID, no cryptographic provenance either way. Third-party AI-text detection is nevertheless real and operating at population scale on these platforms (Pangram Labs classified 41% of LinkedIn long-form public posts and 30% of public comments as entirely AI-generated over Apr-Jun 2026), and LinkedIn now offers readers a 'seems like AI' flag, reported clicked ~1M times by 2026-08-25 — so detection is social as well as algorithmic. The saving grace, unique to this tactic: narrowcast content that actually works is dense with proprietary specifics, which is the strongest available negative signal for AI-generation detectors and for human readers alike. In other words, doing this tactic properly IS the anti-detection strategy. A genuinely useful, specific, first-hand post is not mistaken for slop. Disclosure triggered: none for AI-assisted framing of your own material that you edited and published under your own name (see policy_and_legal). No platform requires disclosure of AI assistance in text as of 2026-09-11.

**reversibility and blast radius**

LOW risk, the lowest in this table. You are optimising for a signal platforms actively reward, using content that is by construction non-generic — there is no known penalty, no shadowban vector, and no enforcement history. The three residual risks, in order: (1) the explicit 'send this to' ask being classified as bait, which costs post-level reach and is fully reversible by dropping the phrase; (2) CONFIDENTIALITY — this is the real blast radius. The tactic demands specifics, and specifics come from client work. A forwarded post is uncontrollable: it lands in Slack channels you will never see, is screenshot-able, and cannot be deleted once forwarded. A post containing an identifiable client detail is therefore not recallable in any meaningful sense — deleting it removes the original and not the forwards. That is a contract and a relationship risk, not an algorithm risk, and it is the one that can actually cost you something; (3) being wrong in public about a specific, since falsifiable claims are the price of forwardability — recoverable with a correction, which is itself forwardable. MITIGATION: run every specific past a confidentiality check before publishing, and assume permanence.

#### practice

**how to apply**

1. START FROM THE ARTEFACT, NOT THE TOPIC. Before writing, name the thing being forwarded: a number, a template, a decision rule, a warning, a checklist. No artefact, no post. This inverts the usual order and is the step people skip.
2. NAME THE RECIPIENT, NOT THE AUDIENCE. Write down a specific person — a real one, by name, privately — who needs this. Then write the post to THEM. The public audience is a side effect.
3. NARROW THE ROLE DESCRIPTOR UNTIL IT HURTS. Run the tightener prompt. Move from category ('founders') to role-plus-constraint ('solo consultants who just made their first hire and are still doing delivery'). Put it in the first two lines so readers self-sort and cross-sort ('that's Anna') immediately.
4. RUN THE OTHER-FOCUS AUDIT. Classify every sentence self-presenting vs recipient-useful. If self-presenting exceeds ~30%, rewrite. Keep the credibility markers, cut the applause-seeking.
5. MAKE THE PAYLOAD SELF-CONTAINED. Remove every 'as I said last week', 'link in comments', 'follow for part 2'. The post must work pasted into Slack with no caption and no author. This is the single most-skipped step and the most damaging.
6. RUN THE RECIPIENT SIMULATION. Six real roles from your network; for each, does it get forwarded and what message goes above it? Under 2/6 → the payload is weak; fix the artefact, not the wording.
7. DO NOT ASK FOR THE SEND. No 'send this to...', no 'tag someone'. The design does the work; the ask triggers bait classification and, worse, flips the reader back into self-focus.
8. FORMAT FOR THE FORWARD. Front-load the payload. Carousel or single reference card where the platform allows it (screenshot-survivable). If there is a link, put it inside the payload rather than in a comment.
9. CONFIDENTIALITY PASS. Every specific: is it mine to share, and is it genuinely anonymised? Assume permanence and uncontrolled redistribution.
10. PUBLISH AND MEASURE THE RATIO, NOT THE COUNT. Track sends-per-reach (and saves-per-reach), not total sends. Compare against your own 30-day baseline for the same format, never against another account.
11. HARVEST THE DARK SIGNAL MANUALLY. Add 'how did you hear about us?' to inbound forms, and when someone DMs you 'a colleague sent me this', log which post. Over 8-12 weeks this hand-built dataset will tell you more than the analytics.
12. ITERATE ON ARTEFACT TYPE. After ~10 posts, compare sends-per-reach by artefact class (number vs template vs warning vs decision rule). One class will dominate for your niche. Make more of that.

**checklist**

PASS/FAIL before publishing:
[ ] I can name the specific artefact being forwarded (number / template / rule / warning / checklist). Not a topic — an artefact.
[ ] I named a real person, before writing, who needs this.
[ ] The audience descriptor is a role plus a constraint, not a category, and it appears in the first two lines.
[ ] Recipient-useful sentences outnumber self-presenting ones by at least 2:1.
[ ] The post makes complete sense pasted into Slack with no caption, no author name, and no knowledge of my other posts.
[ ] Nothing essential lives in a comment, a link-in-bio, or a 'part 2'.
[ ] Recipient simulation scores at least 2 of 6 real network roles, with a plausible covering message for each.
[ ] There is NO explicit 'send this to' / 'tag someone' / 'share with your team' instruction anywhere in the post.
[ ] The post contains at least one specific that would be WRONG if applied to a different company (i.e. it is falsifiable, therefore real).
[ ] Confidentiality pass done: every client/project/person detail is mine to share and genuinely unidentifiable.
[ ] I am measuring sends-per-reach against my own baseline, and I have accepted in advance that the public metrics may look mediocre.
[ ] I am not treating '3-5x' or '84%' as facts in any plan built on this post.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

PRIMARY KPI: sends-per-reach (Instagram native; LinkedIn Sends ÷ impressions since late 2025; TikTok shares ÷ views). Always a RATIO against your own baseline for the same format — absolute send counts are meaningless across account sizes and across post types. SECONDARY: saves-per-reach (highly correlated, and on LinkedIn possibly the stronger signal — AuthoredUp puts a save at ~5x a like); out-of-network / unconnected reach share (the outcome sends are supposed to buy — if sends rise and unconnected reach does not, the mechanism is not firing on your account); DM volume of the form 'a colleague sent me this' (hand-logged; the only direct evidence of the dark path). LEADING INDICATORS, in the order they move: sends in the first 60-90 minutes → unconnected-reach share at 6-24h → profile views and inbound DMs at 24-72h → self-reported 'a friend sent me' attributions over weeks. LAGGING / BUSINESS: inbound enquiries citing a forward, and pipeline from people who never engaged publicly with anything you posted — the signature of dark-social conversion. DO NOT OPTIMISE: likes (weakest of the three Instagram signals and slightly counter-indicated for this tactic), comment count (a forwarded post often generates no public comments at all — that is success, not failure).

**measurement feasibility**

The defining problem of this tactic: the FIRST HOP is measurable, everything after it is invisible. OBSERVABLE NATIVELY: send/share counts and therefore sends-per-reach on Instagram (Insights), TikTok (analytics, with share-destination breakdown) and LinkedIn (Saves and Sends in post analytics since late 2025 — the enabling change that made this measurable on LinkedIn at all); saves; in-network vs out-of-network reach share. NOT OBSERVABLE, AT ALL: who received the forward, whether they opened it, whether they forwarded it again, and any conversion that followed — this is the entire 'dark social' problem, and the reason the unsourced 84% figure has such staying power (it names a real blind spot even though its magnitude is invented). Also not observable: dwell time, and the platform's actual weighting of a send. PRACTICAL PROXIES, ranked: (1) unconnected/out-of-network reach share as a downstream proxy for whether sends translated into distribution; (2) a hand-kept log of inbound DMs and enquiries that mention being sent the post — low-tech, slow, and the only true attribution available; (3) a 'how did you hear about this?' free-text field on any inbound form; (4) UTM-tagged links placed INSIDE the forwardable payload rather than in a comment, which survive the forward and are the only automated dark-social attribution that works at all. Accept up front that you will be optimising a first-hop ratio as a proxy for an effect you cannot see. Budget 8-12 weeks before the hand-built dataset says anything.

### Original data drops

`original-data-drops` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 5 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Original data drops. Category: copy. Definition: a post whose central payload is a number you personally produced — your own experiment, your own client results, your own audit of your own corpus, your own N-of-many analysis — published with the sample size and the method visible, so the reader can carry the number away and re-tell it. Maturity: established as a craft pattern (data journalism and 'state of X' reports predate social feeds) but APPRECIATING in 2026, because it is one of the few content inputs an LLM cannot manufacture on your behalf, and because generative search engines preferentially absorb statistics. Distinct from its sibling item 'Proof-of-work receipts': data drops are the PAYLOAD (the number itself), receipts are the EVIDENCE WRAPPER (the artifact proving the number).

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. Three separate clocks. (1) STABLE — the underlying psychology (practical utility, surprise/novelty and social currency as transmission drivers) rests on Berger & Milkman JMR 2012 and Berger's Annual Review of Psychology 76:559-581 (2025) synthesis; no reason to expect decay. (2) 12-24 MONTHS — the generative-engine advantage: the +33% 'Statistics Addition' visibility lift comes from the GEO paper (KDD 2024), whose own authors warn the methods 'may require adaptation as generative engines evolve'; engine answer-construction changed materially between 2024 and 2026. (3) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER — every platform-side multiplier (LinkedIn document-post engagement rates, dwell-time weighting, the May 2026 LinkedIn low-quality-AI algorithm change, the March 2026 'authenticity update'). Treat clock (1) as the reason to do this at all; never build a plan on clock (3) numbers.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

Mechanism in five moves. (1) INSTRUMENT: you run or already run something measurable — an ad account, a publishing cadence, a client engagement, a repo, an agent pipeline, a personal experiment ('I ran 90 days of X'). The precondition is that measurement exists BEFORE the post idea does; retrofitting a number to a desired conclusion is how this tactic turns into fraud. (2) EXTRACT ONE NUMBER: not a dashboard — one figure that survives being said out loud, ideally counter-intuitive relative to the audience's prior ('reach fell 60% while engagement rate rose'). A number that merely confirms the consensus carries no surprise and therefore no transmission value. (3) SHOW n AND METHOD IN THE POST BODY: sample size, time window, and the one-line method ('1.3M posts, H1 2026, 50k creators'). This is the load-bearing move — it is simultaneously the credibility gate for humans, the citability gate for LLMs, and the anti-slop gate for platform quality classifiers. (4) GIVE AWAY THE TRANSFERABLE RULE: the reader must be able to act on the number without your dataset. A number that is only true for you is a brag; a number that generalises is social currency. (5) MAKE THE NUMBER PORTABLE: one sentence, quotable verbatim, with your name attached to it. The unit of spread is the sentence, not the post. Optional amplification: turn the same dataset into a chart image (X/IG), an 8-10 slide document post (LinkedIn), and a long-form article (the AI-citation surface).

**ranking signal targeted**

Primary: DWELL TIME / scroll depth / 'see more' expansion — a data claim with a method line is read slowly, and dwell is the dominant LinkedIn quality signal in 2026 (see vault note 'Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026', LinkedIn section). Secondary: SAVES/BOOKMARKS (reference value; reported ~5x a like on LinkedIn, ~3x on Instagram) and RESHARE-WITH-COMMENTARY (people re-publish a statistic to claim it as their own insight). Tertiary: SUBSTANTIVE COMMENT DEPTH — numbers invite disagreement about method, which produces long replies rather than 'Great post!'. Also: DM SENDS / narrowcast forwarding ('this is the number I was telling you about'), largely invisible in analytics. On the generative-engine side, a completely different signal: SEMANTIC RELEVANCE + being the ORIGIN of an attributable statistic. IMPORTANT AND HONEST: no platform has ever stated that 'post contains a statistic' is a ranking feature. The lift is entirely indirect, through reader behaviour. Anyone claiming a direct statistics boost is inventing it.

**why it drives reach**

Causal chain: an unfamiliar, specific number creates an information gap that cannot be closed by scrolling past, which buys read-time; read-time is the primary 2026 quality signal on LinkedIn and a strong one elsewhere; a reader who finishes and finds the number useful saves it (lasting-value signal, which extends content half-life through resurfacing) or forwards it privately (a high-weight, largely unmeasurable signal). Separately, the number itself is SOCIAL CURRENCY in Berger's sense — re-telling a proprietary statistic makes the re-teller look informed, so sharing serves the sharer's self-presentation, not just yours. Because the number is yours, every retelling is an attribution event, which compounds into name recognition and, on the AI-search side, into an entity-to-statistic association that generative engines can cite. The reach mechanism therefore runs through the READER'S incentive to repeat you, not through any algorithmic preference for data.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Strictly downstream of the data. What the model must NOT do: produce, estimate, extrapolate or 'illustrate' the number. What it does well: (a) ANALYSE — given the raw export, compute cuts, find the outlier, test whether the headline number survives a different slice; (b) RETRIEVE — RAG over your own notes/past posts/transcripts to find which of your numbers you have never published and which contradict a popular belief; (c) CRITIQUE — act as a hostile methodologist: 'what is the strongest objection to this n, this window, this denominator?'; (d) VARY — 12 framings of the same number, ranked by which prior it violates; (e) PACKAGE — chart spec, slide split, alt text, and the article version for citability. Division of labour that survives audit: human owns the dataset and the claim, AI owns the arithmetic-checking and the wording.

**automation level**

L1 (AI-assisted draft) overall — and the data-generation step is irreducibly L0 (manual): a human must have run the thing that produced the number. The packaging half (chart, slide split, variant hooks, alt text) can sit at L2 (autonomous with guardrails) only if a numeric-integrity gate is enforced — every figure in the output must be traceable to a cell in the source file, and the pipeline fails closed when it is not. Nothing about this pattern is credibly L3, and any tool marketed as 'AI generates data-driven posts for you' is generating statistics, not data — which is the fraud failure mode, not automation.

**prompt patterns**

- ANALYST (grounded, no invention): 'Here is the raw export [attach CSV]. Compute: [list cuts]. Rules: (1) every number you output must be traceable to a cell or a computation over cells in this file; (2) if a figure is not derivable, write NOT_IN_DATA — do not estimate; (3) state n and the date window beside every figure; (4) flag any cut where n < 30 as underpowered.'
- SURPRISE RANKER: 'Below are 14 findings from my dataset. My audience is [ICP] and their current belief about [topic] is [X]. Rank these by how strongly each VIOLATES that belief, not by how impressive it is. For the top 3, name the specific prior each one breaks and the objection a skeptic raises first.'
- HOSTILE METHODOLOGIST: 'Here is my claim and my method: [claim + n + window + denominator]. You are a peer reviewer who wants to reject this. List the 5 strongest methodological objections in descending order, and for each one say what I would have to publish alongside the post to neutralise it.'
- PORTABLE-SENTENCE FORGE: 'Compress this finding into a single sentence under 20 words that contains the number, the sample size, and the subject, and that stays true when quoted with no surrounding context. Give 8 versions. Reject any version where removing the context makes the sentence overstate the finding.'
- TRANSFERABLE-RULE EXTRACTOR: 'Given this finding from my data, write the rule a reader who does NOT have my dataset can apply tomorrow. If the finding does not generalise beyond my situation, say so explicitly instead of writing a rule.'
- CITABILITY PASS (GEO-informed): 'Rewrite this post as a self-contained answer to the question a practitioner would type into ChatGPT. Keep the statistic, the sample size, the date, and the method in the SAME sentence so the claim survives extraction. Add the source attribution inline, not as a footnote.'

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

SPLIT — do not average these. (a) The transmission psychology (practical utility, surprise, social currency drive sharing): MODERATE-TO-STRONG, peer-reviewed and synthesised. (b) The generative-engine citation lift from adding statistics: MODERATE — one peer-reviewed KDD 2024 paper with a 10,000-query benchmark, single study, 2023-24 engine behaviour. (c) The specific social-platform claim 'posts containing original data get more reach': UNVERIFIED — no platform-official or independent large-N test isolates 'contains original statistic' as a variable; the 2026 marketing-blog figures circulating on this are vendor-sourced and mutually citing. (d) The 'original research earns links' finding: MODERATE, large-N but vendor-produced (BuzzSumo/Backlinko) and about web content, not feed posts.

**evidence provenance**

Peer-reviewed: Berger & Milkman (Journal of Marketing Research, 2012); Berger (Annual Review of Psychology, 2025); Aggarwal et al., GEO (KDD 2024, arXiv 2311.09735). Independent large-N but vendor-produced and self-published: van der Blom Algorithm Insights 2026 (1.3M posts / 50k creators — the most-cited independent LinkedIn dataset, but not peer-reviewed and sold as consulting positioning); Semrush AI-citation study (325k prompts / 89k LinkedIn URLs, Jan-Feb 2026); BuzzSumo x Backlinko (912M posts) and BuzzSumo x Majestic (1M posts). Vendor-with-product-to-sell: every 2026 'carousel/data post gets X% more engagement' blog, including several that appear to be AI-generated and cite each other in a loop. Single-creator anecdote: essentially all 'I posted my numbers and got 500k impressions' claims. NOTE the structural irony worth stating in the note itself: the evidence base for 'publish your own data' is itself dominated by vendors publishing their own data.

**effect size and n**

- Berger & Milkman 2012: ~7,000 New York Times articles over ~3 months; practical utility, surprise and interest each positively and independently predict appearance on the most-emailed list, controlling for external attention drivers. Effect reported as coefficients on a sharing outcome, not as a percentage lift usable for social posts.
- GEO (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024; GEO-Bench, 10,000 queries / 8,000 train / 1,000 val / 1,000 test across 25 domains, 9 source datasets): 'Statistics Addition' +33% Position-Adjusted Word Count; 'Cite Sources' +28%; 'Quotation Addition' +41%; 'Keyword Stuffing' -9%. On Perplexity.ai specifically, Statistics Addition reached +37% on Subjective Impression. Largest gains for Statistics Addition in Law & Government, Debate and Opinion domains.
- BuzzSumo x Backlinko, 912M blog posts: 94% of all content earns zero external backlinks; 75% of all social shares come from ~1.3% of articles (power-law, not a normal distribution — the single most important number for expectation-setting here).
- Semrush, Jan-Feb 2026, 325,000 prompts / 89,000 cited LinkedIn URLs: LinkedIn cited in ~11% of responses on average (14.3% ChatGPT Search, 13.5% Google AI Mode), #2 domain behind Reddit; ~95% of cited LinkedIn posts were ORIGINAL rather than reshares; ~59% of cited LinkedIn content came from individual members rather than company pages; median cited post carried only 15-25 reactions.
- van der Blom Algorithm Insights 2026 (1.3M posts, 50k creators, H1 2026): document/PDF posts ~6.60% engagement rate, highest of any LinkedIn format; one external link in the body cuts median reach ~18.8%; replying to comments within 30 minutes associated with 64% more total comments and 2.3x views.
- NO EFFECT SIZE FOUND for the direct claim of interest: there is no credible measurement of how much reach a post gains specifically because it contains an original, first-party statistic. Anyone quoting one is quoting a vendor blog.

**conflicting evidence**

- SHARES vs LINKS DIVERGE: BuzzSumo/Majestic's analysis of 1M posts found essentially no correlation between social shares and backlinks — original research and reference content earn LINKS reliably but not necessarily SHARES, while listicles and quizzes earn shares but not links. So 'publish original data' is a strong authority/citation play and only a conditional virality play. Do not let the authority evidence stand in for virality evidence.
- CITABILITY IS NOT VIRALITY: Semrush's 2026 study found the median AI-cited LinkedIn post carried just 15-25 reactions and at most one comment, and that sub-500-follower creators are cited comparably to large accounts. The same post can be a citation success and an engagement failure. These are two different objective functions and this item scores well on one of them.
- PREDICTABILITY CEILING: Goel, Anderson, Hofman & Watts (Management Science, 2015) show structural virality is a continuum with no bimodal 'viral / not viral' split and that classic tipping-point theory is unsupported — combined with the 1.3%-of-articles-get-75%-of-shares power law, the honest expectation for any single data drop is 'no spread', regardless of quality.
- AI-vs-HUMAN IS UNRESOLVED, and it cuts both ways here: UMinn/GPT-4 work finds LLM-written posts can outperform human ones, while a peer-reviewed within-subjects Instagram field experiment (24 alternating posts) found human posts won on likes (42.6 vs 39.6), comments (5.3 vs 2.3) and ER (6.73% vs 5.96%); a vendor study of 10,024 posts claims +31% for AI-assisted. This item's premise — that the human-supplied number is what carries the post — is consistent with the human-wins result and in tension with the AI-wins result. Leave it unresolved.
- 'MORE DATA = MORE AUTHORITY' vs FEED FATIGUE: the 2026 feed is saturated with unverifiable statistics, much of it AI-generated, which is a reason audiences increasingly discount numbers without a visible method — the same trend that makes n-and-method disclosure valuable also makes bare statistics cheaper than they were in 2022. No measurement of this discount rate was found.
- CADENCE: Buffer's 2M+ post analysis reports ~3x engagements per post at 11+/week, while most 2026 LinkedIn guidance says 2-4/week maximises per-post reach. Since a genuine data drop costs hours, this item is structurally incompatible with the high-cadence branch of that conflict; that is a constraint, not a refutation.
- **correction_2026_09_11_instagram_study_is_a_null_result**: CORRECTION (2026-09-11, verified against the full PDF): this file quotes raw means from Flesheriu & Fron (2025), Oeconomica Jadertina 2/2025, DOI 10.15291/oec.4845 (likes 42.58 vs 39.58, comments 5.33 vs 2.33, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%). The means are accurate but NONE of the differences is statistically significant: Mann-Whitney U gives likes p=.91, comments p=.07, shares p=.17, saves p=.79, reach p=.89, impressions p=.51, ER p=.64. The paper states 'H1 was not supported' and concludes EQUIVALENCE, not human superiority. Dropping one launch-day outlier flips ER in the AI direction (5.95% vs 5.79%); readers significantly PREFERRED the AI-written captions (U=8.0, p=.045); and 7 of the 12 top-performing posts were AI. Scope limits that further weaken it as evidence about AI TEXT: a single account with 770 followers, 24 alternating posts, a culinary niche, and AI-generated IMAGERY bundled with the caption - the authors attribute 64% of engagement to the visual. Do not cite this study as showing that human-written posts outperform AI-written posts.
