#### fit

**platform and format fit**

BEST: LinkedIn — dwell-time-dominant ranking, professional audience that argues about method, and the #2 AI-citation domain; deliver as a text post (150-300 words, number in the first line before the 'see more' fold) or an 8-10 slide PDF document post, with the long-form article version as the durable citation surface. STRONG: X/Twitter — a single chart image plus a quotable sentence; the platform's 2026 ranker weights dwell and video-watch, and a chart earns inspection time. STRONG: a newsletter — algorithm-independent and the most citable artifact you own. CONDITIONAL: Reddit — the most demanding and most rewarding venue for real data, but only as a genuine contribution in the relevant subreddit with the method exposed and zero self-promotion; promotional framing gets removed. Instagram: workable as a carousel with one chart per slide, but the audience is weaker for B2B numbers. BACKFIRES: TikTok and Shorts — a statistic is not a retention device; the format rewards demonstration, so show the experiment, do not narrate the table. Threads/Facebook: weak fit, conversational surfaces with low tolerance for methodology. GENERAL BACKFIRE CONDITION: anywhere the audience cannot evaluate the denominator, a data drop reads as a brag. Cross-reference the vault note above rather than re-deriving per-platform mechanics.

**audience fit**

B2B >> B2C. Technical and practitioner audiences >> general. Works best where the reader has a decision the number changes — pricing, cadence, tool choice, hiring. EN vs PL: English is where the citation upside lives (generative engines index it far more densely and the audience is larger), Polish is where the competitive density is lower and a first-party number stands out more against a thinner local benchmark supply — the PL market has fewer people publishing their own numbers, so a modest dataset buys disproportionate local authority. For a Poland/EU-based creator the defensible split is: publish the number in EN for citation and reach, and a PL adaptation that names the local context, rather than a straight translation.

**scales with**

Capped by MEASURABLE ACTIVITY VOLUME, not by follower count. If you do not run enough instrumented things, you run out of numbers in a quarter — this is the binding constraint and it is why most people abandon the tactic. Secondary caps: size of your existing corpus (an agent can only surface unpublished numbers that exist); client confidentiality (the best numbers are often the least publishable); and analytical skill (a wrong cut is worse than no post). Note the divergent ceilings: for AI CITATION there is effectively no account-size floor (Semrush found sub-500-follower creators cited comparably), but for VIRALITY the usual network-position ceiling applies — the same data drop from a 50k-follower account and a 500-follower account produce very different distributions. Team size helps at the packaging stage only; it cannot manufacture the input.

**decay and saturation**

The TACTIC does not saturate the way hook templates did, because its input is scarce by construction — you cannot copy someone else's proprietary number and still be doing the tactic. Estimated shelf life 3+ years. What DOES decay: (1) each individual dataset — a 2026 benchmark is stale by 2027, so plan a refresh cadence rather than a one-off; (2) the bare-statistic format — as AI-generated pseudo-statistics flood feeds, an unsourced number is worth progressively less, which shifts value from the number to the METHOD DISCLOSURE and to the receipts; (3) the generative-engine edge — the GEO paper's own caveat plus two years of engine drift make the +33% figure directionally useful and numerically stale. Practical read: the durable half of this tactic is 'show your method', and that half is appreciating.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- n too small for the claim — 'I tested 12 posts' presented as a finding; the first skeptical comment names the sample size and the thread becomes about your rigour rather than your result.
- The number confirms consensus — no surprise, no transmission; it reads as a slide from a pitch deck.
- No transferable rule — the finding is true only inside your business, so the reader has nothing to carry away and no reason to re-tell it.
- Vanity denominator — impressions, followers, 'reached 2M people'. Audiences in 2026 explicitly discount reach metrics; revenue, time, error rate and conversion survive scrutiny, reach does not.
- Method hidden to make the number look bigger — works once, then someone reproduces it and the correction outlives the post.
- Cherry-picked window — the same dataset with a different start date says the opposite; if you cannot show the window, you do not have a finding.
- Publishing a client's number without permission — kills the relationship and the tactic simultaneously.
- Running out of data and back-filling with model-estimated figures. This is the terminal failure mode and it converts the tactic into its own opposite.
- Treating one data drop as a campaign — the power law (1.3% of articles get 75% of shares) means the expected outcome of any single drop is nothing; the tactic only pays across a series.

**ai slop risk**

HIGH on one specific axis and LOW on the rest. The dangerous axis is FABRICATED STATISTICS: models fluently produce plausible percentages with no source because they pattern-match the shape of a statistic, and this is one of the best-documented hallucination patterns in marketing copy. The tells, in order of reliability: (1) a suspiciously clean number (exactly 40%, 3x, 10x) with no n; (2) no date window; (3) attribution to 'a recent study' or 'research shows' with no nameable author or institution; (4) several statistics in one post that all point the same direction — real data is messier and usually contains one inconvenient figure; (5) a statistic that is quotable but not checkable. On the prose axis the slop risk is genuinely low: a post built around a number you actually measured is close to the definition of what LinkedIn's 2026 quality scoring is probing for — original insight rather than perspective-free templated text. MITIGATION: a fail-closed numeric-integrity gate (every figure traceable to a source cell, model emits NOT_IN_DATA rather than an estimate) and a human read of every figure before publishing. Never let a model write the number.

**human input required**

NON-SUBSTITUTABLE, and unusually clean for this table: the human must OWN THE DATASET. Specifically — (a) the human ran or has legitimate access to the thing measured; (b) the human can produce the raw source on request; (c) the human made the judgement call about which cut is the honest one (the choice of denominator and window is editorial, not computational); (d) the human accepts accountability for the claim, including publishing a correction if it is wrong. Everything else in the workflow is substitutable by a model. This is the checkable gate: if you cannot answer 'where did this number come from, and can you show me?', the post is not a data drop and should not be published as one.

**detectability and disclosure**

TEXT: AI-assisted drafting of the prose around your own number is not reliably machine-detectable, and public AI-text detectors have material false-positive rates — so detection is not the live risk. The live risk is the inverse: a FABRICATED number is checkable by anyone, permanently, and by AI search itself, which is now a fact-checking surface. CHARTS AND IMAGES: a chart rendered by code (Datawrapper, Flourish, matplotlib) carries no synthetic-content provenance and triggers no labelling; a chart or background produced by an image model may carry C2PA Content Credentials or SynthID, which platforms read — Meta surfaces 'AI Info' from C2PA, TikTok joined the C2PA steering committee (2026-07-27) and LinkedIn is among the few platforms that preserve credential chains through upload, so an AI-generated visual can be auto-labelled regardless of your intent. PRACTICAL DISCLOSURE POSTURE: disclose the DATA PROVENANCE loudly (n, window, method, source) and the AI ASSISTANCE quietly and only where it materially shaped the output — note the disclosure paradox recorded elsewhere in this research (disclosure erodes perceived authenticity, but process-level disclosure mitigates that). For this item the asymmetry is favourable: method disclosure BUILDS trust, so lead with it.

**policy and legal**

Assume a Poland/EU-based creator. (1) EU AI ACT ART. 50 — applicable since 2026-08-02, with a grace period to 2026-12-02 for pre-existing systems; disclosure duties attach to deepfakes and to AI-generated TEXT published on matters of public interest, with an exemption where the text underwent human editorial review and a person or organisation holds editorial responsibility. A data drop written over your own dataset with human verification of every figure sits squarely inside that exemption; an AI-generated chart of a person or an AI avatar presenting the data does not. Fines up to EUR 15M or 3% of worldwide turnover. (2) SUBSTANTIATION — you are liable for the truth of a claim regardless of who or what drafted it; the FTC restated this in 2026 and EU/Polish unfair-commercial-practices law reaches misleading business claims the same way. If the number supports a commercial claim about your own service, you need the underlying data retained and producible. (3) GDPR — if the dataset concerns identifiable people (clients, users, employees), publish only aggregates, check re-identification risk in small cells (an n of 8 in a named niche is identifiable), and confirm the lawful basis; 'it is my data' is not one. (4) CONTRACT — NDAs and client agreements routinely forbid publishing performance figures even anonymised; get written permission or genericise beyond recognition. (5) Platform ToS adds little here beyond the general prohibition on deceptive content.

**reversibility and blast radius**

Platform-side: LOW risk — nothing about publishing your own numbers triggers shadowban, comment restriction or suspension. Reputational: HIGH and asymmetric — a wrong number is screenshot-able, permanently quotable, and now also ingestible by AI search, so a debunked statistic can outlive the correction and keep being cited back at you. A confidentiality breach is worse and irreversible: it costs the client relationship and, potentially, a contractual claim. Recovery protocol: correct in a new top-level post (not a buried edit), state what was wrong and why, publish the corrected method — done openly this is usually net-positive for credibility, which is the one genuine upside of the blast radius here. Practical rule: the recoverable mistakes are analytical, the unrecoverable ones are ethical.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- STEP 0 — BUILD THE SUPPLY (one-off, ~2h): list everything you already measure that nobody has published — ad account, publishing log, client engagements, agent-pipeline traces, repo history, personal experiments. This inventory is the constraint on the whole tactic; if the list is short, fix that before writing anything.
- STEP 1 — PICK ONE QUESTION (15 min): a question your ICP argues about and your data can actually answer. Write the question down before looking at the data, so you cannot retrofit the conclusion.
- STEP 2 — RUN THE ANALYSIS WITH THE INTEGRITY GATE (45-120 min): feed the raw export to the ANALYST prompt with the NOT_IN_DATA rule. Compute the cut, then compute the two cuts that would most plausibly overturn it.
- STEP 3 — STRESS-TEST (20 min): run the HOSTILE METHODOLOGIST prompt. If the top objection is fatal, kill the post — this is the step that protects the whole tactic, and killing posts here is a success, not a failure.
- STEP 4 — CHOOSE THE SURPRISE (15 min): run the SURPRISE RANKER over the findings. Keep exactly one headline number. A second number in the hook halves the memorability of both.
- STEP 5 — FORGE THE PORTABLE SENTENCE (15 min): the quotable line that contains number + n + subject and stays true out of context. This sentence is the actual product; the post is packaging.
- STEP 6 — WRITE THE POST (30 min): line 1 = the number with its n, before the 'see more' fold. Lines 2-3 = the method in one breath. Middle = what surprised you and the two cuts that could have overturned it. End = the transferable rule. Close with a specific methodological question, not 'thoughts?'. Keep 150-300 words for the feed version; no external link in the body (~-18.8% median reach on LinkedIn per van der Blom 2026) — put it in a comment or the profile.
- STEP 7 — ATTACH THE RECEIPT (20 min): one chart image or one screenshot of the source, redacted. See the sibling item 'Proof-of-work receipts'.
- STEP 8 — VERIFY EVERY FIGURE AGAINST THE SOURCE (10 min, non-negotiable): read the published draft with the source file open. Any figure you cannot point to gets cut.
- STEP 9 — PUBLISH THE DURABLE VERSION (60 min, same week): a LinkedIn article or newsletter issue with the full method, the table, and the date. This is the AI-citation surface; the feed post is the promotion for it.
- STEP 10 — HARVEST (ongoing, 2 weeks): answer methodological comments with detail, log which objections recurred, and note who asked to reuse the number. Re-run and re-publish the same benchmark on a fixed cadence so the dataset becomes a recurring franchise rather than a one-off.

**checklist**

- PASS/FAIL — Can I produce the raw source for every figure in this post right now? (If no: do not publish.)
- PASS/FAIL — Are n, the date window and the denominator stated in the post itself, not just implied?
- PASS/FAIL — Does the headline number violate a belief my audience actually holds? (If it confirms consensus: kill or reframe.)
- PASS/FAIL — Did I run the hostile-methodologist pass, and is the strongest objection survivable in a comment?
- PASS/FAIL — Is there a transferable rule a reader without my data can apply tomorrow?
- PASS/FAIL — Is the headline metric a real outcome (revenue, time, error rate, conversion) rather than a vanity metric (impressions, followers, reach)?
- PASS/FAIL — Does the quotable sentence stay TRUE when quoted with zero surrounding context?
- PASS/FAIL — Confidentiality: do I have the right to publish this, and are small cells safe from re-identification?
- PASS/FAIL — Did a human (me) read every number against the source after the model touched the draft?
- PASS/FAIL — Is there exactly one headline number, not three?
- PASS/FAIL — No external link in the post body; long-form/citable version exists or is scheduled.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- LEADING (first 60-90 min): number of comments that engage with the METHOD rather than the conclusion — the highest-quality early signal that the post will travel, because methodological comments are long and long comments are dwell.
- LEADING: 'see more' expansion / read-through proxy — whether the number in line 1 bought the click.
- PRIMARY: saves/bookmarks — the reference-value signal that extends half-life via resurfacing.
- PRIMARY: reshares WITH commentary (a bare repost is worth much less; a reshare where someone re-states your number in their own words is the transmission event you are engineering).
- PRIMARY: unprompted re-quotation — other people using your number, with or without attribution, in their own posts. This is the real objective and it lags by weeks.
- SECONDARY: inbound DMs and 'can I cite this?' requests — the narrowcast signal, invisible in analytics but countable in your inbox.
- SECONDARY (different objective function): AI-citation appearances — does ChatGPT/Perplexity/Google AI Mode surface your figure when asked the underlying question?
- DELIBERATELY DEMOTED: impressions and likes. Given the power law, a single post's impression count carries almost no information about whether the tactic is working.
- PORTFOLIO-LEVEL: across 10+ drops, the share that produced any re-quotation at all. Judge the tactic here, never on one post.

**ai search citability**

HIGHEST of any item in the copy category — this is arguably the tactic's strongest justification in 2026, stronger than its virality case. Three converging reasons: (1) GEO (KDD 2024) measured 'Statistics Addition' at +33% visibility in generative-engine responses (+37% subjective impression on Perplexity) and 'Cite Sources' at +28%, with statistics gaining most in Debate/Opinion/Law domains — i.e. exactly the argumentative terrain a benchmark post occupies; (2) being the ORIGIN of a statistic makes you the attributable node an engine must name, rather than one of many pages restating someone else's figure; (3) Semrush's 2026 data shows ~95% of cited LinkedIn posts are original rather than reshares, ~59% of cited LinkedIn content comes from individual members, and there is effectively no follower floor for citation. Practical consequence: publish the durable long-form version (article/newsletter) with the number, n, date and method IN THE SAME SENTENCE so the claim survives extraction, and accept that the citation payoff arrives on a different timescale — and against a different metric — from the feed payoff.

#### omitted as uncertain

- cost and time to execute
- measurement feasibility
- prompt artifact link
- tool examples
- worked example

### Personal narrative arcs

`personal-narrative-arcs` · automation L1 · evidence STRONG · 6 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Personal narrative arcs
- **category**: copy
- **definition**: Micro-storytelling in a feed post: a compressed arc - situation, complication, turn, consequence - built from something that actually happened to the author, used as the carrier for the point rather than as decoration around it.
- **maturity**: established, and the most durable item in the copy category - but its dominant executions (the vulnerability confession, the humblebrag arc) are saturated and now carry a credibility cost.
- **one line**: The one layer a model cannot generate, because it requires having been there - and consequently the layer platform classifiers are effectively hunting for.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **the mechanism named**: Narrative transportation: the reader is absorbed into the story world, which reduces counter-arguing and raises affective involvement, and persuasion follows as a side effect of absorption rather than as a response to argument. Green and Appel's 2024 review is the current authoritative summary; van Laer et al.'s 2014 Journal of Consumer Research meta-analysis is the quantitative anchor.
- **the minimum viable arc**: Four beats, and a feed post has room for exactly four. (1) SITUATION - a specific, dated, located starting state ('Two years ago we were shipping onboarding in 14 days'). (2) COMPLICATION - the thing that went wrong, named concretely, with a cost. (3) TURN - the decision or realisation, including what you almost did instead. (4) CONSEQUENCE - what changed, measured. The generalisable point comes after beat 4, in one line, not before beat 1.
- **why the order matters**: Leading with the lesson converts the story into an illustration and kills transportation - the reader now knows the destination and evaluates rather than travels. This is the single most common structural error, and it is exactly what LLMs do by default, because they are trained to be helpful and front-load conclusions.
- **specificity is the transport mechanism**: Transportation runs on concrete detail: the named tool, the exact figure, the time of day, the thing someone actually said. Generic detail ('a client', 'a while back', 'a big number') produces no mental imagery and therefore no transportation. This is also the property that makes the arc unfakeable - a model can invent a detail but cannot invent YOUR detail, and invented specifics are brittle under follow-up questions in the comments.
- **the moderators that matter**: van Laer et al.'s 2019 meta-analysis (64 articles, 138 effect sizes) found the transportation effect is stronger when the story is in a commercial rather than non-commercial domain, when it is USER-generated rather than professionally produced, and when it is received by one story-receiver at a time. All three describe a feed post read alone on a phone, which is a genuinely favourable finding for this tactic.
- **arc types that work in feed length**:
  - The reversed decision - 'we built X, then killed it, here is what the six months taught us'
  - The expensive mistake - a named cost, owned, with the mechanism explained
  - The client moment - one scene, one quote, one constraint (anonymise the client, keep the constraint exact)
  - The changed mind - what you publicly believed, what changed it, what you believe now
  - The boring middle - the unglamorous work between the announcement and the result, which is the arc least colonised by AI because it requires having done the work
- **arc types that are burnt**: The rejection montage, the airport/taxi-driver epiphany, the fired-then-founded arc, the 'I almost quit' confession that resolves into a product pitch, and any story whose complication is trivial relative to its claimed insight.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **primary**: Dwell time and completion. A story is the only text structure that makes stopping mid-way feel costly to the reader, which is precisely the behaviour dwell-based rankers reward. LinkedIn confirms dwell as a ranking signal; TikTok's watch-time-per-impression is the video equivalent.
- **secondary**:
  - Reply depth and comment substance - stories produce first-person responses ('the same thing happened to us') rather than 'Great post!', and substantive multi-sentence comments are among the heaviest 2026 LinkedIn signals
  - Sends / DM shares - a specific story about a specific situation gets forwarded to the one person it applies to, which is the highest-intent distribution signal on Meta surfaces and TikTok
  - Saves - lower than for reference content; stories are shared more than they are saved
- **the signal it uniquely targets**: The human authenticity classifier. This is not a ranking signal in the classical sense but it now gates distribution: LinkedIn suppresses content exhibiting recycled structure and absent first-hand perspective, and a genuine narrative arc is the cheapest way to be unambiguously on the right side of that line.
- **honest caveat**: None of this is a measured coefficient. The chain story -> transportation -> dwell -> reach is inferred from separate literatures that have never been joined on a live feed.

**why it drives reach**

Three compounding effects. (1) Mechanically: rankers now score quality-per-impression with dwell and completion as the dominant inputs, and narrative is the oldest known technology for making someone finish something. (2) Socially: a specific story generates specific replies, and reply depth is weighted far above reactions on every 2026 surface - a reader who recognises their own situation in yours writes three sentences, not an emoji. (3) Competitively, and this is the part that is new in 2026: with roughly four in five sampled LinkedIn long-form posts classified as likely-AI, first-hand narrative has become scarce. The tactic's value comes less from stories being intrinsically more persuasive - the best meta-analytic evidence is notably lukewarm on that - and more from stories being the only content type whose supply cannot be increased by buying more tokens. Its edge is a supply constraint, not a psychological one, and that is a more honest and more durable reason to use it.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **does well**:
  - Interviewing you. The single highest-value use: 'Ask me one question at a time about this incident until you have the scene, the stakes, the turn and what I almost did instead. Do not write anything yet.' This extracts detail you would not have volunteered.
  - Structuring raw recall into the four beats without adding facts.
  - Cutting. First drafts of personal stories are 3x too long and the excess is almost always in the setup.
  - Finding the beat that is missing - usually the complication's real cost, which people instinctively soften.
  - Flagging where you slipped from specific to generic ('a client' where you meant something nameable).
  - Generating the closing generalisation, which is the one part of the post that is genuinely commodity writing.
- **does badly or must not do**:
  - Inventing or embellishing detail. This is not a quality problem, it is a fabrication problem: a made-up specific is a false statement published under your name, and the comments are where it gets tested.
  - Smoothing the voice. The texture that makes a story land - the odd word choice, the unresolved bit, the sentence that runs long because you were annoyed - is exactly what a polish pass removes.
  - Choosing the story. Judging which incident is worth telling requires knowing your audience and your own reputation.
- **the rule**: The model may reorganise, question and cut. It may not add a single fact. That is the whole governance model for this tactic.

**automation level**

L1 AI-assisted draft, with a hard floor: the raw material must be human-supplied and unembellished. This is the one tactic in the set where higher automation is not merely lower-quality but actively harmful - an L2 loop generating plausible personal anecdotes is a fabrication engine, and the failure is reputational rather than statistical. Correct configuration is inverted from the usual: human generates, AI edits. Note that tools marketed as producing 'authentic personal stories' from a topic prompt are producing fiction; the honest ones are interview tools.

**prompt patterns**

- **pattern 1 the interview**: 'I want to write about [incident]. Ask me one question at a time until you have: the scene (when, where, who), the stakes (what it cost or risked), the complication (what went wrong, specifically), the turn (the decision, and what I almost did instead), and the consequence (measured). Do not write the post. Do not suggest answers. Stop when you have all five.' The one-question-at-a-time constraint is what makes this work - batched questions get batched, shallow answers.
- **pattern 2 fact locked draft**: 'Here are my raw answers. Write the post using ONLY facts present in my answers. If a sentence would need a detail I did not give you, write [MISSING: what you need] instead of inventing it. Four beats. The lesson goes last, in one line.' The [MISSING] convention turns hallucination into a visible to-do.
- **pattern 3 specificity audit**: 'Mark every noun phrase in this draft as SPECIFIC (a reader could picture or verify it) or GENERIC. For each GENERIC, ask me the question that would make it specific.' Runs the transportation mechanism directly - generic nouns are exactly where transportation fails.
- **pattern 4 lesson placement**: 'Find every sentence that states the general lesson. Tell me where each one sits in the post. Move them all to the end and show me the result.' Front-loaded lessons are the default LLM failure mode and this prompt fixes it mechanically.
- **pattern 5 the cringe check**: 'Read this as a skeptical senior person in my field who dislikes LinkedIn performance. Where does it read as performed rather than told? Where am I claiming more insight than the incident supports? Where would you stop reading out of embarrassment?' The third question is the one that matters - performative vulnerability is a documented credibility risk, not just a taste issue.
- **pattern 6 the stakes test**: 'What did this actually cost me? If the answer in the post is vague or zero, say so.' A story with no real cost is an anecdote, and readers can tell.
- **anti pattern**: 'Write a personal story about [topic] for LinkedIn.' This instructs the model to fabricate. There is no prompt-engineering fix; the input is wrong.

**tool examples**

- Claude / GPT-class models used strictly as interviewer and editor; ~$20/mo. The interview mode is the load-bearing feature, not the writing mode.
- Voice capture - any dictation tool, or a phone voice memo transcribed. Speaking a story produces better raw material than typing one, because you keep the detail you would edit out while typing.
- This Obsidian vault - dated notes as the first-hand corpus; the brain-qa skill to retrieve what actually happened rather than what you remember happening.
- AuthoredUp (~$12.46-19.99/mo) - for the fold, since the complication has to be visible above the ~140-character mobile cut for the story to be opened at all.
- MagicPost - source of the post-type engagement medians quoted below; sells a LinkedIn tool.
- Explicitly NOT recommended: any tool that generates 'personal stories' from a topic. Those produce fabricated anecdotes under your name.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

Genuinely mixed, and the mix is the interesting part. (a) That narrative transportation exists and correlates with persuasion outcomes: strong - multiple peer-reviewed meta-analyses. (b) That narrative content is MORE persuasive than equivalent non-narrative content: weak and actively contested - the most recent meta-analysis found no statistically significant difference. (c) That transportation can be reliably manipulated by a writer on demand: weak - Green and Appel report that manipulation attempts produce inconsistent results with no method that reliably works. (d) That personal-story posts outperform advice posts on LinkedIn engagement: moderate-but-correlational, one large-N vendor corpus. (e) That first-hand perspective protects against AI-slop suppression: moderate - platform-stated intent, not measured effect.

**evidence provenance**

- **peer reviewed**: van Laer, de Ruyter, Visconti and Wetzels (2014), Journal of Consumer Research 40(5):797-817 - the extended transportation-imagery model meta-analysis. van Laer, Feiereisen and Visconti (2019), Journal of Business Research - 64 articles, 138 effect sizes, digital-era moderators. Rahmani, Montano, Groves and Green (2025), Behavioural Public Policy - 77 experiments, 57 articles, 24,380 respondents, 377 findings. Green and Appel (2024), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology - the current review, including the manipulation-inconsistency finding. Orgad (2025), New Media and Society - 'Posting vulnerability on LinkedIn'. Plus work on conditional effects of LinkedIn vulnerability disclosure (authentic vs performative perception) and on vulnerability disclosure and perceived authenticity.
- **platform official**: LinkedIn's stated slop-detection target (recycled structure, restated ideas, no first-hand perspective) and the 2026-07-30 product changes, via the CPO's own announcement as reported by TechCrunch, Fortune and Social Media Today.
- **independent large n**: None joining story structure to feed distribution. The academic meta-analyses are lab and field experiments on persuasion outcomes, not on algorithmic reach.
- **vendor with product to sell**: MagicPost's post-type engagement medians (1,141,932-post corpus, sells a LinkedIn tool); Originality.ai's AI-prevalence and engagement comparisons (sells the detector).
- **the important provenance point**: The strongest evidence for this tactic is psychological and the strongest evidence against its uniqueness is also psychological, from the same literature. The marketing evidence sits in between and is correlational. Anyone presenting 'storytelling works' as settled science is over-reading a body of work that has become more cautious over time, not less.

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **works best**:
  - **LinkedIn**: The strongest fit anywhere. Long character budget, dwell-ranked, comment-depth weighted, and an audience whose professional identity makes them respond to work stories with work stories. The post-type data puts lived-experience posts at 2-2.5x the platform median.
  - **X / Threads / Bluesky**: As threads, not single posts. A 4-8 post thread is a natural arc container and threads generate roughly 3x the replies of standalone posts on Bluesky.
  - **TikTok / Reels**: Talking-head micro-story is one of the highest-completion formats there is, because an unresolved complication is the strongest completion driver available in 15-40 seconds.
  - **Substack Notes / newsletters**: Room for a full arc and an audience that opted in to your voice specifically.
  - **Reddit**: Works, but only as genuine account-of-experience with no promotional turn. The moment the arc resolves into a pitch it is downvoted.
- **backfires**:
  - **Instagram feed for B2B**: The image carries the post; a text arc in the caption is mostly unread.
  - **Corporate or brand accounts**: A 'we' narrative has no narrator and produces no transportation. This tactic requires a named individual.
  - **Regulated contexts**: Client stories in legal, medical or financial work carry confidentiality exposure that usually outweighs the reach.
  - **Pitch-adjacent posts**: An arc that resolves into a product CTA converts the story retrospectively into an ad and costs more credibility than the reach is worth.
  - **Bluesky's follow-graph surface**: No ranking at all there, and no dwell optimisation - the arc still reads well but earns no algorithmic return.
- **format note**: The complication must be visible above the fold (~140 chars mobile on LinkedIn). A story whose setup consumes the entire pre-fold budget never gets opened, which is the most common way a good story dies.

**scales with**

- **what it needs**: A supply of lived experience. This is a hard, non-purchasable constraint and it is the entire story of this tactic's economics.
- **what caps it**: Your own rate of doing things worth telling. Nobody has more than a few genuinely good stories per quarter, and the pressure to post weekly is what drives people to inflate trivial incidents into arcs - which is the main failure mode.
- **account size**: Near-neutral for engagement rate, which is why it suits small accounts: dwell and comment depth are normalized per impression, so a small engaged network reading a real story out-signals a large network skimming a generic one.
- **corpus size**: Strongly positive and under-exploited. A dated archive of what you actually did - notes, commits, invoices, a vault like this one - converts vague recall into the specific detail transportation requires. The bottleneck is usually retrieval, not experience.
- **team size**: Scales badly. The arc requires a named narrator; ghostwritten stories are the version readers detect most reliably, because the ghostwriter does not know which detail is the strange one.
- **objective dependence**: Best-in-class for trust, inbound and comment depth. Middling for raw reach (an inspirational generic post can out-reach it). Poor for saves relative to reference content.

**decay and saturation**

- **the mechanism**: Does not decay. Narrative transportation is a property of human cognition, not of a ranking system.
- **specific arc shapes**: 12-24 months. The rejection montage, the airport epiphany and the fired-then-founded arc are already burnt on LinkedIn and now read as parody.
- **the vulnerability register**: Actively decaying and arguably past peak. Enough performed vulnerability has been published that readers now apply a performative-versus-authentic judgment by default - which the peer-reviewed work confirms is a real, conditional distinction, not merely cynicism.
- **the tactic overall**: Counter-cyclical and rising. As generated content saturates the feed, the scarcity premium on genuine first-hand material increases. This is the only item in the copy category whose expected return is going up.
- **what makes a given story immune**: Being true and specific to you. It cannot be copied because nobody else has it. Saturation applies to shapes, never to contents.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- Inflated stakes - a trivial incident narrated as a turning point. The single most common failure, driven by posting cadence outrunning lived experience. Readers calibrate stakes accurately and discount the author permanently.
- Performative vulnerability - disclosure as a technique rather than as disclosure. Peer-reviewed work finds this is a real, detectable distinction with credibility consequences, not a matter of taste.
- The bait-and-switch resolution - a genuine arc that lands on a product pitch, retroactively reframing the story as an ad.
- Lesson-first structure - stating the generalisation before the story, which kills transportation and is the default LLM output shape.
- Generic detail - 'a client', 'a while back', 'a big improvement'. No mental imagery, no transportation, and it is also the tell that the story may not be real.
- Fabricated or embellished specifics - a category error rather than a craft error. It is a false statement published under your name, and the comments are where it gets tested.
- Confidentiality leakage - identifiable client or colleague detail. Not recoverable, and in regulated fields it is a professional matter, not a content matter.
- Fold failure - the complication buried below the ~140-character cut, so nobody expands.
- Self-repetition - the same three stories recycled quarterly, which is what happens when the tactic outruns its raw material.

**ai slop risk**

- **level**: Paradoxical, and worth stating precisely: LOWEST risk when done correctly - a true specific story is the strongest anti-slop artefact available - and HIGHEST risk when done incorrectly, because AI-generated fake personal stories are the single most recognisable form of slop on the feed.
- **why the paradox**: Everything that makes a real story work is unfakeable detail, and everything a model produces in its absence is archetype. There is no middle ground, which makes the failure very visible.
- **specific tells of a fabricated arc**:
  - Round or archetypal numbers: 47 rejections, 3 AM, a $10,000 lesson, exactly 100 days
  - A stranger who delivers the insight - the taxi driver, the barista, the elderly neighbour
  - Emotional escalation on a fixed curve, resolving cleanly with no residue
  - No specific proper nouns anywhere - no named tool, city, role, or month
  - The lesson generalises perfectly, with no leftover part that does not fit (real experience always has a leftover)
  - Dialogue that is too well-formed - people do not speak in complete parallel sentences
  - The narrator is never unsympathetic, never petty, never wrong in an unflattering way
  - The arc is legible in one read with nothing to re-read
- **the one test**: Could a stranger who knows your industry, but not you, have written this? If yes, it is not a personal narrative - it is an archetype wearing the first person.
- **mitigation**: Keep one true detail that does not serve the lesson. Real stories carry irrelevant specifics; constructed ones do not, because every element was generated to serve the point.

**human input required**

- **minimum non substitutable contribution**: The entire raw material. Uniquely in this research set, the human input is not a gate applied to AI output - it is the input, and the AI contribution is editorial only.
- **the five things only you have**: (1) What actually happened, in order; (2) what it cost, precisely; (3) what you almost did instead - the counterfactual nobody else knows; (4) the detail that does not serve the point; (5) the judgment about whether it is worth telling at all.
- **checkable gate**: Remove every sentence a competent stranger could have written about your industry. If what remains is not a coherent story, the post is an archetype and should not ship.
- **second gate**: Can you answer three hostile follow-up questions about this story in the comments, with specifics, without hedging? If not, you do not know it well enough to publish it - or it did not happen the way you wrote it.
- **why this is the right gate**: It is precisely what platform classifiers are probing for. LinkedIn's stated target is absence of first-hand perspective, not machine involvement; an AI-edited true story is safe, a human-typed archetype is not.
- **time cost**: The recall and interview step, 20-40 minutes. The writing is the cheap part.

**detectability and disclosure**

- **machine detectable**: The fabrication is more detectable by humans than by machines - readers catch archetypal structure that detectors miss, and detectors flag genuine non-native writing that readers would accept. Seven detectors flagged non-native English writing as AI-generated 61% of the time, unanimously on ~20% of samples (Liang et al.), which is directly relevant to a Polish author writing English narrative: your true story is at elevated risk of a false AI flag, and the defence is specificity, not style.
- **provenance standards**: None applicable. C2PA is unsolved for plain text and breaks on screenshots; SynthID covers Google-generated media. There is no way to cryptographically attest that a story is true, and there never will be.
- **what actually flags you**: Readers, via LinkedIn's 'Seems like AI slop' button (live since 2026-07-30), whose reports both moderate and train LinkedIn's classifiers, with private feedback to authors whose content readers find inauthentic. A fabricated personal story is the most report-prone content type on the platform, because readers who recognise the archetype feel actively deceived rather than merely bored.
- **disclosure triggered**: None for AI-assisted editing of a true story. There is, however, a real editorial line: if the AI added facts, the post contains fabrication and the issue is honesty, not disclosure. No platform rule covers this; your own standard has to.

**policy and legal**

- **eu ai act art 50**: Applicable since 2026-08-02. AI-edited narrative text is within scope in principle, but the duty attaches only to text 'published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest', and is disapplied where the content 'has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility'. A first-person story you lived, dictated and reviewed sits squarely inside the exemption. Practitioner guidance notes the review must be substantive rather than cursory - trivially satisfied here, since you are the source of the facts.
- **the bigger legal surfaces are not ai law**:
  - GDPR and confidentiality: a client story containing identifiable detail about an individual is personal-data processing. Anonymise the party, keep the constraint exact. For a Poland/EU-based consultant this is the real exposure in this tactic, and it is larger than anything in the AI Act.
  - Contractual NDAs: most consulting agreements restrict naming clients or describing engagements. A story does not become permissible by being flattering.
  - Defamation / reputational claims: a story about a named former employer or colleague that portrays them unfavourably is actionable in Poland regardless of truth if it damages reputation and cannot be justified.
  - Advertising law: a personal success story used to promote a service becomes a commercial claim and falls under unfair-commercial-practices rules; fabricated testimonial-like content is a straightforward consumer-protection breach.
- **platform rules**: No platform prohibits personal narrative. Inauthentic-behaviour and misrepresentation policies apply to fabricated experience, though enforcement against an individual post is in practice reader-driven.
- **practical position**: The AI-law exposure is negligible; the confidentiality exposure is real and recurring. Get consent or anonymise properly, every time.

**reversibility and blast radius**

- **worst case**: The largest blast radius of any tactic in this research set - and uniquely, the damage is not algorithmic. A fabricated or inflated story that is publicly called out damages credibility permanently and in a way no amount of subsequent good content repairs, because the doubt attaches to everything you publish afterwards.
- **second worst case**: A confidentiality breach involving a client. Professional and contractual consequences, potentially a lost relationship or a claim. Not reversible by deleting the post - it has already been seen and screenshotted.
- **algorithmic blast radius**: Minimal. There is no ranking penalty for a story that simply does not land; a weak arc costs one post's reach.
- **recoverability**: Asymmetric and worth internalising: the algorithmic downside is trivially recoverable, the reputational downside is close to permanent. That asymmetry is the argument for never letting a model add a fact.
- **the cheap insurance**: Tell true stories, anonymise third parties, understate rather than inflate the stakes. All three are free, and together they eliminate essentially the entire downside.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 1**: Start from an incident, never from a topic. If you are searching for a story to illustrate a point you already wanted to make, stop - that is the path to inflation. Keep a running list of things that actually happened; this vault's dated notes are the natural home for it.
- **step 2**: Test the stakes honestly. What did it cost - money, time, a relationship, a belief? If the answer is nothing, it is an anecdote, and anecdotes do not carry arcs.
- **step 3**: Run the AI interview: one question at a time until the model has scene, stakes, complication, turn and consequence. Do not let it write yet. Dictate the answers if you can - speaking preserves detail that typing edits away.
- **step 4**: Have it draft using only your facts, with [MISSING: x] wherever it would need to invent. Fill the gaps yourself or cut those beats.
- **step 5**: Check the order. Complication early, turn late, lesson last and in one line. Move any lesson sentence that appears before the final beat.
- **step 6**: Run the specificity audit - every generic noun phrase either becomes specific or gets cut. Then deliberately keep one true detail that serves nothing.
- **step 7**: Set the fold so the complication (not the setup) is visible in the first ~140 characters on mobile. Verify in a real preview.
- **step 8**: Run the cringe check and the stakes test: where does this read as performed, and am I claiming more insight than the incident supports? Cut the claim, not the story.
- **step 9**: Confidentiality pass - anonymise every third party, remove anything identifying, confirm no NDA surface. Non-negotiable and it takes two minutes.
- **step 10**: Publish, then be present in the comments for the first 90 minutes, answering follow-ups with more specifics. This is where a real story compounds and a fabricated one collapses - and the author-reply lift is itself a documented reach mechanic.
- **step 11**: Log the arc type and the outcome. Over time this tells you which of your own stories your audience actually wants, which is the only story-selection data that exists.

**checklist**

- PASS/FAIL: Did this actually happen, to me, in the way I have written it?
- PASS/FAIL: Every specific in the post is real - no number, quote, date or detail added by the model?
- PASS/FAIL: Real stakes - I can name what it cost?
- PASS/FAIL: Complication visible above the ~140-character mobile fold, not just the setup?
- PASS/FAIL: Lesson appears once, at the end, in one line?
- PASS/FAIL: At least three specifics a stranger could not have invented (named tool, month, exact figure, actual quote)?
- PASS/FAIL: One true detail kept that does not serve the lesson?
- PASS/FAIL: Passes the stranger test - a competent outsider in my field could NOT have written this?
- PASS/FAIL: Not performative - would I tell this the same way to a skeptical peer over coffee?
- PASS/FAIL: Third parties anonymised; no NDA or GDPR exposure?
- PASS/FAIL: I can answer three hostile follow-up questions with specifics?
- PASS/FAIL: The arc does not resolve into a pitch?
- PASS/FAIL: Not a shape I have used in my last three posts?

**worked example**

- **real measured finding 1**: The academic counterweight, quoted, because it is the most useful single sentence anyone writing stories for a feed can hold onto. Rahmani, Montano, Groves and Green (2025), Behavioural Public Policy, across 77 experiments and 24,380 respondents: 'Although narratives seem to have somewhat stronger average effects, no statistically significant difference was detected between narrative and non-narrative treatments,' and 'conditional on audiences sitting down to view or listen, narrative content is not markedly more persuasive than non-narrative content.' Their alternative account of the advantage - that narratives 'attract and engage large and diverse audiences' - is the correct reason to use this tactic in a dwell-ranked feed. Use stories to be read, not to be believed.
- **real measured finding 2**: The practitioner counterweight, from MagicPost's 1,141,932-post LinkedIn corpus: posts about a challenge overcome show a 1.03% median engagement rate and posts about a genuinely hard moment 0.80%, against a 0.39% platform median and 0.44% for the most-published type, punchy advice (N=142,301). Lived experience runs roughly 2-2.5x the median. Correlational, vendor-produced, and entirely consistent with the alternative explanation that people with real experiences also write better posts.
- **real structural example**: van Laer et al. (2019), across 64 articles and 138 effect sizes, found transportation strongest when a story is user-generated rather than professionally produced and received by one person at a time. That is a peer-reviewed description of a phone-held feed post written by an individual - the format advantage is real and measured, even if the narrative-versus-argument advantage is not.
- **constructed illustration**: CONSTRUCTED, and labelled as such because fabricating a quoted 'real post' would be the exact failure this entry warns about. WEAK (lesson-first, generic, archetypal): 'Failure is the best teacher. Last year I learned this the hard way when a big project didn't go as planned. It taught me that resilience matters more than talent. Here are 3 lessons...' - no scene, no cost, no counterfactual, no specific; a stranger could have written every word. STRONG (four beats, specifics, lesson last): 'In March we shipped a migration that took the client's reporting offline for nine hours.' [complication above the fold] / 'I had flagged the rollback plan as untested two weeks earlier and let it go, because the deadline was political and I did not want to be the person slowing it down.' [stakes + the unflattering truth] / 'We restored from a backup I had argued against keeping.' [the turn, plus the true detail that does not serve the lesson] / 'Now nothing ships without a rollback we have actually executed once, in staging, with a stopwatch.' [measured consequence] / 'The cost of being the person who slows things down is always lower than you think it is.' [lesson, last, one line]. Note what makes the strong version work: it contains a fact the author would rather not publish, which is the property no generator produces.

**cost and time to execute**

- **per post**: 45-90 minutes, the most expensive copy tactic in this set. Recall and interview 20-40 min (the real cost), drafting 10 min, structural and specificity passes 15 min, confidentiality pass 2 min, comment presence in the first 90 minutes 15-30 min.
- **hidden ongoing cost**: Living a life that generates stories. Not chargeable, but it is the actual input, and it caps output regardless of how much time you spend writing.
- **per month**: At 2-4 story posts per month: 3-6 hours, plus comment time. Attempting more than about one genuine arc per week is what causes stake inflation - the constraint is supply, not effort.
- **tooling**: ~$20/mo for an LLM; ~$12.46-19.99/mo for AuthoredUp if you want the fold preview; a dictation tool (often free). Materially cheaper in tools and dearer in time than any other tactic here.
- **comparison**: Versus a 10-minute AI repurpose, this is 5-9x the time. Versus a 4-hour original-data post, it is cheaper and reusable across formats - one true story feeds a LinkedIn post, an X thread, a Reel and a newsletter section. Amortised across four surfaces, a 90-minute story is competitive with anything in this research.
- **the asset argument**: Stories accumulate. A file of 30 true, specific work incidents is a durable content asset that AI cannot reproduce and competitors cannot copy. That file is the thing worth building; the posts are just withdrawals from it.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **leading**:
  - Comment substance in the first 90 minutes - specifically, comments that tell a story back. This is the highest-fidelity signal that transportation actually occurred, and it appears within the hour.
  - Reply depth - multi-turn threads rather than single comments
  - DM responses, which stories produce at unusually high rates and which do not appear in any analytics dashboard
  - Profile visits, the standard trust proxy after a personal post
- **lagging**: Follower quality (not count), inbound enquiries, and whether people reference the story back to you weeks later - the last being the only real measure of whether it landed.
- **what moves first**: Comment character count. Watch it, not the comment count. Stories produce fewer but far longer comments than engagement-bait, which is exactly the trade the 2026 rankers reward.
- **what not to watch**: Reactions. A story that gets 200 likes and no comments did not transport anyone; it was recognised as a genre and reacted to as one.
- **objective specific**: For trust and inbound, the KPI is DMs and enquiries. For reach, comment depth. These come apart - the most-read story is often not the one that generates business.

**measurement feasibility**

- **observable**: Comment count and content, reply depth, profile visits, follower change, video view duration for talking-head versions. Comment content is the unusual case here: it is qualitative but genuinely informative, and reading it manually beats any available metric.
- **not observable**: Dwell time and completion on text posts, and DM shares - the two signals the tactic most directly moves. Dark-social forwarding (someone sending your story to a colleague in Slack) is entirely invisible and is plausibly this tactic's largest real effect.
- **usable proxies**: (1) Average comment length as a transportation proxy; (2) ratio of first-person comments ('this happened to me too') to generic ones - the single best available indicator; (3) unsolicited DMs within 48 hours; (4) whether people bring the story up later, tracked informally.
- **honest limit**: This is the tactic whose main value - trust, memorability, being the person someone thinks of six months later - is the least measurable thing in the entire research set. Any attempt to justify it on measured engagement alone will undersell it, and any attempt to optimise it against engagement metrics will push it toward the inflated, performative versions that destroy its actual value. Measure it lightly and on long horizons, or not at all.
- **practical advice**: Keep a simple log: arc type, whether people replied with their own stories, and any DM or enquiry that referenced it. Thirty entries in, you will know which of your stories your audience wants. No dashboard will tell you this.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- as of date and volatility
- audience fit
- conflicting evidence

### Persuasion formulas

`persuasion-formulas` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 6 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Persuasion formulas (PAS, AIDA, BAB, 4U)
- **category**: copy
- **definition**: Fixed four-to-five-beat message skeletons imported from direct-response advertising and applied to social posts: PAS (Problem-Agitate-Solution), AIDA (Attention-Interest-Desire-Action, E. St. Elmo Lewis, c.1898-1903), BAB (Before-After-Bridge), 4U (Urgent-Unique-Ultra-specific-Useful, Michael Masterson/AWAI). Each prescribes the ORDER of moves, not the substance.
- **maturity**: decaying as a differentiator, established as a floor. The underlying psychology (tension-then-resolution, contrast, specificity) is stable; the visible template is now the single most reliable AI tell on LinkedIn and X, because every LLM trained on marketing corpora emits it by default.
- **one line verdict**: Use the formula as a private scaffold you delete before publishing, never as the visible surface of the post.

**as of date and volatility**

- **as of**: 2026-09-11
- **stable layer**: The persuasion psychology is stable / decade-scale: Witte & Allen (2000) fear-appeal meta-analysis, Loewenstein (1994) information-gap curiosity, Berger (2025, Annu. Rev. Psychol. 76:559-581). These do not rot.
- **volatile layer**: The PLATFORM fit of these formulas is quarter-to-quarter. X replaced its entire ranking stack in Jan 2026 (open-sourced at github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm, Apache-2.0, committed to ~4-weekly public updates) and shipped its largest update 2026-05-15. LinkedIn's 360Brew LLM ranker was confirmed via its engineering blog (Mar 2026) and changed comment ranking to per-viewer relevance in Aug 2026. Link suppression on X tightened ~Mar 2026.
- **rot rate**: Mechanism claims: 6-12 months. Specific weights/penalties: quarter-to-quarter — but X's are now readable from source, so they can be re-checked rather than re-guessed. Re-verify the X param.rs weights and the LinkedIn format benchmarks before relying on any number here.
- **decay direction**: Monotonically worse for the VISIBLE template, roughly flat for the underlying moves. Each new model generation makes the template cheaper to emit and therefore cheaper to recognise.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **the four formulas**:
  - **PAS**: Problem (name a pain the reader already feels) -> Agitate (make the cost of the pain vivid and near-term) -> Solution (the move that removes it). The agitation step is a fear appeal in Witte's sense: it raises perceived severity and susceptibility.
  - **AIDA**: Attention (hook) -> Interest (relevance/proof) -> Desire (the outcome as wanted state) -> Action (the ask). Built for a linear funnel that terminates in a click.
  - **BAB**: Before (current unsatisfactory state) -> After (transformed state) -> Bridge (the mechanism that crosses between them). A contrast frame; the persuasion sits in the delta, not in either state.
  - **4U**: A headline/first-line filter rather than a body structure: is the promise Urgent, Unique, Ultra-specific, Useful? It grades a hook, it does not generate one.
- **the shared engine**: All four open a gap and then close it. Loewenstein's (1994) information-gap theory is the common mechanism: curiosity is aroused by a perceived discrepancy between current and desired knowledge, and the reader keeps reading to close it. PAS and BAB open the gap with a felt cost; AIDA opens it with a promise; 4U grades how motivating the gap is.
- **what actually transfers to 2026 social**: Three of the moves survive the move from a sales page to a feed: (1) SPECIFICITY — the 'Ultra-specific' U is the only one of the four Us that a platform NLP classifier can distinguish from generic marketing language, because it requires a proper noun, a number, or a date; (2) CONTRAST — BAB's delta is the cheapest way to justify why a post exists at all; (3) DELAYED RESOLUTION — the gap must not close before the 'see more' fold on LinkedIn or before the dwell threshold on X.
- **where the structure now fails mechanically**:
  - AIDA's 'Action' step assumes an outbound click. X discounts standalone external-link posts to near-zero median engagement for non-Premium accounts (tightened ~Mar 2026), and LinkedIn's ranker deprioritises off-platform links in the post body. The final beat of AIDA is the beat the ranker punishes.
  - PAS's 'Agitate' step is high-arousal negative language. On X this raises the predicted probability of the actions that carry the heaviest negative weights in the published scorer: ReportWeight -234.0, MuteAuthorWeight -58.8, NotInterestedWeight -43.2, BlockAuthorWeight -31.2, against FavoriteWeight +0.5. Agitation buys likes at +0.5 and risks mutes at -58.8.
  - PAS in its short social form resolves the tension in 4-6 lines. LinkedIn's dominant practitioner-observed signal is DWELL TIME; a tightly closed loop ends dwell early. The formula is optimised for conversion-per-impression on a page you already landed on, not for time-on-post in a feed.
  - Witte & Allen (2000): strong fear appeals paired with LOW efficacy produce the greatest DEFENSIVE responses (avoidance, reactance) rather than message acceptance. A social-length PAS post almost never has room for a credible efficacy step — the 'Solution' is usually a slogan or a CTA, not a demonstrated capability. That is the theoretical reason short-form PAS underperforms its sales-page ancestor.
  - Template collision: because every general-purpose LLM emits PAS/AIDA as its default marketing shape, the structure now correlates with low-effort AI output in the reader's mind and (per vendor reporting) in platform classifiers. The formula has become a negative quality signal by association.

**ranking signal targeted**

- **primary**: Dwell time / scroll depth / 'see more' expansion (LinkedIn). The formula's only real ranking job in 2026 is to keep the gap open past the fold.
- **secondary**: Reply depth. PAS and BAB both end on a claim; a claim invites disagreement or corroboration, which produces substantive comments. On X, ReplyWeight is +5.0 and QuoteWeight +5.0 versus FavoriteWeight +0.5 — the reply is worth 10x the like.
- **explicitly NOT targeted**: Saves and share-via-DM. A closed persuasive loop gives the reader nothing to keep or forward; these formulas were built to move one reader down a funnel, not to be passed sideways. ShareViaCopyLinkWeight is +20.0 and ShareViaDmWeight +5.0 on X — the two highest positive weights in the published table — and classic persuasion formulas target neither.
- **honest answer**: Largely UNKNOWN at the formula level. No platform exposes a 'structure' feature. The formulas do not move a signal directly; they move reader behaviour, which moves the signals. Any claim that 'PAS gets more reach' is inferring two steps back from the ranker.

**why it drives reach**

- **causal chain**: Formula -> an unresolved gap at the fold -> reader expands and keeps reading -> dwell time and scroll depth rise -> LinkedIn's 360Brew / X's Phoenix ranker read sustained attention plus (if the claim is arguable) replies -> post escalates beyond the seed audience.
- **the weak link**: Step 2. The formula guarantees a gap but not an INTERESTING gap. Robertson et al. (2023, Nature Human Behaviour) and Banerjee & Urminsky's Upworthy analysis converge on the same uncomfortable point: structural/textual cues move click-through by low single-digit percentages, and prior persuasion research does not reliably predict even the DIRECTION of those effects. The variance that matters lives in the substance, not the skeleton.
- **counter causal path**: On X the chain can run negative. Agitation -> a slice of readers who feel accused rather than understood -> P(mute)/P(report) rises -> the -58.8 / -234.0 weights dominate the +0.5 likes -> the post is suppressed despite visible engagement. Worse, the account-level model (Agatha) labels accounts from 'blocks, reports and spam reports relative to favorites' — so habitual agitation is a slow account-level tax, not just a per-post risk.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **what the model is good at here**:
  - STRUCTURE DETECTION on your own past posts: 'label the rhetorical move of each line in these 30 posts of mine' — reveals which formula you already use unconsciously and which of your top posts broke it.
  - CRITIQUE against the formula rather than generation from it: score a human draft on 4U (is each U evidenced by a concrete token?) and return only the failing U.
  - VARIATION at the line level: 12 alternative Agitate lines given a fixed, human-written Problem and Solution.
  - ADVERSARIAL reading: 'who would feel accused by this post, and what would make them mute the author?' — a cheap proxy for the P(mute)/P(report) term that actually decides X distribution.
- **what it is bad at**: Generating the post from the formula. Asked for 'a PAS post about X', every frontier model produces the same artefact: three-beat cadence, uniform 18-24 word sentences, see-saw negation ('It's not X. It's Y.'), rule-of-three lists, and zero proper nouns or numbers. That is the shape readers now screenshot and mock.
- **the inversion**: Use the formula as a REVIEW rubric, not a GENERATION template. Generation from the formula produces the tell; critique against the formula removes weaknesses without imposing the shape.

**automation level**

- **level**: L1 (AI-assisted draft), with the critique loop sitting at L1/L2 boundary.
- **why not higher**: The non-substitutable inputs — which problem is real for THIS audience, whether the solution actually worked, the proprietary number — are exactly the inputs the model does not have. An L2 autonomous run produces a structurally perfect post with nothing in it.
- **where L2 is safe**: Scoring and gating: an automated pass that rejects drafts with zero proper nouns, zero numerals, or >0.8 cadence uniformity can run unattended, because its failure mode is a false rejection, not a published post.
- **caveat**: Most tools marketed as 'AI agents' for social are L1 schedulers with a prompt box. Nothing credible sits at L3 in 2026 for this task.

**prompt patterns**

- **pattern 1 reverse engineering**: SYSTEM: You are a rhetorical analyst, not a copywriter. USER: Here are 30 of my posts with their impression and comment counts. For each, label the rhetorical move of every line (claim / evidence / concession / question / anecdote / instruction / ask). Then report: (a) which move sequences appear in my top decile by comments, (b) which appear in my bottom decile, (c) any sequence that appears in BOTH — those are noise, not signal. Do not recommend a formula.
- **pattern 2 formula as rubric**: You will NOT rewrite this draft. Score it against 4U and return a table: for each of Urgent / Unique / Ultra-specific / Useful, quote the exact span of my text that earns it, or write MISSING. A U is only earned by a concrete token: a date, a number, a named person, a named tool, or a named client. Abstract claims earn nothing. Return only the MISSING rows and one question per missing row that only I can answer.
- **pattern 3 agitation ceiling**: Here is my Problem and my Solution, both fixed — do not change them. Write 10 candidate Agitate lines on a severity ladder from 1 (understated, describes a cost) to 10 (accusatory, describes a failure of the reader). For each, answer: who reads this line and feels ACCUSED rather than understood? I will pick from the bottom half of the ladder.
- **pattern 4 gap placement**: My LinkedIn first 210 characters are what shows before 'see more'. Here is my full post. Find the single sentence whose removal from the visible portion leaves the largest unresolved question, and show me the post reordered so that sentence sits just BELOW the fold. Do not add words.
- **pattern 5 anti template pass**: Rewrite this draft to destroy its template signature while preserving every factual claim and the argument order. Hard constraints: vary sentence length so the standard deviation exceeds 8 words; delete every 'It's not X, it's Y' construction; delete every three-item list; the post must contain at least two proper nouns and one number I supplied. Return a diff, not a new post.
- **anti pattern**: 'Write me a PAS post about [topic]' and 'Make this more engaging'. Both produce the median of the training distribution, which is precisely the shape being filtered out.

**tool examples**

- **drafting and critique**: Claude (Opus/Sonnet, 2026), ChatGPT (GPT-5.x, 2026), Gemini — all four formulas are in every model's default repertoire, which is the problem, not the feature. Use them for critique passes.
- **linkedin native suites**: Taplio (Starter $39/mo, Growth $69/mo — AI drafting starts at Growth, Pro $199/mo; ~25% off annual, as of 2026); Hypefury (~$6/mo per channel, scheduling-first with limited AI writing); SuperGrow, Supergrow/Contentin-class competitors. These ship formula libraries as templates — the exact thing to avoid using verbatim.
- **anti slop and style**: Vale (prose linter, free, enforces house style rules like 'no see-saw negation'), Pangram / originality classifiers for detection-risk checks, sloptrim-class filters. See [[Marketing Agent Research]].
- **measurement**: Native LinkedIn analytics (impressions, members reached, engagement rate — NOT dwell), Shield or Taplio analytics for per-post history, X native analytics (impressions, engagements, profile clicks, bookmarks).
- **primary source to read rather than a tool**: github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm — home-mixer/params/param.rs holds the actual scoring weights, updated roughly every four weeks. Reading it directly beats any vendor blog about 'the X algorithm'.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

MIXED, and the split matters. STRONG for the underlying psychology (Witte & Allen 2000 meta-analysis; Loewenstein 1994; Chen & Berger 2013; Berger 2025 review). STRONG/platform-official for the X scoring weights that determine whether an agitation-heavy post survives (published source code). WEAK-to-VENDOR-CLAIM for every quantitative statement about how PAS/AIDA/BAB/4U specifically perform on 2026 social feeds — there is no independent large-N study of copywriting-formula structure versus social reach. ANECDOTAL for the 'these formulas no longer work' consensus, which is real but is practitioner observation plus template-fatigue reasoning, not measurement.

**evidence provenance**

- **peer reviewed**: Witte & Allen (2000) Health Education & Behavior 27(5):591-615 — fear-appeal meta-analysis. Loewenstein (1994) Psychological Bulletin — information-gap theory. Chen & Berger (2013) Journal of Consumer Research 40(3):580 — controversy/conversation. Berger (2025) Annual Review of Psychology 76:559-581 — current word-of-mouth synthesis. Robertson et al. (2023) Nature Human Behaviour — headline negativity.
- **platform official**: github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm (Apache-2.0, xAI, Jan 2026, major update 2026-05-15): scorer weights, predicted-action list, Grox/Agatha/BDSM content-and-account classifiers, visibility filtering. LinkedIn engineering blog + 360Brew arXiv papers (Mar 2026).
- **working paper not peer reviewed**: Banerjee & Urminsky, 'The Language That Drives Engagement: A Systematic Large-scale Analysis of Headline Experiments' (SSRN 3770366, Chicago Booth). The circulating version is explicitly labelled PRELIMINARY RESULTS FROM AN EXPLORATORY DATASET with a note that confirmatory results are likely to differ — cite its direction, never its magnitudes.
- **vendor with product to sell**: Taplio, Socialinsider, Buffer, Contentin, SocialPilot, dozens of 'LinkedIn algorithm 2026' blogs. A large fraction of the 2026 copywriting-formula content that ranks on this query is itself AI-generated and cites other AI-generated posts; treat the entire genre as circular.
- **specific laundering risk flagged**: The claim circulating as 'Setup-Stat-Reframe cadence earns 42% citation rate on Google AI Mode versus 0% for unstructured prose' appears only in vendor copywriting-framework blogs with no methodology, no sample, and no primary link. Do NOT propagate it. Same for 'founders using structured formulas see 2x-3x higher engagement'.
