#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **cross reference**: Ranking mechanics are not re-derived here — see [[Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026]] (17 platforms, 2026-07-06) for per-platform signals, golden hour and half-life.
- **linkedin**: PARTIAL FIT. BAB is the best-fitting formula because the Before/After contrast naturally survives being split across the 'see more' fold, and the Bridge is a professional-expertise payload that earns dwell. PAS backfires in its short form: it closes too fast for dwell and its agitation reads as manufactured urgency in a professional-identity context. AIDA's Action step fights the link penalty. 4U works purely as a first-line grader.
- **x**: POOR FIT for PAS/AIDA as written. The published weights reward reply (+5.0), quote (+5.0), DM-share (+5.0) and copy-link-share (+20.0), and punish report (-234.0) and mute (-58.8). A formula whose second beat is agitation is optimising the cheap signal and risking the expensive one. BAB compressed to two lines works because contrast is quotable. 4U is genuinely useful at X length.
- **instagram tiktok shorts**: MISFIT. These are watch-time-and-completion surfaces; a text persuasion skeleton is the wrong primitive. The only transferable element is the 3-second hook, which is 4U's 'Urgent + Ultra-specific' test applied to a spoken or on-screen first line.
- **newsletters and long form**: BEST FIT, and the honest home of these formulas. On owned surfaces the Action step can be a link without penalty, and there is room for the efficacy step that Witte & Allen show fear appeals require. If you want to use AIDA properly in 2026, use it in the newsletter, not the post.
- **format note**: LinkedIn document/carousel posts are the strongest engagement format (Socialinsider 2026: documents ~7.00% ER on 1.3M business posts, +14% YoY) — but a persuasion formula spread over 8-10 slides becomes an obvious sales deck. If you carousel a formula, put the Bridge on slide 2, not slide 9.

**audience fit**

- **b2b**: Workable but constrained. B2B readers recognise the templates from their own marketing departments, which raises the cynicism floor. The formulas survive when the Problem is one only an insider would name precisely.
- **b2c**: More tolerant of AIDA and 4U, especially on consumer-offer content, because the transactional frame is expected.
- **technical audiences**: HOSTILE. Engineers and technical practitioners treat the PAS/AIDA silhouette as a reliability signal in reverse. The winning register is claim-plus-evidence-plus-caveat, which is closer to an abstract than to a sales page.
- **en vs pl**: EN audiences have the highest template fatigue because they see the most of it. PL-language professional feeds are roughly 12-24 months behind on saturation, so a clean BAB structure still reads as competent rather than canned — but this window is closing, and a machine-translated EN formula post reads worse in PL than a natively written one. Idiom, not grammar, is where translated formulas break.
- **personal brand vs company page**: Formulas cost a personal account more than a company page, because a person is judged on sincerity and a brand is expected to sell.

**scales with**

- **not capped by account size**: The formula itself is size-neutral — it is a writing scaffold, available identically to a 200-follower and a 200,000-follower account.
- **capped by problem inventory**: The real ceiling. PAS needs a genuinely felt, specific problem; BAB needs a real before-state you witnessed. Most people have 5-15 of these, not 500. Past that inventory, the formula starts generating problems that do not exist, which is the exact failure the audience detects.
- **capped by corpus**: Effective use of the critique prompts requires 30+ of your own posts with performance data before the structure analysis says anything non-obvious.
- **network position**: On LinkedIn distribution still starts with your own network, so a formula post from a poorly-connected account in a dense niche outperforms the same post from a well-connected account in a diffuse one.
- **objective dependent ceiling**: For AI-citation visibility the ceiling is different and lower for these formulas specifically: persuasive structure is not extractable structure. Sub-500-follower accounts are cited by AI engines comparably to large ones, but a PAS post is a poor citation candidate regardless of account size because it makes a pitch rather than an answerable claim.

**decay and saturation**

- **shelf life**: The underlying moves: indefinite. The visible template: already past its decay point on EN LinkedIn and X, roughly 12-24 months of residual usefulness on PL-language professional feeds.
- **the precedent**: Broetry is the canonical case and the right mental model. Coined ~2017, popularised by Josh Fechter, it worked by forcing 'see more' clicks; within roughly 24 months the feed filled with copycats, the format became shorthand for performative humility ('I failed 7 times'), and by 2026 it is a thing people screenshot to mock. Nothing about the psychology changed — only the number of people using it.
- **why formulas decay faster now**: Before LLMs, copying a template took effort and spread at human speed. Now the marginal cost of emitting a perfect PAS post is one prompt, so saturation that used to take two years takes two quarters. Formula decay rate is now a function of model availability, not of creator learning curves.
- **leading indicator of death**: When the format appears in parody accounts and in 'how to spot AI writing' listicles, its distribution advantage is already gone. 'It's not X, it's Y' — a see-saw negation that top creators used as a signature — crossed that line in 2026.
- **what does not decay**: Specificity. A post containing a number nobody else has cannot be saturated, because nobody else can write it.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- TEMPLATE RECOGNITION. The reader identifies the formula before the argument, and the post is read as marketing rather than as thinking. Once recognised, the remaining content is discounted regardless of quality.
- AGITATION WITHOUT EFFICACY. The Witte & Allen failure: severity is raised, no credible capability is offered, and the reader resolves the discomfort by scrolling past (defensive avoidance) or by rejecting the author (reactance). Social-post length makes this the DEFAULT outcome of PAS, not an edge case.
- PREMATURE RESOLUTION. The gap closes above the fold, dwell time never accumulates, and the post dies in the seed audience despite being well written.
- MANUFACTURED PROBLEM. The formula demands a Problem; when the author has none, the model invents one. Readers who do not have the invented problem feel talked past, and readers who do have it notice it was described generically.
- CTA COLLISION. AIDA's Action step collides with two independent penalties: external-link demotion, and engagement-bait classifiers that flag explicit interaction solicitation ('Agree? Comment below').
- INVERTED-U OVERSHOOT. Chen & Berger (2013): controversy raises discussion up to a moderate level and DECREASES it beyond, because discomfort overtakes interest. An Agitate step tuned for maximum intensity lands past the peak.
- CADENCE COLLAPSE. Formula-driven output is cheap, so volume rises, per-post quality falls, and the account's average engagement-per-impression drops — which on a per-impression-normalised ranker like 360Brew hurts subsequent posts too.
- PORTFOLIO HOMOGENEITY. Twenty PAS posts in a row train your own audience to recognise your shape and skip it, independent of any algorithm.

**ai slop risk**

- **risk level**: HIGHEST of any item in this research. These formulas are the LLM default output shape for anything labelled 'marketing copy'. Asking a model for a persuasive post without constraints returns a formula post essentially every time.
- **specific tells**:
  - Cadence uniformity — a run of 18-24 word sentences, paragraph after paragraph. Reported in 2026 as the single most reliable marker, more so than any lexical tic.
  - See-saw negation: 'It's not about X. It's about Y.' Learned by models from top creators, then over-applied until it became a tell.
  - Rule-of-three lists everywhere, including where the real answer has two or five items.
  - Zero proper nouns and zero numerals — no named tool, client, date, or measured quantity anywhere in the post.
  - A Solution step that describes a category ('the right systems', 'a clear process') rather than a specific thing you did.
  - Perfect beat symmetry: each of P/A/S or B/A/B occupying a near-identical number of lines.
  - Em dashes are NO LONGER a reliable tell in 2026 — GPT-5.1 suppresses them by default and their prevalence in human professional writing is comparable. Do not use em-dash counting as a gate.
- **why the tells matter twice**: They cost you reader trust, and (per vendor reporting, unverified) they cost you a distribution test — LinkedIn commentary claims templated AI-shaped posts are throttled before reaching a real test audience. Direction plausible, magnitude unverified.
- **mitigation**: Invert the workflow: human writes the substance and the argument order, AI critiques against the formula, human writes the final prose. Never let the model produce the surface text of the beats.

**human input required**

- **minimum non substitutable contribution**: ONE verifiable particular that the model could not have known, placed inside the Solution or Bridge beat — not in the hook. Hooks are cheap; the beat that carries the claim is where the classifier and the reader both look.
- **acceptable forms**:
  - A number from your own work: a measured result, a cost, a duration, a conversion, a headcount, an error rate.
  - A named artefact: the specific tool, library, version, vendor, or document, with the version or date.
  - A first-hand incident with a time and a place: what broke, when, and what you did in the next hour.
  - A named client or project (with permission), or an anonymised but structurally specific one ('a 40-person logistics firm in Wrocław').
  - A judgement call with its counterfactual: what you chose, and the option you rejected and why.
- **the gate**: If every sentence of the post would still be true and publishable by a competitor in the same niche, the human contribution is zero and the post should not ship. This is a pass/fail test, not a scale.
- **why this is what classifiers probe for**: Platform NLP quality signals and AI-citation engines are both, in effect, searching for the same thing: unique, attributable, checkable assertions. Specificity is simultaneously the anti-slop gate, the persuasion upgrade (4U's Ultra-specific), and the citability requirement.
- **time cost of the gate**: 5-15 minutes of retrieval, not of writing. The bottleneck is having kept the number, not producing it.

**policy and legal**

- **jurisdiction assumed**: Poland / EU-based creator.
- **eu ai act article 50**: Applicable since 2026-08-02. Article 50 creates transparency duties for AI-generated or manipulated content. Two duties matter here and they are different: (a) DEEPFAKES (synthetic image/audio/video depicting real people or events) must be disclosed — not triggered by text drafting; (b) AI-GENERATED TEXT PUBLISHED TO INFORM THE PUBLIC ON MATTERS OF PUBLIC INTEREST must be disclosed, WITH AN EXPRESS EXEMPTION where the content underwent HUMAN REVIEW OR EDITORIAL CONTROL and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility. Fines reach EUR 15M or 3% of worldwide turnover; a grace period runs to 2026-12-02 for pre-existing systems.
- **what this means for persuasion formulas specifically**: A PAS post selling your own consulting service is commercial speech about your business, not 'information to the public on a matter of public interest' — Art. 50(4) is not the binding constraint. It DOES bite when the formula is applied to public-interest topics: AI policy, health, employment law, elections, safety. Since PAS and AIDA both push authors toward urgency framing on exactly such topics, this is a live risk rather than a theoretical one. The mitigation is already your quality workflow: genuine human editorial review, documented.
- **advertising law**: Where the Action step promotes a product or paid service, EU/PL consumer-protection and unfair-commercial-practice rules apply to the CLAIM regardless of how it was drafted. Agitation that overstates a risk in order to sell a remedy is a misleading-practice exposure, and 'the AI wrote it' is not a defence.
- **ftc divergence**: US FTC guidance focuses on endorsement disclosure and substantiation of claims rather than AI authorship, so a Poland-based creator writing for a US audience faces the EU transparency duty plus US substantiation expectations, not a single harmonised rule.
- **platform tos**: All major platforms permit AI-assisted text. The prohibited categories are inauthentic/mass-produced content (YouTube's Inauthentic Content Policy, 2026), engagement bait, and undisclosed deceptive synthetic media. Formula-driven text at low volume violates none of these; formula-driven text at scale starts to resemble mass-produced content.

**reversibility and blast radius**

- **typical worst case**: LOW and fully reversible. A recognisably templated post underperforms and is forgotten within the platform's content half-life (LinkedIn ~24-72h; X minutes-to-hours). No enforcement action attaches to using a copywriting formula.
- **the compounding risk**: Account-level, and this is the part that is NOT cheap to reverse. On X, the Agatha model labels accounts from 'blocks, reports and spam reports relative to favorites' — so a sustained diet of high-agitation posts degrades the account's standing rather than just individual posts. On LinkedIn, per-impression normalisation means a run of low-quality-per-impression posts drags subsequent ones. Recovery is measured in weeks of better posting, not in deleting one post.
- **brand damage**: The realistic tail risk is being quoted as an example of AI slop or LinkedIn cringe by a larger account. This is reputational, spreads faster than the original post, and is not deletable.
- **enforcement risk**: Near zero for the formula itself. Non-zero if the Action step uses engagement bait or link-spam patterns, which carry post suppression and, on repetition, account-level reach restriction.
- **recovery playbook**: Delete nothing (deletion signals nothing useful and loses the data). Stop posting formula-shaped content for 2-3 weeks, publish 3-5 posts carrying proprietary numbers or first-hand incidents, and reply substantively in others' comment sections. Both platforms' rankers are per-impression and recency-weighted, so the average recovers with volume of good posts.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 0 precondition**: Before opening any model, write down the one verifiable particular this post will carry — a number, a name, a date, an incident. If you cannot, stop: no formula will rescue a post with nothing in it. This takes 2 minutes and kills roughly half of bad post ideas.
- **step 1 pick the formula by objective not by habit**: Reader has a problem they already feel and you have a demonstrated fix -> PAS, but only with a real efficacy step. Reader does not yet see the gap and you can show a concrete transformation -> BAB (best default for LinkedIn). You are grading a first line, not structuring a body -> 4U. You are writing a newsletter or landing page with a legitimate click at the end -> AIDA. You are writing for X at 280 characters -> BAB compressed, or no formula at all.
- **step 2 draft the substance yourself out of order**: Write the Solution/Bridge beat FIRST and in your own words, because it carries the verifiable particular. Then write the Problem/Before beat to match the fix you actually have, not the fix you wish you had. Writing in beat order is what produces invented problems.
- **step 3 set the agitation ceiling**: Run prompt_pattern_3 (agitation ladder 1-10). Pick from the bottom half. Chen & Berger's inverted U means the intensity that maximises interest is well below the intensity that maximises discomfort; on X the asymmetry is brutal — a reply is +5.0, a mute is -58.8.
- **step 4 place the fold**: Run prompt_pattern_4. On LinkedIn, ensure the first ~210 characters end with the gap OPEN. The single most common structural mistake is resolving PAS's tension in the visible portion, which caps dwell time before it starts.
- **step 5 destroy the signature**: Run prompt_pattern_5 as a diff, then apply the diff by hand. Target: sentence-length standard deviation above 8 words, no see-saw negation, no three-item list unless the real answer has three items, at least two proper nouns and one number.
- **step 6 gate then publish**: Run the checklist below. Any FAIL sends the draft back to step 2, not to the model.
- **step 7 measure the right thing**: Record impressions, comments (substantive vs one-line), saves, and — on LinkedIn — whether the post kept earning impressions past 24h. Do not compare posts on likes; likes are the weakest signal on both platforms (X: FavoriteWeight +0.5).
- **step 8 rotate**: Never run the same formula more than twice in any five consecutive posts. Format decay is driven by repetition frequency far more than by elapsed time.
- **total time**: 25-40 minutes for a post that carries a real particular, of which only ~10 minutes is AI-assisted.

**checklist**

- **gate type**: pass/fail — any FAIL blocks publication
- **items**:
  - SUBSTANCE: the post contains at least one number, proper noun, date, or named artefact that a competitor in my niche could not have written. FAIL = do not publish.
  - COMPETITOR TEST: if I swapped my name for a rival's, would the post still be entirely true and publishable? If yes, FAIL.
  - EFFICACY: if the post agitates a problem, does it show a capability rather than assert one? A slogan-level Solution is a FAIL (Witte & Allen).
  - FOLD: are the first ~210 characters (LinkedIn) leaving a question open rather than answering it? FAIL if the tension resolves above the fold.
  - AGITATION CEILING: would a reasonable person in my audience feel ACCUSED rather than understood by any line? FAIL — rewrite that line down the ladder.
  - CADENCE: is the standard deviation of my sentence lengths above ~8 words? A uniform 18-24 word rhythm is a FAIL.
  - SIGNATURE: zero 'It's not X, it's Y' constructions; no gratuitous three-item lists; no perfectly symmetrical beat lengths. Any present = FAIL.
  - CTA: no engagement bait ('Agree? Comment below', 'Tag someone who...'), and no external link in the post body on X or LinkedIn. FAIL if present.
  - ROTATION: have I used this same formula in either of my last two posts? If yes, FAIL — change the shape or the format.
  - LEGAL: if this post informs the public on a matter of public interest (health, law, elections, AI policy, safety), have I genuinely reviewed and edited it, and can I evidence that editorial control? FAIL if the answer is 'the model wrote it and I skimmed'.
  - CLAIM SUBSTANTIATION: every factual or performance claim is one I can evidence if challenged. FAIL otherwise — 'the AI wrote it' is not a defence under EU/PL unfair-commercial-practice rules.

**cost and time to execute**

- **per post time**: 25-40 minutes end to end for a formula-scaffolded post carrying a real particular. Breakdown: 2 min deciding the particular, 10-15 min drafting substance by hand, 5 min AI critique passes (patterns 2-5), 5-10 min applying the diff, 3 min checklist. A no-particular formula post takes 5 minutes and should not be published.
- **per post time if the particular must be retrieved**: Add 15-60 minutes to dig out the actual number from analytics, invoices, or logs. This retrieval cost — not writing — is the real constraint on formula-based publishing.
- **per month time**: At 3 posts/week: roughly 6-8 hours/month, plus a one-off 2-3 hours to build the reusable rubric prompts and run the structure analysis over your own back catalogue.
- **tool subscriptions**: Minimum viable: one frontier model subscription, ~USD 20-30/month (ChatGPT Plus / Claude Pro tier). That is genuinely sufficient for every prompt pattern above. Optional: Taplio Starter $39 / Growth $69 / Pro $199 per month (AI drafting begins at Growth; ~25% off annual, 2026 pricing); Hypefury ~$6/month per channel for scheduling. Vale is free.
- **total monthly**: USD 20-30/month for the model-only workflow; USD 60-100/month if a LinkedIn-native suite is added.
- **comparison anchor**: A formula post is the CHEAP end of the spectrum — comparable to a 10-minute repurpose, far below a 4-hour original-data post. That is exactly why it is saturated: low marginal cost invites volume, and volume is what killed broetry.
- **hidden cost**: The rotation requirement. Because formulas decay with repetition, a formula-only strategy forces you to keep acquiring new formulas, which is an ongoing research cost that a substance-first strategy does not carry.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **leading first 60 90 minutes**:
  - Substantive comments (>10 words, containing a specific question or a personal experience) in the first hour — the earliest reliable read. One-line comments are near-worthless under LinkedIn's NLP filtering.
  - 'See more' expansion behaviour, proxied by whether impressions keep climbing after the first 30 minutes rather than flattening.
  - On X: replies and quotes in the first 30-60 minutes (weights +5.0 each) rather than likes (+0.5).
- **lagging 24 72h**:
  - Members reached / unique impressions versus your own trailing median — always compare to your baseline, never to someone else's benchmark.
  - Saves/bookmarks — the strongest signal that the Bridge/Solution beat carried real utility.
  - Follower conversion (X FollowAuthorWeight +4.0) — the clean test of whether the post demonstrated capability rather than asserted it.
  - Profile views, which on both platforms indicate the post made the author interesting rather than merely the topic.
- **formula specific diagnostic**: Compute comments-per-impression separately for posts that resolve above the fold versus below it. If the below-fold group does not win on your own data, your gap is not interesting — a substance problem that no structural fix will solve.
- **negative indicators to watch**: A rising ratio of one-line-to-substantive comments across your last 10 posts is the earliest sign your formula has been recognised: people are engaging with the shape out of habit rather than with the content.
- **what not to track**: Likes as a primary metric, and engagement rate borrowed from industry benchmarks — the denominators differ so wildly between sources (Socialinsider 5.20% average LinkedIn ER vs Buffer's 21.77% median for carousels) that cross-source comparison is meaningless.

**measurement feasibility**

- **directly observable**: Impressions/members reached, reactions, comments (and their text, so quality can be judged by hand), reposts, follower delta, profile views. All available natively on LinkedIn and X at no cost.
- **NOT observable**: Dwell time — the signal these formulas are primarily aimed at is invisible in creator analytics on both LinkedIn and X. X's published scorer uses dwell, click-dwell time and active seconds as ranking inputs; none of these are exposed to the author. Also invisible: 'see more' expansion rate, share-via-DM counts (X ShareViaDmWeight +5.0), and copy-link shares (+20.0, the single highest positive weight) — the two highest-value positive actions in X's own scorer are the two you cannot see.
- **best available proxies**:
  - Dwell proxy: impressions accruing over 2-24h rather than front-loading. A post that keeps gaining impressions on day 2 was read, not scrolled.
  - Expansion proxy: comments-per-impression, which requires reading past the fold to produce.
  - Dark-social proxy: unexplained profile-view or follower spikes with no matching public engagement, and inbound DMs referencing the post. Ask directly — 'how did you find this?' in DM replies is crude but is the only instrument you actually have.
- **measurement honesty**: Per-post attribution for a structural choice is not feasible at individual-creator volume. To detect a formula effect against normal post-to-post variance you would need tens of posts per condition. Treat formula choice as a craft decision informed by mechanism, not as something you can A/B test on your own account.
- **instrumentation note**: Export your own post history monthly (native export, Taplio, or Shield) and keep a local table with a 'formula used' column. After ~50 posts this is the only dataset about your audience that actually exists.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- conflicting evidence
- detectability and disclosure
- effect size and n
- prompt artifact link

### Proof-of-work receipts

`proof-of-work-receipts-originality` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 8 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Proof-of-work receipts. Category: copy. Definition: attaching verifiable artifacts to a claim — screenshots, raw exports, logs, terminal output, before/after pairs, timestamps, commit hashes, invoices, dashboards, named sources and direct quotations — so the reader can check the claim rather than trust it. It is the EVIDENCE WRAPPER, distinct from its sibling item 'Original data drops', which is the PAYLOAD; receipts can also wrap a claim that contains no data at all ('I shipped this', 'the client said this'). Maturity: established in build-in-public culture since ~2013 (Buffer's Open Startup, later Pieter Levels' public revenue dashboards) but SHARPLY APPRECIATING in 2026 for two new reasons: it is the clearest available anti-slop signal in a feed saturated with AI-generated assertion, and evidence markers are the highest-lift optimization measured for generative-engine citation.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. Four clocks. (1) STABLE — 'evidence beats assertion' as a credibility mechanism; no expiry. (2) 12-24 MONTHS — the generative-engine lift: the GEO paper (KDD 2024) measured Quotation Addition +41% and Cite Sources +28%, but its authors explicitly caveat that methods 'may require adaptation as generative engines evolve', and engine answer-construction has moved substantially since the 2023-24 measurement window. Treat the DIRECTION (evidence markers help citation) as solid and the 40% MAGNITUDE as a two-year-old single-study figure, not a 2026 fact. (3) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER — LinkedIn's originality/authenticity scoring (announced changes March 2026 and 20 May 2026), Meta/TikTok/LinkedIn C2PA handling, and every vendor engagement-rate figure. (4) DEGRADING FAST — the trustworthiness of a screenshot as evidence, now that image editing and generation are trivially available; this clock runs against the tactic and is the main thing to watch.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

Mechanism in five moves. (1) MAKE THE CLAIM CHECKABLE, NOT LOUDER: replace an intensifier with an artifact — 'we cut onboarding from 11 days to 4' plus the exported log beats 'we dramatically improved onboarding'. The artifact does not need to be impressive; it needs to be inspectable. (2) SHOW THE UGLY PART: an un-cropped screenshot including the failed run, the flat week, the caveat row. Perfectly clean evidence reads as manufactured; the imperfection IS the credibility signal, and it is the part a model cannot invent for you. (3) TIMESTAMP AND LOCATE: date, tool, version, commit hash, 'taken 2026-09-03 from X's export'. Provenance metadata in the CAPTION, since platform upload strips most file-level metadata. (4) QUOTE AND CITE NAMED SOURCES VERBATIM: direct quotation with attribution, plus a named source for any third-party figure. This is the same move the GEO study measured as the highest-lift optimization, and it doubles as the human-credibility move. (5) MAKE THE ARTIFACT THE VISUAL: the screenshot is the image slot, so it competes for the scroll-stop; a legible, cropped-to-the-point artifact with one thing circled outperforms both a stock graphic and a raw unreadable dump. The compound effect: a reader who zooms into a screenshot has spent dwell time, and a reader who can verify a claim is measurably more willing to re-transmit it, because re-telling an unverifiable claim carries reputational risk for THEM.

**ranking signal targeted**

Primary: DWELL TIME — an artifact is inspected, not skimmed; on LinkedIn (dwell-dominant in 2026) tapping and reading a screenshot is one of the cheapest legitimate ways to buy read-time. Secondary: the QUALITY/ORIGINALITY CLASSIFIER — LinkedIn's 2026 scoring reportedly assesses whether content reads as generic, templated and perspective-free; a first-party artifact is close to definitionally not that, so receipts act as insurance against the AI-slop reach penalty rather than as a booster. Tertiary: SAVES (a checkable reference is worth keeping) and DM SENDS (forwarding evidence to a colleague is a low-risk act; forwarding an unverifiable claim is not). On the generative-engine side, a genuinely different target: EXTRACTABLE ATTRIBUTED STATEMENTS — quotations and cited sources are what answer-engines lift. HONEST CAVEAT: no platform states that 'contains a screenshot' or 'contains a citation' is a ranking feature. Every effect here is indirect, via reader behaviour and via the negative classifier you are avoiding. Where the truthful answer is 'unknown', it is unknown.

**why it drives reach**

Two chains, one defensive and one offensive. DEFENSIVE (the more reliable of the two in 2026): platforms now suppress content scored as generic/perspective-free, with reported reach reductions in the tens of percent; receipts are the most legible possible demonstration that a human did a specific thing at a specific time, so they move you out of the suppressed bucket. Reach gained by not being penalised is still reach, and it is the more defensible half of the case. OFFENSIVE: evidence lowers the reputational cost of re-transmission — Berger's word-of-mouth work frames sharing as self-presentational, and sharing something that could be debunked threatens the sharer's self-presentation, so verifiability removes a brake on forwarding rather than adding an accelerator. Additionally the artifact buys inspection time (dwell), invites specific rather than generic comments ('what tool is that in row 3?'), and produces the saves that extend content half-life. The AI-search chain is separate: attributed, quotable statements are structurally easier for an answer engine to lift and cite.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

The model never produces the evidence. It (a) IDENTIFIES which claims in a draft are unsupported assertions and demands an artifact for each — the highest-value use, run as an audit pass over your own copy; (b) SUGGESTS which artifact would actually settle each claim (a log line, an export, a timestamped screenshot); (c) DRAFTS the caption that carries the provenance (tool, date, what to look at, what the caveat is); (d) WRITES ALT TEXT for the artifact, which is both an accessibility duty and an indexability gain; (e) EXTRACTS quotable attributed sentences from named sources for the citation layer; (f) REDACTION-CHECKS — vision models can scan a screenshot for names, emails, tokens, client identifiers and open browser tabs before you publish, which is a real and underused safety win. What it must NOT do: generate or edit the artifact, re-render a 'cleaner' version of a screenshot, or invent a quotation or a source. Fabricated quotations are a documented hallucination mode and this tactic's worst failure.

**automation level**

L1 (AI-assisted draft) — and the evidence-capture step is irreducibly L0. The audit pass ('which claims here lack a receipt?') and the redaction scan can be run at L2 (autonomous with guardrails) as a pre-publish gate that fails closed: no artifact, no publish. Nothing here is L3, and a tool that offers to 'generate proof visuals' is offering to fabricate evidence, which is a different activity with a different risk profile. Note for tool evaluation: most 2026 products marketed as AI social agents are L1 schedulers with a template library; none of them can supply a receipt.

**prompt patterns**

- RECEIPT AUDIT (the core pass): 'Read this draft. For every factual or performance claim, output a row: CLAIM | TYPE (first-party result / third-party fact / opinion) | RECEIPT I ALREADY HAVE | RECEIPT I WOULD NEED. Flag every claim with no possible receipt as UNSUPPORTED. Do not suggest wording improvements — only the evidence table.'
- ARTIFACT CHOOSER: 'Claim: [X]. I have access to [list of systems/exports]. Name the single smallest artifact that would let a skeptical reader verify this claim, and say exactly what should be visible in it and what should be cropped out.'
- PROVENANCE CAPTION: 'Write a 2-line caption for this screenshot. Line 1: what the reader should look at, naming the one element that proves the claim. Line 2: provenance — tool, date captured, what has been redacted and why. No adjectives, no hype.'
- REDACTION SCAN (vision): 'Examine this screenshot as if you were trying to deanonymise it. List every element that could identify a person, a client, an account, an internal URL, a token, or a document title — including browser tabs, sidebar entries, notification badges and partially visible text. Then list what must be cropped or masked.'
- QUOTATION AND CITATION PASS (GEO-informed): 'For each third-party claim in this draft, supply a direct verbatim quotation with the speaker or organisation named and the publication date, or mark it NO_SOURCE. Never paraphrase a source into a quotation. Never invent an author, a title, or a URL.'
- ANTI-FABRICATION GUARD (system-level, persistent): 'You may not produce quotations, statistics, source names, URLs or dates that I have not supplied. When a draft needs one, emit the literal token NEEDS_RECEIPT and continue. Emitting a plausible placeholder is a failure.'
- SKEPTIC SIMULATION: 'You are a hostile reader who assumes this screenshot is cherry-picked or staged. Write the three comments you would post. For each, say what additional artifact would shut it down.'

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

SPLIT, and the headline number in this item's own description needs demoting. (a) 'Evidence markers raise generative-engine visibility': MODERATE — one peer-reviewed study (GEO, KDD 2024, 10,000-query benchmark). Note the description's framing 'stats + quotes + cited sources lift generative-engine visibility up to 40%' is a compression of THREE separately measured interventions (Quotation +41%, Statistics +33%, Cite Sources +28%) into one round number; the 40% figure is the quotation result specifically, not a combined effect, and no combined-stack effect was measured. (b) 'Receipts raise social-platform reach': UNVERIFIED — no platform-official or independent large-N test isolates it; the mechanism is plausible and the direction is widely reported by practitioners, but there is no number. (c) 'Generic AI content is suppressed, so demonstrating non-genericness protects reach': MODERATE on direction (LinkedIn publicly announced quality/authenticity changes in March and May 2026), VENDOR-CLAIM on magnitude (the circulating 47% reach reduction and 94% detection accuracy figures trace to marketing blogs, not to LinkedIn engineering communications). (d) 'Verifiability increases willingness to share': ANECDOTAL as applied here — the underlying self-presentation account is peer-reviewed (Berger), but the specific receipt-to-share link is an inference, not a measured effect.

**evidence provenance**

Peer-reviewed: Aggarwal et al., GEO (KDD 2024, arXiv 2311.09735) — the only hard number in this item. Berger (Annual Review of Psychology 76, 2025) and Berger & Milkman (JMR 2012) — for the self-presentation and practical-utility mechanisms, applied by inference. Platform-official: LinkedIn's own 2026 announcements about deprioritising low-quality AI content (March and 20 May 2026) — official as to the POLICY, silent as to the magnitudes. Industry-consortium official: C2PA membership and platform behaviour (TikTok joining the C2PA steering committee 2026-07-27; Meta 'AI Info' labels; LinkedIn preserving credential chains). Government-official: FTC 2026 policy statement material (claim substantiation survives AI authorship); EU AI Act Art. 50. Vendor-with-product-to-sell: essentially all 2026 numeric claims about AI-content penalties, detection accuracy and carousel/engagement lifts — several of these blogs appear themselves AI-generated and cite each other circularly, which is a live illustration of the problem this tactic addresses. Single-creator anecdote: the entire build-in-public evidence base (Buffer, Levels, Cheung).

**effect size and n**

- GEO (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024; GEO-Bench: 10,000 queries, 8,000/1,000/1,000 split, 25 domains, 9 source datasets), relative improvement in Position-Adjusted Word Count: Quotation Addition +41%; Statistics Addition +33%; Cite Sources +28%; Fluency Optimization +29%; Authoritative tone +18%; Easy-to-Understand +14%; Technical Terms +10%; Unique Words +6%; Keyword Stuffing -9%. On Perplexity.ai, Statistics Addition +37% on Subjective Impression. Domain skew: Quotation Addition strongest in People & Society, Explanation and History; Cite Sources strongest in Statement, Facts and Law & Government.
- Semrush, Jan-Feb 2026, 325,000 prompts / 89,000 cited LinkedIn URLs across ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode and Perplexity: LinkedIn cited in ~11% of responses on average, #2 domain behind Reddit; ~95% of cited LinkedIn posts were original rather than reshares; ~59% of cited content came from individual members; median cited post carried only 15-25 reactions and at most one comment.
- LinkedIn AI-content suppression: reported ~47% organic reach reduction for generic AI content after the March 2026 authenticity update and ~94% detection accuracy — BOTH VENDOR-SOURCED AND CIRCULAR. LinkedIn has confirmed the policy direction, not these magnitudes. Do not restate them as fact.
- van der Blom Algorithm Insights 2026 (1.3M posts, 50k creators, H1 2026): reach down ~60% for active creators over two years; a reported ~80% of comments arriving in the first five minutes of his posts are AI-written — a useful proxy for how saturated the assertion layer has become.
- NO EFFECT SIZE FOUND for the central social-media claim: nobody has measured how much reach, dwell or sharing a post gains specifically from attaching a verifiable artifact. Treat the tactic as mechanism-plausible and number-free on the feed side; its only quantified benefit is the citation one.

**conflicting evidence**

- THE 40% FIGURE IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE: the research item's own description implies a combined 'stats + quotes + cited sources' lift of up to 40%. The source study measured these as SEPARATE single interventions (+41%/+33%/+28%) against a baseline, on a 2023-24 benchmark, against academic-style content — not as a stacked effect on social posts. No stacking experiment exists. The honest statement is 'each evidence marker independently improved citation visibility by roughly a quarter to two-fifths in one 2024 study', not 'receipts give you +40%'.
- CITABILITY vs VIRALITY PULL APART: Semrush's median AI-cited LinkedIn post carried 15-25 reactions. Optimising a post for extractable, attributed, evidence-dense statements can make it drier and LESS shareable. These are two objective functions and receipts serve one much better than the other.
- SCREENSHOTS ARE DEGRADING AS EVIDENCE: the same generative capability that makes receipts valuable makes screenshots forgeable, and 2026 creator-economy commentary explicitly argues that screenshotable metrics (followers, views, reach) are no longer meaningful proof. So a receipt's credibility is not intrinsic — it depends on the artifact being costly to fake (a live URL, a CI run, a third-party dashboard) rather than merely being an image. Expect this to worsen.
- TRANSPARENCY IS NOT MONOTONIC: the 2019 build-in-public norm of maximum disclosure has been explicitly revised in 2026 toward selective disclosure; more receipts is not linearly better, and over-sharing of process reads as performance rather than proof.
- THE DISCLOSURE PARADOX CUTS BOTH WAYS: disclosing AI assistance erodes perceived trustworthiness, authenticity and competence — sharpest in social and interpersonal writing — yet rich, process-level disclosure (naming the tool, the verification step, the sources) mitigates it. Receipts are process-level disclosure, so they sit on the mitigating side; but a post that foregrounds 'here is how the AI made this' can still lose more in warmth than it gains in credibility. No effect size found for the net.
- AI-vs-HUMAN PERFORMANCE REMAINS UNRESOLVED: UMinn/GPT-4 work finds LLM posts outperform human ones; a peer-reviewed within-subjects Instagram field experiment (24 alternating posts) found human posts won on likes (42.6 vs 39.6), comments (5.3 vs 2.3) and ER (6.73% vs 5.96%); a vendor study of 10,024 posts claims +31% for AI-assisted. Receipts are premised on the human-advantage side of this; that premise is not settled.
- **correction_2026_09_11_instagram_study_is_a_null_result**: CORRECTION (2026-09-11, verified against the full PDF): this file quotes raw means from Flesheriu & Fron (2025), Oeconomica Jadertina 2/2025, DOI 10.15291/oec.4845 (likes 42.58 vs 39.58, comments 5.33 vs 2.33, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%). The means are accurate but NONE of the differences is statistically significant: Mann-Whitney U gives likes p=.91, comments p=.07, shares p=.17, saves p=.79, reach p=.89, impressions p=.51, ER p=.64. The paper states 'H1 was not supported' and concludes EQUIVALENCE, not human superiority. Dropping one launch-day outlier flips ER in the AI direction (5.95% vs 5.79%); readers significantly PREFERRED the AI-written captions (U=8.0, p=.045); and 7 of the 12 top-performing posts were AI. Scope limits that further weaken it as evidence about AI TEXT: a single account with 770 followers, 24 alternating posts, a culinary niche, and AI-generated IMAGERY bundled with the caption - the authors attribute 64% of engagement to the visual. Do not cite this study as showing that human-written posts outperform AI-written posts.

**sources**

- Aggarwal, P., Murahari, V., Rajpurohit, T., Kalyan, A., Narasimhan, K. & Deshpande, A. (2024), 'GEO: Generative Engine Optimization', KDD 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735 (HTML: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2311.09735v3) — [peer-reviewed] — source of the +41%/+33%/+28% figures and of the authors' own decay caveat.
- Berger, J. (2025), 'What Gets Shared, and Why? Interpersonal Communication and Word of Mouth', Annual Review of Psychology 76:559-581 — https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-psych-013024-031524 — [peer-reviewed] — self-presentation and audience moderators.
- Berger, J. & Milkman, K. (2012), 'What Makes Online Content Viral?', JMR — https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1509/jmr.10.0353 — [peer-reviewed] — practical utility and surprise as independent transmission drivers.
- Semrush AI-citation study coverage (325k prompts / 89k LinkedIn URLs, Jan-Feb 2026) — https://almcorp.com/blog/linkedin-ai-search-citations-2026/ ; https://blendin.ai/blog/linkedin-ai-search-citations ; https://blog.mean.ceo/startup-news-leveraging-89k-linkedin-urls-for-ai-visibility-2026/ — [independent large-N, vendor-produced; accessed via secondary coverage].
- Neil Patel, 'LinkedIn Is Suppressing AI Slop: What That Means for You' — https://neilpatel.com/blog/linkedin-ai-slop-crackdown-content-strategy/ — [vendor-with-product-to-sell] — useful for the mechanism description (behavioural scoring, not AI classification), not for magnitudes.
- SocialNexis, 'LinkedIn's originality scoring and what low-signal posts cost' — https://socialnexis.com/guides/linkedin-ai-originality-reach-penalty — [vendor-with-product-to-sell] — origin-class example of the circulating 47% figure.
- ZoomSphere, 'LinkedIn Algorithm 2026: Why Generic AI Content Kills Your Organic Reach' — https://www.zoomsphere.com/blog/linkedin-algorithm-2026-why-generic-ai-content-kills-your-organic-reach — [vendor-with-product-to-sell].
- Richard van der Blom, Algorithm Insights 2026 (1.3M posts / 50k creators) — https://richardvanderblom.com/ ; summary https://podcast.creatorscience.com/richard-van-der-blom-2/ — [independent large-N, self-published].
- buildinpublic.so, 'Build in Public — The 2026 Definitive Guide' — https://www.buildinpublic.so/blog/build-in-public — [vendor/community] — history (Buffer Open Startup 2013, Levels' public revenue dashboards) and the 2026 shift from maximum to selective transparency.
- Yahoo Finance / creator-economy commentary, '2026: Transparency Becomes a New Standard in the Creator Economy' — https://finance.yahoo.com/news/2026-transparency-becomes-standard-creator-090000982.html — [trade press] — the 'screenshotable metrics are not meaningful' argument.
- FTC, 'Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems' (Federal Register, 2026-07-07) — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/07/2026-13628/policy-statement-concerning-the-suppression-of-accuracy-in-artificial-intelligence-systems — [government-official]; related analysis on advertiser substantiation liability: https://kr.law/news/article-detail/ai-marketing-claims-come-under-ftc-scrutiny — [law-firm commentary].
- influencers-time, 'AI Hallucination Detection Protocol for Creator Briefs' — https://www.influencers-time.com/ai-hallucination-detection-protocol-for-creator-briefs/ — [vendor] — catalogue of invented-statistic and invented-certification patterns.
- Vault cross-reference (do not re-derive): 'BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/INFO/Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026' (dwell-time primacy, saves weighting, engagement-bait throttling, generic-AI reach limiting) and 'PROJECTS/AGENTIC-SYSTEMS/Marketing Agent Research.md' (anti-slop gate, LLM-as-judge rubrics, HITL approval).

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

BEST: LinkedIn — dwell-dominant ranking, an audience that inspects screenshots, and an explicit 2026 penalty for perspective-free content that receipts directly counter; deliver as a text post with one annotated screenshot, or as a document post where each slide is a different artifact. STRONG: X/Twitter — the native home of the receipt ('here's the log'), especially in build-in-public and dev communities; a single legible screenshot is the whole post. STRONG: Reddit — receipts are close to mandatory; an unsupported claim in a technical subreddit gets dismantled, and a well-documented one earns disproportionate engagement (Reddit is also the #1 AI-cited domain, so the citation upside is real). GOOD: GitHub/dev.to/Hacker News for engineering artifacts. CONDITIONAL: Instagram — works as a carousel where slides 2-4 are artifacts, but the audience skews toward aesthetic consistency and a raw dashboard screenshot fights the grid. BACKFIRES: TikTok and Shorts — a static screenshot is a retention killer; the native equivalent is screen-recording the thing happening, not photographing the result. BACKFIRES ALSO: any context where the artifact is unreadable at phone width (a full-screen spreadsheet), and any context where it exposes a client. Cross-reference the vault note above for per-platform ranking mechanics.

**scales with**

Capped by ARTIFACT SUPPLY, which is capped by how much verifiable work you actually do — the tactic is self-limiting by design and that is precisely why it is a credible signal. Secondary caps: CONFIDENTIALITY (the most compelling artifacts are usually client-owned and unpublishable), REDACTION LABOUR (every screenshot is a data-leak surface, and this cost does not fall with scale), and LEGIBILITY (an artifact must survive phone-width viewing, which caps how complex it can be). Does NOT scale with team size or tooling — an agency cannot buy receipts. Ceilings diverge by objective: for AI CITATION there is effectively no account-size floor (sub-500-follower creators are cited comparably), while for VIRALITY the normal network-position ceiling applies. For a solo creator the binding constraint is almost always 'I did not capture the screenshot at the time' — which is a workflow problem, not a content problem.

**decay and saturation**

The PRINCIPLE (evidence beats assertion) does not decay. The IMPLEMENTATION decays on two clocks. (1) 12-24 months: the screenshot specifically. Image generation and editing have made a static screenshot cheap to fake, and 2026 commentary already argues that screenshotable metrics prove nothing; expect audiences to discount bare screenshots and to reward artifacts that are expensive to fake — a live URL, a public repo, a third-party dashboard, a CI run, a signed document, a named person willing to be quoted. Migrate up that ladder over time. (2) 6-12 months: the anti-slop DIFFERENTIATION value. Receipts are currently a strong non-slop signal because most AI-assisted posts have none; as the practice spreads (and as tools start auto-attaching decorative 'proof' visuals), the signal weakens toward baseline and becomes table stakes rather than an edge. NOT decaying: the citation value of named sources and verbatim quotations, which is structural to how answer engines assemble responses.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- The artifact does not actually support the claim — a dashboard screenshot showing a spike next to a claim about revenue. Readers check; the mismatch is worse than no artifact.
- Unreadable at phone width — a full spreadsheet or a 200-line log. If nothing is circled, nothing is proven.
- Too clean to be true — a perfect chart with no bad week reads as staged, especially in 2026.
- Cherry-picked window with the axis cropped. This is the most common dishonest form and the easiest to catch.
- Receipts substituting for a point — a wall of artifacts and no thesis; evidence is not an argument.
- Confidentiality leak: a client name in a sidebar, an internal URL, a notification badge, an open tab, a token in a terminal. Irreversible the moment it is posted.
- Fabricated or mis-attributed quotations and sources introduced by the model. This is the failure that destroys the tactic's entire premise, and it is a documented hallucination pattern.
- Metric theatre — using reach/followers/views as the receipt, which the 2026 audience explicitly discounts.
- Receipt fatigue — every post carrying proof of something trivial; the signal inflates and stops meaning anything.
- Optimising so hard for extractable, attributed statements that the post becomes a dry citation stack nobody wants to read.

**ai slop risk**

LOW for the artifact itself (a model cannot produce your real screenshot) and HIGH for the surrounding text, in a specific and dangerous way: this is the format most likely to tempt a model into INVENTING a supporting quotation, source, URL, author or date, because the draft has an obvious evidence-shaped hole and models fill holes. Fabricated citations are among the best-documented hallucination modes, and a fake citation inside a post whose whole claim is 'I show my evidence' is a self-destructing artifact. THE TELLS: (1) a quotation with no nameable speaker and no date; (2) a source cited as 'a recent study' or 'research from [big institution]' with no title; (3) a plausible-looking URL that 404s; (4) an artifact described in the caption but not actually visible in the image; (5) captions written in generic marketing register ('the results speak for themselves') rather than in the flat, specific register real evidence invites; (6) every cited source conveniently agreeing. MITIGATION: the persistent ANTI-FABRICATION GUARD prompt (model emits NEEDS_RECEIPT rather than a plausible placeholder), a human click-through on every URL before publishing, and treating any model-supplied quotation as unusable until verified against the original.

**human input required**

NON-SUBSTITUTABLE and unusually explicit: the human must (a) HAVE DONE the work the artifact records; (b) CAPTURE the artifact at the time — this is a workflow habit, not a writing step, and it is where the tactic usually fails; (c) DECIDE what may lawfully and ethically be shown, including the confidentiality call; (d) PERFORM THE REDACTION and take responsibility for what leaks; (e) VERIFY every third-party quotation and source by opening it. As a checkable gate before publishing: 'name the artifact, say where it came from, and open the source' — if any of the three fails, the post is an assertion wearing evidence costume and must be reframed as opinion. This gate is also, in effect, what the platform quality classifiers are probing for.

**policy and legal**

Assume a Poland/EU-based creator. (1) GDPR IS THE DOMINANT RISK HERE, more than for any other item in this table: a screenshot is a data-disclosure surface. Client names, employee names, email addresses, user IDs, avatars, chat content and internal document titles are personal data; publishing them without a lawful basis is a breach regardless of how small the audience. Redact by default, aggregate small cells, and remember that blurring is reversible if done badly — mask with solid blocks. (2) CONFIDENTIALITY AND CONTRACT: NDAs and MSAs commonly forbid disclosing engagement details, metrics or even the client's identity; written permission before publishing a client artifact, every time. (3) EU AI ACT ART. 50 — in force since 2026-08-02, grace period to 2026-12-02 for pre-existing systems, fines up to EUR 15M or 3% of worldwide turnover: AI-generated TEXT on matters of public interest requires disclosure unless it underwent human editorial review with a responsible person or organisation — a receipts-based post with a human verification gate sits inside that exemption; an AI-generated IMAGE depicting a real person or a realistic scene triggers deepfake transparency duties, which is a further reason never to generate a 'proof' visual. (4) SUBSTANTIATION: you remain liable for claims regardless of AI authorship (FTC restated this in 2026; EU/Polish unfair-commercial-practices law reaches misleading business claims equivalently). (5) COPYRIGHT AND PLATFORM ToS: screenshotting third-party UIs and quoting others' posts is generally defensible as quotation/reporting but is not unlimited — quote a bounded excerpt with attribution, and check the ToS before screenshotting paywalled or gated tools.

**reversibility and blast radius**

Bimodal. Platform-side: NEGLIGIBLE — receipts do not trigger shadowbans, comment restrictions or suspensions; they are the opposite of the behaviour platforms police. Content-side: LOW and recoverable — a misread chart is fixed with a correction post and usually nets out positive. CONFIDENTIALITY-SIDE: SEVERE AND IRREVERSIBLE — a published screenshot is archived, screenshotted back, cached and potentially ingested by crawlers within minutes; deleting the post does not unpublish the data. The realistic worst cases are a lost client, a contractual claim, a GDPR complaint to UODO, and reputational damage that is worse than any algorithmic penalty because it attaches to the one asset this tactic exists to build — trust. A fabricated receipt is the other unrecoverable case: it converts your credibility play into the proof of its opposite. Mitigation is entirely pre-publish: the redaction scan and the permission check are the only controls that work, because there is no post-publish remedy.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- STEP 0 — INSTALL THE CAPTURE HABIT (one-off): the binding constraint is that artifacts must be captured at the moment the work happens. Set up a single 'receipts' folder, bind a screenshot hotkey, and capture the before-state as reflexively as the after-state. Nothing downstream works without this.
- STEP 1 — WRITE THE CLAIM FIRST (10 min): one sentence, specific and falsifiable. If it cannot be false, it needs no receipt and is not this kind of post.
- STEP 2 — RUN THE RECEIPT AUDIT (10 min): the audit prompt over the draft. Every claim gets a row. Anything marked UNSUPPORTED is either cut, downgraded to explicit opinion ('my read is…'), or held until you can evidence it.
- STEP 3 — CHOOSE THE SMALLEST SUFFICIENT ARTIFACT (10 min): the one screenshot, log line or export that settles the claim. Prefer artifacts that are expensive to fake — a live URL, a public commit, a third-party dashboard — over ones that are merely images.
- STEP 4 — CROP, ANNOTATE, REDACT (15 min, non-generative tools only): crop to the claim; circle or arrow the one element that proves it; solid-block every name, address, ID, token, internal URL, tab title and notification. Never use a generative 'clean up' or 'expand' feature on a receipt.
- STEP 5 — RUN THE VISION REDACTION SCAN (5 min): ask a vision model to deanonymise your own screenshot. Fix whatever it finds. This step catches the sidebar entry you stopped seeing months ago.
- STEP 6 — CHECK PERMISSION (5 min): if any client, employer or third party is identifiable or inferable, get written permission or genericise until they are not.
- STEP 7 — WRITE THE PROVENANCE CAPTION (10 min): what to look at, then tool/date/what-was-redacted. Flat register, no adjectives. Add alt text describing the artifact — accessibility duty plus indexability gain.
- STEP 8 — ADD THE CITATION LAYER (10 min): for every third-party fact, a named source and, where it carries weight, a verbatim quotation with speaker and date. Open every URL yourself. This is the step that does double duty as GEO.
- STEP 9 — INCLUDE ONE INCONVENIENT FACT (5 min): the flat week, the failed variant, the caveat. It is the highest-credibility sentence in the post and the one no model would have volunteered.
- STEP 10 — RUN THE SKEPTIC SIMULATION (10 min): three hostile comments, and either pre-empt them in the post or hold the answers ready for the comment thread, where they become the long substantive replies that drive distribution.
- STEP 11 — PUBLISH AND STAFF THE THREAD (ongoing): answer artifact questions with specifics in the first 30-60 minutes; van der Blom's 2026 data associates replying within 30 minutes with substantially more comments and views. Keep external links out of the post body.
- STEP 12 — MAINTAIN A CORRECTION PROTOCOL: if an artifact is later shown to be wrong or misread, correct in a new top-level post naming the error. Silent edits are the reputational failure, not the original mistake.

**checklist**

- PASS/FAIL — Does the artifact ACTUALLY demonstrate the specific claim, or merely sit near it?
- PASS/FAIL — Is the proving element legible and marked at phone width?
- PASS/FAIL — Redaction scan run and clean: no names, emails, IDs, tokens, internal URLs, tab titles, notification badges, document titles?
- PASS/FAIL — Do I have the right to publish this artifact (client permission / employer policy / GDPR basis)?
- PASS/FAIL — Did any part of the artifact pass through a GENERATIVE editor? (If yes: recapture. Non-negotiable.)
- PASS/FAIL — Caption carries provenance: tool, date captured, what was redacted?
- PASS/FAIL — Every third-party quotation is verbatim, attributed to a named speaker with a date, and I opened the source myself?
- PASS/FAIL — Zero model-supplied statistics, sources or URLs survive unverified in the final text?
- PASS/FAIL — Does the post contain at least one inconvenient or unflattering fact?
- PASS/FAIL — Is there a thesis, not just a pile of evidence?
- PASS/FAIL — Alt text written for every artifact?
- PASS/FAIL — Would I be comfortable if the subject of this screenshot read the post? (If no: stop.)

#### measurement

**ai search citability**

VERY HIGH — and this is the item where the citation case is strongest and best evidenced. The GEO study (KDD 2024) measured exactly this family of interventions and found the largest single lifts of any technique tested: Quotation Addition +41%, Statistics Addition +33%, Cite Sources +28% (against Keyword Stuffing at -9%), with the citation-style gains concentrated in Statement/Facts/Law & Government and quotation gains in People & Society/Explanation/History. Mechanistically an answer engine needs extractable, attributable, self-contained statements, and a receipts-dense post supplies them by construction. Semrush's 2026 LinkedIn analysis reinforces the fit: ~95% of cited posts are original rather than reshares, ~59% of citations go to individual members, there is effectively no follower floor, and the median cited post has only 15-25 reactions — which is both the opportunity and the warning. TWO CAVEATS: the +40%-class numbers are single-study, two years old, measured on academic-style content, and were never tested as a stacked combination; and optimising for extractability trades against warmth, so the citation-optimised version of a post is often the less shareable one. Practical move: put the artifact-backed claim, its source and its date in the SAME sentence, publish a long-form version for the durable surface, and treat the feed post as its promotion.

#### omitted as uncertain

- audience fit
- cost and time to execute
- detectability and disclosure
- kpis and leading indicators
- measurement feasibility
- prompt artifact link
- tool examples
- worked example

## D. Virality science and constraints

### AI citation visibility as a second objective function

`ai-citation-visibility-vs-virality` · automation L1 · evidence STRONG · 12 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: AI citation visibility as a second objective function
- **category**: science
- **definition**: Treating 'gets retrieved and quoted by ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode and Perplexity' as a distinct optimization target with its own reward function, its own winning formats and its own scaling law — rather than as a downstream benefit of posts that already perform well on engagement.
- **maturity**: emerging as a practice, established as a mechanism. The structural half (what makes a passage citable) has peer-reviewed evidence from KDD 2024. The distributional half (which platforms and which posts actually get cited in 2026) is a single large vendor study plus a handful of unreviewed preprints.
- **the claim in one line**: The median LinkedIn post cited by an AI engine has 15-25 reactions and fewer than one comment. If that is true, citation selection is close to orthogonal to engagement, and optimizing for one does not get you the other.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **the two layer model**: Answer engines have a parametric layer (entity associations baked into weights — slow, consensus-built) and a retrieval layer (live fetch per query — fast, freshness-driven). Social posts act almost entirely on the retrieval layer. You are not trying to be remembered; you are trying to be FETCHED and then QUOTED.
- **the pipeline a post passes through**:
  - 1. INDEXABILITY. The engine's crawler must be able to read the post. This is a platform property, not a content property, and it is why LinkedIn and Reddit dominate while closed platforms do not appear at all. You inherit your platform's indexability; you cannot improve it.
  - 2. RETRIEVAL. A query fires; the engine fetches candidate documents. Semantic relevance to the query decides candidacy. Semrush measured LinkedIn's semantic similarity to cited queries at 0.57-0.60 against Reddit's 0.53-0.54 and Quora's 0.435 — LinkedIn content is, on that measure, a tighter semantic match to the queries it gets pulled into.
  - 3. CHUNKING. The document is split. This is where most social content dies: a post whose meaning depends on the hook two paragraphs above, or on a thread's context, does not survive chunking as a self-contained claim.
  - 4. SELECTION AND WEIGHTING. The synthesiser decides which chunks to lean on. THIS is the step Aggarwal et al. measured, and it is the only step with peer-reviewed causal evidence attached.
  - 5. QUOTATION AND ATTRIBUTION. The chunk is paraphrased or quoted and a citation is emitted. Zero-click by construction — the value is the named mention, not the traffic.
- **what the geo paper actually did**: GEO-Bench: 10,000 queries split 8K/1K/1K across nine source datasets and 25 domains, preserving a real-world mix (~80% informational, 10% transactional, 10% navigational), each query augmented with the cleaned text of the top five Google results. The generative engine was SIMULATED: fetch top-5, then GPT-3.5-turbo synthesises an answer, five samples at temperature 0.7. Nine content modifications were applied one at a time to a randomly selected source, and impression measured two ways — Position-Adjusted Word Count (how much of the answer comes from your source and how prominently) and Subjective Impression (seven sub-metrics scored by GPT-3.5 via G-Eval).
- **the headline mechanism**: Adding evidence-shaped material to a passage — a direct quotation, a concrete statistic, an explicit source attribution — makes a synthesiser lean on that passage more, without the passage saying anything new. The paper's own qualitative examples are blunt about this: a Swiss-chocolate passage gained 132.4% visibility purely by appending '(According to a survey conducted by The International Chocolate Consumption Research Group)'. The mechanism is credibility signalling to a model, and it is cheap.
- **the distribution side**: Semrush ran 325,000 unique prompts through ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode and Perplexity in January-February 2026 and extracted 89,000 unique LinkedIn URLs from the responses. LinkedIn came out as the second most-cited domain overall at ~11% of responses on average — 14.3% on ChatGPT Search, 13.5% on Google AI Mode, 5.3% on Perplexity. Within LinkedIn, articles (500-2,000 words) took 50-66% of citations and feed posts (50-299 words) 15-28%; 95% of cited posts were original rather than reshares; 54-64% were knowledge-sharing or practical-advice in intent.
- **the finding that makes it a second objective function**: The median cited LinkedIn post carried 15-25 reactions and fewer than one comment. That is at or below ordinary baseline engagement. Whatever the retrieval stack is selecting on, it is not the engagement signal — which means the two objectives can be pursued separately, and a post can succeed completely at one while failing at the other.

**why it drives reach**

- **it drives a different thing than reach**: Citation is not distribution in the feed sense. There is no follower graph, no in-network path and no accumulation: 100% of it is query-triggered discovery, and it is overwhelmingly zero-click. What it produces is a NAMED MENTION inside the answer a buyer is reading at the moment of evaluation.
- **the causal story**:
  - A prospect asks an answer engine a question inside your domain rather than running a search. The engine synthesises and cites. Your name or your company appears as the attributed source of the specific claim the prospect just accepted as true.
  - That is a categorically different event from a feed impression: pre-qualified (they asked), high-intent (they are researching), and endorsed (the engine chose you as evidence). It converts without a click.
  - It also compounds in a way feed reach does not. A feed post's half-life on LinkedIn is roughly 24-72 hours. A cited article stays in the retrievable corpus and can be re-cited for every future matching query — and LinkedIn's own 2026 change to resurface older posts by semantic relevance pushes in the same direction.
- **the zero sum warning nobody quotes**: Aggarwal et al. Table 2 measures what happens when EVERY source optimizes simultaneously, broken down by the source's own search rank. The pattern reverses by position: Cite Sources moves a rank-5 source +115.1% and a rank-1 source -30.3%. Quotation Addition: rank-5 +99.7%, rank-1 -22.9%. Statistics: rank-5 +97.9%, rank-1 -20.6%. So GEO is a redistribution mechanism, not a pure expansion — it transfers visibility from established high-rank sources to lower-ranked ones. For a small creator that is the whole opportunity. It also means the advantage shrinks as adoption spreads, which is the decay mechanism for this entire entry.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **draft**: Generate the answer-shaped version of a claim you already hold. The model is good at the transformation 'take this paragraph and make it self-contained, claim-first, with the evidence attached' and bad at supplying the evidence. Keep that division absolute.
- **critique**: The highest-value role here. Ask a model to read a draft as a RETRIEVER would: 'If this post were chunked into 150-word passages, would any single passage answer the question <Q> without the rest? Quote the passage or state that none does.' That is a checkable, mechanical critique and it catches the most common failure (meaning distributed across the whole post).
- **score**: Approximate the GEO interventions as a rubric: does the passage contain a direct quotation, a concrete statistic with its source, an explicit attribution? Three booleans, no LLM judgement required for two of them. Do NOT build an LLM-as-judge 'citability score' — the GEO paper's own Subjective Impression metric was GPT-3.5 scoring GPT-3.5 output via G-Eval, which is exactly the circularity to avoid reproducing.
- **retrieve**: Pull the actual numbers from your own corpus so the statistics being added are yours. This is the step that separates a legitimate evidence-density improvement from fabrication, and it is where a vault-grounded RAG setup earns its keep.
- **vary**: Generate multiple query phrasings a prospect might use, then check whether your passage answers each one. Cheap, and it directly targets the semantic-match step.
- **what the model must not do**: Invent statistics or attributions. The GEO mechanism rewards the APPEARANCE of evidence, which is precisely why it is dangerous to automate: a model asked to 'add a supporting statistic' will produce one. Every number must resolve to a source you can name, or the tactic degrades into machine-generated misinformation that happens to rank.

**automation level**

- **level**: L1 for the writing, L2 for the checking.
- **detail**: The structural transformation (claim-first, self-contained, evidence attached) is an AI-assisted draft step with a human supplying the substance — L1. The verification (does every number resolve to a source? does any single chunk stand alone?) is a deterministic-enough gate to run unattended — L2. Monitoring (running your prompt set weekly across engines and logging where you appear) is fully automatable — L2 with guardrails, since the output is a log rather than a publication.
- **nothing here is L3**: The non-substitutable input is the proprietary fact. A fully autonomous citation-optimization loop would have to generate its own evidence, which is the failure mode, not the goal.
- **vendor label warning**: The 2026 'AI visibility' tool category (Profound, Peec, Otterly, Scrunch and the rest) is monitoring, not optimization — they tell you where you are cited. That is genuinely useful and is not what the marketing implies. None of them is an agent that improves your citability; they are dashboards with a prompt scheduler.

**prompt patterns**

- **patterns**:
  - **name**: Query-first inversion | **shape**: Here is a claim I can support: <claim>. List the 8 distinct questions a practitioner would type into ChatGPT or Perplexity that this claim is a correct and complete answer to. Phrase them as real users type, not as keywords. Then pick the ONE question my claim answers most completely, and write a 120-180 word passage that answers exactly that question, claim first, with my evidence attached in the first three sentences. | **why**: Inverts the normal drafting order. You are not writing a post that happens to be citable; you are writing the answer to a specific retrievable query. The 'pick ONE' constraint is what forces self-containment — a passage trying to answer three questions answers none of them completely enough to be lifted.
  - **name**: Chunk-survival test | **shape**: Split this draft into passages of roughly 150 words at natural boundaries. For EACH passage, answer: (a) does it state a complete claim without depending on any other passage; (b) does it carry at least one concrete number, named source or direct quotation; (c) if a retrieval system returned only this passage, what question would it be a good answer to. Mark any passage that fails (a) or (b). | **why**: This is the single highest-leverage prompt in the entry. It simulates the chunking step that most social writing fails at, and it produces a specific, fixable list rather than a score.
  - **name**: GEO intervention pass, applied honestly | **shape**: Apply exactly these three modifications to the passage, and refuse any you cannot do truthfully: (1) QUOTATION — add a direct quote from a named person with the attribution inline; (2) STATISTICS — add one concrete figure with its source and date; (3) CITE SOURCES — attribute each factual claim to where it came from. For each modification you SKIP, state why the truthful version is unavailable. Do not invent a quote, a number or a source under any circumstances. | **why**: These are the three top-performing interventions in GEO-Bench (Quotation ~+41%, Statistics ~+31%, Cite Sources ~+28% on Position-Adjusted Word Count against the no-optimization baseline). The 'refuse and explain' clause is load-bearing — without it this prompt is a fabrication engine, because the model can always satisfy the request by making something up.
  - **name**: Keyword-stuffing removal | **shape**: This draft was written with SEO habits. Remove every instance of keyword repetition that does not serve the sentence. Report what you removed. Then confirm the passage still contains the query's core terms once each, naturally placed. | **why**: Keyword Stuffing was the only GEO-Bench modification that scored BELOW the unoptimized baseline. Legacy SEO instinct is actively counterproductive here, and it is the habit most likely to be imported by anyone with search-marketing background.
  - **name**: Dual-objective split brief | **shape**: I have one piece of substance: <substance>. Produce TWO separate artifacts, and do not compromise either toward the other. (A) A LinkedIn feed post optimized for engagement: hook, tension, rhythm, a reason to comment. (B) A 700-1,200 word article optimized for citation: claim-first sections, one question answered per section, every claim sourced, no hook, no narrative. Then state in one line what each one gives up. | **why**: The operational consequence of the whole entry. Trying to serve both objectives in one artifact produces a post that is too structured to be engaging and too narrative to be chunked. Two artifacts from one substance costs perhaps 20 extra minutes and serves both functions properly.

**tool examples**

- **monitoring**:
  - Profound — the largest independent dataset in this space (~700,000 social citations extracted from ChatGPT response URLs, Oct-Dec 2025, US English). Vendor, but the method is disclosed.
  - Semrush AI visibility tracking — the vendor behind the 325K-prompt study; the study exists to sell the tool, which is the standard caveat.
  - Peec AI, Otterly.ai, Scrunch — the 2026 monitoring tool cohort. All do the same thing: run a fixed prompt set across engines on a schedule and diff the citations.
- **diy alternative**: A weekly scripted run of 30-50 priority prompts across ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode, logging cited domains and URLs. This is what every tool in the category does; at a personal-brand scale the DIY version costs an afternoon plus API fees and avoids a subscription. Recommended over buying, until the prompt set exceeds a few hundred.
- **for indexability**: Bing Webmaster Tools (feeds ChatGPT Search and Copilot) and Google Search Console — relevant for owned properties, irrelevant for LinkedIn content where you inherit the platform's indexability.
- **for the content side**: No special tooling. The GEO interventions are writing decisions, not tool outputs. Anything sold as a 'GEO optimizer' in 2026 is a prompt wrapper around the three interventions in this entry.

#### evidence

**evidence provenance**

- **peer reviewed**: Aggarwal, Murahari, Rajpurohit, Kalyan, Narasimhan, Deshpande — 'GEO: Generative Engine Optimization', KDD '24 (ACM SIGKDD, Barcelona, Aug 25-29 2024). Read from the paper PDF directly, including Tables 1-5 and Section 5.3, not from a secondary summary.
- **vendor with product to sell**: Semrush (Margarita Loktionova, published 2026-03-10) — large-N, disclosed method, direct commercial interest in the conclusion that AI visibility is trackable and worth paying to track. Profound — same category, independent dataset, same caveat.
- **vendor without disclosed method**: Cloro's 'LinkedIn article citations fell 65% in six months' — no method published. Included specifically as the contrary datapoint on volatility, not as a finding.
- **preprint not peer reviewed**: arXiv 2603.29979 (GEO-SFE, structural features, +17.3% citation rate across six engines, submitted 2026-03-31); arXiv 2604.25707 (citation-selection to citation-absorption measurement framework); arXiv 2603.09296 (diagnosing and repairing citation failures).
- **internal compiled**: content/BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/INFO/Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026.md §12 — orientation for index dependencies and the zero-click framing.
- **notable absence**: No PLATFORM-OFFICIAL source exists for any of this. Neither OpenAI, Google nor Perplexity publishes citation-selection criteria or source-share statistics. Every distribution number in this entry is reconstructed from the outside by companies selling visibility tools. That is the structural weakness of the whole field and it will not improve.
