#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **cross reference**: Ranking mechanics per platform live in content/BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/INFO/Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026.md. Only the citation layer is covered here.
- **linkedin**: The best-evidenced surface for this objective. #2 cited domain at ~11% of responses. Within LinkedIn the format ordering is unambiguous and inverse to feed intuition: ARTICLES (500-2,000 words) take 50-66% of citations, feed POSTS (50-299 words) 15-28%. Newsletters and Pulse articles are effectively evergreen and searchable. If citation is the objective, the article is the artifact and the feed post is the promotion for it.
- **reddit**: The #1 cited domain by broad agreement, and structurally advantaged by content licensing (Google and OpenAI both pay Reddit). Genuine, on-culture answers in relevant subreddits are the highest-citation-per-hour writing available anywhere — and the least compatible with a personal brand, since Reddit punishes promotion and the citation attaches to a pseudonymous comment.
- **youtube**: Transcript-rich structured video gets cited; chapters matter disproportionately (per the vault note, only ~31% of AI-cited videos have chapters — a large and cheap opportunity gap).
- **x threads bluesky**: Poor citation surfaces. Short, context-dependent, and on X the index access is restricted. Almost nothing in this entry transfers.
- **instagram tiktok**: Effectively zero for text-based citation. Captions are short and the substance is in the video.
- **your own site**: The format nobody in the social-first framing mentions, and the one you actually control. An article on your own domain is indexable, refreshable, citation-attributable to YOU rather than to a platform, and immune to a platform's share collapsing 65% in six months. The strongest version of this strategy publishes the article on an owned property and the promotion on LinkedIn.
- **format summary**: Long-form, educational, self-contained, evidence-dense, original (not reshared), on an indexable platform. Note how little that overlaps with the viral-post format: hook, tension, brevity, narrative, emotional payload. The two format specs conflict at nearly every point, which is the practical content of the 'second objective function' claim.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- **fabricated evidence**: The dominant failure and the one the mechanism actively invites. The interventions reward the presence of a statistic and a source; a model asked to add them will comply. The result is a passage optimized to be cited AND wrong, with your name attached as the attributed source in someone else's answer.
- **optimizing the wrong artifact**: Applying the interventions to a 200-word feed post. Feed posts take 15-28% of LinkedIn's AI citations; articles take 50-66%. Structuring a short post for citability makes it stiff and worse at its actual job without materially improving its citation odds.
- **chasing both objectives in one post**: Produces the characteristic 2026 failure: a post with a hook it does not earn, headings it does not need, a statistic that interrupts the narrative, and no emotional payload. Too structured to engage, too narrative to chunk. Split the artifact.
- **importing seo habits**: Keyword stuffing is the only tested intervention that scores BELOW the unoptimized baseline. Anyone arriving from search marketing will do this by reflex.
- **measuring by traffic**: Citation is zero-click by construction — up to ~93% of AI Mode sessions end without a visit. Judging this objective by referral traffic will show it failing while it works.
- **platform concentration**: Building the whole strategy on LinkedIn's ~11% share. It is a share of someone else's retrieval mix, measured over two months, and it can move 65% in six.
- **invisible stagnation**: Because you cannot observe citation without deliberately checking, a strategy that stopped working six months ago looks identical to one that is working. The monitoring loop is not optional here — it is the only sensory organ this objective has.

**ai slop risk**

- **risk level**: HIGH, and structurally so — higher than for any engagement tactic, because the reward function is satisfiable by counterfeit.
- **why it is worse here**: Engagement tactics fail visibly when the content is empty: nobody comments. Citation tactics can SUCCEED with empty content, because the retrieval stack is reading for the SHAPE of evidence, not verifying the evidence. A fabricated statistic with a plausible attribution is, to the selection step, indistinguishable from a real one. That is a reward-hacking surface, and the 2026 web is visibly full of content that has already found it.
- **the specific tells**:
  - Statistics with no named source, no date and no n. 'Studies show 73% of B2B buyers...' — the canonical form, and it is nearly always synthetic.
  - Attribution to a plausible-sounding organisation that does not exist. Note that the GEO paper's own best qualitative example is literally '(According to a survey conducted by The International Chocolate Consumption Research Group)' — a fictional body, used illustratively by the authors, and a perfect demonstration of how cheaply the signal can be counterfeited.
  - Quotations attributed to a well-known figure with no source, date or context.
  - Uniform section structure across every post — the fingerprint of a template, and the thing YouTube's Inauthentic Content Policy names directly as mass-produced and low-variation.
  - Round numbers. Real data is 1,247 and 23.4%; synthetic data is 1,000 and 25%.
- **the gate that actually works**: Every number resolves to a source you can name, with a date and a sample size, and you can produce the source on demand. Not 'the model said it came from somewhere'. This is a mechanical, checkable gate and it is the single most important control in this entry.
- **the second order risk**: If enough people reward-hack this, engines will add source-quality discounting and the honest practitioners lose the advantage alongside the dishonest ones. The tragedy-of-the-commons dynamic is already visible in how fast 2026 GEO content degraded.

**human input required**

- **the non substitutable contribution**: THE EVIDENCE ITSELF. A number from your own work, a quote from a conversation you actually had, a named case with a real outcome, a date you can defend. The model can structure all of it and supply none of it, and the gap between those two facts is the whole risk profile of this entry.
- **why this is a harder gate than elsewhere**: For engagement tactics the human contribution is a judgement call about tone or timing — real, but soft. Here the human contribution is a verifiable fact with provenance, which is binary: either the number came from somewhere you can name, or the post is a fabrication dressed as research. There is no partial credit.
- **the second contribution**: The DECISION about which claim is worth defending. Citation attaches your name to a specific assertion in front of a stranger who will act on it. That is an editorial and reputational judgement, not a formatting one.
- **the checkable gate**: For each factual claim in the draft: name the source, the date, and the n. Three fields, all mandatory, none of which an LLM can fill truthfully on its own. If any field is empty, the claim is cut — not softened, cut.
- **what the engines are effectively probing for**: Exactly this. The retrieval stack cannot verify your statistic, but the humans who read the cited answer can, and the reputational feedback loop runs through them. Over a long enough horizon, verifiable evidence is the only version of this strategy that survives contact with its own audience.
- **the art 50 connection**: For content on matters of public interest, human review with editorial responsibility is also the legal basis for the labeling exemption. The gate that makes the content honest and the gate that makes it compliant are the same gate.

**policy and legal**

- **jurisdiction assumed**: Poland / EU creator.
- **eu ai act article 50**: Applies from 2026-08-02, with a grace period to 2026-12-02 for marking obligations on systems placed on the market before August and no retroactive labeling of earlier content. The deployer duty relevant here is Art. 50(4): AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be labeled UNLESS it underwent human review or editorial control with a person holding editorial responsibility. The Commission FAQ defines that as substantive examination by a knowledgeable person, with authority to approve, alter or reject — spell-checking does not qualify. Most B2B commercial content is outside the obligation on subject-matter grounds; content on health, environment, politics, justice, migration or consumer safety is inside it.
- **deployer status**: The Commission FAQ excludes purely personal, non-professional use — but states that regular economic benefit, or business/freelance activity, makes you a deployer. A consultant publishing to generate leads is a deployer. Penalties reach EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide turnover, and for SMEs it is the LOWER of the two.
- **platform terms**: No platform prohibits writing for citability. LinkedIn's relevant rules are the authenticity and inauthentic-behaviour policies, which bite on mass-produced and coordinated content, not on well-structured content. There is no 'GEO' clause anywhere.
- **the real legal exposure is not ai law**: It is MISREPRESENTATION. A fabricated statistic presented as research, amplified by an answer engine to people making purchasing decisions, is a consumer-protection and unfair-commercial-practices question long before it is an AI Act question — and in the EU that regime is mature, enforced, and does not care how the text was produced. Under the UCPD framework, misleading factual claims in commercial communication are actionable regardless of authorship.
- **third party content**: Quotation Addition is the top-performing intervention and it means quoting real people. Short attributed quotations for commentary or criticism are generally safe under EU quotation exceptions, but attributing a quote someone did not say is defamation-shaped, not copyright-shaped, and the answer engine will repeat it at scale with your name on it.
- **practical position**: For a Poland-based consultant writing sourced B2B articles with real editorial review: no Art. 50 duty, no platform violation, no copyright issue. The entire legal risk surface of this tactic reduces to one question — are the numbers real.

**reversibility and blast radius**

- **best case failure**: You optimize and nothing gets cited. Cost is the extra 20-40 minutes per article. Fully reversible, and the content is still better content.
- **middle case**: You build on LinkedIn and LinkedIn's citation share collapses. Recovery means republishing the corpus on an owned property, which is work but not loss — the substance transfers. This is a strong argument for keeping the canonical version somewhere you control.
- **worst case reputational**: A fabricated or wrong statistic gets cited by an answer engine, repeated across thousands of responses with you named as the source, and is then corrected publicly. Effectively irreversible: you cannot recall a citation, cannot edit an engine's cached answer, and cannot control how long a stale passage stays in the retrieval corpus. The blast radius is larger than a bad viral post because attribution is explicit and the context is authoritative — the reader was told this is the evidence.
- **worst case platform**: Essentially nil. No account risk from this tactic. The one adjacent risk is the cadence collision: publishing at the volume that helps citation can trip authenticity classifiers built for mass-produced content.
- **asymmetry summary**: Downside is concentrated entirely in one failure mode — publishing a false fact — and that failure is uniquely hard to reverse because the distribution mechanism is a machine that quotes without checking and remembers longer than a feed does. Everything else here is cheap and recoverable.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 1 accept the split**: Stop treating citation as a bonus outcome of good posts. Run it as a second objective with its own artifact type, its own cadence and its own metric. Concretely: a viral-objective post and a citation-objective article are different deliverables produced from the same substance, and neither should be compromised toward the other.
- **step 2 build the question inventory**:
  - List 30-50 questions a real prospect asks inside your domain — phrased as people type them into an engine, not as keywords. Mine your own DMs, sales calls and comment sections for the actual phrasings; do not have a model invent them.
  - For each question, mark whether you hold PROPRIETARY evidence (your own data, a named case, a first-hand observation) or only synthesised opinion.
  - Rank by proprietary-evidence strength, not by search volume. The questions where you are the only possible source are where the ceiling is highest and the competition is zero.
- **step 3 produce the citation artifact**:
  - Target 500-2,000 words — the band that takes 50-66% of LinkedIn's AI citations. A LinkedIn article, a newsletter issue, or (better) a post on your own site.
  - One question per section. Section heading states the question; the first sentence answers it completely. Everything after the first sentence is support.
  - Apply the three verified interventions to each section, and only where truthful: a direct QUOTATION with named attribution; a concrete STATISTIC with source, date and n; explicit SOURCE ATTRIBUTION for each factual claim. Expected effect on the primary metric in GEO-Bench: roughly +28% to +41% each, individually, against an unoptimized baseline.
  - Run the chunk-survival test. Any passage that fails self-containment gets rewritten, not deleted.
  - Strip keyword repetition. It is the one tested intervention with a negative effect.
  - Do NOT add a hook. This artifact is not being scrolled past; it is being retrieved.
- **step 4 produce the engagement artifact separately**: From the same substance, write the feed post that does the feed's job — hook, tension, one idea, a reason to reply — and link or reference the article. Two artifacts, one research effort. The marginal cost of the second is roughly 20 minutes.
- **step 5 publish where you can be indexed and keep the canonical copy**: Publish the article on LinkedIn for the distribution AND on an owned property for durability. If the two must differ, the owned one is canonical. This is the single cheapest insurance against a platform's citation share moving.
- **step 6 cadence**: 5+ publications per four weeks is the pattern associated with ~75% of cited authors. Not all need to be articles — but the indexed surface area is the input, so a slow month is a month with no new retrieval candidates. Note the tension with engagement-side over-posting limits and resolve it by artifact type, not by volume.
- **step 7 monitor**:
  - Fix a prompt set of 30-50 questions from step 2. Run them weekly across ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode.
  - Log: which of your URLs were cited, which competitor sources appeared, and which questions returned nothing of yours.
  - The gap list drives the next month's publishing plan. This is the entire feedback loop and it is the only way to observe this objective at all.
- **step 8 refresh**: Re-update key pieces at least quarterly — dates, numbers, examples. Freshness is a retrieval-layer input and a stale article silently stops being selected without any visible signal.

**checklist**

- **gate type**: Pass/fail before publishing a citation-objective artifact. Any FAIL blocks.
- **items**:
  - [ ] This artifact has ONE objective and I can state which. (FAIL if it is trying to be both a viral post and a citable article.)
  - [ ] Every factual claim resolves to a named source with a date and, where relevant, a sample size — and I can produce that source on demand. (FAIL on any unsourced number. This is the non-negotiable gate.)
  - [ ] No statistic, quotation or attribution in this piece was generated by a model. (FAIL is terminal.)
  - [ ] Every section heading is a question a real person actually asks, in their phrasing. (FAIL on keyword-shaped headings.)
  - [ ] Each section's first sentence answers its question completely, without needing the rest. (FAIL on any section that requires context from above.)
  - [ ] The chunk-survival test passes: every ~150-word passage states a complete claim and carries at least one concrete number, named source or direct quotation. (FAIL per-passage.)
  - [ ] No keyword repetition beyond natural use. (FAIL — this is the one intervention with a measured negative effect.)
  - [ ] Length is in the 500-2,000 word band, or there is a stated reason it is not.
  - [ ] A canonical copy exists on a property I control. (WARN if LinkedIn-only.)
  - [ ] This piece is in the weekly monitoring prompt set. (FAIL if unmeasured — an unmonitored citation strategy is invisible to itself.)

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **primary kpi**: Citation share on your fixed prompt set: of N monitored questions, how many return an answer citing one of your URLs. Tracked weekly, read monthly. This is the only direct measure of the objective and it requires deliberate measurement — it will never appear in a platform dashboard.
- **secondary kpis**:
  - Distinct cited URLs — depth of the corpus that works, not just whether one piece is a lucky outlier.
  - Citation persistence: how many weeks a given URL keeps being cited. This is the compounding metric and the one that distinguishes this objective from feed reach.
  - Share of voice against named competitors on the same prompt set.
  - Coverage gaps: questions where nothing of yours appears. The publishing backlog writes itself from this list.
- **leading indicators**:
  - PUBLICATION CADENCE of citation-objective artifacts. Fully in your control, and the input most strongly associated with being cited (~75% of cited authors at 5+/four weeks). Moves weeks before citations do.
  - EVIDENCE INVENTORY — how many unpublished proprietary facts you are sitting on. When this hits zero the strategy stalls or turns dishonest; it is the earliest possible warning and nobody tracks it.
  - Semantic coverage of your question inventory: what fraction of your 30-50 questions has a dedicated, self-contained passage somewhere in your corpus.
  - Freshness age of your top-cited pieces. Passing roughly 3 months without a refresh is the point where retrieval selection starts drifting away, per the general freshness guidance in the vault note.
- **the metric to explicitly stop using**: Reactions and comments on citation-objective artifacts. The median cited post has 15-25 reactions and fewer than one comment. Judging these pieces by engagement will cause you to kill the ones that are working.

**ai search citability**

- **self referential note**: This entry IS the citability objective, so the field is about second-order effects rather than a fresh assessment.
- **does pursuing it also help engagement**: Weakly and indirectly. The habits it enforces — specificity, real numbers, sourced claims, questions people actually ask — improve any writing, and the vault note records that LinkedIn's 2026 ranker resurfaces older evergreen posts by semantic relevance, which means a citation-shaped article has a longer feed tail than a hot take. But the FORMAT specs conflict directly: hooks, brevity and narrative tension drive engagement and do nothing for citation; headings, self-containment and evidence density drive citation and flatten engagement. Expect a modest positive spillover from the habits and a clear negative from the format if you try to merge them.
- **the compounding property engagement does not have**: A feed post's half-life is 24-72 hours on LinkedIn. A cited article is a retrieval candidate indefinitely, subject to freshness. Over 24 months the citation corpus accumulates and the feed archive does not, which inverts the apparent productivity of the two objectives on a long enough horizon.
- **the strategic read**: For a sub-1,000-follower specialist with proprietary data, citation is the BETTER first objective. The mechanism evidence says low-ranked sources gain most (up to +115% for rank-5 in GEO-Bench), the distribution evidence says cited posts do not need engagement, and the ceiling is set by your knowledge rather than your network. Virality requires a network you do not have; citability requires facts you might. Run citation first, and let the engagement objective come second once there is an audience for it to act on.

#### omitted as uncertain

- as of date and volatility
- audience fit
- conflicting evidence
- cost and time to execute
- decay and saturation
- effect size and n
- evidence strength
- measurement feasibility
- prompt artifact link
- ranking signal targeted
- scales with
- worked example

### AI slop and the authenticity penalty

`ai-slop-authenticity-penalty` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 9 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: AI slop and the authenticity penalty. Category: science (with a hard platform-mechanics layer). Definition: the combined cost of publishing content that reads as machine-written — an algorithmic cost (demotion from out-of-network recommendation by platform classifiers tuned against low-effort AI output) and a social cost (readers who recognise the pattern disengage, distrust, and since 2026-07-30 on LinkedIn can report it with one tap). Maturity: ESTABLISHED as a direction and newly ENFORCED as a mechanic — 2026 is the year it stopped being an aesthetic complaint and became a distribution rule. Critical framing that most coverage gets wrong: neither LinkedIn's policy nor its classifier targets AI AUTHORSHIP. Both target LOW EFFORT AND ABSENCE OF UNIQUE PERSPECTIVE. LinkedIn explicitly permits AI assistance. The penalty is on genericness; AI is merely its most productive cause.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

Two independent penalty mechanisms that people routinely merge into one. MECHANISM 1 — THE ALGORITHMIC GATE. LinkedIn's ranking runs through a text-native decoder model (360Brew, 150B parameters, Mixtral 8x22B base, over 30 predictive tasks, arXiv 2501.16450), so the ranker reads the post rather than only its engagement counters. Since 2026-05-20 the stated policy is that content judged low-effort AI — polished on the surface, lacking real unique perspective or substance — is removed from RECOMMENDATIONS TO PEOPLE OUTSIDE YOUR NETWORK while remaining visible to your direct connections and followers. That is the whole mechanic and its precision matters: the post is not deleted, your followers still see it, and your metrics do not collapse to zero. What disappears is the only reach that compounds — the out-of-network impressions that grow an audience. This makes the penalty nearly invisible from inside creator analytics: you see a normal-looking post with a quiet impression number and no cause. Named targets in the same policy: engagement bait, recycled thought leadership, generic AI-constructed phrasing such as the 'it is not X, it is Y' antithesis, and automated commenting — LinkedIn reports blocking hundreds of thousands of automated comment attempts daily and millions of other automation attempts in recent months. Since 2026-07-30 the classifier has a human training signal: readers tap 'seems like AI slop' on a post, and LinkedIn states the reports provide signal used to tune its models and to reduce slop in out-of-network suggested content. MECHANISM 2 — THE AUDIENCE PENALTY, which operates even where no classifier exists. The peer-reviewed mechanism is effort-signalling into parasocial connection: Carney, Riveros and Tully (Journal of Consumer Research 2026), using TikTok data from its disclosure-policy rollout plus eight preregistered experiments, find that AI-associated content reduces engagement, and that the cause is NOT perceived quality, NOT AI skepticism and NOT general AI aversion — it is a drop in the one-sided emotional bond between viewer and creator, mediated by PERCEIVED CREATOR EFFORT. This is the load-bearing insight of the whole item: the audience is not penalising machine involvement, it is penalising the inference that you did not bother. It predicts the shape of the damage precisely — the effortful engagement types (comments, shares, DMs) fall first and hardest, while passive ones (impressions, likes) hold up, which is exactly the split observed in the Instagram field data recorded in the sibling item. It also predicts the fix, which is not concealment: anything that raises perceived effort — a proprietary number, a named client, a first-hand scene, visible work — restores the bond regardless of how the sentences were produced. WHY THE TWO MECHANISMS CONVERGE: the platform classifier is a machine proxy for exactly the same judgement the reader is making. Both are probing for whether a human with something to say was present. That is why one defence covers both, and why humaniser tools — which optimise text against provenance detectors — defend against neither.

**ranking signal targeted**

Primarily a NEGATIVE GATE rather than a graded signal, and naming it that way is the practical difference. THE GATE: pass/fail on 'does this read as low-effort generic AI', evaluated by a text-native ranker, determining eligibility for out-of-network recommendation on LinkedIn. Failing it does not reduce a score, it removes a distribution channel. NEW SINCE 2026-07-30: reader reports ('seems like AI slop') as a training and moderation signal — a social signal converted into an algorithmic one, which means your audience now has a direct input into your classifier score. DOWNSTREAM SIGNALS THE AUDIENCE PENALTY MOVES, in order of sensitivity: substantive COMMENT DEPTH and SHARES first (effortful acts, most sensitive to a perceived-effort drop), then SAVES and DM SENDS, then DWELL TIME and see-more expansion, with LIKES and IMPRESSIONS least sensitive and therefore the worst early-warning metrics. SIGNAL NOT TARGETED, despite folklore: there is no evidence of a provenance-based penalty — nothing suggests a platform is checking whether a model was involved, and LinkedIn says the opposite. 'Unknown' is the honest answer for the exact feature set: LinkedIn has never published the classifier's inputs, its threshold, or any per-post feedback, and no number in circulation about the size of the demotion comes from LinkedIn.

**why it drives reach**

Inverted causal story — this item explains reach LOST, and the chain is short and well-evidenced at both ends with a documented gap in the middle. Chain: generic output leaves no trace of the author, so (a) the platform classifier declines to recommend it out-of-network, which removes the compounding impressions, and (b) readers who do see it infer low effort, which weakens the parasocial bond and suppresses exactly the effortful engagement types that feed back into ranking. Those two effects are multiplicative, not additive: fewer out-of-network impressions means a smaller pool from which the weakened per-impression engagement rate can draw, so a post can lose most of its potential distribution without anything visibly going wrong. The three links are evidenced unevenly and should be cited that way: the policy link is PLATFORM-OFFICIAL (LinkedIn stated it); the audience link is PEER-REVIEWED (JCR 2026, eight preregistered experiments, effort-mediated parasocial mechanism); the JOIN between them — how much reach a given post actually loses — is UNMEASURED by anyone credible. Every percentage in circulation for the size of the penalty is vendor-sourced. The direction is safe to act on; the magnitude is not safe to quote. One further amplifier worth stating: at 40.5% AI share of LinkedIn long-form supply, the classifier is operating on a corpus where slop is close to a plurality, which means a genuinely specific post is competing in a thinner field than the raw post count suggests — the penalty for slop and the premium for substance are the same phenomenon seen from two sides.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

In this item the model is the HAZARD, and the same technology is also the mitigation, which is the part worth engineering. AS HAZARD: a model asked to write a post from a topic rather than from substance will produce fluent, structurally correct, entirely unfalsifiable text — the exact object both the classifier and the reader are screening for. The failure is not quality, it is the absence of anything only you could have said, and no amount of prompting for 'authentic, human tone' fixes it because the missing ingredient is an input, not a style. AS MITIGATION, three useful roles: (1) CRITIQUE — a second model instance, in a FRESH context, scoring a draft against a slop rubric and returning only violations; running this in the drafting thread produces a model grading its own work and passes almost everything; (2) DETECTION — running your own draft through a detector before publishing tells you something real, but only about provenance-style genericness, not about the effort signal that actually matters, so treat a clean detector score as necessary-at-best and never as sufficient; (3) RETRIEVAL — RAG over your own notes, transcripts and past work to surface the specific you already own but forgot, which is the single highest-leverage AI use in this item because it attacks the actual deficit (missing substance) rather than its symptom (generic prose). What the model must never do here: originate the claim, invent the number, or supply the example.

**automation level**

L1 is the ceiling for anything published under a personal name, and in 2026 that is a platform-imposed ceiling rather than a taste preference. L0 (manual) is the reference condition and is not slop-exposed at all. L1 (AI-assisted draft with human-supplied substance and human final edit) is the operating point this item defends — it clears both the classifier gate and the effort inference, provided the human input is real. L2 (autonomous with guardrails) is defensible ONLY when the guardrail is a hard human approval before publish plus a substance gate that can fail a post, and it degrades to slop the first time the gate is skipped 'just this once'. L3 (fully autonomous) is self-defeating on LinkedIn by construction: the classifier is looking precisely for the human layer that L3 removes, and automated commenting — the most common L3 pattern — is named explicitly in the May 2026 policy and is the one behaviour in this whole research with genuine account-suspension exposure. Note the marketing gap: most tools sold in 2026 as 'AI social media agents' are L1 drafters bolted to a scheduler, which is fine; the risk is operators who use the L1 tool at L3 discipline by never reading the output.

**prompt patterns**

Detection-and-repair prompts, not generation prompts — the generation side belongs to the ghostwriting item. (A) SLOP RUBRIC IN A FRESH CONTEXT, the highest-value pattern and useless if run in the drafting thread: 'You are a hostile reviewer. Score this draft 1-5 on each and quote the offending line for anything under 4: (i) contains at least one number, name, date or artefact that only the author could supply; (ii) zero banned constructions; (iii) sentence length varies, with at least one line under 6 words and one over 25; (iv) the closing line follows from the argument rather than being bolted-on engagement bait; (v) every claim is falsifiable — a reader who disagreed could point at something specific. Return only the failures.' (B) THE SUBSTANCE INTERROGATION, run BEFORE drafting and the one that prevents slop rather than detecting it: 'Here is my topic. Ask me five questions whose answers only I could give — about what I measured, who I talked to, what failed, what it cost, what I changed my mind about. Do not write anything until I have answered at least two.' (C) BANNED-CONSTRUCTION BLOCK, pasted verbatim into every generation prompt and rotated quarterly because model defaults move: ban 'it is not X, it is Y', 'stop X, start Y', 'here is the thing', 'let that sink in', 'the result?', 'in today's fast-paced world', 'here is what nobody tells you', rhetorical-question-followed-by-one-word-paragraph, perfectly balanced triads, and an em-dash in every second sentence. (D) THE REPORT-BUTTON TEST, which is the 2026-specific addition: 'Read this as a LinkedIn user who has the seems-like-AI-slop button available. Would you tap it? Quote the line that would make you tap it.' This reframes the check from a detector question to a social one, which is the correct frame since 2026-07-30. (E) INVERSION CHECK: 'Rewrite this post as it would appear if a competitor with no access to my data wrote it. If the rewrite is nearly identical to mine, my post contains nothing proprietary.'

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

Split by sub-claim, and the split is the point. STRONG / PLATFORM-OFFICIAL: that LinkedIn demotes content its classifier reads as low-effort AI, that the mechanism is suppression from out-of-network recommendation rather than removal, that AI assistance remains permitted, and that a reader-facing report button exists. These are stated by the platform and reported by mainstream press. STRONG / PEER-REVIEWED: that AI-associated content reduces engagement through reduced parasocial connection mediated by perceived creator effort (JCR 2026, eight preregistered experiments plus TikTok policy-rollout data). MODERATE / PEER-REVIEWED: that AI-labelled content is rated less credible than human content (AIES 2025, N=207) and that audiences discount AI-labelled headlines even when they are true or human-made (PNAS Nexus 2024). MODERATE / INDEPENDENT LARGE-N BUT VENDOR-OWNED: the prevalence numbers — how much of LinkedIn is machine-written. ANECDOTAL-TO-UNVERIFIED: everything about the SIZE of the reach penalty. VENDOR-CLAIM AND CIRCULAR: the 30% and 47% penalty figures this item was briefed with, plus '-45% engagement', '-60% for bait', '2% organic reach for AI-flagged pages'. NO PRIMARY METHODOLOGY was located for any of them in this research. Overall verdict to carry: DIRECTION STRONG, MAGNITUDE UNKNOWN. Act on the direction; never quote the magnitude.

**conflicting evidence**

FIRST CONFLICT — AI-vs-HUMAN PERFORMANCE, mandatory and unresolved. This item assumes an authenticity penalty; the sibling item 'AI vs human content performance — unresolved' records that whether AI content actually underperforms is contested: Huang and Zhou (Public Relations Review 2025, peer-reviewed) find GPT-4 posts OUTPERFORM human ones on brand X accounts, while the only peer-reviewed field experiment (Flesheriu and Fron 2025, 24 alternating Instagram posts) found NO statistically significant difference on any metric, with raw means leaning human on comments and leaning AI on reach. Note carefully that the version of that study which circulates — 'human posts won on likes 42.6 vs 39.6, comments 5.3 vs 2.3, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%' — omits that every one of those comparisons was non-significant (p from .07 to .91) and that the authors concluded equivalence. The authenticity penalty is therefore NOT established as a general performance law; what is established is a POLICY penalty on one platform plus an EFFORT-mediated audience effect. These are compatible: AI writing can be good and still be demoted for being generic, and the same post can gain reach on X while losing recommendation eligibility on LinkedIn.
SECOND CONFLICT — DOES DETECTION EVEN WORK? Top detectors report 94-96% accuracy on unedited frontier output, but independent testing puts real-world accuracy far lower once text is edited or paraphrased, the RAID benchmark shows accuracy and false-positive rate are traded against each other so cross-tool comparisons without the FPR are meaningless, and a 2023 Patterns study plus later follow-ups document heavy false-positive bias against non-native English writers. Pangram's 0.01% FPR claim sits at the extreme optimistic end of this literature and is self-reported. So the same evidence base that supplies the prevalence numbers also undermines confidence in them, and 'flagged as AI' and 'is AI' are not the same proposition in either direction. This matters directly for a Poland-based creator writing English.
THIRD CONFLICT — CONCEALMENT VS DISCLOSURE. The naive response to an authenticity penalty is to hide AI use. But the sibling item 'The AI disclosure paradox' documents that disclosure itself erodes trust (Schilke and Reimann, OBHDP 2025, 13 experiments) — while the JCR 2026 finding says the mediator is perceived EFFORT and that effort-signalling disclosure mitigates the loss. These pull in opposite directions on tactics and agree on mechanism: what the audience punishes is the inference of low effort, not the fact of AI use. A disclosure that reveals effort helps; one that reveals shortcut hurts; concealment is a third option with its own downside, since being exposed by a reader's report button is worse than either.
FOURTH CONFLICT — MAGNITUDE SOURCES CONTRADICT EACH OTHER. '+31% for AI-assisted content across 10,024 posts' and '-45% for AI posts across 3,368 posts' circulate in the same corner of the internet, frequently in the same article. They cannot both be true. Both are untraced. Their coexistence is the strongest available argument for treating the entire observational vendor layer as unusable, and for the confound this item was created to keep in view: in observational data 'AI-detected' and 'low-effort' are the same population, so every such study estimates the cost of GENERICNESS and reports it as the cost of AI.

CORRECTION (2026-09-11, verified against the full PDF): this file quotes raw means from Flesheriu & Fron (2025), Oeconomica Jadertina 2/2025, DOI 10.15291/oec.4845 (likes 42.58 vs 39.58, comments 5.33 vs 2.33, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%). The means are accurate but NONE of the differences is statistically significant: Mann-Whitney U gives likes p=.91, comments p=.07, shares p=.17, saves p=.79, reach p=.89, impressions p=.51, ER p=.64. The paper states 'H1 was not supported' and concludes EQUIVALENCE, not human superiority. Dropping one launch-day outlier flips ER in the AI direction (5.95% vs 5.79%); readers significantly PREFERRED the AI-written captions (U=8.0, p=.045); and 7 of the 12 top-performing posts were AI. Scope limits that further weaken it as evidence about AI TEXT: a single account with 770 followers, 24 alternating posts, a culinary niche, and AI-generated IMAGERY bundled with the caption - the authors attribute 64% of engagement to the visual. Do not cite this study as showing that human-written posts outperform AI-written posts.
