#### fit

**audience fit**

B2B AND PROFESSIONAL AUDIENCES: highest exposure, because the audience is small, repeated and evaluative — people are deciding whether to hire or work with you, so the effort inference is not an aesthetic reaction but a competence signal. TECHNICAL AUDIENCES: fastest detection and the most public punishment; they have read the same model's default rhythm a hundred times this week and will say so in the comments, which converts a quiet demotion into a visible one. B2C AND CASUAL AUDIENCES: the effect is weaker but not absent, and the Instagram survey data is a useful humility check — readers actually preferred AI-written captions when they did not know which was which, so 'people can always tell' is false as a general claim. What people reliably detect is not machine authorship but EMPTINESS. GENERAL AUDIENCES ON VISUAL PLATFORMS: least sensitive to text tells, most exposed to auto-labelling of AI imagery. PL vs EN, and this is the asymmetry that matters for a Poland-based creator: writing in Polish, model output is stiffer and more translationese, so the tells are more obvious to a Polish reader and the bar for editing is higher; writing in English, third-party detectors carry documented false-positive bias against non-native writers, so hand-written English by a Polish author can be flagged as machine-written regardless of how it was produced. Practical consequence: do not use a public detector score as your own quality gate, and do not let a reader's detector screenshot define the argument — the defence is specificity, which is checkable, not a detector result, which is not.

**scales with**

What caps exposure and what caps the defence. (1) PUBLISHING VOLUME: exposure scales linearly with posts, and the whole hazard is created by cadence pressure — nobody produces slop on the day they have something to say. The binding resource is not writing time but SUBSTANCE SUPPLY, i.e. the rate at which you accumulate proprietary numbers, first-hand scenes and named artefacts. (2) CORPUS AND MEMORY: a large searchable body of your own work (this vault) raises the ceiling, because retrieval can surface a specific you already own instead of inventing one. This is the main structural advantage a knowledge base confers on this item. (3) REVIEW CAPACITY: the human edit does not compress; realistic ceiling is a few posts a day before the human layer degrades, and the degradation is invisible to you and obvious to readers. (4) NICHE SATURATION: in a niche where 40%+ of supply is machine-written, both the penalty and the premium are larger — being specific is worth more, being generic costs more. (5) ACCOUNT AGE AND RELATIONSHIP DEPTH: the parasocial mechanism means an established account has more to lose (a bond exists that can be damaged) and more buffer (followers still see suppressed posts). A new account has no bond to break but also no floor. (6) WHAT IT DOES NOT SCALE WITH: follower count. The classifier does not care, and the effort inference operates per-post. Note the objective split recorded elsewhere in this research: sub-500-follower accounts are cited by AI answer engines at broadly comparable rates to large ones but do not go viral comparably, so for a citation objective this penalty is about quality, not scale.

**decay and saturation**

Unusually, the RISK is appreciating while the SPECIFIC TELLS decay fast. THE PENALTY ITSELF is not a tactic that saturates — it is a direction of platform travel, and every 2026 data point (LinkedIn's May policy, its July report button, its removal of its own AI writer, TikTok's C2PA steering-committee membership from 2026-07-27) points the same way. Expect enforcement to tighten, not loosen. Shelf life of the DIRECTION: years. WHAT DECAYS IN ONE QUARTER: the banned-construction list. Model defaults move with every upgrade, so 'it is not X, it is Y' is a 2026 tell that will be a 2027 non-signal, replaced by whatever the next default register produces. Any fixed phrase blacklist needs quarterly rotation or it defends against last year's slop. WHAT DECAYS IN 6-12 MONTHS: every prevalence number, and with it the strategic reading — at 40.5% AI share and rising, the eventual inversion is that machine-written becomes the baseline and the classifier's notion of 'normal' shifts, at which point the defensible position is not 'does not read like AI' but 'could only have been written by this person'. Build toward the second, because it is invariant. WHAT DOES NOT DECAY AT ALL: the effort-signalling mechanism. A proprietary number with its denominator, a named client, a dated first-hand scene — these defeat both the classifier and the reader inference under any model generation, any policy version and any saturation level, because they are not stylistic properties but informational ones. That is the durable core of this item and the only part worth building a system on.

#### risk

**failure modes**

(1) DEFENDING AGAINST THE WRONG DETECTOR — the most expensive error. You run drafts through a provenance detector, pass, and publish something with nothing in it. LinkedIn's classifier is not looking for model fingerprints; it is looking for absence of unique perspective. 'Humaniser' tools optimise against the wrong objective entirely and can make text worse by adding noise instead of substance. (2) SUBSTANCE HOLLOWING UNDER CADENCE PRESSURE: once drafting is cheap you publish on days you have nothing to say. This is the single most common real-world path into slop and it is invisible from inside, because each individual post looks fine. (3) INVISIBLE PENALTY, MISDIAGNOSED: the demotion produces a normal-looking post with quiet reach and no notification, so authors attribute it to timing, the algorithm, or seasonality and respond by posting MORE — which compounds the problem. There is no feedback channel; you will never be told. (4) SELF-CRITIQUE THEATRE: running the slop rubric in the drafting thread, where the model grades its own output and passes nearly everything. (5) COMMENT-LAYER EXPOSURE: automated or generic commenting, which is the one behaviour in this area with genuine account risk and which many 'growth' tools still ship by default. (6) STYLE-ONLY REMEDIATION: stripping banned phrases from an empty post produces an empty post with better rhythm; the tells were symptoms. (7) READER REPORT CASCADE: since 2026-07-30 a single recognisable archetype — especially a fabricated personal story — can draw reader reports that feed the classifier, converting a one-off into a persistent signal. (8) OVERCORRECTION: refusing all AI assistance on authenticity grounds, which costs throughput for a penalty that platform policy explicitly does not impose on AI assistance per se.

**ai slop risk**

This item IS the slop risk, so the field is its taxonomy. TELLS, ordered by diagnostic value rather than by how often they are listed: (a) NO PROPER NOUNS, NO NUMBERS, NO DATES — no named tool, client, person, place or figure anywhere in the post. This one test catches most slop and almost nothing else. (b) UNFALSIFIABLE CLAIMS: nothing a disagreeing reader could point at and dispute. (c) THE ANTITHESIS FAMILY: 'it is not X, it is Y', 'stop X, start Y', 'the result?', 'here is what nobody tells you'. (d) RHETORICAL QUESTION FOLLOWED BY A ONE-WORD PARAGRAPH. (e) UNIFORM PARAGRAPH LENGTHS and an em-dash in every second sentence. (f) HOLLOW QUANTIFIERS: 'many leaders', 'most teams', 'in my experience' with no experience attached. (g) PERFECTLY BALANCED TRIADS and parallel structure with no ragged edge — real expertise produces uneven emphasis because some parts of a real answer are harder than others. (h) BOLTED-ON ENGAGEMENT-BAIT CLOSER that does not follow from the post. (i) A STATISTIC WITH NO DENOMINATOR, NO DATE AND NO SOURCE — note that this one appears in slop ABOUT this very topic, which is how the 30%/47% figures propagate. THE PLATFORM'S OWN FORMULATION is the cleanest standard to internalise: low-effort AI-generated content that may sound polished on the surface but lacks any real unique perspective or substance. Polish is not the defence; polish is the symptom. THE ONE-QUESTION DISCRIMINATOR: if a competitor with no access to your data, your clients and your week rewrote this post from the same topic, would it come out nearly the same? If yes, it is slop regardless of who or what typed it.

**human input required**

The minimum non-substitutable contribution, supplied BEFORE generation and never retrofitted afterwards — at least ONE of: a PROPRIETARY NUMBER with its denominator and date (your error rate, your before/after, your client's result with permission, your own audit of your own corpus); a FIRST-HAND SCENE with a time and a place ('Tuesday, third client call, they asked X'); a NAMED ARTEFACT you can point at (a repo, a pull request, a deck, a tool with a version, a person with attribution); or a JUDGEMENT CALL you would defend in a room of peers who could push back. Plus one non-optional act regardless of which you chose: you write the first two lines and the last line by hand, every time. WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT GATE and not merely good advice: it is simultaneously (i) what the platform classifier is a proxy for — LinkedIn's stated bar is that posts represent your voice and your perspectives and that the ultimate value comes from the human behind the tool; (ii) what the peer-reviewed audience mechanism measures — perceived creator effort, the mediator in the JCR 2026 parasocial finding; and (iii) the only property that is invariant to model upgrades, policy changes and detector accuracy. It also converts an unfalsifiable instruction ('do not post slop') into a binary you can check in ten seconds. THE OPERATIONAL DISCIPLINE that makes it real: if you cannot write the three-to-five-line brief containing that asset before the model writes anything, you do not have a post. Stop there. The willingness to not publish on a scheduled day is the actual scarce resource in this entire item.

**policy and legal**

Assuming a Poland/EU-based creator. PLATFORM RULES, which are the binding constraint here and are not law: LinkedIn's Professional Community Policies require authentic identity and prohibit inauthentic engagement; the May 2026 ranking policy demotes low-effort AI content from out-of-network recommendation while explicitly permitting AI assistance; automated commenting and mass automation are prohibited and actively blocked at scale. The practical hierarchy is worth stating plainly: AI-assisted writing is permitted, generic output is demoted, automated engagement is enforced against. EU AI ACT ARTICLE 50(4), applicable since 2026-08-02: deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose artificial generation — with a human-review carve-out where a knowledgeable person deliberately examined the substance including fact-checking and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility (a spelling or grammar pass does not qualify), and a public-interest threshold that ordinary professional posting does not obviously cross. AI-assisted text does not trigger the deepfake duties in Art. 50(2); an AI avatar, synthetic voice or manipulated image would, and that is the more likely exposure for a creator using generated visuals. GDPR is not engaged by drafting as such, but is engaged if your prompt corpus or RAG index contains third parties' personal data — a real consideration when the anti-slop defence is 'use your own client transcripts'. Get consent before a client's number appears in a post. POLISH/EU COMMERCIAL LAW, the under-noticed exposure: if slop-adjacent claims appear in material that sells something — repeating an untraced '47% penalty' statistic in a pitch deck or a course — the relevant regime is unfair-commercial-practices law (UOKiK enforcement of the UCPD implementation), not the AI Act. FTC rules are a US regime about material connections and do not govern drafting method.

**reversibility and blast radius**

ASYMMETRIC — the algorithmic half is recoverable, the social half is not, and people insure against the wrong one. ALGORITHMIC WORST CASE, documented and mild: suppression from out-of-network recommendation, with the post still visible to direct connections and followers. Change what you publish and distribution recovers. There is no stated permanent penalty and no account-level consequence for AI-assisted text. One caveat with weak evidence: a vendor claim that consecutive AI-heavy weeks produce compounding account-level suppression that also drags down later human posts is plausible given account-level quality scoring but unverified — treat as a reason for caution, not as a fact. ACCOUNT SUSPENSION is not on the table for AI-assisted writing; it IS on the table for automated commenting and mass automation, which LinkedIn names and blocks explicitly. That is the one place where the blast radius reaches the whole account. SOCIAL WORST CASE, and the one that does not heal: being publicly identified by peers as a slop account. In B2B the audience that matters is small, repeated and has a long memory; a screenshot of your post next to a detector score circulates independently of any algorithm change. Since 2026-07-30 this can now happen through a platform-sanctioned mechanism rather than only through a quote-post. The reputational loss is capped at one identity but is not reversible on any useful timescale. CHEAPEST INSURANCE, in order: never automate commenting; never skip the human-input gate 'just this once'; and keep at least one visibly proprietary artefact in every post, so that any accusation is answerable with evidence rather than denial.

#### practice

**how to apply**

PER POST, the gate (10-15 minutes, and it is the whole system). 1. BEFORE opening a model, write three to five rough lines by hand containing the non-substitutable asset — a number with its denominator and date, a first-hand scene with a time and place, a named artefact, or a defensible judgement. If you cannot write those lines, you do not have a post today; stop, and do not treat that as a failure. 2. Draft however you like, with the banned-construction block pasted into the prompt and an explicit 'add no facts I did not give you; if something is missing, ask rather than invent'. 3. Run the slop rubric (prompt pattern A) in a SECOND, FRESH context that holds only the rubric and the draft — never in the drafting thread. Fix violations yourself. 4. Apply the inversion check: would a competitor with no access to your data produce nearly this post from the same topic? If yes, go back to step 1. 5. Hand-write the first two lines and the last line. 6. Run the report-button test: read it as a LinkedIn user with the 'seems like AI slop' button available, and find the line that would make someone tap it. 7. Run the checklist below as a hard gate; any fail means do not post. SYSTEM LEVEL, one-off (2-3 hours). 8. Build the substance pipeline, which is the real fix: a standing note where you log, weekly, every number you produced, every named thing you shipped, every conversation that changed your mind. In this vault, content/ already is that corpus — a retrieval step over it is worth more than any style prompt. 9. Set a cadence you can supply with substance, not the maximum the tooling allows. Publishing three substantive posts a week beats twelve empty ones under both mechanisms simultaneously, since the classifier gate is per-post and the effort inference is per-post. 10. Never automate comments. Write fewer, longer, specific ones by hand. MAINTENANCE, quarterly. 11. Rotate the banned-construction list against current model defaults — it is the fastest-rotting component in the system. 12. Re-check the platform policy layer (LinkedIn changed it twice in 2026) and re-read the prevalence numbers, because saturation changes what 'normal' means. 13. Once a quarter, re-read your own last ten posts cold and mark which ones a stranger could have written. That count is your real slop rate, and it is the only measurement of this you will ever get.

**checklist**

Hard pass/fail gate before publishing. Any FAIL means do not post. 1. The post contains at least one number, name, date or artefact that only I could supply. PASS/FAIL. 2. I wrote the brief containing that asset before the model wrote anything. PASS/FAIL. 3. A competitor with no access to my data could NOT produce nearly this post from the same topic. PASS/FAIL. 4. At least one claim in it is falsifiable — a disagreeing reader could point at something specific. PASS/FAIL. 5. Zero hits on the current banned-construction list. PASS/FAIL. 6. Sentence length varies: at least one line under 6 words and one over 25. PASS/FAIL. 7. First two lines and last line written by hand. PASS/FAIL. 8. The critique pass ran in a fresh context, not the drafting thread. PASS/FAIL. 9. The closing line follows from the argument rather than being bolted-on engagement bait. PASS/FAIL. 10. No statistic appears without its denominator, date and source — including any statistic about AI content itself. PASS/FAIL. 11. If it is a comment rather than a post: I wrote it by hand and it references something specific in the post I am replying to. PASS/FAIL. 12. Reading it as a stranger with the 'seems like AI slop' button available, I would not tap it. PASS/FAIL.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

The defining measurement problem: the penalty is never reported to you, so every direct KPI is unavailable and you must instrument the INPUT instead of the outcome. LEADING, fully under your control, and these should be primary: (1) SUBSTANCE RATE — share of published posts containing a proprietary number, named artefact or first-hand dated scene. Target 100%; anything below 80% is a system failure, not a bad week. (2) BRIEF-FAILURE RATE — how often you abandon a post because you could not write a substantive brief. A healthy number is NOT zero; zero means the gate is not binding. (3) EDIT DISTANCE between model draft and published text — it should stabilise, not fall; trending to zero means you have stopped supplying the human layer. (4) HAND-WRITTEN-COMMENT RATIO, since comments are the highest-risk surface. MIDDLE, days to a week, and the first place a real penalty shows: (5) COMMENTS PER IMPRESSION and SHARES PER IMPRESSION — the effortful engagement types, which the peer-reviewed mechanism predicts fall first; (6) NON-FOLLOWER REACH SHARE, the closest available proxy for out-of-network recommendation eligibility and therefore the nearest thing to a direct read on the classifier gate. Watch this one against your own rolling median, never against published benchmarks. LAGGING and noisiest: (7) impressions relative to your own rolling 8-week median; (8) follower growth; (9) inbound DMs and conversations. ORDER OF MOVEMENT: substance rate and brief-failure rate move immediately, comments-per-impression and non-follower share within a week, impressions last and least interpretably. ANTI-KPI: do not track likes. They are the least sensitive metric to the effort mechanism and will reassure you while the thing that matters is decaying.

**measurement feasibility**

Honest split, and the honest conclusion is that the outcome is largely unobservable. NOT OBSERVABLE AT ALL: whether any given post was flagged by LinkedIn's classifier. There is no notification, no dashboard field, no appeal and no API. You see a reach shortfall and never a cause, which means you can never attribute a bad post to slop rather than to timing, topic or cold-start variance. This is the central measurement fact of the item and it should be stated whenever someone quotes a penalty percentage — those numbers are inferred from detector-labelled observational data, not from platform feedback, which is precisely why they disagree with each other. ALSO NOT NATIVELY OBSERVABLE: dwell time (LinkedIn exposes impressions, reactions, comments, reposts and members reached, not per-post dwell); DM and dark-social forwarding; and how many readers tapped the report button on your post. PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE AND THE BEST AVAILABLE PROXY: non-follower reach share, which is exposed on Instagram directly and approximable on LinkedIn from 'members reached' against follower count. Because the stated penalty mechanism is specifically removal from OUT-OF-NETWORK recommendation, a sustained drop in non-follower share against your own baseline is the closest thing to a signal that exists — still confounded by topic and cadence, so read it as a trend over 8-10 posts, never per post. FULLY OBSERVABLE BECAUSE YOU OWN IT: substance rate, brief-failure rate, edit distance, hand-written-comment ratio, and the quarterly cold re-read of your own last ten posts. Make these the spine of measurement precisely because they are the only clean numbers, and accept that this item is managed by controlling inputs rather than by reading outcomes.

**ai search citability**

Two opposite effects, and they resolve in favour of the same behaviour. NEGATIVE: being classified as machine-written is a citation risk as well as a reach risk. Answer engines have an obvious incentive to discount sources that read as synthetic, and the competitive environment is already saturated — 40.5% of LinkedIn long-form public posts and 30.6% of Medium long-form were classified as fully AI-generated in mid-2026, so you are competing for citation inside a corpus engines have every reason to start down-weighting. POSITIVE AND LARGER: the exact properties that defeat the slop penalty are the properties that earn citation — attributable statistics with denominators and dates, named entities, original first-hand claims, and being the ORIGIN of a fact rather than a restater of one. An engine must name the source of a number it uses; a post full of unsourced generalities gives it nothing to name. So the anti-slop gate and the citability strategy are the same gate, which is a rare alignment in this research and worth exploiting. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS VAULT: the citable artefact is the durable long-form version published on an open URL you control (brain.lipowczan.pl), with the claim, its n, its date and its method in the SAME SENTENCE so it survives extraction; the social post is a pointer, and LinkedIn is in any case a poor citation surface because much of it is gated from crawlers. CAUTION: date-stamp every platform-mechanics claim in-line, because a well-structured page is extracted confidently even when stale, which turns a citable asset into a liability faster than an unstructured one. Note finally that follower count is close to irrelevant for citation while decisive for virality — so for a citation objective, slop discipline is the entire strategy.

#### omitted as uncertain

- as of date and volatility
- cost and time to execute
- detectability and disclosure
- effect size and n
- evidence provenance
- platform and format fit
- prompt artifact link
- tool examples
- worked example

### AI vs human content performance — unresolved

`ai-vs-human-performance-evidence-conflict` · automation L2 · evidence STRONG · 7 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: AI vs human content performance — unresolved. Category: science. Definition: the open empirical question of whether LLM-written social content out-performs or under-performs human-written content on engagement, and under what conditions. Maturity: EMERGING AND CONTESTED — this is an active dispute, not a settled finding, and its purpose in this research is to stay open. The honest one-line answer as of 2026-09-11: the two best-designed studies point in opposite directions, they measured different constructs on different platforms in different policy regimes, and the decisive experiment (same author, same substance, randomised AI-draft vs hand-written, post-May-2026 LinkedIn) has not been run by anyone. IMPORTANT CORRECTION made during this research: the framing this item was handed — 'human posts won on likes 42.6 vs 39.6, comments 5.3 vs 2.3, ER 6.73% vs 5.96%' — is descriptively accurate but inferentially wrong. Those are raw means from a study whose own Mann-Whitney tests found NONE of the differences significant and whose stated conclusion is equivalence (hypothesis not supported). See effect_size_and_n.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. Four clocks, and they run at very different speeds. (1) FIXED: the published studies themselves do not change — Huang and Zhou (Public Relations Review 2025) and Flesheriu and Fron (Oeconomica Jadertina 2025) are what they are. (2) STABLE-ISH, 2-4 YEARS: the underlying psychology of what people engage with. (3) 6-12 MONTHS: model capability — every frontier upgrade moves the AI side of the comparison, and every published comparison is a snapshot of one model generation (GPT-4 for Huang and Zhou; a free consumer image tool for the Instagram study). (4) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER AND DECISIVE: the platform policy layer. Both published studies were run BEFORE the 2026 suppression regime — LinkedIn announced demotion of low-effort AI content on 2026-05-20 and shipped a reader-facing 'seems like AI slop' report button on 2026-07-30, and X rewrote its ranker in Jan 2026 and again in May 2026. This is not a normal decay note: the platforms changed the DEPENDENT VARIABLE. Before mid-2026, 'does AI content get more engagement' was a question about audiences. After mid-2026 on LinkedIn it is a question about audiences AND a classifier that explicitly demotes text it reads as generic. No pre-2026 result transfers cleanly across that boundary, in either direction.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

The dispute has a specific shape, and most people arguing about it are comparing incommensurable things. THREE EXPERIMENTAL FAMILIES, each answering a different question. (A) STIMULUS-LEVEL LAB COMPARISON — generate a post with a model, generate or select a matched human post, show both to panelists or score both against a historical corpus, measure preference or predicted engagement. Huang and Zhou (2025) is the best instance: three studies built around the FIIT model (Fluency, Interactivity, Information, Tone), validated on a Fortune 500 X/Twitter corpus, then an experimental consumer-preference study, then a head-to-head in which trained public relations professionals, given the framework and paid incentives, could not match GPT-4. Strength: controlled, replicable, and it isolates the writing. Weakness: it measures preference and predicted engagement for BRAND-account copy, in a period with no provenance-based suppression, against human writers who were doing a cold task rather than publishing under their own name to their own audience. (B) FIELD EXPERIMENT ON A REAL ACCOUNT — publish alternating AI and human posts on a live account and read the platform's own analytics. Flesheriu and Fron (2025) is the only peer-reviewed instance in this research: 24 single-image culinary posts, 12 human and 12 AI, alternating on one Instagram account with 770 followers, measured at 48 hours. Strength: real distribution, real audience, within-subjects. Weakness: n=24 posts is powered only to detect very large effects, one niche, one account, static images. (C) OBSERVATIONAL DETECTOR-BASED CORPUS ANALYSIS — run an AI-text detector over a large scrape and compare engagement of flagged vs unflagged posts. This family produces all the big circulating numbers (+31% for AI-assisted across 10,024 posts; -45% for AI posts across 3,368 posts) and it is the family that CANNOT answer the question at all. THE STRUCTURAL CONFOUND, which is the single most important thing in this entry: in observational data, 'AI-detected' and 'low-effort' are not two populations, they are one. Detectors fire on genericness, hedging, uniform rhythm and absence of specifics; those same properties are what low-effort human writing has; and low effort predicts low engagement whether or not a model was involved. A detector-based corpus study therefore estimates the effect of GENERICNESS and reports it as the effect of AI AUTHORSHIP. The bias is not random and not small. It is made worse by a second measurement problem: detector false positives are heavily concentrated in non-native English writing, so the mislabelled group is systematically different from the correctly-labelled one on exactly the dimension (register, idiom) that also affects engagement in English-language feeds. Direction of the resulting bias is not even guaranteed — a vendor whose product is AI writing will tend to publish corpus studies showing a positive delta, and a vendor whose product is AI detection will tend to publish ones showing a negative delta. Both are drawing from the same confounded well. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE IT: a within-author randomised field experiment — one author, a fixed brief containing the substance, two executions (voice-matched AI draft edited to publish standard vs hand-written to publish standard), random assignment of execution to slot, one platform, pre-registered, several hundred posts, run inside the current policy regime, with reach and engagement-rate as primary outcomes. Nobody has published this. Until someone does, the correct posture is the one this item exists to enforce: hold the question open and stop citing whichever side supports the decision you already made.

**ranking signal targeted**

Not a tactic, so strictly: not applicable — but naming what each study actually measured is the whole value of this entry. Huang and Zhou measured engagement outcomes on brand X/Twitter posts (likes, comments, shares) plus stated consumer preference, i.e. AUDIENCE RESPONSE, with FIIT (fluency, interactivity, information, tone) as the proposed linguistic mediator. Flesheriu and Fron measured Instagram Insights at 48 hours: likes, comments, shares, saves, accounts reached, impressions, profile visits, follows, engagement rate and an engagement-score formula — i.e. a mix of INTERACTION signals and REACH signals, and the two split in opposite directions (human slightly ahead on interaction, AI slightly ahead on reach). Neither study measured DWELL TIME, sends/DM shares, or the signal that now gates out-of-network distribution on LinkedIn: the platform genericness classifier. That classifier is a pass/fail gate, not a graded signal, and it did not exist as a ranking input when either study was run. So the honest statement of the signal is: the published evidence speaks to audience-facing interaction and reach signals in a pre-suppression regime, and is SILENT on the signal that matters most in 2026.

**why it drives reach**

There is no single causal story here, because the finding is not single. The three candidate mechanisms in play, stated so they can be tested rather than asserted: (1) PRO-AI mechanism (Huang and Zhou): models write more fluently, structure interactivity more reliably, pack more information per character and hit a more consistently positive tone than a human writing under time pressure — and those four properties, not authorship, are what predict engagement. If true, AI wins wherever the copy is the product and the author is a brand rather than a person. (2) PRO-HUMAN mechanism (the relational side of Flesheriu and Fron, and the Journal of Consumer Research 2026 effort/parasocial finding recorded in the disclosure item): engagement on personal accounts is partly a relationship transaction — a comment is a social act toward a person, and perceived creator effort is what licenses it. AI-produced content signals lower effort, which weakens the parasocial bond and specifically suppresses the effortful engagement types (comments, shares) while leaving passive ones (likes, impressions) roughly intact. Flesheriu and Fron's pattern is exactly this shape: the largest effect in the whole study is on COMMENTS (rank-biserial -.42, favouring human), while likes and reach are flat or slightly favour AI. (3) 2026 PLATFORM mechanism: none of the above matters if a classifier removes the post from out-of-network recommendation before an audience ever sees it. On LinkedIn since 2026-05-20 this is the binding constraint, and it targets genericness rather than provenance — which means the operative variable is not 'was a model involved' but 'is there anything in this post only this human could have supplied'. The practical synthesis is that all three can be true simultaneously and apply to different objectives: AI-heavy execution may win on reach-type metrics for brand-voice content, lose on relationship-type metrics for personal-voice content, and be gated entirely on one platform regardless.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

In this item the model is the OBJECT of study, not a tool — but the distinction the literature keeps collapsing is worth stating as a role taxonomy, because it is the reason the studies disagree. The published comparisons test FULLY-GENERATED content (a model produced the post, or the post plus the image) against FULLY-HUMAN content. Almost nobody in practice operates at either pole. The practically relevant comparison — an AI-assisted draft where a human supplied the proposition, the proprietary number and the final edit, versus that same human writing unaided — is exactly the comparison NOT covered by any study located in this research. That gap is the most actionable finding in this entry: the evidence base tests the two configurations nobody uses, and is silent on the one everybody uses. When reading any new study on this question, the first thing to establish is which of the three the 'AI' condition actually was, and the second is whether the human condition was an incentivised stranger performing a writing task (Huang and Zhou, study 3) or a person publishing to their own audience.

**automation level**

Taxonomy applied to the EVIDENCE rather than to a tactic. Huang and Zhou's AI condition is effectively L2/L3 — model output treated as the deliverable. Flesheriu and Fron's AI condition is L2 with light guardrails: the authors report they had to alter recipes because the image tool could not render the requested dishes, which is a human intervening in the AI arm and, by their own admission, compromising ecological validity. The human conditions in both are L0. NOTHING IN THE PEER-REVIEWED RECORD TESTS L1 — the AI-assisted draft with human-supplied substance and human final edit — against L0. Nothing credible sits at L3 for social publishing in 2026, and the 2026 platform regime makes L3 actively self-defeating on LinkedIn, because the classifier is looking precisely for the absence of the human layer that L3 removes. Note also that a tool marketing itself as an 'autonomous posting agent' is almost always an L1 drafter attached to a scheduler, and buying one does not move you to L2, let alone L3.

**prompt patterns**

This is a science item, so the useful prompts are evaluation prompts, not generation prompts. (A) EVIDENCE-CLASSIFICATION PROMPT, run against any new claim before it enters the vault: 'For this claim about AI vs human content performance, answer in this order and refuse to proceed if a step is unknown: 1. What exactly was the AI condition — fully generated, AI-assisted with human substance, or detector-inferred from observational data? 2. What was the human condition — a paid stranger performing a task, or a person publishing to their own audience? 3. Platform, date window, and was it before or after 2026-05-20? 4. Is the comparison randomised, within-subject, or observational? 5. Who funded it and do they sell either AI writing or AI detection? 6. Is the reported number a raw mean or a tested difference, and if tested, what is the p-value and the effect size?' Question 6 is the one that would have caught the mis-citation this entry corrects. (B) CONFOUND PROBE for any corpus study: 'If this dataset were re-analysed with an effort proxy — presence of a number with a denominator, a named entity, a date, or a first-person specific — as a covariate, would the reported AI effect survive? If the authors did not control for it, state that the estimate is confounded with genericness and cannot be attributed to authorship.' (C) HOSTILE-REPLICATION PROMPT before you act on your own A/B result: 'Here are my post-level results. Compute the within-author variance of engagement across my last 50 posts, then tell me how large a difference my test would need to detect at 80% power given that variance and this n. If my observed difference is smaller than that, say so plainly and tell me to stop drawing a conclusion.' Most personal A/B tests on social are radically underpowered, and this prompt is the cheapest available guard against reading noise as signal.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

moderate overall, and deliberately not resolved into a direction — but the strength differs sharply by sub-claim, and collapsing them is how this question gets mis-cited. STRONG: that the question is genuinely open (two peer-reviewed studies, opposite headline framings, neither refuted). MODERATE: that GPT-4-written brand-account posts can outperform human-written ones on engagement and stated preference in a controlled comparison (Huang and Zhou 2025, peer-reviewed, three studies, but magnitudes unpublished in the accessible record). MODERATE-TO-WEAK: that human and AI content perform EQUIVALENTLY on a real account (Flesheriu and Fron 2025 — peer-reviewed and correctly analysed, but n=24 posts on a 770-follower account is a null from an underpowered test, which is weak evidence of equivalence rather than evidence of no difference). WEAK / SELF-REPORT: that human-generated content has a stronger effect on user engagement than AI-generated content (Stanikzai and Mittal 2025, N=324 creators, CB-SEM on survey perceptions, not behaviour). VENDOR-CLAIM AND UNUSABLE: every observational corpus number on either side, including '+31% for AI-assisted across 10,024 posts' and '-45% for AI posts across 3,368 posts'. PLATFORM-OFFICIAL AND STRONG, but about a different proposition: that LinkedIn demotes content its classifier reads as low-effort AI.

**conflicting evidence**

THIS ENTRY IS THE CONFLICT, so the job here is to state each side at its strongest and then say precisely why they do not cancel.
SIDE A — AI WINS. Huang and Zhou (2025, Public Relations Review, peer-reviewed, three studies): GPT-4-generated social posts outperform human-written ones on engagement, consumers prefer them, and trained PR professionals given the same framework and paid incentives cannot match the model. Scope: brand accounts, X/Twitter, corporate register, pre-suppression regime, GPT-4.
SIDE B — HUMANS WIN, AS USUALLY CITED. Flesheriu and Fron (2025): on a live Instagram account, human posts beat AI posts on likes (42.58 vs 39.58), comments (5.33 vs 2.33), shares (0.25 vs 0) and engagement rate (6.73% vs 5.96%).
SIDE B AS THE PAPER ACTUALLY REPORTS IT — and this correction is the most useful thing in this entry: none of those differences is statistically significant (all p between .07 and .91), the authors explicitly state H1 was not supported, and their own conclusion is that AI-generated content 'can perform similarly to, and at times even surpass, human-generated content'. Dropping a single launch-day outlier flips the engagement-rate comparison in AI's favour. Anyone citing this study as evidence that humans win is citing the descriptive table against the paper's own inference. The defensible reading is: no detectable difference, with a non-significant human lean on relational metrics (comments, shares) and a non-significant AI lean on reach metrics (impressions, profile visits, non-follower reach).
WHY A AND B DO NOT CANCEL — four incommensurabilities. (1) CONSTRUCT: Huang and Zhou compared AI-WRITTEN TEXT against human-written text; Flesheriu and Fron compared AI-GENERATED IMAGES PLUS CAPTIONS against human photographs plus captions, in a niche (food) where the photograph is the product — their own survey attributes 64% of engagement to the visual. These are not the same experiment with different results; they are different experiments. (2) AUTHOR TYPE: brand account with no parasocial relationship vs a personal account whose 770 followers know the poster. The effort/parasocial mechanism (see the disclosure item) predicts exactly that AI would do better in the first setting and worse on comments in the second — which is what both papers found. (3) REGIME: both pre-date LinkedIn's 2026-05-20 demotion policy and its 2026-07-30 reader report button; on the platform where most professional writing happens, the distribution rule changed after the evidence was collected. (4) POWER: n=24 posts detects only enormous effects; a null there is weak evidence of equivalence, not proof of it.
SIDE C — THE OBSERVATIONAL VENDOR LAYER, which contradicts itself and should be excluded from the adjudication entirely: '+31% for AI-assisted, N=10,024' vs '-45% for AI posts, N=3,368 across 99 profiles' vs MagicPost's within-author phrase penalties of -4.3% to -6.7%. These cannot all be true, they are all untraced to primary methodology, and the parties publishing them sell AI writing tools, AI detectors, or both. More fundamentally they are structurally incapable of answering the question, because 'AI-detected' and 'low-effort' are the same population in observational data — see how_it_works.
SIDE D — ADJACENT AND OFTEN MISREAD AS EVIDENCE FOR HUMANS: LinkedIn's own policy. It is platform-official and strong, but it is a statement about LOW-EFFORT GENERIC content, not about AI authorship; LinkedIn explicitly permits AI assistance. Citing the policy as proof that AI content underperforms is a category error, though it does mean that in 2026 the two questions have different practical answers on that platform.
NET POSITION TO HOLD: unresolved, with a defensible working prior that authorship per se matters less than (i) whether anything in the post could only have come from the author and (ii) whether the account's relationship with its audience is parasocial or transactional. Do not upgrade this to a finding without the within-author randomised experiment described in how_it_works.

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

The answer is platform-shaped, which is itself the finding. X / TWITTER, BRAND ACCOUNTS: the only setting with peer-reviewed evidence favouring AI (Huang and Zhou). Plausible reason: corporate register rewards fluency and consistency, and there is no parasocial bond for AI to erode. INSTAGRAM, SINGLE-IMAGE, VISUAL NICHE: the only setting with a peer-reviewed field experiment, and it returns equivalence with a split — human slightly ahead on comments and hashtag-driven impressions, AI slightly ahead on profile visits and non-follower reach. Note the study's own attribution of 64% of engagement to the visual: on image-first platforms the text comparison is largely swamped, so a claim about 'AI captions' generalises poorly from it. LINKEDIN: NO peer-reviewed head-to-head exists, and it is the platform where the question matters most for a B2B creator — and the one where the answer is now partly decided by policy rather than by audience, since 2026-05-20. Treat any LinkedIn-specific AI-vs-human number as vendor-derived until a study appears. REDDIT: outside the evidence base entirely, and the environment where detected AI writing carries the harshest and least recoverable penalty, because enforcement is human moderators rather than a ranking function. Pangram's scan puts Reddit at 4.4% AI overall vs LinkedIn's much higher share, which is consistent with the norm being enforced. FORMAT: the evidence covers short brand posts and single-image posts. Nothing located covers carousels, video scripts, threads or long-form articles, so do not transfer the finding across formats. Cross-reference [[Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026]] for the per-platform ranking mechanics rather than re-deriving them here.

**scales with**

What caps the usefulness of this question, rather than of a tactic. (1) OBJECTIVE: if the objective is reach, the evidence tilts neutral-to-AI; if it is relationship, comments and inbound conversations, it tilts neutral-to-human. Decide the objective before consulting the evidence, or you will pick the study that suits you. (2) ACCOUNT TYPE: brand accounts sit in the regime where AI did well; personal accounts sit in the regime where the effort/parasocial mechanism operates. (3) AUDIENCE SIZE AND YOUR OWN ABILITY TO TEST: a personal A/B test needs enough posts to beat within-author variance, and almost nobody has them — at typical variance you need low-hundreds of posts to detect a 10-15% difference, so accounts publishing 12 posts a month are structurally unable to resolve this for themselves within a year. This is the real ceiling: not the account, the sample. (4) NICHE DENSITY: in a niche where AI content is already 40% of long-form supply (LinkedIn, per Pangram), the marginal AI post competes against a saturated field, which makes the population-level answer drift over time even if the individual-level answer does not. (5) OBJECTIVE-DEPENDENT CEILING worth noting: small accounts are cited by AI answer engines at broadly comparable rates to large ones but do not go viral comparably, so for a citation objective this whole dispute is close to irrelevant.

**decay and saturation**

The QUESTION does not decay; every published ANSWER does, and unusually fast, for three independent reasons. (1) MODEL DRIFT: Huang and Zhou tested GPT-4; frontier models have moved two generations since. Any 'AI wins/loses by X%' number is a statement about one model version. Shelf life 6-12 months. (2) POLICY DRIFT: the 2026-05-20 demotion policy and the 2026-07-30 report button changed the distribution function on LinkedIn mid-year; a further 'ranking update' in any quarter can flip the sign of the platform term. Shelf life one quarter. (3) SATURATION: as AI-generated supply rises (40.5% of LinkedIn long-form by mid-2026), the counterfactual changes — 'AI content' stops being a distinctive treatment and becomes the baseline, at which point the interesting comparison inverts into 'does visibly human content now outperform the norm'. That inversion is the most likely 2027 shape of this item and is worth watching for. PRACTICAL SHELF LIFE OF THIS ENTRY: re-check at 6 months; treat any magnitude in it as expired at 12. The structural claims — the observational confound, the L1-vs-L0 evidence gap, the construct mismatch between the two studies — do not decay and are the durable part.

#### risk

**failure modes**

How this item stops being useful, which for a science entry means how it gets misused. (1) CHERRY-PICKING BY CONVENIENCE, the dominant failure: you have already decided to use AI heavily, so you cite Huang and Zhou; or you are selling authenticity, so you cite the Instagram means. Both are available, both are peer-reviewed, and neither citation is honest on its own. (2) MEAN-WITHOUT-TEST, the failure this entry was written to correct: quoting 42.6 vs 39.6 without p=.91 turns a null into a finding. Once that restatement is in circulation it is almost never corrected, because the corrected version is less quotable. (3) CONSTRUCT COLLAPSE: treating 'AI-generated food photos plus captions on Instagram' and 'GPT-4 brand copy on X' as two readings of one quantity. (4) REGIME BLINDNESS: applying a pre-May-2026 result to post-May-2026 LinkedIn. (5) OBSERVATIONAL LAUNDERING: a vendor corpus number gets quoted in a blog, the blog gets quoted in a newsletter, and by the fourth hop it is 'studies show'. The 10,024-post +31% claim is already at this stage — it appears without methodology everywhere it appears. (6) SELF-EXPERIMENT OVERREADING: you run 10 AI posts and 10 human posts, see a 20% difference, and conclude. At realistic within-author variance that test has almost no power; you have measured noise. (7) STALE-MODEL ARGUMENT: rebutting the pro-AI evidence on the grounds that 'GPT-4 was bad at this' while your own counter-evidence is also from 2025.

**ai slop risk**

Meta-level, and real: this item is itself a magnet for slop. The topic is exactly the shape LLMs produce confident empty text about — a contested empirical question with quotable numbers floating free of their methods — and a material share of the secondary sources restating these studies are themselves machine-written (Pangram measured 40.5% of LinkedIn long-form public posts as fully AI-generated in mid-2026, and marketing blogs are a denser AI population than that). THE SPECIFIC TELLS in slop written about this question: (a) a percentage with no n, no date and no platform ('AI content gets 45% less engagement'); (b) 'studies show' with no study named; (c) a confident resolution of the dispute in either direction in a single sentence; (d) the Instagram means quoted without the p-values — a near-perfect diagnostic, because a source that read the paper would have to mention that H1 was not supported; (e) both the +31% and the -45% claims appearing in the same article without the author noticing they contradict each other; (f) treating LinkedIn's anti-slop policy as evidence about AI performance. THE DISCRIMINATOR when you read any new piece on this: does it name the AI condition, the human condition, the platform and the date, and does it distinguish a raw mean from a tested difference? If not, discard it regardless of how authoritative it sounds.

**human input required**

For this item the non-substitutable human contribution is JUDGEMENT ABOUT EVIDENCE, and it is genuinely non-substitutable — a model asked to summarise this literature will, with high probability, reproduce the 42.6-vs-39.6 framing without the p-values, because that framing dominates the secondary corpus it learned from. Concretely, the minimum human acts are: (1) READ THE METHODS SECTION of any study you intend to cite, not the abstract and certainly not a summary of the abstract — the entire correction in this entry came from reading pages 30-32 of the source PDF; (2) CHECK WHETHER A QUOTED DIFFERENCE WAS TESTED, and if so at what p and what effect size; (3) NAME THE FUNDER of any corpus study before repeating its number; (4) STATE YOUR OWN OBJECTIVE (reach vs relationship) before consulting the evidence, so the choice of study is not downstream of the conclusion you want; (5) REFUSE TO RESOLVE — the disciplined output here is 'unresolved, and here is why each side is scoped', which is harder to write and less shareable than a verdict. If you are writing a post about this, the non-substitutable asset is your own within-author data, however small, reported honestly with its limitations — that is the one thing in this space nobody else has.

**detectability and disclosure**

Two separate detectability questions live under this item and they are routinely conflated. (1) CAN A READER OR PLATFORM TELL? Third-party text detectors report high accuracy on unedited frontier-model output and materially lower accuracy once text is edited or paraphrased; false positives are concentrated in non-native English writing; Pangram reports a 0.01% false-positive rate for Pangram 3.3, which is a vendor self-report about the detector that produced the prevalence numbers in this entry. LinkedIn's own classifier is the only one with distribution consequences, and it is not a provenance detector — it targets genericness and absence of unique perspective, which is why 'humaniser' tools that optimise against provenance detectors do not help. Since 2026-07-30 detection is also SOCIAL: readers can tap 'seems like AI slop' on a post, and those reports feed LinkedIn's models. (2) DOES DETECTION CONTAMINATE THE EVIDENCE? Yes, and this is the part that matters for a science entry: every observational study of AI-vs-human performance uses a detector as its independent variable, so detector error is measurement error in the treatment assignment, and it is correlated with the outcome (generic writing is both more likely to be flagged and less likely to be engaged with). That is not a nuisance, it is the identifying assumption failing. DISCLOSURE: no platform requires labelling AI-assisted text as of 2026-09-11, and LinkedIn explicitly permits AI assistance. C2PA and SynthID cover synthetic images, audio and video, not text typed into a composer — note that the Instagram study's AI condition WAS image-generated, so a modern replication of it would potentially carry Content Credentials that the 2025 version did not. See the sibling item 'The AI disclosure paradox' for what disclosure does to the audience once you make it.

**policy and legal**

Assuming a Poland/EU-based creator. EU AI ACT ARTICLE 50(4), applicable since 2026-08-02: deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating text PUBLISHED WITH THE PURPOSE OF INFORMING THE PUBLIC ON MATTERS OF PUBLIC INTEREST must disclose that the text is artificially generated. Two limits matter for this item. First, the human-review carve-out — the obligation does not apply where the content underwent human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility, with the Commission's guidance indicating that review means a knowledgeable person deliberately examining the substance including fact-checking, and that a spelling or grammar pass does not qualify. Second, the public-interest threshold, which ordinary professional or personal-brand posting does not obviously cross. A creator who writes the brief, supplies the substance and edits materially normally lands inside both carve-outs. AI-assisted TEXT does not trigger the deepfake/synthetic-media duties; an AI avatar or a synthetic voice would. SPECIFIC TO THIS ITEM: if you PUBLISH CLAIMS about AI-vs-human performance commercially — in a pitch, a course, a proposal — the relevant regime is not the AI Act but unfair-commercial-practices and advertising law (in Poland, the UOKiK regime implementing UCPD): repeating an untraced vendor statistic such as '+31% for AI-assisted' as though it were established, in material that sells a service, is a misleading-claim exposure, not merely a sloppy-citation problem. The mitigation is trivial and should be habitual: attribute the number to its source and its provenance class in the same sentence. PLATFORM ToS: LinkedIn permits AI assistance and demotes generic output; its Professional Community Policies require authentic identity. FTC endorsement rules are a US regime about material connections and do not govern drafting method.

**reversibility and blast radius**

LOW as a publishing risk, MODERATE-TO-HIGH as a decision risk, and the second is the one people underrate. Nothing about holding an opinion on this question can get an account suspended. The real blast radius is STRATEGIC: if you resolve the question wrongly in your own head and build a publishing system on it, the cost is a year of output pointed at the wrong objective — a fully-automated pipeline built on 'AI wins' that gets classifier-gated on LinkedIn from May 2026 onward, or a hand-writing-only policy built on 'humans win' that caps your cadence for a difference the field data could not even detect. Both are recoverable but slowly, on the timescale of rebuilding a publishing habit, and the second is invisible while it happens because you never see the counterfactual. SECONDARY AND SHARPER: repeating a vendor number in a client proposal or a talk and being corrected in public by someone who read the paper — that is a credibility hit in exactly the audience whose opinion has compounding value, and it is fully avoidable by the citation discipline in human_input_required. REVERSIBILITY OF THE ALGORITHMIC SIDE, for completeness: LinkedIn's stated mechanism is suppression from out-of-network recommendation, not removal, and posts stay visible to direct connections — so distribution recovers when the inputs change.

#### practice

**how to apply**

This is a science item, so 'applying' it means using it as a decision procedure rather than a tactic. STEP 1 — STATE THE OBJECTIVE FIRST, in one sentence, before touching any evidence: reach (impressions, non-follower share, new followers) or relationship (comments, DMs, inbound conversations, meetings). The evidence tilts differently for each and choosing afterwards is how you cherry-pick without noticing. STEP 2 — CLASSIFY YOUR ACCOUNT: brand-transactional (no parasocial bond) or personal-relational (readers know you). Huang and Zhou's setting is the first; the effort/parasocial mechanism applies to the second. STEP 3 — ACCEPT THE PLATFORM TERM AS BINDING AND SEPARATE. On LinkedIn since 2026-05-20, whether AI text 'performs better' is downstream of whether it clears the genericness gate at all. Treat the gate as a precondition, not a factor: every post must carry at least one thing only you could have supplied. This requirement is invariant to how the AI-vs-human question eventually resolves, which makes it the one safe commitment available today. STEP 4 — REFUSE TO BUY A CONCLUSION. When a tool, course or consultant quotes a performance delta, ask the six questions in prompt_patterns (A). If they cannot answer 3, 4 and 6, the number is decoration. STEP 5 — RUN THE ONLY EXPERIMENT YOU CAN ACTUALLY RUN, and run it honestly: fix the brief (the substance) first, then randomise the EXECUTION — voice-matched AI draft edited to publish standard vs hand-written to publish standard — assigning execution to slot by coin flip, logging model version, date, slot and objective metric. STEP 6 — BEFORE INTERPRETING IT, compute the power: take the variance of your last 50 posts' impressions and engagement rate, and ask what difference your n could detect. If the answer is 'only a difference bigger than 40%', say so in your notes and do not conclude. STEP 7 — RE-READ THIS ENTRY IN SIX MONTHS and specifically check three things: whether a within-author randomised study has appeared; whether Huang and Zhou has been replicated on a current model; whether LinkedIn's policy has changed again. STEP 8 — WHEN YOU WRITE ABOUT IT PUBLICLY, lead with the unresolved status and your own numbers. In a field where 40%+ of long-form supply is machine-written and every second post resolves this question confidently in one direction, a careful 'here is why nobody knows yet, and here is my own small dataset' is itself the differentiated position.

**checklist**

Pass/fail gate before repeating ANY claim from this area, in a post, a proposal or a vault note. Any FAIL means do not publish the claim. 1. I can name the study or the vendor, not just 'a study'. PASS/FAIL. 2. I know whether the AI condition was fully-generated, AI-assisted, or detector-inferred. PASS/FAIL. 3. I know the platform and the date window, and whether it predates 2026-05-20. PASS/FAIL. 4. If I am quoting a difference, I know whether it was statistically tested, and I state the p-value or say it was untested. PASS/FAIL. 5. I know who funded it and whether they sell AI writing or AI detection. PASS/FAIL. 6. If it is an observational corpus study, I have said out loud that AI-detected and low-effort are the same population in that data. PASS/FAIL. 7. I am not presenting the question as resolved. PASS/FAIL. 8. If I am citing Flesheriu and Fron, I have included that none of the differences reached significance and the authors' own conclusion was equivalence. PASS/FAIL. 9. If I am citing my own A/B result, I have checked it against within-author variance and stated the power limitation. PASS/FAIL. 10. The claim would survive being read by the author of the paper I am citing. PASS/FAIL.

**worked example**

The cleanest worked example is the mis-citation this entry corrects, shown in both forms. AS IT CIRCULATES — and as this very research item was briefed to me: 'A peer-reviewed within-subjects Instagram field experiment with 24 alternating posts found human posts won on likes (42.6 vs 39.6), comments (5.3 vs 2.3) and engagement rate (6.73% vs 5.96%).' Every number in that sentence is correct. The sentence is still wrong, because it converts a null result into a win. AS THE PAPER REPORTS IT, quoted from Flesheriu and Fron (2025), Oeconomica Jadertina 2/2025, p. 30: 'Nevertheless, the differences observed were not statistically significant.' And p. 32: 'However, none of the differences observed were statistically significant, underscoring that AI-generated and human-generated posts exhibit equivalent performance in quantitative engagement metrics. As a result, H1 was not supported.' The test statistics, from the same page: likes U=69.5 p=.91; comments U=102.5 p=.07; engagement rate U=80.5 p=.64. And from the conclusions, p. 35: 'Among the 12 highest-performing posts, five were produced by humans and seven by AI, indicating that AI-generated content can perform similarly to, and at times even surpass, human-generated content.' HOW TO SAY IT HONESTLY IN ONE SENTENCE YOU COULD POST: 'The only peer-reviewed field experiment I can find on this ran 24 alternating posts on a real 770-follower Instagram account and found no statistically significant difference on any engagement metric — the raw means lean human on comments and lean AI on reach, and dropping a single launch-day outlier flips the engagement-rate comparison to AI. Anyone telling you this question is settled has not read the p-values.' SECOND WORKED EXAMPLE, the contradiction test: the same secondary articles that cite '+31% engagement for AI-assisted content across 10,024 posts' frequently also cite '-45% engagement for AI posts'. Putting both in one sentence is the fastest available demonstration that the observational layer is not measuring what it claims to measure.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

For a science item, the KPIs are about the state of the evidence and about your own test, not about a post. EVIDENCE-STATE INDICATORS, checked quarterly, ordered by how much they would move the answer: (1) has a WITHIN-AUTHOR RANDOMISED field experiment been published — this is the single indicator that would resolve the item, and its absence is why the item exists; (2) has Huang and Zhou been REPLICATED on a post-GPT-4 model, or on a personal rather than brand account; (3) has any study appeared that tests L1 (AI-assisted with human substance) against L0 rather than L2/L3 against L0; (4) has any platform published a first-party analysis rather than a policy statement; (5) has the AI share of supply moved (Pangram-style prevalence scans), since saturation changes the counterfactual. YOUR-OWN-TEST INDICATORS, if you run it: leading — number of randomised pairs logged, and the within-author variance of your baseline (compute this FIRST; it determines whether the test is worth running at all); middle — comments-per-impression and profile-visits-per-impression, which are the two metrics where the published field data showed the largest opposite-signed leans and therefore where a real effect would show first; lagging and noisiest — impressions and follower growth, which are dominated by cold-start lottery variance and should never be the primary outcome of a small test. ANTI-KPI, stated explicitly: do not track 'does my AI content get more likes'. Likes had p=.91 and rank-biserial +.04 in the only field experiment available — it is the metric least likely to carry signal and most likely to produce a confident wrong conclusion.

**measurement feasibility**

Poor, and the specific ways it is poor are the reason this stays unresolved. NOT OBSERVABLE AT ALL: whether a given post was flagged by LinkedIn's genericness classifier — never surfaced, so you see the reach shortfall and never the cause, which makes attribution of any reach difference to authorship unreliable on the one platform where the policy term is largest. NOT NATIVELY OBSERVABLE: dwell time (LinkedIn exposes impressions, reactions, comments, reposts and members reached, not per-post dwell), and DM/dark-social forwarding, which is a meaningful share of real distribution and is invisible everywhere. PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE AND ACTUALLY USABLE: Instagram Insights per post (the instrument Flesheriu and Fron used — likes, comments, shares, saves, accounts reached, impressions, profile visits, follows, and non-follower share), read at a fixed lag; their 48-hour standardisation is a good convention to copy. FULLY OBSERVABLE BECAUSE YOU OWN IT: which arm a post was in, the model and version used, the edit distance between draft and published text, and the time you spent. Make these the spine of any self-test, because they are the only clean variables. THE BINDING PROBLEM IS POWER, NOT ACCESS: within-author engagement variance on social is large relative to any plausible authorship effect, so even with perfect measurement a 20-40 post test detects nothing. The proxy worth adopting instead of a formal test: track comments-per-impression and inbound DMs as your relational read, and impressions-per-follower against your own rolling 8-week median as your reach read, and treat any single-post comparison as anecdote by construction.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- audience fit

- evidence provenance
