### Berger word-of-mouth synthesis (STEPPS + 2025 review)

`berger-wom-synthesis` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 3 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Berger word-of-mouth synthesis (the 2025 Annual Review, with STEPPS subordinated to it). Category: science. Definition: the current authoritative academic account of WHY people pass things on - Jonah Berger, 'What Gets Shared, and Why? Interpersonal Communication and Word of Mouth', Annual Review of Psychology 2025, 76:559-581 (DOI 10.1146/annurev-psych-013024-031524; first published as a Review in Advance 2024-08-06; PMID 39107036; CC-BY 4.0, free full text). It organises sharing around SIX SENDER MOTIVATIONS (impression management, accessibility, emotion regulation, information acquisition, social bonding, persuasion) and then shows how FOUR CONTEXT MODERATORS (audience, modality, channel, device) change what those motivations produce. Position of STEPPS: STEPPS (Social currency, Triggers, Emotion, Public, Practical value, Stories) is the popular-book framing from Berger's 'Contagious' (Simon & Schuster, 2013). VERIFIED IN THE PRIMARY TEXT during this research pass: the string 'STEPPS' appears ZERO times in the 2025 review, and 'Contagious' appears exactly once - in the reference list - cited in-text only in support of two narrow claims (self-enhancement, and social currency/status). Berger's own peer-reviewed synthesis does not use his own acronym as its structure. That is the hard evidence that STEPPS is a teaching mnemonic sitting UNDER the review, not a theory sitting above it. Maturity: ESTABLISHED and stable. This is a top-of-field invited review by the most-cited researcher in the area; it is a consolidation, not a frontier.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. STABLE - the slowest-rotting item in this whole research set. Three clocks, all long. (1) The review itself: published January 2025 (Review in Advance August 2024); 29 citations at OpenAlex / 35 at Semantic Scholar as of 2026-09-11. Annual Reviews commissions a replacement on a topic roughly every 8-12 years (Berger's own prior review was J. Consumer Psychology 2014, 24(4):586-607), so expect this to remain the anchor until roughly 2033. (2) The underlying psychology (impression management, accessibility, emotion regulation, information acquisition, social bonding, persuasion): decades old, replicated, essentially not volatile. Berger's own closing line is that 'the fundamental motivations for sharing have remained similar' despite changes in devices and channels. (3) The moderator layer (modality / device / channel) is the youngest part - most of it rests on 2018-2024 work (Melumad et al. 2019; Ransbotham et al. 2019; Berger et al. 2022; Oba & Berger 2024) and a fast-moving device landscape (voice-first interfaces, AI chat as a communication channel in its own right) could extend it within 3-5 years. CRITICAL DATING CAVEAT: the review's evidence base is almost entirely PRE-2024 and largely pre-2020. It says nothing about 2026 algorithmic ranking, LinkedIn's Aug-2026 per-viewer comment ranking, or X's Jan/May-2026 ranker rewrites. It tells you what a HUMAN wants to pass on; it does not tell you what a 2026 RANKER will distribute. Do not treat it as a platform-mechanics source - for that, cross-reference the vault note [[Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026]].

#### mechanism

**how it works**

TWO LAYERS.

LAYER 1 - six motivations that make a person press share (structure taken verbatim from the review's 'WHAT GETS SHARED AND WHY' section):

1. IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT. People share what makes them look good and signals a desired identity. This is the largest cluster in the review and it produces five concrete content properties: (a) ENGAGING things - interesting, funny, surprising, extreme, novel (Berger & Milkman 2012; Heath et al. 2001; Chen & Berger 2013 on moderate controversy; Heath & DeVoe 2005 on extreme narratives - 'Tim caught a 200-pound fish' beats 'Tim caught a 10-pound fish'); (b) SCARCE / EXCLUSIVE / HIGH-STATUS things - hidden bars, limited editions, invite-only access, being first to know (Berger 2013; Goor et al. 2020; Lovett et al. 2013); (c) USEFUL things - because being helpful signals competence (note the mechanism: usefulness works through IMPRESSION, not altruism); (d) things that FACILITATE SOCIAL INTERACTION; (e) VALENCE control - people suppress what makes them look bad. The review flags a real counter-current: high need-for-uniqueness individuals SUPPRESS word of mouth on publicly consumed goods (Cheema & Kaikati 2010) and 'share and scare' - praising a thing while stressing how hard it is to use (Moldovan et al. 2015).

2. ACCESSIBILITY. What is top of mind gets shared. Four sub-levers: RECENT (over 40% of what people discuss is happening right now; another 25-35% is less than a day away - Weingarten & Berger 2024), FREQUENT (chronic accessibility), PRIMED (environmental triggers - orange products around Halloween, Berger & Fitzsimons 2008; advertising raises discussion, Onishi & Manchanda 2012), and PUBLICLY VISIBLE (shirts get discussed more than socks - Berger & Schwartz 2011). This is the STEPPS 'Triggers' pillar with an actual cognitive mechanism attached.

3. EMOTION REGULATION. Sharing is how people manage feeling. Six sub-functions enumerated in the review: generating social support, venting, sense-making, reducing dissonance, taking vengeance, and rehearsing/savouring positive experience. Content consequence: more emotional things, highly positive OR negative things, arousing things, and things evoking specific emotions get shared more. Berger & Milkman (2012) is the anchor - AROUSAL, not valence, is the active ingredient: awe, anger and anxiety (high arousal) increase transmission; sadness (low arousal, deactivating) decreases it.

4. INFORMATION ACQUISITION. People talk in order to GET information, not only to give it. Triggered by decisions that are risky, important, complex or uncertainty-ridden, and by a poor or untrustworthy information environment (brands involving more risk are talked about more - Lovett et al. 2013). This is the driver STEPPS has no slot for at all, and it is the one that underwrites the 'ask a real question' post.

5. SOCIAL BONDING. Sharing as social glue. Phatic communication - messages whose function is rapport rather than information; Rettie (2009) finds almost 6 in 10 text messages are phatic. Loneliness, social exclusion and boredom all raise the drive to reach out.

6. PERSUASION. People share to move others to act. This pushes toward EXTREME content (extremely positive or negative information outperforms moderate information at changing behaviour - Abelson 1995; Craig & Blankenship 2011) and toward AROUSING content, because arousal is an excitatory state that supports action.

LAYER 2 - four moderators that change what those six motivations actually produce. This layer is what the 2025 review adds over every popular treatment:

A. AUDIENCE, on two dimensions. TIE STRENGTH: impression management is stronger with WEAK ties (people prefer self-enhancing topics with strangers - Chen 2017; word of mouth is more positive with weaker ties - Dubois et al. 2016; people are less willing to raise controversial topics with acquaintances - Chen & Berger 2013), while emotional and connecting content flows to STRONG ties, which are better for social support, sense-making and dissonance reduction. AUDIENCE SIZE: broadcasting (many) versus narrowcasting (one). Barasch & Berger (2014, JMR 51(3):286-299, six studies) is the key result - broadcasting triggers egocentric self-focus so people share what makes them look good; narrowcasting triggers other-focus so people share what is USEFUL to that one recipient.

B. MODALITY - speaking vs writing. Speaking produces more personal, social, self-disclosing, informal content; writing produces more formal, detached, complex content and REDUCES emotional expression because it involves more deliberation (Berger et al. 2022). Writing also pushes toward more INTERESTING products and brands (Berger & Iyengar 2013). Mechanism: writing is slower and editable, which buys construction and refinement time; speech is more social and puts the communicator in an interactive, audience-focused mindset.

C. DEVICE - smartphone vs PC, and this is about the PRODUCER, not the reader. Smartphones produce communication that is SHORTER, less focused on specific details, MORE emotional and MORE self-disclosing (Melumad et al. 2019). PCs produce communication that is more ABSTRACT, more EXTREME and more REFLECTIVE (Ransbotham et al. 2019). Mechanisms: learned associations (PC = work, phone = social connection and identity - Melumad & Pham 2020), small screens and buttons making writing effortful (Antoun et al. 2017), and portable use in distracting contexts. Both reduce deliberative capacity.

D. CHANNEL - email vs text vs face-to-face vs ephemeral. Channels differ in SYNCHRONICITY (longer turn gaps buy refinement time), EPHEMERALITY (Snapchat and face-to-face vanish on delivery; email and voice notes persist and can be re-viewed - Barnea et al. 2023), and SOCIAL PRESENCE (Short et al. 1976). Channels also carry tie-strength associations: texting is personal and strong-tie, email is work and weak-tie, so people deliberate more over email.

THE STEPPS MAPPING, made explicit. Social currency -> impression management (status/scarcity sub-branch). Triggers -> accessibility (priming sub-branch). Emotion -> emotion regulation, with the correction that AROUSAL not valence is the operative variable. Public -> accessibility (public visibility) plus impression management. Practical value -> impression management (useful content makes the SENDER look helpful) plus information acquisition. Stories -> not a driver at all; a delivery vehicle. What STEPPS has NO slot for: information acquisition, social bonding, persuasion, and the entire four-moderator layer. That is the case for the subordination in one paragraph.

**ranking signal targeted**

MOSTLY UNKNOWN, and saying so is the honest answer. The review is about human sharing MOTIVATION; it contains no claim whatsoever about algorithmic ranking and cites no ranker. What it targets is the upstream human act - the SHARE / REPOST / SEND - which platforms then weight downstream. Where a mapping is defensible: (a) the narrowcasting branch (Barasch & Berger 2014) maps onto DM sends / share-to-DM, which are heavily weighted on IG and Threads and which X's open-sourced ranker weights explicitly (ShareViaCopyLink 20.0 against FavoriteWeight 0.5 in home-mixer/params/param.rs) - see the sibling items 'Narrowcast / share-to-DM trigger design' and 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes'; (b) the impression-management branch maps onto the public repost or quote, which is more reach-weighted but self-presentation-gated, so it only fires when resharing your post flatters the resharer; (c) the accessibility branch maps onto nothing algorithmic at all - it is about being top of mind at the moment of conversation, i.e. recall, not ranking, and it predicts dark-social and offline mentions that are invisible in every analytics panel; (d) the emotion-regulation and persuasion branches point toward comment depth and reply volume rather than reach. NOT targeted, and not addressed anywhere in the review: dwell time, completion rate, semantic relevance, first-hour velocity, saves. Use this item to decide WHAT to write; use [[Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026]] to decide how the platform will treat it.

**why it drives reach**

The causal chain is deliberately short and it stops before the algorithm. A post is written -> it engages one or more of the six motivations in a reader -> the reader shares (publicly, or privately to one person) -> that share is both a distribution event in itself (a new root node reaching that person's network) and a ranking input the platform weights. The review's contribution is that it tells you which motivation you are actually pulling on, and therefore which of the two share TYPES you will get. Broadcast-flavoured content (status, novelty, being in-the-know, a moral position) recruits impression management and produces PUBLIC reshares. Narrowcast-flavoured content (a specific useful thing for a specific person) recruits other-focus and produces DM FORWARDS. These are different distribution mechanisms with different measurement properties, and most copy advice conflates them. The second contribution is the honest ceiling. This model explains the per-reader PROBABILITY of a share. It does NOT explain cascade size, because - per Goel, Anderson, Hofman & Watts (Management Science 2016), the sibling item 'Limits of virality prediction' - over 99% of cascades die within a single generation and popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest single broadcast. So a well-motivated post raises the base rate of the first share; it does not buy you a cascade. Reach is the product of (share probability, which this item governs) x (network position and platform amplification, which it does not).

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Four roles, in descending order of how well the model actually performs them.

1. CRITIC / MOTIVE AUDITOR (best use). Give the model the six-driver taxonomy plus the draft, and have it name which driver the post recruits IN THE READER and quote the exact span that does it. The failure it catches is the common one: a draft that is interesting to the AUTHOR but recruits no reader motivation at all. Because the taxonomy is closed and small, this is a classification task models do reliably.

2. MODERATOR SIMULATOR (second best). Ask the model to rewrite the same substance under a broadcast frame versus a narrowcast frame (Barasch & Berger 2014), then compare: if the two versions come out nearly identical, the post has no narrowcast trigger and will not be forwarded. The same trick applies to modality - have it contrast a spoken phrasing against the written one and flag where writing has flattened the emotion (Berger et al. 2022).

3. SCORER on a rubric. LLM-as-judge over a six-driver rubric with forced quoting. Useful for RANKING a batch of drafts; unreliable as an absolute score. Anchor it with three to five of your own past posts whose real performance you know. The LLM-as-judge tooling and rubric patterns are already catalogued in [[Marketing Agent Research]] - do not re-derive them.

4. RETRIEVER / CORPUS ANALYST, indirectly. The review's own future-directions section explicitly endorses automated textual analysis for this research - LIWC (Boyd et al. 2022), the Lexical Suite (lexicalsuite.com), topic modelling (Blei et al. 2003), embeddings (Mikolov et al. 2013), and 'large language models such as ChatGPT'. The same tooling applied to your own post corpus tells you which drivers you habitually use and which you never touch.

NOT an AI role: generating the substance. Every driver except accessibility requires something the model does not have - your status signal, your first-hand emotion, your real uncertainty, your relationship with the reader.

**automation level**

L1 - AI-assisted, and it cannot honestly go higher. This item is a JUDGMENT SCAFFOLD, not a generator: it tells you which of six human motives your draft is pulling on, and that verdict is only useful if a human then decides whether that is the motive they want. An L2 'autonomous with guardrails' setup is defensible for the AUDIT half - a gate that blocks publication when the model cannot name a driver or cannot quote the span carrying it - but the rewrite half stays L1. Nothing here belongs at L2 generation or L3. Note also that no commercial tool implements this taxonomy at all: every 'virality scorer' or 'post grader' sold in 2026 is a hook-and-engagement heuristic, typically a repackaged STEPPS checklist, not a motivation model.

**prompt patterns**

Four concrete structures. All force VERBATIM QUOTING, which is what stops the model hallucinating a driver that is not in the text.

1. SIX-DRIVER AUDIT (forced-quote classification):
'Here is a draft post. For each of these six sharing drivers - impression management, accessibility, emotion regulation, information acquisition, social bonding, persuasion - either quote the exact sentence in the draft that recruits it, or write ABSENT. Do not paraphrase; quote verbatim. Then state which single driver is strongest and why. If four or more are ABSENT, say so plainly.'

2. BROADCAST/NARROWCAST SPLIT (Barasch & Berger 2014):
'Two questions about this draft, answered separately. (a) BROADCAST: if someone reposts this publicly, what does it say about THEM? Write the one-line impression they buy. If reposting it makes them look worse, or says nothing, say so. (b) NARROWCAST: name the specific colleague a reader would DM this to, and quote the line that makes it worth forwarding to that one person. If you cannot name a plausible recipient, state that the post has no narrowcast trigger.'

3. MODALITY REPAIR (Berger et al. 2022 - writing suppresses emotional expression through deliberation):
'This was written, so deliberation has likely flattened its emotion. Find the three places where a spoken version would have carried more feeling and show the spoken phrasing beside the written one. Change nothing else. Do not add adjectives - recover the feeling that was edited out.'

4. AROUSAL, NOT VALENCE (Berger & Milkman 2012 - the most common misreading):
'Classify the dominant emotion of this draft on the ACTIVATION axis, not the positive/negative axis. High-activation: awe, anger, anxiety, excitement, amusement. Low-activation (deactivating): sadness, contentment, resignation. If the draft is dominated by a low-activation emotion, name it and say which sentence deactivates the reader. Do not advise making it more positive - valence is not the variable.'

ANTI-PATTERN to avoid: 'make this post more viral using STEPPS.' It produces the acronym as a checklist rather than a diagnosis, and it invites the model to bolt on a fake 'story' and a fake 'trigger'. Always ask for a DIAGNOSIS with quotes, never for an application of a framework.

**tool examples**

For READING the source: the full text is free (CC-BY 4.0) at https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/pdf/10.1146/annurev-psych-013024-031524 - 23 pages, no paywall, no login. Note that the HTML landing page at annualreviews.org/content/journals/... returns HTTP 403 to automated fetchers while the /doi/pdf/ path serves the PDF directly; if a tool tells you this paper is paywalled, it used the wrong URL. Do not pay for it and do not settle for the abstract - the moderator sections (pp. 571-574) are the part absent from every popular summary.

For APPLYING it: any frontier chat model with the rubric pasted in - Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini. The review itself names ChatGPT as an acceptable text-analysis instrument, so this is not a stretch of the source.

For CORPUS analysis of your own posts: LIWC-22 (Boyd et al. 2022, paid individual licence, roughly USD 100+), the free Lexical Suite (https://www.lexicalsuite.com/), or embeddings plus topic modelling over your exported post archive. All three are endorsed by name in the review's 'The Role of Automated Textual Analysis' section (p. 575).

NO commercial tool implements the six-driver taxonomy as of 2026-09-11. Treat any vendor claiming to score 'Berger's framework' as scoring STEPPS off a blog post.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

SPLIT - and the split is the whole point of this entry. (a) As a SYNTHESIS of what psychology currently believes about sharing: STRONG. Invited peer-reviewed Annual Review, top-of-field journal, sole author is the most-cited researcher in the area, CC-BY, 29-35 citations within roughly 13 months of the Review-in-Advance posting. (b) As a source of EFFECT SIZES: WEAK, verging on absent. The review reports no effect sizes, no confidence intervals and no meta-analytic estimates. It is a narrative review, not a meta-analysis. Anyone quoting a percentage 'from Berger 2025' is quoting something that is not in the paper. (c) As a predictor of what performs on a 2026 B2B FEED: UNVERIFIED. The evidence base is dominated by lab experiments, US consumer and student samples, and pre-2020 field data (New York Times emails, Twitter, urban legends, product word of mouth). Almost none of it is professional content, almost none of it is LinkedIn, none of it is 2026 ranking. (d) STEPPS specifically: ANECDOTAL as a causal framework. 'Contagious' is a trade book; its six pillars were never validated as a set, and Berger's own peer-reviewed synthesis does not use them. The individual underlying findings are solid; the acronym is packaging.

**evidence provenance**

PEER-REVIEWED, single-author invited review - the strongest provenance class available for a synthesis, and materially stronger than anything else in this research set. Jonah Berger, Marketing Department, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania. Published by Annual Reviews, whose articles are commissioned and refereed. The author declares no conflicts in the Disclosure Statement.

PROVENANCE CAVEAT WORTH STATING PLAINLY: Berger is reviewing a literature he substantially authored. A large share of the in-text citations are Berger or Berger-and-co-author papers - Berger 2011, 2013, 2014; Berger & Milkman 2012; Berger & Schwartz 2011; Berger & Heath 2005, 2007, 2008; Berger & Fitzsimons 2008; Berger & Iyengar 2013; Berger & Ward 2010; Barasch & Berger 2014; Chen & Berger 2013; Buechel & Berger 2012; Weingarten & Berger 2024; Oba & Berger 2024; Boghrati & Berger 2023; Berger & Packard 2022. That is normal and expected for an invited review by a field's founder, and it does not make the review wrong - but it does mean this is one research programme's account of the field rather than an adversarial one, and it is a commercial as well as an academic programme (Berger sells books and speaking on the same material). The underlying studies are independently peer-reviewed; the SELECTION and EMPHASIS are not independent.

DOWNSTREAM PROVENANCE: every 'STEPPS' blog post, LinkedIn carousel and marketing course is vendor-with-product-to-sell material derived from the 2013 trade book, not from this review. When a 2026 marketing source cites 'Berger', check which one it means - in practice it is almost always Contagious, and almost never the peer-reviewed synthesis.

**effect size and n**

- NO EFFECT SIZE IN THE REVIEW ITSELF. This is the single most important thing to record: the 2025 Annual Review is narrative, reports no coefficients, no IRRs, no R-squared and no confidence intervals, and performs no meta-analysis. Anyone attaching a percentage to 'Berger 2025' is fabricating it.
- Descriptive figures QUOTED INSIDE the review - these are real, and they are the only numbers in it: people spend 50-80% of their day in some form of interpersonal communication (Klemmer & Snyder 1972 - a 1972 estimate, treat as illustrative); over 20 billion texts are sent each day (Giacomini 2021); over 40% of what people discuss is happening RIGHT NOW, with a further 25-35% less than a day away in either direction (Weingarten & Berger 2024); over 50% of stories are distorted in one way or another in the retelling (Marsh & Tversky 2004); almost 6 in 10 text messages are phatic, i.e. carry no information and exist only to signal that the sender is thinking of the recipient (Rettie 2009).
- The load-bearing effect sizes live in the CITED primary studies, not the review. Berger & Milkman (2012), Journal of Marketing Research 49(2):192-205: approximately 7,000 New York Times articles over a three-month period, plus controlled experiments. Findings - positive content more viral than negative; awe, anger and anxiety (high-arousal) increase transmission; sadness (low-arousal, deactivating) decreases it; effects hold controlling for how surprising, interesting and practically useful the content is, and for external attention drivers such as prominence of placement. Reported as regression coefficients on most-emailed status, NOT as a percentage lift usable for a social post.
- Barasch & Berger (2014), Journal of Marketing Research 51(3):286-299: SIX studies. Broadcasting (communicating with multiple people) leads people to avoid sharing content that makes them look bad; narrowcasting (communicating with one person) encourages sharing content useful to the recipient; mediated by communicators' focus of attention (self-focus vs other-focus). Lab and field studies with typical social-psychology sample sizes (hundreds per study), not large-N field data.
- Berger & Packard (2018), Psychological Science 29(7):1178-1184, 'Are Atypical Things More Popular?' - the atypicality/novelty branch of the impression-management driver.
- SAMPLE-COMPOSITION CAVEAT: the review's evidence is overwhelmingly US, overwhelmingly consumer or lay rather than professional, and mostly collected before 2020. There is no N for 'B2B posts on LinkedIn in 2026', because no such study is cited. Write 'no effect size found' for any B2B-feed application of this item rather than borrowing a number from an adjacent study.
