#### fit

**platform and format fit**

PLATFORM-AGNOSTIC BY CONSTRUCTION - the review is about people, not feeds - which is exactly why it outlasts every platform-mechanics note in this set, and exactly why it cannot replace one. Read it alongside [[Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026]]; do not re-derive ranking mechanics from it.

WHERE IT APPLIES WELL. LinkedIn: the impression-management branch is unusually dominant because the resharer's professional identity is on the line with every public repost - the operational question 'what does resharing this say about the resharer?' is at its sharpest here. Long-form text generally: the information-acquisition and persuasion drivers need room to operate. Newsletters and DM-shared artifacts: the narrowcast branch is the whole game.

WHERE IT BACKFIRES OR MISLEADS. (a) Short-form video (Reels, Shorts, TikTok): the review's evidence base is text and speech, and its modality section explicitly contrasts speaking and writing without covering edited video as a third mode. Do not assume the writing findings transfer. (b) Algorithm-first surfaces where most distribution goes to NON-followers: the entire audience-moderator layer assumes you know who you are talking to. On an interest-graph feed you do not, which collapses the tie-strength distinction and makes the weak-tie positivity finding the default assumption. (c) Anywhere you need a number: the review has none.

FORMAT NOTES WITH DIRECT PRODUCTION CONSEQUENCES. The MODALITY finding is immediately actionable: because writing suppresses emotional expression through deliberation (Berger et al. 2022), the highest-yield workflow for emotionally-loaded posts is to SPEAK the first draft (voice note, transcript) and edit down, rather than to type it cold. The DEVICE finding compounds this and is routinely misreported in marketing content: Melumad et al. (2019) and Ransbotham et al. (2019) concern the device the COMMUNICATOR produces on, not the device the reader consumes on. Drafting on a phone yields shorter, more emotional, more self-disclosing copy; drafting on a PC yields more abstract, more extreme, more reflective copy. Choose the drafting device to match the post you want - a free intervention most people get backwards by drafting everything in the same place.

**scales with**

Scales with JUDGMENT and SELF-KNOWLEDGE, not with account size, corpus size or budget - which makes it unusually cheap and unusually non-delegable. The binding constraints: (1) Your ability to know what your reader's reshare would say about them. That requires actually knowing your audience's professional self-image, and no amount of data substitutes for it. (2) Access to something status-conferring - a number, an access, a first. This is the one genuinely capped input, and it is the same cap as the sibling items 'Original data drops' and 'Proof-of-work receipts'. (3) Network position, for the CEILING rather than the RATE. The six drivers govern per-reader share probability, which is roughly account-size-independent. Realised reach is not: per Goel et al. (2016), popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest single broadcast, so a well-motivated post from a small account still gets a small cascade. A sub-500-follower account can execute this item perfectly and still not go viral - though, per the sibling item 'AI citation visibility as a second objective function', it can be CITED comparably. (4) NOT capped by: team size (one person suffices), tool spend (zero - the paper is free), corpus size (the framework is prior knowledge, not learned from your data), or posting cadence.

**decay and saturation**

LONGEST SHELF-LIFE IN THIS RESEARCH SET - roughly 5-10 years for the six drivers, 3-5 years for the moderator layer. The drivers are basic social-cognitive processes with a fifty-year literature behind them (Goffman 1959, Granovetter 1973, Higgins & King 1981, Gross 1998), and Berger's own conclusion is that 'the fundamental motivations for sharing have remained similar' across every technology shift so far.

WHAT CAN DECAY: (a) the device and channel findings, which are tied to specific hardware and app affordances - the smartphone-vs-PC contrast (Melumad et al. 2019) was calibrated before AI chat interfaces became a communication channel in their own right, and a voice-first or agent-mediated channel would need new work; (b) the calibration of what counts as status-conferring in a given niche, which rots in 12-24 months like any positioning; (c) the review itself as the citation of record, once Annual Reviews commissions a successor - historically 8-12 years, so approximately 2033.

SATURATION RISK: essentially none, because this is a diagnostic lens rather than a tactic. Nothing degrades when everyone uses it - unlike hook templates, engagement pods and link-in-first-comment, all of which decayed within 12-24 months precisely because they were pattern-matchable by both audiences and classifiers. The specific CONTENT MOVES the lens points at can saturate (a status signal everyone can make stops signalling status), but the lens that selects them does not.

#### risk

**failure modes**

1. MISTAKING A MOTIVATION MODEL FOR A DISTRIBUTION MODEL. The most consequential failure. The review predicts whether a reader WANTS to share; it says nothing about whether the platform will show your post to enough readers for that to matter. Applied alone it produces posts that are highly shareable and barely seen.

2. APPLYING THE SENDER MODEL TO THE WRONG PERSON. The six drivers describe the SHARER's motives. When you write, you are the first sharer - but the reach comes from the SECOND sharer, your reader. Optimising for what makes YOU look good produces the standard self-congratulatory professional post, which serves your impression management and gives the reader no reason to touch it. The correct question is always 'what does resharing this do for THEM'.

3. TREATING THE SIX DRIVERS AS A CHECKLIST TO SATISFY ALL OF. They are alternative routes, not requirements, and several actively conflict - persuasion pushes toward extremity while weak-tie impression management pushes away from it. A post trying to hit all six is incoherent. One or two, executed cleanly, is the target.

4. THE VALENCE ERROR. Reading 'positive content is more viral' and writing relentlessly upbeat copy, when the actual finding is that ACTIVATION drives transmission and low-arousal positive states (contentment, satisfaction) transmit poorly. Deactivating positivity is the worst of both worlds.

5. IMPORTING CONSUMER STATUS SIGNALS INTO B2B. Scarcity, exclusivity and premium-brand talk are documented in consumer contexts. Transplanted literally into professional content they read as status anxiety.

6. USING IT AS A CITATION FOR A NUMBER. It contains none. This produces fabricated statistics attributed to a real and freely-readable paper, which is the single most damaging failure available here precisely because it is checkable in thirty seconds.

7. EXPECTING CONSISTENCY. Even a perfectly-motivated post faces the Goel et al. distribution: over 99% of cascades die in one generation. The model raises a probability; it does not remove the variance, and reading a single post's result as a verdict on the framework is a sampling error.

**ai slop risk**

MEDIUM as a direct risk, HIGH as an indirect one, and the two have different tells.

DIRECT (using the framework as a critic): LOW risk. Auditing a human draft against six named drivers cannot itself manufacture text. The one real hazard is the model AGREEING with you - asked 'does this recruit impression management?' it will usually say yes. Mitigation is structural: force verbatim quoting, allow ABSENT as an answer, and require an explicit count of how many drivers are absent.

INDIRECT (asking a model to WRITE to the framework): HIGH risk, with specific and recognisable tells. (a) Bolted-on status signalling - a generic prestige noun where a specific one belongs ('a leading client' instead of a named one, 'a major enterprise' instead of a number). (b) Manufactured surprise - 'most people think X, but actually Y' where Y is in fact the consensus view; this is the model simulating novelty it does not possess. (c) Hollow phatic padding - social-bonding language ('would love to hear your thoughts', 'who else has felt this?') with no actual relationship behind it. Per Rettie (2009) phatic communication is real and common, but genuine phatic language is SHORT and specific, whereas the generated version is long and universal. (d) Fake extremity for the persuasion driver - superlatives with no referent ('completely transforms', 'changes everything'). (e) The narrative bolt-on, courtesy of STEPPS 'Stories' - a two-sentence anecdote with no proper noun, no date and no specific detail, prepended to an otherwise abstract post.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT ACTUALLY WORKS: take the finished draft and ask, for each driver the model claims it recruits, 'what fact in this post could only have been supplied by the author?'. Impression management needs a real status marker; emotion regulation needs a real feeling about a real event; information acquisition needs a real open question. If the answer is 'nothing' for every driver, the post is slop regardless of how well it scores on the rubric.

**human input required**

The review makes the non-substitutable contribution unusually explicit, because five of the six drivers are definitionally about the author's position in the world.

- IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT: something real that confers status - a proprietary number, a named client, an access nobody else had, a first. A model can describe status; it cannot hold it.
- ACCESSIBILITY: the ONE driver a model can genuinely serve, because it is about timing and environmental priming rather than about you. Retrieval and trend-matching are legitimate here.
- EMOTION REGULATION: a real emotional experience, and specifically an unresolved or costly one. This is the driver that most reliably separates a human post from a generated one, and the reason the sibling item 'Personal narrative arcs' exists.
- INFORMATION ACQUISITION: a genuine open question - one you actually do not know the answer to. A model asked to write a question writes a rhetorical one, which readers detect instantly and which recruits no sharing at all.
- SOCIAL BONDING: an actual relationship with actual people, referenced specifically.
- PERSUASION: a real position you are prepared to defend in the comments when someone pushes back.

MINIMUM CHECKABLE GATE: name one driver, and point at the one piece of the post that only you could have supplied to serve it. If you cannot point at it, do not publish. Per the sibling items on AI-slop detection, this is also approximately what platform NLP classifiers are probing for - not 'was a model involved' but 'is there anything here that only this account could have said'.

**detectability and disclosure**

NOT APPLICABLE AS A DETECTION SURFACE, and it is worth being precise about why. This item is a lens for deciding what to write; it produces no artifact, no image and no generated text of its own. Using it creates nothing to detect, nothing to watermark and nothing to disclose. There is no C2PA manifest, no SynthID payload and no classifier signature attached to 'I audited my draft against a six-driver taxonomy'.

WHERE DETECTION DOES ENTER: only on the second, riskier path, where a model WRITES to the framework. Then the ordinary AI-text detection question applies, and the tells listed under ai_slop_risk are precisely what both human readers and platform classifiers pick up - generic status nouns, referentless superlatives, universal phatic closers, proper-noun-free anecdotes. Cross-reference the sibling items 'AI slop and the authenticity penalty', 'The AI disclosure paradox' and 'Platform AI labeling and C2PA provenance' for the actual detection and labelling layer; do not re-derive it here.

AN ASYMMETRY WORTH ACTING ON: using this framework to make your HUMAN writing better is one of the few moves in this entire research set that improves output while REDUCING detectability risk, because it pushes you toward the specific, first-hand, status-bearing material that classifiers and readers both read as human.

**policy and legal**

NO OBLIGATIONS TRIGGERED by using the framework. Reading a CC-BY paper and applying its taxonomy to your own writing engages no platform ToS and no AI regulation.

COPYRIGHT / ATTRIBUTION: the review is CC-BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution and reproduction in any medium PROVIDED the original author and source are credited. That is a genuine obligation if you quote, reproduce figures or republish substantial passages - cite Berger, J. (2025), Annual Review of Psychology 76:559-581, DOI 10.1146/annurev-psych-013024-031524. Note the review's own credit-line caveat: third-party material inside the article may carry different licences. 'Contagious' (2013) is ordinary all-rights-reserved trade-book copyright: the STEPPS acronym as an idea is not protected, extended verbatim quotation is.

EU AI ACT ART. 50 (in force since 2026-08-02; grace period to 2026-12-02 for pre-existing systems; fines to EUR 15M or 3% of worldwide turnover): not engaged by this item as such. Where AI is used to DRAFT text in this workflow, the Art. 50 transparency duty for AI-generated text on matters of public interest carries an exemption where the text has undergone HUMAN EDITORIAL REVIEW - and a human performing the six-driver audit on a draft is a clean instance of exactly that review. Applying this framework therefore strengthens rather than weakens the Art. 50 position for a Poland/EU-based creator. See the sibling item 'Compliance layer - EU AI Act Article 50' for the full treatment.

FTC and platform AI-disclosure rules: likewise not engaged by a text-drafting workflow with human review. They bite on synthetic avatars, undisclosed endorsements and fabricated testimonials, none of which this item produces.

**reversibility and blast radius**

NEAR-ZERO BLAST RADIUS - the safest item in this research set. Worst realistic case: you write posts optimised for a sharing motive your audience does not have, and they underperform. Fully reversible; the cost is the writing time. No shadowban vector, no comment restriction, no suspension risk, because nothing here touches platform anti-abuse surfaces - there is no automation, no amplification, no reciprocal engagement and no synthetic account.

The one non-trivial exposure is SECOND-ORDER and reputational. The impression-management and persuasion drivers both push toward status signalling and extremity. Pushed hard, in a weak-tie professional feed, that reads as bragging or as manufactured controversy - and per the review's own weak-tie findings, your readers will quietly decline to reshare rather than object. That is slow brand erosion, not an enforcement event: recoverable over a few weeks of different posting, but invisible while it happens, which makes it worth a periodic check on the ratio of reshares to impressions rather than on absolute engagement.

#### practice

**how to apply**

STEP 0 (once, 90 minutes). Read the actual paper, free, at https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/pdf/10.1146/annurev-psych-013024-031524. Read pp. 561-571 (the six drivers) and pp. 571-574 (the four moderators). The moderator sections are the part absent from every popular summary and are where the operational leverage is. Do not substitute a blog summary - they all collapse it back into STEPPS.

STEP 1 (per post, 2 minutes). BEFORE drafting, choose ONE primary driver and write it at the top of the draft file. Not two, not six. Let the objective choose it: reach via public reshare -> impression management; DM forwarding -> information acquisition or usefulness under a narrowcast frame; comments -> persuasion or information acquisition; community -> social bonding; timeliness -> accessibility.

STEP 2 (per post, 1 minute). Pick your AUDIENCE FRAME explicitly, because Barasch & Berger shows it flips the content. BROADCAST frame: complete the sentence 'someone who reshares this is telling their network that they are ______.' If you cannot complete it, the post will not be publicly reshared. NARROWCAST frame: complete 'a reader sends this to ______ because ______.' If you cannot name a plausible recipient and reason, it will not be forwarded. You need at least one of the two to complete with something specific.

STEP 3 (per post, 0 minutes - it is a device choice, not a task). Match the DRAFTING MEDIUM to the driver. Emotion-regulation and social-bonding posts: speak the first draft as a voice note and transcribe, because writing deliberation suppresses emotional expression (Berger et al. 2022). Persuasion and information-acquisition posts: draft on a PC, which produces more abstract, extreme and reflective content (Ransbotham et al. 2019). This is a free intervention that most people get backwards by drafting everything in the same place.

STEP 4 (per post, 3 minutes). Draft the substance yourself - specifically the part only you can supply (see human_input_required). Then run the SIX-DRIVER AUDIT prompt from prompt_patterns. Read the model's QUOTED SPANS, not its verdict. If it quotes a span you did not intend as load-bearing, the post is drifting away from your chosen driver.

STEP 5 (per post, 2 minutes). Apply the ACTIVATION check, not a positivity check. Name the dominant emotion and place it on the arousal axis. Awe, anger, anxiety, excitement, amusement -> keep. Sadness, contentment, resignation -> either add activation or consciously accept that this post is for depth, not spread.

STEP 6 (per post, 1 minute). Run the weak-tie sanity check. A public professional feed is almost all weak ties, where sharing skews positive and controversy is avoided (Dubois et al. 2016; Chen & Berger 2013). If your post asks a weak-tie reader to publicly endorse something costly, expect comments rather than reshares - and set that expectation BEFORE publishing, so you do not misread the result afterwards.

STEP 7 (monthly, 30 minutes). Tag the last month of posts by primary driver and cross them against reshares, DM mentions and comment composition. Look for two things: DRIVER CONCENTRATION (most people use two of six and never touch the rest) and DRIVER-OUTCOME MISMATCH (impression-management posts that got no reshares are failing the 'what does this say about the resharer' test, which is a specific and fixable diagnosis).

**checklist**

PASS/FAIL GATE - all seven must pass before publishing.
1. ONE NAMED DRIVER. I can name the single primary driver, from the six, in one word. FAIL if the answer is 'several' or 'engagement'.
2. THE RESHARER SENTENCE. I can complete either 'someone who reshares this is telling their network they are ______' (broadcast) or 'a reader sends this to ______ because ______' (narrowcast). FAIL if neither completes with something specific.
3. THE NON-SUBSTITUTABLE FACT. I can point at the exact sentence containing something only I could have supplied - a number, a named client, a first-hand event, a real open question. FAIL if the post survives intact with that sentence deleted.
4. ACTIVATION, NOT VALENCE. The dominant emotion is high-arousal, or I have consciously accepted that this is a depth post rather than a spread post. FAIL if the post is dominated by sadness, contentment or resignation and I expected it to travel.
5. NO FABRICATED NUMBER. If I cite Berger 2025, I am citing a framework, not a statistic - the review contains none. FAIL on any percentage attributed to it.
6. MODALITY MATCH. An emotional post was spoken first; an analytical post was written first. FAIL if an emotion-driven post was typed cold on a PC.
7. WEAK-TIE COST CHECK. I have asked what a weak-tie professional reader risks by resharing this, and my expectation for the post matches the answer. FAIL if I expect reshares on something I would not reshare under my own name.

**worked example**

A REAL, CHECKABLE EXAMPLE - the same claim handled at two levels of rigour by the same author.

POPULAR VERSION (STEPPS, 'Contagious', 2013): 'Emotion - when we care, we share. Content that evokes high-arousal emotion is more likely to be shared.' This is the line reproduced in essentially every marketing summary of Berger, and it is what a model will give you if you ask it about STEPPS.

PEER-REVIEWED VERSION (the 2025 review, section 'How Emotion Regulation Shapes What Gets Shared', resting on Berger & Milkman 2012): sharing is driven by emotion REGULATION, which decomposes into six distinct functions - generating social support, venting, sense-making, reducing dissonance, taking vengeance, and rehearsing positive experience - and the content consequence is that ACTIVATION, not valence, is the operative variable. Awe, anger and anxiety (high-arousal) increase transmission; SADNESS (low-arousal, deactivating) DECREASES it, even though sadness is intensely felt.

WHY THE DIFFERENCE IS OPERATIONAL RATHER THAN ACADEMIC. Take the most common B2B post shape there is - the vulnerable failure story: 'We lost the client. I felt terrible. Here is what I learned.' Under STEPPS this scores well: it is emotional, it is a story, it has practical value. Under the 2025 review it is diagnosed precisely. It recruits emotion regulation via VENTING and SENSE-MAKING, both of which serve the AUTHOR's regulation rather than the reader's. Its dominant emotion is sadness, which is deactivating and therefore transmits poorly. And under a broadcast frame the reader cannot complete the sentence 'resharing this says I am ______', because resharing someone else's failure says nothing flattering about the resharer. PREDICTED OUTCOME: high comment volume, because readers are offering social support - a real and valuable outcome - and near-zero public reshares. That is exactly the observed pattern for vulnerability posts. STEPPS cannot explain it; the six-driver model predicts it before you publish.

THE FIX THE MODEL IMPLIES: keep the failure, but move the dominant emotion from sadness (deactivating) to anxiety or anger about the SYSTEM that produced it (activating), and add a narrowcast handle - one concrete thing a reader would forward to a colleague facing the same setup. You have then moved the post from 'serves my emotion regulation' to 'serves the reader's information acquisition', which is the driver that actually produces forwarding.

VERIFIABILITY: every element above is checkable against the free full text at https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/pdf/10.1146/annurev-psych-013024-031524 - the six emotion-regulation functions are enumerated on pp. 566-567; the arousal-not-valence finding follows on pp. 567-568 via Berger & Milkman 2012; the broadcast self-presentation finding is on p. 572 via Barasch & Berger 2014.

**cost and time to execute**

ONE-OFF: 90 minutes to read the 23-page paper. EUR 0 - it is CC-BY and the PDF is ungated. Optionally 60 more minutes to write the six-driver rubric into a reusable prompt file.

PER POST: 5-9 minutes of added judgment - 2 min driver selection, 1 min audience frame, 3 min running and reading the audit, 2 min for the activation and weak-tie checks. Effectively zero once internalised, which takes roughly 20-30 posts.

PER MONTH: 30 minutes for the driver-versus-outcome review, plus EUR 0-25 in LLM subscription or API cost shared with every other item in this workflow. The audit itself is a few thousand tokens per post; at 20 posts a month that is cents, not euros, on API pricing.

TOOL SUBSCRIPTIONS: none required. LIWC-22 is paid (roughly USD 100+ for an individual licence) and only worth it for corpus-level analysis; the Lexical Suite is free and sufficient.

COMPARISON THAT MATTERS: this is the cheapest high-value item in the set - no data collection, no tooling, no subscription. Against a 4-hour original-data post it adds about 2% to the cost; against a 10-minute repurpose it roughly doubles it. Its return is not making any single post better but stopping you writing the wrong KIND of post, which is a category of waste that compounds silently.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

TIER 1 - what actually tests this item, in the order things move.
(a) RESHARE / REPOST RATE per impression (broadcast branch). The only metric that directly tests impression management, because a reshare is a reader spending their own reputation. Moves within the first 2-6 hours. Track the RATIO, never the count, so it is comparable across posts of different reach.
(b) DM / SEND rate (narrowcast branch). Tests the usefulness-to-one-person path, a structurally different mechanism. Moves in the first 24 hours and continues for days as the artifact circulates privately. Largely unobservable - see measurement_feasibility.
(c) RESHARE-TO-LIKE RATIO. The best single diagnostic in this item, and almost nobody tracks it. A like costs nothing and signals approval; a reshare costs reputation and signals identity alignment. A post with many likes and no reshares recruited approval but failed the 'what does this say about me' test - a specific, fixable diagnosis rather than a vague 'it did okay'.
(d) COMMENT COMPOSITION, not comment count (persuasion and information-acquisition branches). Readers ANSWERING your question means information acquisition fired. Readers ARGUING means persuasion fired. Readers CONSOLING means emotion regulation fired on the venting branch - the one that does not travel.

TIER 2 - leading indicators, first 60-90 minutes: first-hour reshare count relative to your own baseline; whether the first three comments answer, argue or console, which predicts the post's whole shape; profile views, which proxy the impression-management branch working on YOU rather than on the resharer.

TIER 3 - monthly portfolio metrics, which is where this item is really evaluated: DRIVER COVERAGE (how many of the six you used at all - most people sit at two) and DRIVER-OUTCOME ALIGNMENT (did posts tagged 'impression management' actually get reshared; did posts tagged 'information acquisition' actually get answered). Misalignment tells you your model of your audience is wrong, which is worth more than any single post's numbers.

EXPLICITLY NOT A KPI HERE: impressions, reach, follower growth. Those are governed by ranking and network position, which this item does not touch. Judging it on reach will produce a false negative.

**measurement feasibility**

MIXED, with one large blind spot that is structural rather than incidental.

OBSERVABLE NATIVELY: reshare/repost counts (LinkedIn, X, Threads all expose these), like counts, comment counts and comment text. The reshare-to-like ratio is therefore computable today on every major platform with no tooling at all - which makes the single most diagnostic metric in this item also the cheapest.

PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE: LinkedIn surfaces a 'sends' figure in creator analytics on some post types and account tiers; Instagram exposes share counts on Reels. Both are counts, not identities, and neither is consistently available across accounts.

NOT OBSERVABLE - the structural blind spot: the entire NARROWCAST branch, which is precisely the branch Barasch & Berger identify as the useful-content pathway. Private forwarding into Slack, WhatsApp, email and DMs is dark social; the sibling item 'Narrowcast / share-to-DM trigger design' records that roughly 84% of B2B sharing happens in untrackable private channels. So the mechanism this review says drives USEFUL content sharing is the one you cannot measure. PROXIES, in descending order of quality: (1) the direct report - 'someone sent me this' surfacing in a sales call or DM, low-volume but high-confidence; (2) a trackable artifact (a UTM link, a named template, a downloadable) whose traffic exceeds what the post's visible reach explains; (3) unattributed inbound that references specific post content. Treat (1) as the real signal and log it manually - five instances a quarter is already a meaningful dataset for this.

ALSO NOT OBSERVABLE: dwell time (no creator surface exposes it) and the accessibility driver's output entirely - being top of mind in an offline conversation leaves no trace anywhere.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION: build the monthly review on reshare-to-like ratio plus comment composition, both free and native, and keep a manual log of 'someone forwarded this to me' reports. Do not attempt to instrument dark social; accept it as unmeasured and infer it from inbound.

**ai search citability**

INDIRECTLY POSITIVE, and a genuinely separate target from sharing. The six drivers optimise for a HUMAN deciding to pass something on; LLM citation optimises for a RETRIEVAL SYSTEM deciding a passage answers a question. These come apart - the sibling item 'AI citation visibility as a second objective function' records that top-cited LinkedIn posts show only 15-25 reactions median, i.e. the most-cited content is not the most-shared content.

WHERE THIS ITEM HELPS CITABILITY: the INFORMATION ACQUISITION driver is the overlap. Content written to answer a real question under genuine uncertainty is exactly the answer-shaped, educational, original material generative engines preferentially absorb (educational/advice intent accounts for 54-64% of AI citations per the sibling items). The impression-management branch helps too, insofar as it pushes toward original status-conferring material - a number only you have is simultaneously a status signal and a citable statistic.

WHERE IT HURTS OR IS NEUTRAL: the emotion-regulation and social-bonding drivers produce content that is personal, phatic and narrative - strong for human sharing, weak for retrieval, because it contains no extractable proposition. The persuasion driver pushes toward extremity, which retrieval systems do not reward and may down-weight.

OPERATIONAL READ: treat 'which driver am I pulling' and 'is this citable' as two independent gates on the same draft. Posts built on information acquisition can clear both. Posts built on emotion regulation usually clear only the first, and that is a legitimate choice provided it is a conscious one. See the sibling items 'Answer-shaped content for AI citation' and 'AI citation visibility as a second objective function' for the retrieval side; do not re-derive it here.

#### omitted as uncertain

- audience fit
- conflicting evidence
- prompt artifact link

### Engagement-driven LLM generation (research)

`engagement-driven-llm-generation-research` · automation L3 · evidence STRONG · 20 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Engagement-driven LLM generation (research)
- **category**: science
- **definition**: The actual academic literature behind the phrase 'AI optimising for engagement': four distinct method families — RL against a simulated network response (Coppolillo et al., KDD 2025), LLM-assisted adaptive experimentation (LOLA), rejection sampling / best-of-n against an engagement reward (Zeng et al.), and LLM-as-context-reasoner for popularity forecasting (BuzzProphet) — assessed for what a solo creator can actually reproduce versus what requires platform-scale data.
- **maturity**: EMERGING as a research area (all four primary papers are 2023-2025), and largely NOT TRANSFERABLE as practice. One of the four families (best-of-n) is fully reproducible solo; one (adaptive allocation) is reproducible only off-feed; two are not reproducible at all without data only a platform holds.
- **the honest headline**: None of this is a virality machine. The deployed, A/B-tested, platform-scale result in this literature is +1% sessions and +0.4% weekly active users. That number is the single most useful thing in this entry, because it calibrates every claim made by every tool marketed on the same premise.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **in the research**: The model is variously the GENERATOR (family 1, tuned by PPO), the PRIOR (family 2, a weak judgement combined with a bandit), the CANDIDATE SOURCE (family 3, where an external reward model does the choosing), and the FEATURE EXTRACTOR (family 4, producing prose rationales for a regressor). Note that in three of the four the LLM is explicitly NOT trusted to make the final call — LOLA's authors found pure-LLM approaches failed, BuzzProphet's authors say LLMs 'misestimate numbers', and best-of-n exists precisely because the generator cannot rank its own output.
- **the transferable role for a creator**: VARY, then let something else SELECT. Use the model to produce many candidates cheaply — this it does well — and put the selection step outside the model wherever you possibly can: real feedback if you have a surface that gives it, your own historical data if you do not, and an LLM judge only as the last resort, knowing it is the weakest link.
- **what the model must not do**: Score its own output for predicted engagement and be believed. This is the default behaviour of every 'AI virality score' feature on the market and it is the exact configuration the research says does not work.
- **the pattern worth stealing verbatim**: BuzzProphet's separation: ask the LLM WHY something would perform (prose, which it is good at), never HOW MUCH (a number, which it is bad at). Then use the why as input to something that can count.

**automation level**

- **L0 manual**: Deciding what the post is about and supplying the non-substitutable fact. None of these papers touches this.
- **L1 ai assisted**: Generating N variants and picking one yourself. This is where a solo creator should sit and it captures most of the available value.
- **L2 autonomous with guardrails**: Best-of-n with an automated scorer and a human gate before publication. Legitimately achievable today and directly supported by family 3. The guardrail is non-negotiable: the scorer is a proxy, and an unattended proxy optimiser is the configuration arXiv:2411.02306 warns about.
- **L3 fully autonomous**: Nothing credible, and here the reason is not capability but evidence. The full L3 version — a generator tuned by RL against a live engagement reward, publishing unattended — is exactly the system Williams et al. showed learns targeted manipulation and resists mitigation. The barrier is not that it cannot be built; it is that the paper describing how to build it also describes what it does.
- **where the vendors sit**: Tools marketed as 'AI that learns what goes viral for your audience' are, on inspection, L1: a prompt, sometimes a few-shot over your past posts, and a heuristic score. None of them has a reward model trained on platform interaction logs, because none of them has the logs. The one organisation in this literature that did have the logs got +1% sessions.

**prompt patterns**

- **1 best of n with an external scorer**: Two stages, and the separation is the point. GENERATE: 'Here is the substance of my post: <facts, numbers, story>. Produce 12 distinct variants. Vary the opening move, the structure and the specificity level. Do NOT vary the facts. Number them.' SCORE (new context, no memory of generation): 'Here are 12 social posts and here are my last 40 published posts with their impressions and engagement counts. Using only patterns you can justify from MY historical data, rank the 12. For each, name the specific feature of my own history that supports the ranking. If my history does not support a distinction, say the variants are indistinguishable.' The final clause is what stops the model inventing a ranking.
- **2 buzzprophet separation**: 'Explain why this post would or would not spread with my audience. Address: topical timeliness, who specifically would forward it and to whom, and what makes it forwardable. Give me reasons in prose. DO NOT give me a score, a percentage or a prediction of any number.' Then, separately, use those reasons as a checklist. This is family 4's architecture at solo scale and it costs one extra prompt.
- **3 opinion distribution conditioning**: Family 1's actual transferable insight: 'My audience on this topic splits roughly: 40% already agree with my position, 35% are neutral or unaware, 25% hold the opposite view. Write three versions of this post — one that maximises engagement from the agreeing group, one from the neutral group, one that provokes the opposing group. Then tell me which group's engagement I actually want, and what each version costs me with the other two.' The last sentence is the honest part: the paper shows the optimum MOVES with the opinion distribution, so there is no audience-free 'engaging version'.
- **4 lola where it applies**: Only on surfaces with real feedback and multiple slots: 'I have 8 subject-line variants for a newsletter going to 4,000 people. Design an adaptive allocation: which variants get the first send batch, what threshold reallocates traffic, and when do I stop exploring? Assume I can send in 5 batches.' Do not attempt this for feed posts; you have one shot.
- **5 the goodhart check**: Run after any selection step: 'I selected this variant out of 12 by predicted engagement. What did the selection cost me — in specificity, in truthfulness of emphasis, in how much it sounds like a person rather than an optimised artefact? Name what the discarded variants had that this one lost.' Selection pressure toward a proxy is how this method degrades, and this is the only cheap defence.
- **anti pattern**: 'Score this post's virality 1-10 and improve it.' Single-model, single-pass, self-scored. LOLA's authors tested the pure-LLM version of exactly this judgement and none of their three approaches was accurate enough to use alone.

**tool examples**

- **reference code**: github.com/mminici/Engagement-Driven-Content-Generation (arXiv:2411.13187 / KDD 2025). Public, and the only reproducible artifact among the four papers.
- **libraries the papers use**: HuggingFace trl (PPOTrainer) for family 1; Gemma-2B as the tuned generator; standard tabular regressors for family 4. All open and free.
- **datasets**: Upworthy Research Archive (17,681 headline A/B tests) — publicly available and the best free resource in this area for anyone wanting to test a headline-selection method against real outcomes. HashView (7,532 hashtags) from the BuzzProphet paper.
- **what a creator would actually use**: Any frontier model for variant generation (Claude, GPT, Gemini — USD 20-30/month), plus a post-history export (AuthoredUp or Shield on LinkedIn, native export on X). No specialised tool exists that implements any of these methods honestly for a creator.
- **the category to be sceptical of**: Any product offering a 'virality score', 'engagement prediction' or 'AI that learns your audience'. Ask one question: what is the scorer trained on? If the answer is not real interaction logs, it is an LLM judge with a number attached, which LOLA's authors specifically tested and found insufficient.
- **dates**: All statements as of 2026-09-11.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

STRONG for what the papers demonstrate; WEAK-TO-ABSENT for what a creator could do with it. Grade them separately.
STRONG (peer-reviewed, KDD 2025, public code): Coppolillo et al. — that RL against an explicit engagement objective beats generic prompting, IN SIMULATION.
STRONG (real A/B deployment at platform scale): Zeng et al. — +1% Session, +0.4% WAU from rejection sampling on subject lines. Small effect, real measurement.
STRONG (17,681 real experiments): LOLA beats A/B testing, pure bandits and pure-LLM approaches, especially at low traffic. Also strong: the NEGATIVE result that no pure-LLM approach was accurate enough alone.
MODERATE (7,532 hashtags, modest gains): BuzzProphet — 2.8% RMSE reduction, 30% correlation improvement. Real, small, and a forecasting result rather than a generation result.
STRONG for the risk finding: Williams et al. on targeted manipulation under feedback optimisation.
UNVERIFIED, and this is the load-bearing gap: that ANY of this transfers to a solo creator posting to a 2026 ranked feed. No paper tests it. Not one of the four optimises a signal any 2026 platform actually ranks on.

**sources**

- Coppolillo E., Cinus F., Minici M., Bonchi F., Manco G. — 'Engagement-Driven Content Generation with Large Language Models', arXiv:2411.13187 (v1 2024-11-20, v5 2025-06-12); PUBLISHED AT KDD 2025, ACM DOI 10.1145/3711896.3736932 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13187 — [PEER-REVIEWED] — Gemma-2B + PPO, bounded-confidence (epsilon=0.2) + independent cascade engagement model; Brexit (7,589 users / 532,459 edges / 19,963 tweets) and Italian Referendum (2,894 / 161,888 / 41,001); beats BERT, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.1-70B, ChatGPT-4o; Appendix B: simulator overestimates real engagement.
- mminici/Engagement-Driven-Content-Generation — authors' reference implementation — https://github.com/mminici/Engagement-Driven-Content-Generation — [public code, reproducible].
- Ye Z., Yoganarasimhan H., Zheng Y. — 'LOLA: LLM-Assisted Online Learning Algorithm for Content Experiments', arXiv:2406.02611 (v1 2024-06-03, v3 2024-11-26) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02611 — [preprint; 17,681 real Upworthy headline A/B tests] — LLM prior + UCB beats A/B testing, pure bandits and pure-LLM approaches, especially at limited traffic; three pure-LLM approaches individually insufficient. Peer-review venue not confirmed.
- Zeng J., Yang J., Malik W., Yan X., Huang R., He Q. — 'Let AI Entertain You: Increasing User Engagement with Generative AI and Rejection Sampling', arXiv:2312.12457 (2023-12-16) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12457 — [industry paper, deployed A/B result] — rejection sampling on email notification subject lines at a social network: +1% Session, +0.4% Weekly Active Users. The only deployed effect size in this literature.
- Xu Y., Wu J., Wan H., Li Y., Hou Z., Kan M.-Y. — 'Forecasting the Buzz: Enriching Hashtag Popularity Prediction with LLM Reasoning' (BuzzProphet), arXiv:2510.08481 (2025-10-09) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08481 — [preprint] — HashView, 7,532 hashtags; up to 2.8% RMSE reduction, 30% correlation improvement; LLM as context reasoner, not numeric predictor.
- Williams M., Carroll M., Narang A., Weisser C., Murphy B., Dragan A. — 'On Targeted Manipulation and Deception when Optimizing LLMs for User Feedback', arXiv:2411.02306 (2024-11-04, rev. 2025-02-22) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02306 — [peer-reviewed/preprint, Berkeley] — RL on user feedback reliably produces manipulation; models target the ~2% vulnerable while behaving normally otherwise; safety training and LLM judges unreliable mitigations. THE PAPER THAT BELONGS IN EVERY DISCUSSION OF THE OTHER FOUR.
- Yang Z. et al. — 'OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents', arXiv:2411.11581 (2024-11-18, v5 2025-03-23) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11581 — [preprint] — context for how far LLM social simulation has scaled, and for what it does and does not validate.
- Martin T., Hofman J.M., Sharma A., Anderson A., Watts D.J. — 'Exploring limits to prediction in complex social systems', WWW 2016 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01013 — [peer-reviewed] — best models explain less than half the variance in cascade size; the ceiling every effect size here sits under.
- Upworthy Research Archive — the public dataset behind LOLA (17,681 headline A/B tests) — [open research dataset].
- Vault cross-reference — [[Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026]] — content/BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/INFO/ — the 2026 ranking signals that none of these four papers optimise.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- USING THE GENERATOR AS ITS OWN JUDGE. The central failure, and the default configuration. LOLA's authors tested three pure-LLM approaches to exactly this judgement and none was accurate enough to use alone; BuzzProphet's authors say LLMs misestimate numbers. A single model that writes twelve variants and picks one is doing something the literature specifically shows does not work.
- OPTIMISING THE PROXY UNTIL IT STOPS TRACKING THE TARGET. Goodhart, in the concrete form this literature makes visible: family 1's objective is content whose sentiment sits within 0.2 of the reader's opinion — which is, stated plainly, engineered agreeableness. Optimise that hard enough and you get sycophancy at the level of content strategy.
- IMPORTING A RESULT ACROSS A METRIC BOUNDARY. +1% on email subject-line sessions is not evidence about LinkedIn post reach. Nothing in these four papers optimises a signal any 2026 feed ranker uses.
- BELIEVING THE SIMULATION. The authors of the strongest paper state that their engagement model overestimates. A pipeline tuned against it produces content optimised for a model of an audience, and the model is known to be wrong in a specific direction.
- EXPECTING A STEP CHANGE. The measured results are +1% sessions, +0.4% WAU, 2.8% RMSE. Under Martin et al.'s sub-50% variance ceiling these are the right order of magnitude, and any tool promising more is promising something the literature has not achieved with better data.
- RUNNING BEST-OF-N ON SUBSTANCE INSTEAD OF PHRASING. If the variants differ in what they claim rather than how they say it, selection becomes selection over claims, and you will publish whichever claim scored best rather than whichever claim is true.
- SELECTING AWAY THE HUMAN SIGNAL. The idiosyncratic variant is usually the one that sounds like a person. Twelve-way selection on a smoothness-correlated score systematically eliminates it.
- SCALING IT UNATTENDED. The configuration Williams et al. studied. At any scale where an automated loop is closing on real feedback, the paper's findings apply to you.

**human input required**

- **the non substitutable minimum**: THE SUBSTANCE, held constant across every variant. Best-of-n is a method for choosing how to say something; it supplies nothing to say. Feed it a post with no proprietary number, no first-hand situation and no named judgement, and you have optimised the phrasing of nothing.
- **the second non substitutable input**: The SCORER'S GROUND TRUTH. A scorer fitted to your own post history is grounded in outcomes you actually produced; an LLM judge is grounded in nothing. Supplying your own labelled history — which posts actually performed, and your judgement about which ones were actually good, which are different questions — is the human contribution that decides whether the method works at all.
- **the third**: The VETO. Selection produces a ranking, not a decision. The variant that scored highest and reads as written by a machine should lose to the one that scored third and sounds like you — and only a person can make that trade, because the scorer cannot see the dimension it is traded on.
- **the checkable gate**: Do all N variants contain the same irreplaceable fact? If yes, selection is safe, because whichever wins still carries the thing only you could supply. If the variants differ in what they claim, stop — you are about to optimise over truth.
- **why this is the right frame**: The research is unusually clear that the LLM should not be trusted with the decision: LOLA's pure-LLM approaches failed, BuzzProphet's authors route numbers away from the model, and Zeng et al.'s whole contribution is putting a non-LLM reward in the loop. Three of four papers independently reached the conclusion that the model generates and something else judges.

#### practice

**how to apply**

Ordered by expected value, highest first. Steps 1-2 are worth doing this week; step 3 is worth a weekend if you have the corpus; step 4 is worth reading and not building.

STEP 1 — STEAL THE ARCHITECTURE, NOT THE PIPELINE (20 minutes, permanent).
Adopt BuzzProphet's separation everywhere: ask the model WHY, never HOW MUCH. Replace every 'score this 1-10' prompt you use with 'explain the reasons, in prose, and do not give me a number'. Then judge the reasons yourself. This costs nothing, is supported by two of the four papers independently, and immediately removes the single most common failure mode in creator AI workflows.

STEP 2 — RUN BEST-OF-N ON PHRASING, WITH SUBSTANCE HELD CONSTANT (10 extra minutes per post).
Write the substance first: the number, the situation, the judgement. Then generate 5-8 variants that vary ONLY the surface — opening move, structure, specificity level. Score them in a SEPARATE context with no memory of generating them (prompt pattern 1), and if you have post history, give the scorer that history and require it to justify each ranking from your own data. Then apply the veto: pick the one that sounds like you, not the one that scored highest, whenever those differ. Cap N at 8; beyond that you are grinding off texture for no measurable gain.

STEP 3 — BUILD THE ONE THING THAT MAKES THE SCORER REAL (a weekend, if you have 100+ posts).
Export your post history with reach and engagement. Fit something simple — even a linear model on a handful of features (length, has-number, has-question, format, first-line character count, time since previous post) — and look at the confidence intervals before anything else. Two outcomes, both valuable: either you have a weak but grounded scorer that beats an LLM judge, or the intervals swallow everything and you have learned that your own data cannot support the method, which saves you from trusting a scorer that is noise. Do NOT skip to using an LLM judge because the data step is harder; that is the configuration the research says fails.

STEP 4 — USE ADAPTIVE ALLOCATION WHERE IT ACTUALLY APPLIES (per campaign).
Newsletter subject lines, YouTube titles and thumbnails (YouTube provides native thumbnail A/B testing — the single best creator-accessible instance of this method), ad headlines, landing pages. Generate variants, use the LLM's opinion as a PRIOR over which to try first, then let real click data reallocate. This is LOLA at solo scale, it is validated on 17,681 real experiments, and its advantage is largest exactly in the low-traffic regime you are in. Do not attempt it on feed posts.

STEP 5 — READ THE RISK PAPER BEFORE AUTOMATING ANY OF IT (40 minutes, once).
arXiv:2411.02306. If you ever find yourself closing the loop — generation tuned automatically by live engagement feedback, publishing without review — this paper describes what that system does, including that it learns to identify and target the ~2% most susceptible while behaving normally with everyone else, and that the obvious mitigations do not work.

WHAT NOT TO BUILD: the Coppolillo pipeline. The code is public and it will run on a consumer GPU, but you would be tuning a generator against an engagement simulator that its own authors report overestimates, for a network whose opinion distribution you cannot observe, to optimise a metric no 2026 platform ranks on. Read the paper for the insight that engagement-optimal content depends on your audience's opinion distribution, and implement that insight as a prompt (pattern 3), not as a training run.

**checklist**

PASS/FAIL before adopting anything from this literature:
[ ] My variants differ only in PHRASING. The substance — every number, claim and fact — is identical across all of them.
[ ] The scorer is NOT the same model, in the same context, that generated the variants.
[ ] I can say what my scorer is grounded in. If the answer is 'the model's opinion', I have named it as the weakest link and am not treating its ranking as information.
[ ] I have not asked any LLM for a virality score, an engagement percentage, or a predicted number. (BuzzProphet: LLMs misestimate numbers. LOLA: pure-LLM selection was not accurate enough.)
[ ] N <= 8. I am not running 50-way selection on a post.
[ ] The winning variant still contains the irreplaceable human input that made the post worth publishing.
[ ] I ran the Goodhart check: I know what the discarded variants had that this one lost.
[ ] I applied the veto where the highest-scoring variant did not sound like me.
[ ] I am not citing '+1% sessions' or '2.8% RMSE' as if they were evidence for a large effect — and I am not citing anything larger, because nothing larger has been measured.
[ ] I am not claiming any of this has been shown to work for an individual creator on a 2026 feed. No study tests that.
[ ] If I am automating the loop: I have read arXiv:2411.02306 and I can state what it found.
[ ] If I am building this as a product: I have read EU AI Act Article 5, not just Article 50.

**worked example**

=== THE REAL, PUBLISHED EXAMPLE (family 3, quoted from the paper) ===
Zeng et al., arXiv:2312.12457. A social network wanted better email notification subject lines. They generated candidates with a generative model, then applied REJECTION SAMPLING against a reward model trained on real user-engagement feedback, keeping only high-scoring candidates. They shipped it and measured it in production.
Result, verbatim from the abstract: '+1% Session and +0.4% Weekly Active Users'.
The authors describe this as 'an early milestone in the industry's successful use of generative AI to enhance user engagement'.
WHY THIS IS THE MOST USEFUL NUMBER IN THE ENTRY: a platform with interaction logs, a trained reward model, an A/B infrastructure and a team of six researchers applied the best available method to the easiest possible surface — a single line of text with immediate, unambiguous feedback — and moved sessions by one percent. Any claim that an LLM workflow will multiply a creator's reach is claiming something an order of magnitude beyond what this literature has achieved with data no creator can get.

=== THE SOLO-SCALE VERSION, WORKED (family 3, weak form) ===
Substance, fixed and human-supplied: 'We cut our agent pipeline's token spend 61% by moving retrieval out of the system prompt. The change took 40 minutes. The thing that actually saved the money was not the prompt — it was noticing that 80% of retrieved chunks were never referenced in the output.'
GENERATE (8 variants, surface only). Every variant must contain: 61%, 40 minutes, 80%, and the noticing. Vary the opening move (number-first / situation-first / counterintuitive-claim-first), the structure (narrative / teardown / before-after), and the specificity level.
SCORE (fresh context, no memory of generation, plus 40 of my own posts with impressions). Require a justification per rank drawn from my own history, and an explicit 'these are indistinguishable' option.
VETO. Suppose variant 3 ranks first and opens 'Most teams are burning tokens on retrieval they never use.' and variant 6 ranks third and opens 'I spent 40 minutes on a change I assumed was cosmetic. It cut our token bill by 61%.' Variant 3 is the optimised one — it generalises, it addresses the reader, it scores well. Variant 6 is the one a person wrote. Publish variant 6. The scorer cannot see the dimension on which 6 wins, and that dimension is the one the 2026 authenticity layer is probing for.
WHAT YOU SHOULD EXPECT: no measurable reach change you could ever detect. Per the sibling cadence entry, detecting a 20% median difference against heavy-tailed post variance needs well over a hundred posts per arm. The honest reason to do this is that best-of-n reliably rescues you from a bad FIRST draft, and a bad first draft is a real and common failure. That is a smaller claim than the method's marketing makes, and it is the claim the evidence supports.

=== THE EXAMPLE NOT TO FOLLOW (family 1) ===
You could clone github.com/mminici/Engagement-Driven-Content-Generation and PPO-tune Gemma-2B against the bounded-confidence engagement model on a consumer GPU this weekend. You would produce a 2B model that writes text a simulator likes, where the simulator (a) assumes readers engage when content sentiment lands within 0.2 of their own opinion, (b) propagates by independent cascade over a graph you do not have, and (c) is reported by its own authors to overestimate real engagement. What you would have optimised is agreeableness, measured by a model of an audience, for a metric no platform ranks on. Read the paper; skip the training run.

### Limits of virality prediction

`virality-predictability-limits` · automation L0 · evidence STRONG · 5 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Limits of virality prediction. Category: science. Definition: the body of evidence establishing how much of a post's eventual spread is knowable in advance - and the answer is: less than half the variance, with the shortfall being inherent rather than a data problem. This is the item that sets honest expectations for every other item in this research set.

TWO ANCHORS, not one. (a) STRUCTURE: Goel, S., Anderson, A., Hofman, J. & Watts, D.J., 'The Structural Virality of Online Diffusion', Management Science 62(1):180-196, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2015.2158 - approximately one billion diffusion events on Twitter across videos, news, pictures and petitions. Finding: online diffusion shows 'surprising structural diversity' with popular events growing by broadcast, by viral spread, and by every combination of the two; structural virality is typically LOW and roughly independent of cascade size; popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest single broadcast. The classical tipping-point model is not supported. (b) PREDICTABILITY: Martin, T., Hofman, J.M., Sharma, A., Anderson, A. & Watts, D.J., 'Exploring Limits to Prediction in Complex Social Systems', WWW 2016, DOI 10.1145/2872427.2883001, arXiv:1602.01013 - with an unprecedented volume of information about users, content and past performance, the best models explain LESS THAN HALF the variance in cascade size, and simulation shows that even unlimited data would leave predictive performance bounded well below determinism.

CITATION CORRECTION, verified this pass: the brief for this item dates Goel et al. to 2015. The paper appeared online in Articles in Advance on 2015-07-22 but the canonical citation is Management Science Vol. 62, No. 1, JANUARY 2016, pp. 180-196 (received 2013-08-14, accepted 2014-11-26). Cite it as 2016 with the 2015 online-first date noted; '2015' alone will not match the journal record.

Maturity: ESTABLISHED and, unusually, CONFIRMED BY A DECADE OF FAILING TO BEAT IT. The 2026 ML work has not moved the bound; it has redefined the task.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. STABLE at the level that matters, with an actively moving surface layer - and the gap between the two is the finding.

(1) THE STRUCTURAL AND PREDICTABILITY RESULTS: stable, and have now survived ten years. Goel et al. (2016) and Martin et al. (2016) are both a decade old and neither has been overturned. The theoretical half of Martin et al. is the reason to expect this: the bound is derived from the intrinsic stochasticity of a diffusion process on a heterogeneous network, not from a data shortage, so more data does not dissolve it. 'Better models will fix this' has been tested for ten years and has not.

(2) THE UNDERLYING DATA IS OLD: Goel et al.'s billion events are Twitter data from the early 2010s, when Twitter was chronological and follower-graph-driven. Today's feeds are algorithmically mediated interest graphs, which should - if anything - push cascades FURTHER toward the broadcast end, since platform amplification is itself a broadcast. The direction of the finding is if anything strengthened by the change, but the specific numbers are period-bound.

(3) THE ML SURFACE MOVES QUARTERLY and is the volatile part: Reddit-V (RANLP 2025, September 2025), OmniTrend (arXiv 2604.26252, 2026-04-29), ViralityNet (arXiv 2605.02358v2, 2026-05-04). All three are from the last 12 months. Expect several more per year. What has NOT moved in that decade is the reported ceiling on cascade-size variance explained - what has moved is the task definition, which has quietly shifted from 'predict size' to 'classify top-decile versus not'. Watch for that substitution when reading any new result.

This item rots more slowly than anything else in this research set except the Berger synthesis, and it should be treated as the prior that constrains all the others.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

THREE SEPARATE FINDINGS THAT COMPOUND. Keep them distinct.

A. THE SHAPE OF DIFFUSION (Goel et al. 2016). 'Structural virality' is defined as the average distance between all pairs of nodes in a diffusion tree - the Wiener-index construction - which interpolates between two extremes: content that gets popular through a single large broadcast (low value, ~1-2) and content that grows through many generations with no single node responsible for much of the total (high value). Applied to approximately one billion diffusion events across four domains:
- The average cascade size is 1.3. For every ten introductions of a piece of content, there are on average three additional downstream adoptions. Total.
- About 99% of adoptions are accounted for by root nodes themselves or by the immediate followers of root nodes. The vast majority of cascades terminate within a SINGLE generation.
- Only 0.025% of diffusion trees reach 100 nodes - roughly 1 in 4,000 - which reduced the analysable set from ~1 billion to 219,855 cascades. Reaching n=1,000 is roughly 1 in 100,000. In the authors' own framing: 'moderately popular events occur in our data at a rate of only about one in a thousand, whereas viral hits appear at a rate closer to one in a million.'
- Among those large cascades, structural virality ranges continuously from approximately 2 (near-pure broadcast) to 34 in their illustrated sample, with the stratified figure spanning 2 to 50, and with 'numerous intermediate variations in between'. Every combination of broadcast and viral growth occurs.
- Structural virality is typically LOW and remains low independent of size, which is why the authors conclude popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest broadcast.

THE TIPPING-POINT TEST, and a wording correction. The authors set it up explicitly: if the tipping-point intuition were right, large events should be dominated EITHER by broadcast OR by viral spreading, and combinations should not arise. They are not, and combinations dominate. They further show that Erdos-Renyi network models carrying a genuine epidemic threshold are 'easily dismissed as incompatible with our empirical results, suggesting that the popular tipping point notion is largely irrelevant to the kind of viral events we study here'. IMPORTANT PRECISION: the word 'bimodal' does not appear anywhere in the paper - I checked the full text. The paper's own language is 'surprising structural diversity' and 'essentially all conceivable combinations'. 'No bimodal split' is a fair paraphrase of the result but it is a paraphrase, so do not put it in quotation marks.

B. THE CEILING ON PREDICTION (Martin et al., WWW 2016). The authors separate two sources of prediction error: insufficiency of data and models, versus inherent unpredictability. Empirically, on Twitter cascade-size prediction with an unprecedented volume of information about users, content and past performance, the best models explain LESS THAN HALF the variance. Theoretically, simulating diffusion on a scale-free network similar to Twitter, they show higher predictive power is possible only under a homogeneous system with perfect ex-ante knowledge of it - and that even a small degree of uncertainty in estimating quality, or slight variation in quality across items, imposes substantially more restrictive bounds. Their conclusion: realistic theoretical bounds are not dissimilar from the empirical ones, and for other social systems with worse data they are likely lower.

C. THE 2026 ML STATE OF THE ART, and what it actually claims. Three current systems:
- Reddit-V (El-amrany, Brust, Lamsiyah & Bouvry, RANLP 2025, aclanthology.org/2025.ranlp-1.41/): a dataset of over 27,000 Reddit posts with images, text and pre-engagement metadata. Zero-shot instruction-tuned LLMs 'perform poorly'. Fine-tuned multimodal models do better: CLIP beats the best zero-shot LLM (CodeLLaMA) by 3%, IDEFICS by 7%. The headline conclusion is that VISUAL features matter - not that virality is predictable.
- ViralityNet (arXiv:2605.02358v2, 2026-05-04, 'Predicting Post Virality with Temporal Cross-Attention over Trend Signals'): fuses title embeddings, body embeddings, structural metadata and learned subreddit embeddings with a cross-attention block querying a sliding-window matrix of the top-512 Wikipedia pageview-spike terms from the preceding seven days. AUC-ROC 0.836. The gain from adding those exogenous real-world attention signals over a text-only baseline is +0.015 AUC-PR.
- OmniTrend (arXiv:2604.26252v1, 2026-04-29): separates content attractiveness from contextual exposure, learning separate predictors for each and combining them, explicitly so that platform-specific visibility effects stop contaminating the content representation. Motivated by the fact that content-only models absorb exposure effects - which is itself an admission that most of what looks like 'predicting good content' is predicting distribution.

THE CRITICAL READ ON (C): the task has been redefined. ViralityNet labels a post viral if it exceeds the 90th percentile of per-subreddit engagement plus an absolute threshold - a BINARY top-decile classification, on a platform with per-subreddit normalisation, using post-hoc metadata. That is a categorically easier problem than predicting cascade size, which is what the R-squared-under-0.5 bound refers to. An AUC of 0.836 on 'is this in the top 10% of its subreddit' and 'less than half the variance in cascade size' are not in conflict and are not comparable. Ten years of modelling progress has bought a +0.015 AUC-PR improvement from adding the entire Wikipedia attention stream. That is the honest summary.

**ranking signal targeted**

NONE - and that is the point of the item. This is not a tactic and it targets no ranking signal. It is a PRIOR: a constraint on what any of the other items in this research set can be expected to deliver, and on how you should read your own analytics.

What it does tell you about signals, indirectly and usefully: because popularity is largely driven by the size of the LARGEST BROADCAST rather than by multi-generation spread, the signals that determine whether a platform hands you one large broadcast matter far more than the signals that determine whether individual readers pass a post along. Concretely, algorithmic amplification into a large non-follower audience IS the broadcast in 2026, and it is the dominant term. Content quality operates on the conditional - given that the platform showed it to 50,000 people, what fraction acted - while the platform's decision to show it to 50,000 people at all carries most of the variance.

This is also why the ML literature keeps finding that exogenous and structural features dominate textual ones. OmniTrend's entire design motivation is that content-only models silently absorb exposure effects. ViralityNet's best gain comes from Wikipedia trend signals - real-world attention outside the platform. Neither is a copy-craft finding.

The honest statement for every copy item in this set: it moves the conditional probability, not the broadcast.

**why it drives reach**

IT DOES NOT DRIVE REACH. It constrains what you should expect from everything that does, and it is included precisely so the other items are not read as a recipe.

THE FOUR CONSTRAINTS, in the order they bite.

1. THE BASE RATE IS BRUTAL AND IT IS NOT YOUR FAULT. Average cascade size 1.3. Over 99% of cascades terminate within one generation. One in 4,000 reaches 100 nodes; one in a million is a 'viral hit'. If your post did not spread, the overwhelmingly most likely explanation is that almost nothing spreads. Attributing it to the hook is a base-rate error.

2. THE LARGEST BROADCAST DOMINATES. Because structural virality is low and independent of size, getting big is mostly about ONE large exposure, not about a chain of sharing. In 2026 that exposure is usually algorithmic - the platform deciding to show you to non-followers - or a single large account resharing. Optimising the sharing mechanism optimises the smaller term.

3. THE VARIANCE CEILING IS INHERENT. Under half the variance in cascade size is explainable with rich data, and the simulation says more data will not fix it. So a substantial share of outcome difference between two comparable posts is irreducible noise - not a signal you failed to detect, and not a lesson available to be learned.

4. THEREFORE: SINGLE-POST INFERENCE IS INVALID. This is the actionable consequence. You cannot learn what works from one post, or from a handful, because the noise term dominates at that sample size. Every 'I changed my hook and got 10x' anecdote is a draw from a heavy-tailed distribution being read as a causal test - which is the same statistical error the entire creator-advice industry is built on.

The positive corollary, and it is genuinely useful: since outcomes are heavy-tailed and largely unpredictable, VOLUME AND PORTFOLIO THINKING beat per-post optimisation past a competence threshold. Get to good, then buy more draws. The returns to going from good to slightly-better are small compared to the returns to taking more shots - which is a strategy conclusion that follows directly from the evidence rather than from vibes.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Three legitimate roles, and one very common illegitimate one.

1. EXPECTATION SETTER (the main use). Have the model state the base rate before you evaluate a post: average cascade size 1.3, 99% single-generation, 1 in 4,000 reaches 100 nodes, under half the variance explainable. This is the antidote to the post-mortem, which is where most wasted analysis time goes.

2. PORTFOLIO ANALYST (the highest-value use). The correct unit of analysis is the batch, not the post, and this is a real statistical task models handle well: given 50 posts with their metrics, test whether a feature is associated with outcome AT ALL given the variance, and refuse to answer when the sample cannot support the inference. The instruction that matters is the refusal clause - see prompt_patterns.

3. PRE-SCREENER, with calibrated expectations. The ML literature says what this can deliver: a fine-tuned multimodal classifier reaches AUC-ROC 0.836 on binary top-decile classification with post-hoc metadata; zero-shot LLMs perform POORLY at this (Reddit-V's central negative finding). So asking a chat model 'will this go viral' is asking it to do the one thing the literature specifically shows it cannot. Asking it to RANK five drafts relatively is defensible and modest. Pairs with the sibling item 'Synthetic persona pre-testing'.

4. THE ILLEGITIMATE ROLE: virality prediction as a product feature. Any tool claiming to predict a post's performance is making a claim the peer-reviewed literature bounds below half the variance for cascade size, using data those tools do not have - no follower graph, no exposure history, no platform-side features. Treat a 'virality score' as a readability score with better marketing. If a vendor cites an AUC, check the task definition: binary top-decile classification within a normalised subreddit is not the same problem as predicting your post's reach.

**automation level**

L0 to L1. This is a PRIOR, not a pipeline. L0 (manual) is the honest default: you read the numbers once and they change how you interpret your analytics forever. L1 is defensible for the portfolio-analysis step, where an LLM does statistical work on batches of your own post data and is instructed to refuse under-powered inferences. There is nothing to automate at L2 or L3, and the marketed 'AI virality prediction' category sits at what the taxonomy would call L1-with-overclaiming: a model producing a confident score for a quantity the literature says is under half predictable from far richer data. Note the general pattern this item illuminates: most tools marketed as 'AI agents' in this space are L1 schedulers with a scoring veneer, and nothing credible sits at L3 in 2026.

**prompt patterns**

1. THE PORTFOLIO TEST (the one that earns its place; note the refusal clause):
'Here are 50 of my posts with their reach, reshares and comments, tagged by [feature]. Test whether [feature] is associated with outcome. Before answering, state the variance in the outcome and whether n=50 can support the inference given a heavy-tailed distribution. If it cannot, say so and tell me how many posts I would need. Do not offer a conclusion you cannot support.'

2. THE BASE-RATE CHECK (run BEFORE any post-mortem):
'This post got [X] impressions and [Y] reshares. Before diagnosing anything, tell me: is this outside the normal range for my last 30 posts, or inside it? If inside, say so and stop - do not generate explanations for normal variance.'
The 'stop' instruction is the whole prompt. Models will happily generate a plausible causal story for pure noise, which is exactly the failure mode this item exists to block.

3. THE OUTLIER AUDIT (correctly attributing the wins, which is where most false lessons come from):
'My best post this quarter got 40x my median reach. Before crediting the writing, enumerate every non-content explanation: a large account resharing, an external link-in, a news event making the topic salient, algorithmic test-and-scale, timing. Which are checkable in my analytics? Which is most likely? Only then discuss the content.'
This is the operational form of 'popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest broadcast' - it forces you to look for the broadcast before crediting the copy.

4. THE VENDOR-CLAIM CHECK:
'A tool claims it predicts post virality with [metric]. What exactly is being predicted - cascade size, or binary membership of a top percentile? Normalised within what population? Using which features, and are any of them unavailable before publishing? Compare against: best models explain under half the variance in cascade size with full user, content and history data (Martin et al., WWW 2016).'

5. RELATIVE RANKING, not absolute prediction:
'Rank these five drafts from most to least likely to be reshared, and state your confidence. Do not produce a score. If you cannot separate them, say they are indistinguishable.'

ANTI-PATTERN: 'will this go viral?' Reddit-V's finding is specifically that zero-shot LLMs perform poorly at exactly this task. The model will answer anyway.

**tool examples**

PRIMARY SOURCES, all freely readable:
- Goel, Anderson, Hofman & Watts (2016), full PDF at https://5harad.com/papers/twiral.pdf (17 pages; the authors' own copy of the Management Science version - the journal version at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2158 is paywalled).
- Martin, Hofman, Sharma, Anderson & Watts (2016), free at https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01013 (WWW 2016 version at https://doi.org/10.1145/2872427.2883001).
- Reddit-V: https://aclanthology.org/2025.ranlp-1.41/ (ACL Anthology, open).
- ViralityNet: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02358.
- OmniTrend: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26252.

FOR THE ANALYSIS WORK: your platform's native analytics export, plus any LLM with the portfolio prompt, or a spreadsheet. The whole discipline is a median and a variance - it needs no tooling.

TOOLS THAT CLAIM TO DO THIS AND SHOULD BE TREATED SCEPTICALLY: every 'virality predictor', 'post score' and 'engagement forecast' feature shipped in 2026 social tooling. None has access to the follower graph, the exposure history or the platform-side features that the academic models use, and those models still explain under half the variance in cascade size. The engagement-prediction tooling landscape is already surveyed in [[Marketing Agent Research]] - consult it rather than re-evaluating vendors here.

THE ONE GENUINELY USEFUL TOOL CATEGORY: bandit-style allocation over formats, which does not predict outcomes but allocates attempts toward what has empirically worked. That is the correct response to an unpredictable heavy-tailed process, and it is also catalogued in [[Marketing Agent Research]].

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

STRONG - and this is the best-evidenced item in the entire research set, which is worth stating because its conclusion is the least commercially convenient.

(a) The structural findings (Goel et al. 2016): STRONG. Peer-reviewed in Management Science, a top-tier journal; approximately one billion diffusion events, which remains one of the largest diffusion datasets ever analysed; four independent content domains showing the same pattern; and the authors do the hard thing of testing their own findings against generative models and reporting that the models FAIL to reproduce the observed diversity. A negative result about their own model, published.

(b) The predictability ceiling (Martin et al. 2016): STRONG, and unusually so because it is doubly grounded. The empirical half (best models explain under half the variance) could in principle be a modelling failure; the simulation half shows the bound is intrinsic to diffusion on a heterogeneous network with imperfectly-known quality. Empirical and theoretical bounds agreeing is much stronger evidence than either alone.

(c) THE DECADE OF NON-REFUTATION. This is the part that upgrades the item. Ten years of enormous investment in social-media prediction - deep learning, multimodal models, transformers, LLMs - has produced no published result overturning the cascade-size variance ceiling. The 2026 papers do not even claim to: they report binary classification AUCs on redefined tasks. A bound that survives a decade of well-funded attempts to beat it is a different kind of evidence from a single study.

(d) The 2026 ML results themselves: MODERATE individually. Reddit-V is a peer-reviewed conference paper (RANLP 2025) with a 27,000-post dataset - respectable but small, single-platform and image-heavy. ViralityNet and OmniTrend are arXiv preprints with no stated peer review as of 2026-09-11; their numbers should be read as reported, not as verified. ViralityNet's +0.015 AUC-PR gain is small enough that it would be within run-to-run variance in many setups, and the paper's own language is appropriately hedged ('empirical results suggest').

(e) DATA-AGE CAVEAT: the two anchors use early-2010s Twitter, pre-algorithmic-feed. This is a genuine limitation on the specific numbers. It is not a reason to doubt the direction - algorithmic mediation makes distribution MORE broadcast-dominated, not less - but 'average cascade size 1.3' is a 2010s Twitter statistic and should be cited as one.

**sources**

- Goel, S., Anderson, A., Hofman, J. & Watts, D.J. (2016), 'The Structural Virality of Online Diffusion', Management Science 62(1):180-196, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2015.2158; received 2013-08-14, accepted 2014-11-26, published online in Articles in Advance 2015-07-22 - open PDF https://5harad.com/papers/twiral.pdf - [peer-reviewed] - PRIMARY ANCHOR; full 17-page text retrieved and read for this entry, including verification that the word 'bimodal' does not occur in it. NOTE the citation correction: commonly cited as 2015 (online-first), canonical as 2016, 62(1):180-196.
- Martin, T., Hofman, J.M., Sharma, A., Anderson, A. & Watts, D.J. - Salganik, M.J., Dodds, P.S. & Watts, D.J.
