#### fit

**platform and format fit**

APPLIES EVERYWHERE, and with more force in 2026 than when it was written.

MEASURED ON: Twitter (Goel et al., Martin et al., Cheng et al. on Facebook) in the early-to-mid 2010s; Reddit for the 2026 ML work; an artificial music market for Salganik et al. Not measured on LinkedIn, TikTok, Instagram or YouTube - but the mechanism is a property of diffusion on heterogeneous networks, not of any platform's implementation, and no platform has published anything contradicting it.

WHY IT BINDS HARDER IN 2026, not less. Every major feed is now algorithmically mediated, which means the 'largest broadcast' term - already dominant in Goel et al.'s data - is now largely a PLATFORM DECISION rather than an audience one. From the creator's seat that is strictly worse for predictability: the dominant term in your outcome is decided by a system you cannot observe, using features you do not have, after you publish. The variance ceiling was derived in a world where the follower graph did most of the work. Algorithmic mediation adds a large unobservable term on top.

FORMAT-SPECIFIC NOTES. Short-form video is the most extreme case: algorithmic cold-start means a single post can be shown to millions or to two hundred with no observable difference in the artifact, and the distribution of outcomes is correspondingly more heavy-tailed than anything in the 2010s Twitter data. LinkedIn is the mildest, because reach is more bounded by network position and less by a global recommendation pool - which means outcomes there have lower variance and, correspondingly, that per-post inference is slightly less invalid. Slightly.

WHERE THIS ITEM 'BACKFIRES': as fatalism. The correct reading is not 'nothing matters' - the sharing drivers and copy craft in the sibling items do move the conditional probability, and Goel et al.'s own data shows enormous variation in outcomes. The correct reading is 'a large share of per-post variance is irreducible, so make decisions on portfolios and buy more draws'. Cross-reference [[Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026]] for the platform layer; this item tells you how much of it is knowable in advance, which is: less than you would like.

**scales with**

This item describes a CEILING rather than a lever, so the question is what the ceiling scales with.

(1) PREDICTABILITY SCALES WITH SAMPLE SIZE, not with sophistication. You cannot learn what works from one post; you can from a hundred. This is the only lever that actually moves, and it is the reason posting volume has an epistemic value independent of its reach value - more posts means more information about your own audience, which is worth something even when each individual post underperforms.

(2) PREDICTABILITY SCALES INVERSELY WITH AUDIENCE SIZE, which surprises people. The larger and more heterogeneous your potential audience, the heavier the tail and the noisier each outcome. A 200-person niche has lower-variance and more interpretable outcomes than a 200,000-person one.

(3) THE BOUND DOES NOT SCALE WITH DATA. This is the Martin et al. result and it is the one that kills the intuitive fix: they had an unprecedented volume of user, content and history data and still explained under half the variance, and the simulation shows unlimited data would not close it. Nothing you can buy, instrument or model your way to changes this.

(4) NETWORK POSITION SETS THE CEILING ON OUTCOME, not on predictability. Because popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest broadcast, having access to a large broadcast - a big account who reshares you, a newsletter, a conference stage, or an algorithm that has decided to test you - is the dominant term. That is the thing to invest in if reach is the goal, and it is a distribution problem rather than a writing problem.

(5) WHAT DOES NOT HELP: tooling, prediction models, more careful hook optimisation past a competence threshold, or any vendor product. The bound is not a tooling gap.

**decay and saturation**

VERY LONG SHELF-LIFE for the core findings - 10+ years, and they have already served ten. These are structural properties of diffusion on heterogeneous social networks, not platform features. A platform cannot patch away the fact that outcomes on a heavy-tailed process are hard to predict; if anything, algorithmic mediation has made it worse from the creator's seat.

WHAT WILL DATE: the specific 2010s Twitter numbers. 'Average cascade size 1.3' and '1 in 4,000 reaches 100 nodes' are measurements of a chronological follower-graph feed. A 2026 equivalent has not been published - platform research APIs closed, and nobody has a billion-event dataset with tree structure any more, which is itself why the replication does not exist. Cite the numbers with their era attached.

WHAT DECAYS FAST: the ML state of the art. Reddit-V, ViralityNet and OmniTrend are all from the last 12 months and will be superseded within another 12. But note the pattern that has NOT decayed in a decade: each new generation reports a better number on an easier task rather than a better number on the original one. Expect the next paper to do the same, and read it accordingly.

SATURATION: none possible. This is a constraint, not a tactic - nothing degrades when more people know it. There is a mild irony worth naming: this item is UNDER-adopted rather than saturated, because the entire creator-advice economy has a commercial incentive to ignore it, which means understanding it is a small durable edge in how you allocate your own effort.

THE SIGNAL TO WATCH: a published post-2020, large-scale, tree-structured diffusion analysis on an algorithmic feed. If one appears, it supersedes the specific numbers here. None exists as of 2026-09-11.

#### risk

**failure modes**

1. SINGLE-POST INFERENCE - the dominant failure in all creator practice. A post does well, its features are credited, the lesson is generalised, and the lesson is noise. With under half the variance explainable and a heavy-tailed distribution, n=1 supports no inference whatsoever. Every 'I changed X and got 10x' story is this error.

2. SURVIVORSHIP ANALYSIS OF VIRAL POSTS. Studying what viral posts have in common, without the comparison set of identical posts that did not spread. Goel et al.'s data makes the scale of the problem concrete: viral hits occur at roughly one in a million, so the non-viral comparison set is a million times larger and is never examined. Almost all published 'we analysed the top N viral posts' content has this structure.

3. CREDITING THE COPY FOR THE BROADCAST. The single most common misattribution. If popularity is largely driven by the size of the largest broadcast, then the most likely explanation for your best post is that someone large reshared it, a news event made the topic salient, or the algorithm tested and scaled it - not that the hook was better. Prompt pattern 3 exists for this.

4. BUYING A PREDICTION TOOL. Paying for a virality score is paying for a number the literature bounds below half the variance using features the tool does not have. The tell is that the tool never reports its task definition or its baseline.

5. READING THE 2026 AUCs AS PROGRESS ON THE ORIGINAL PROBLEM. AUC-ROC 0.836 on per-subreddit top-decile binary classification is not a refutation of 'under half the variance in cascade size'. Conflating them produces the false conclusion that ML has solved this.

6. FATALISM - the failure in the other direction, and a real one. 'It's all random so nothing matters' is wrong: the drivers in the sibling items genuinely move the conditional probability, and the variation across posts is enormous. The finding is about IRREDUCIBLE variance in the outcome, not about the absence of signal in the input.

7. OVER-TUNING ON A LUCKY OUTLIER. The most expensive version of failure 1: restructuring a whole content strategy around one anomalous result, thereby abandoning a portfolio approach in favour of chasing a draw that will not repeat.

**ai slop risk**

LOW as a content risk, HIGH as an ANALYTICAL risk - and the analytical one is worth spelling out because it is subtle.

AS CONTENT: essentially no slop risk. Writing about the limits of prediction requires citing specific numbers from specific papers, which is exactly the material a model cannot fabricate convincingly and which a reader can check in one click. The failure mode is not slop but mis-citation - the numbers are specific and easy to get subtly wrong (2015 versus 2016; 1 in 4,000 versus 1 in 1,000; AUC versus R-squared).

AS ANALYSIS - the real risk: LLMs are exceptionally good at generating plausible causal explanations for random variation. Ask why a post underperformed and you will get a confident, well-structured, entirely fictional answer, because the model has no access to the variance and every incentive from its training to be helpful. This is the exact failure this item exists to prevent, and using an LLM naively for post-mortems actively amplifies it - it converts noise into an articulate lesson, which is more dangerous than no lesson at all.

THE TELLS OF ANALYTICAL SLOP: a confident single-cause explanation for a single post's outcome; a 'lesson learned' derived from one data point; a comparison of two posts treated as an experiment; any post-mortem that does not mention the variance or the sample size; and any answer to 'why did this do well' that does not first check whether a large account reshared it.

MITIGATION, and it is structural: every analysis prompt must include the refusal clause - state the variance, state whether the sample supports the inference, and decline if it does not. See prompt patterns 1 and 2. A model that is allowed to refuse will; one that is not, will confabulate.

**human input required**

THE DISCIPLINE TO NOT DRAW A CONCLUSION - which is a genuinely difficult, genuinely non-substitutable human contribution, and the only one this item asks for.

Concretely:
(1) Deciding the minimum sample before a content decision is allowed, and then actually honouring it when a single post tempts you to break it. A model can compute the threshold; only you can refuse to act before it is met.
(2) Distinguishing an outlier caused by a broadcast from an outlier caused by the writing - which requires knowledge the analytics do not contain: who reshared it, what was in the news, whether you were on a podcast that week.
(3) Setting the expectation before publishing, so that a normal result is not retro-fitted into a lesson.
(4) Accepting that a significant share of the outcome is not a referendum on your work. This is emotional rather than analytical labour and it is the part people actually fail at, because a bad post feels like a verdict.

NOTE THE INVERSION: for almost every other item in this research set, the non-substitutable human input is content - a number, a story, a client. Here it is RESTRAINT. That makes it the hardest item to operationalise, because the failure mode is doing something rather than doing nothing, and nothing does not feel like work.

**detectability and disclosure**

NOT APPLICABLE - and worth stating rather than stretching. This item produces no content, no artifact and no output. It is a prior that changes how you read numbers. There is nothing to detect, nothing to watermark, no C2PA manifest, no SynthID payload, no classifier surface, and no disclosure obligation of any kind.

THE ONLY ADJACENT DETECTION QUESTION, and it runs the other way: if you WRITE ABOUT this research - which is good citability material, see ai_search_citability - then ordinary AI-drafting considerations apply to that post like any other, and are covered in the sibling items 'AI slop and the authenticity penalty' and 'Platform AI labeling and C2PA provenance'.

ONE GENUINELY RELEVANT NOTE ON DETECTION IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION: the same unpredictability documented here is why platform integrity systems cannot simply look at outcome distributions to detect manipulation - a genuine heavy-tailed process and an artificially boosted one can produce similar-looking tails. That is background for the sibling item 'Anti-pattern - inauthentic amplification', not a claim about your own content.

**reversibility and blast radius**

ZERO DIRECT BLAST RADIUS. There is no output, no automation, no platform interaction and therefore no shadowban, restriction, suspension or brand risk. Nothing to reverse.

THE BLAST RADIUS THIS ITEM PREVENTS is the point of including it, and it is substantial. Not knowing it costs: money on prediction tooling that cannot work; strategy churn from restructuring around noise; abandoning approaches that were working but had two bad draws; and, most expensively, the opportunity cost of spending hours on per-post optimisation with a bounded ceiling instead of on distribution, which is the dominant term.

THE ONE MISAPPLICATION RISK: using it as a licence for low standards. 'It's unpredictable anyway' is a misreading - the finding is about irreducible variance in the OUTCOME, not about the absence of signal in the INPUT. The craft items in this set do move the conditional probability. Fully reversible if caught, but it can quietly erode quality over a quarter before anyone notices, because the feedback loop that would catch it is exactly the one this item says is too noisy to read at short horizons.

#### practice

**how to apply**

THIS IS A DISCIPLINE, NOT A TACTIC. The steps install a prior and a set of refusals.

STEP 0 (once, 2 hours). Read both anchors. Goel et al. (2016) at https://5harad.com/papers/twiral.pdf - Section 4 (Results) is the load-bearing part. Martin et al. (2016) at https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01013 - the abstract and the simulation section. You are extracting four numbers: average cascade size 1.3; ~99% single-generation; 1 in 4,000 reaches 100 nodes; under half the variance explainable.

STEP 1 (once, 15 minutes). Write those four numbers on a card and put it where you read your analytics. This sounds trivial and is the highest-ROI step in the item, because the failure it prevents is emotional rather than analytical and it happens at the moment you open the dashboard.

STEP 2 (once, 30 minutes). Establish YOUR baseline distribution. Export your last 50 posts. Compute median reach, and the 25th and 75th percentiles. Everything inside that interquartile range is NORMAL and requires no explanation. Most people have never computed this and consequently treat every below-median post as a failure - which, by construction, half of them must be.

STEP 3 (set a rule, once). Fix your minimum sample for a content decision. A defensible default: no change to format, cadence or topic on fewer than 20 posts per variant. Write the rule down, because its entire function is to be binding when you do not want it to be.

STEP 4 (per post, 30 seconds). BEFORE publishing, write your expected outcome. Afterward, compare. This converts every post into a calibration data point and, more importantly, makes it impossible to retro-fit a lesson onto a normal result.

STEP 5 (per post-mortem, 2 minutes). Run prompt pattern 2 before diagnosing anything. If the result is inside your interquartile range, STOP. Do not explain it. Do not change anything. This is the single most-violated rule in content practice and the one that costs the most.

STEP 6 (per outlier, 10 minutes). Run prompt pattern 3. For any post above your 90th percentile, enumerate the non-content explanations FIRST - a large account resharing, an external link-in, a news event, algorithmic test-and-scale, unusual timing - and check which are visible in your analytics. Only credit the content after eliminating the broadcast. Per Goel et al., the broadcast is the more likely explanation.

STEP 7 (monthly, 45 minutes). Analyse the PORTFOLIO, not the posts. Run prompt pattern 1 with the refusal clause. Look for associations across 30-50 posts, and accept 'the sample cannot support this' as a legitimate and common answer.

STEP 8 (strategic, ongoing). Reallocate. Since the largest broadcast dominates, spend the effort you save on post-mortems on DISTRIBUTION instead: relationships with people who have large audiences, newsletters, podcasts, conference talks, communities. That is the term that actually moves the outcome, and it is the conclusion the evidence supports rather than the one the advice industry sells.

**checklist**

PASS/FAIL GATE - applies to ANALYSIS, not to posts. Run before acting on any content data.
1. SAMPLE. The conclusion rests on at least 20 posts per variant. FAIL on any decision drawn from one post or one comparison.
2. BASELINE. I have computed my own median and interquartile range and checked whether this result is outside it. FAIL if I am explaining a result I have not established as abnormal.
3. BROADCAST FIRST. For any outlier, I have checked who reshared it, whether the topic was in the news, and whether the platform scaled it - BEFORE crediting the writing. FAIL on content-first attribution of a win.
4. REFUSAL AVAILABLE. Any model I asked for analysis was permitted to answer 'the sample cannot support this', and I would have accepted it. FAIL if the prompt made a conclusion mandatory.
5. NO PURCHASED PREDICTION. I am not paying for a virality score. FAIL otherwise.
6. TASK DEFINITION. If I am citing a prediction metric, I know what the label is, when it becomes observable, and what population it is normalised within. FAIL on an unqualified AUC or accuracy figure.
7. EXPECTATION RECORDED. I wrote down what I expected before publishing. FAIL if the lesson was formed after seeing the result.

**worked example**

THE PAPER'S OWN FIGURE 3 IS THE WORKED EXAMPLE, and it is the most useful single image in this research set.

Goel et al. drew a stratified random sample of cascades, restricted to those with between 100 and 1,000 adopters - so all of comparable SIZE - ranked them by structural virality, log-binned them, and drew one at random from each bin. They note explicitly that they ran this selection ONCE, 'to avoid hand selection of the best random sample' - a small methodological detail that tells you how carefully the result was made.

What the figure shows: cascades of essentially identical size with radically different shapes. Top left, a near-pure broadcast at structural virality approximately 2 - one node reaching a hundred others directly, the shape of a single account with reach posting something. Bottom right, an ideal-type multi-generation branching structure at 34 - the shape everyone means by 'it went viral'. And between them, every intermediate combination, with the figure caption spanning 2 to 50. The cumulative adoption curves printed beneath each cascade differ just as much - some complete in under two hours, others take days.

WHY THIS IS THE EXAMPLE THAT MATTERS. Every one of those cascades is 'a post with 100-1,000 shares'. In your analytics they would be indistinguishable. But they were produced by completely different mechanisms - one by a single large exposure, one by genuine person-to-person spread, most by some mixture - and only one of them is the thing the advice industry teaches you to engineer. The authors' aggregate finding is that structural virality is typically LOW and stays low as size increases, which means the leftmost shape is the common case: most 'viral' posts are one big broadcast, not a chain.

THE DIRECT PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE. When your post does 40x your median, the prior says: look for the broadcast. Someone with a large audience reshared you, or the algorithm tested and scaled you, or the topic was in the news. That is the most likely mechanism, and it is checkable in most analytics panels in about ninety seconds. Only after eliminating it should the hook get the credit.

THE TIPPING-POINT TEST, in the authors' own construction: if the tipping-point intuition were right, large events in the n=100 (about 1 in 4,000) to n=1,000 (about 1 in 100,000) range should be dominated EITHER by broadcasts OR by viral spreading, with combinations not arising. Figure 3 is what not-arising fails to look like.

VERIFIABILITY: Figure 3 and its caption are on p. 185 of the open PDF at https://5harad.com/papers/twiral.pdf; the cascade-size statistics are in Section 4 on p. 184; the tipping-point setup is on pp. 184-185; the ER-model dismissal is on p. 189.

**cost and time to execute**

ONE-OFF: 2 hours to read both anchor papers (both free), 15 minutes for the base-rate card, 30 minutes to compute your own baseline distribution. EUR 0 in tooling.

PER POST: 30 seconds to record an expectation before publishing. That is the entire per-post cost.

PER POST-MORTEM: 2 minutes for the base-rate check - and this step SAVES time rather than costing it, because most post-mortems end at 'this is inside the normal range, stop' rather than running for twenty minutes.

PER MONTH: 45 minutes for the portfolio analysis, which replaces rather than adds to whatever ad-hoc analysis you were doing.

TOOL SUBSCRIPTIONS: none. A spreadsheet and a chat model.

THIS ITEM IS NET TIME-NEGATIVE, which is unusual and worth stating plainly. It costs about 3 hours up front and then RETURNS time by eliminating unjustified post-mortems, unjustified strategy changes and the evaluation of prediction tooling. Set against a 4-hour original-data post, the entire setup cost is less than one post. Set against the cost of restructuring a content strategy around a lucky outlier - which is where most creators lose a quarter - it is the cheapest insurance in this research set.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

THE CENTRAL MOVE: change the unit of analysis from the post to the PORTFOLIO. Everything else follows.

PORTFOLIO METRICS, which is what you should actually watch:
- MEDIAN reach per post over a rolling 30 posts, never the mean. A heavy-tailed distribution makes the mean a function of your luckiest post, which is why mean-based dashboards are actively misleading here.
- The INTERQUARTILE RANGE of reach. This is your normal-variation band and the single number that tells you whether any given result requires explanation. Almost nobody computes it.
- The RATIO of your 90th percentile to your median. This quantifies how heavy your own tail is, and therefore how many posts you need before any inference is supportable - a heavier tail means a longer required window.
- COUNT OF ATTEMPTS. Since outcomes are heavy-tailed and largely unpredictable, the number of draws is a real input. Track it as an input metric, not as vanity.

PER-POST METRICS, and what they are actually for: record them, but for CALIBRATION rather than diagnosis. Expected versus actual, logged over 50 posts, tells you whether your model of your audience is any good - which is a real and useful signal, and is entirely different from diagnosing an individual post.

LEADING INDICATORS: within the first hour, the only question worth asking is whether the post is inside or outside your normal band. Inside - do nothing, and specifically do not explain it. Outside and high - run the broadcast audit. Outside and low - still probably noise; check again at 24 hours before concluding anything.

EXPLICITLY NOT KPIs HERE: any single post's performance, week-over-week comparisons at low volume, and any 'viral score' from any tool. All three are measurements of noise presented as signal.

THE META-KPI, and the one that tells you this item has landed: how often you change your content strategy. If the answer is more than once a quarter, you are almost certainly responding to variance.

**measurement feasibility**

HIGHLY FEASIBLE - and this is the rare item in this research set where everything you need is already in your own analytics export and needs no proxy at all.

FULLY OBSERVABLE, natively, on every platform: reach or impressions per post, reshares, comments, and the date. That is the entire input. The whole discipline reduces to computing a median, an interquartile range and a 90th percentile over your own last 30-50 posts, which is a spreadsheet operation. No tooling, no API, no subscription, no proxy.

OBSERVABLE WITH A LITTLE WORK - the broadcast audit (step 6 of how_to_apply): most platforms show you WHO reshared a post, which is exactly what you need to check the 'was this a broadcast rather than the copy' question on any outlier. LinkedIn and X both surface reshare lists; where they do not, a single large referrer usually shows up in the follower-growth curve on the same day.

NOT OBSERVABLE - and worth being explicit, because these are the quantities the academic literature actually measured: the DIFFUSION TREE. You cannot see who saw your post through whom, how many generations it travelled, or what its structural virality was. Goel et al. needed platform-internal data covering a billion events to compute it; no creator has any part of that. So you can measure your own OUTCOME distribution precisely and your own diffusion STRUCTURE not at all. Practically this does not matter, because the actionable conclusions all follow from the outcome distribution.

ALSO NOT OBSERVABLE: the platform's exposure decision - how many people it chose to show you to, and why. This is the dominant term in your outcome per Goel et al., and it is invisible before publishing and only partially visible afterward (as impressions, without the reason). This is precisely why the variance ceiling binds harder in 2026 than when it was derived.

WHAT MAKES THIS ITEM UNUSUAL: for most items in this set the predictor is measurable and the outcome is not, or vice versa. Here the thing you need - your own outcome distribution - is free, native, exact and already sitting in an export you have never opened. The barrier is not measurement, it is the discipline to compute an interquartile range before explaining a result.

**ai search citability**

STRONGLY POSITIVE - this is, somewhat unexpectedly, one of the best citability plays in this research set, for three converging reasons.

(1) The material is exactly what generative engines absorb. Specific statistics from named peer-reviewed sources with DOIs: 'average cascade size 1.3', '99% of cascades terminate within one generation', '1 in 4,000 reaches 100 nodes', 'best models explain under half the variance'. Per the GEO findings recorded in the sibling item 'Proof-of-work receipts' (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024, GEO-Bench, 10,000 queries): Quotation Addition +41%, Statistics Addition +33%, Cite Sources +28%. Content built on this item naturally does all three, without any optimisation effort.

(2) It is CONTRARIAN AND CORRECT, which is a rare combination and the most defensible version of the contrarian play in the sibling item 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes'. The consensus position in marketing content is that virality is engineerable. The peer-reviewed position is that it is bounded below half predictable. Taking the against-the-grain side while holding the stronger evidence is the only form of contrarianism that survives contact with a knowledgeable reader - and, critically, it targets a PRACTICE (overclaiming) rather than a person, which keeps it clear of the mute-and-report mechanics documented in the moral-emotional item.

(3) It answers questions people actually ask retrieval systems - 'can virality be predicted', 'why did my post not go viral', 'do virality prediction tools work' - with a specific, sourced, checkable answer. That is answer-shaped content in the precise sense the sibling item 'Answer-shaped content for AI citation' describes, and the educational/advice intent it carries accounts for 54-64% of AI citations.

THE CAVEAT THAT MAKES IT WORK: cite accurately. Management Science 62(1):180-196 (2016, online-first 2015), not '2015'. 'Under half the variance in cascade size', not 'R-squared of 0.4'. 1 in 4,000 at 100 nodes, not 1 in 1,000. A post correcting the record on virality research with a wrong citation is worse than not writing it - and the papers are free, so anyone can check in one click.

#### omitted as uncertain

- audience fit
- conflicting evidence
- evidence provenance
- policy and legal
- prompt artifact link

### Moral-emotional language — quantified effect

`moral-contagion-effect-size` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 4 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Moral-emotional language - quantified effect ('moral contagion'). Category: science. Definition: the finding that messages containing words that are simultaneously MORAL and EMOTIONAL (the overlap of a moral dictionary and an emotional dictionary - the paper's own examples are 'hate', 'disgust', 'greed') are shared more than messages without them, now pinned to a replicated effect size rather than a direction. Anchor: Brady, W.J., Rathje, S., Globig, L.K. & Van Bavel, J.J. (2025), 'Estimating the effect size of moral contagion in online networks: A pre-registered replication and meta-analysis', PNAS Nexus 4(11), article pgaf327, published 2025-10-14, DOI 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf327, PMID 41179848, PMCID PMC12578369, CC-BY-NC 4.0.

THE NUMBER, STATED CORRECTLY (the research brief for this item had it slightly wrong, and the distinction matters): the pre-registered REPLICATION (N=849,266) produced a mean IRR of 1.17 across its five datasets - that is where '+17% per additional moral-emotional word' comes from. But the paper's own BEST POPULATION ESTIMATE is the META-ANALYTIC one: IRR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.06, 1.20], from 5 labs / 27 studies / N = 4,821,006. So the defensible headline is +13% (CI 6-20%), not +17%. Quote 1.13 as the estimate and 1.17 as this particular replication's mean.

Maturity: ESTABLISHED as a finding and stable; the 2025 paper is a consolidation that closed a four-year methodological dispute (Burton, Cruz & Hahn 2021, Nature Human Behaviour). Its APPLICABILITY to professional B2B content, however, is entirely unestablished - see evidence_strength.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. STABLE, with a sharp caveat about what is stable.

(1) The EFFECT ESTIMATE is stable and unlikely to move much. It rests on a pre-registered direct replication plus a meta-analysis of all locatable data, with a publication-bias check (Egger's intercept 3.049, p = 0.171) and a p-curve showing evidential value. The paper was submitted 2024-10-16, revised 2025-09-23, accepted 2025-10-31 and published online 2025-10-14 in issue 4(11); it is 11 months old and is the current last word. The next meaningful update would be a new meta-analysis including post-2023 platform data, which nobody has published.

(2) The UNDERLYING DATA IS OLD AND FROZEN. Every dataset in the replication is Twitter, collected on specific dates in 2018-2020: Kavanaugh hearings 2018-09-16 (N=195,567), the border-wall shutdown 2019-01-16 (N=200,000), the transgender military ban 2019-01-23 (N=53,649), the George Floyd killing (N=200,000), and COVID mask-wearing 2020-05-27 (N=200,000). The outcome variable is the retweet count on a platform that has since been renamed, re-ranked twice in 2026 alone, and closed its research API. Nothing in this literature was measured on a 2026 feed.

(APPARENT ERROR IN THE SOURCE, flagged for honesty: the paper's Table 1 dates the George Floyd collection '2020 March 27'. George Floyd was killed on 2020-05-25 and the protests began in late May. The March date is not possible and appears to be a data-entry error in the published table; the sample itself is presumably late May or June 2020. This does not affect the effect size but you should not reproduce that date.)

(3) The APPLICABILITY to B2B professional content is not a clock at all - it has never been measured, so it cannot decay. It can only be established or not.

Do not treat this item as a platform-mechanics source. Cross-reference [[Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026]] for anything about how a 2026 ranker treats emotionally charged content.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

THE MEASUREMENT. Three word-count predictors are built from two lexicons. The MORAL-EMOTIONAL category is the INTERSECTION of a moral lexicon and an emotional lexicon; the words left over in each lexicon form 'distinctly moral' and 'distinctly emotional' categories. The paper's own worked examples of moral-emotional words are 'hate', 'disgust' and 'greed'. Each tweet gets a count for each of the three categories.

THE MODEL. A negative-binomial regression with maximum-likelihood estimation (chosen because retweet counts are massively overdispersed - Hilbe 2011), predicting retweet count from the three word-category counts plus pre-registered covariates known to affect retweeting independently of content: the author's follower count, whether media or a URL was attached, and whether the author was a verified account. Reported as an incident rate ratio (IRR), i.e. the multiplicative change in expected retweet count per one-unit increase in the predictor.

THE RESULT, dataset by dataset (dictionary method, pre-registered replication, N=849,266): Kavanaugh IRR = 1.05; Trump wall IRR = 1.07; Transgender ban IRR = 1.66; COVID masks IRR = 1.12; George Floyd IRR = 0.97 - all p < 0.001. Four of five positive and significant, one significantly NEGATIVE. Unweighted mean across the five: 1.17.

THE DISTRIBUTION CAVEAT YOU MUST CARRY (this is my arithmetic on the paper's own numbers, not a claim from the paper): the 1.17 mean is an UNWEIGHTED average of five datasets and is dragged upward by a single outlier - the transgender-ban dataset at 1.66, which is also the SMALLEST sample in the set (53,649 tweets, 6.3% of the replication N). The median of the five is 1.07. Four of the five sit between 0.97 and 1.12. So the typical dataset shows roughly a 5-12% effect, and the headline 17% is an artefact of averaging an outlier at equal weight. The meta-analytic 1.13, which is inverse-variance weighted, is the number that handles this properly - which is precisely why it is the one to quote.

THE META-ANALYSIS. All published and unpublished replications locatable via PsycINFO and OSF searches on 'moral contagion' and 'moral-emotional language', restricted to studies that reproduced the Brady et al. (2017) method: 5 labs, 27 studies, N = 4,821,006. Generic inverse-variance weighting, random-effects model, Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman estimator for between-study variance, Q-profile method for the CI on tau-squared. Result: IRR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.06, 1.20].

THE LLM REPLICATION. The same analysis was re-run with GPT-3.5 scoring moral-emotional content instead of a dictionary. Mean IRR across datasets = 1.16 - but note the UNIT CHANGE: this is per STANDARD DEVIATION of the GPT score, not per word. The paper gives the dictionary equivalent on the same standardized scale for comparison: +8% per SD. That standardized pair (+8% dictionary, +16% GPT per SD) is the honest magnitude for anyone thinking in terms of 'how much more moral-emotional should this post be', and it is considerably less dramatic than '+17% per word'.

ROBUSTNESS. Adding sentiment and discrete emotions (sadness, anger, fear, joy, negativity) to the model did not change the moral-emotional coefficient, which the authors read as moral-emotional language being a unique predictor over and above non-moral emotion.

**ranking signal targeted**

THE RETWEET / RESHARE COUNT, and nothing else. The outcome variable throughout this entire literature - the 2017 original, the 2025 replication, the meta-analysis - is the raw retweet count on a tweet. That is a user ACTION, not a ranking signal, and the papers make no claim about any ranker.

What this means operationally: the finding is about what makes a human press retweet, and the platform-ranking consequence has to be inferred separately. On X, reshare-type actions are weighted heavily in the open-sourced ranker (ShareViaCopyLink 20.0 against FavoriteWeight 0.5 in home-mixer/params/param.rs), so the inference is reasonable there. On LinkedIn, the reshare is one signal among dwell time, comment depth and per-viewer comment ranking, and there is no evidence at all connecting moral-emotional language to any of them.

THE SIGNAL THIS ITEM ALSO MOVES, IN THE WRONG DIRECTION: negative actions. Moral-emotional language is by construction the language of outrage ('hate', 'disgust', 'greed'). X's ranker weights negative actions an order of magnitude harder than positive ones - ReportWeight -234.0, MuteAuthorWeight -58.8, NotInterestedWeight -43.2, BlockAuthorWeight -31.2 - and the Agatha system labels ACCOUNTS by blocks and reports relative to favorites. See the sibling item 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes', which established this from the primary source. So on X specifically, moral-emotional language buys you a +13% expected-reshare multiplier while loading an account-level penalty term that is roughly 470x the weight of a favourite. The moral-contagion literature measured only the first half of that trade.

NOT targeted, and nowhere addressed: dwell time, completion rate, saves, semantic relevance, first-hour comment velocity.

**why it drives reach**

The mechanism in the literature is not 'emotion is engaging'. It is specifically GROUP-BASED MORAL SIGNALLING, and that is what makes the B2B translation hard.

The chain: a message contains language that frames something as a moral violation -> that language is a cue for group identity and moral position, not merely for feeling -> resharing it signals the resharer's own moral alignment to their in-group at essentially zero cost -> the reshare is both a distribution event and, on engagement-weighted platforms, a ranking input. The original Brady et al. (2017, PNAS 114(28):7313-7318) finding was that the effect operated WITHIN ideological groups rather than across them, and the single largest dataset in the whole meta-analysis - Rathje, Van Bavel & van der Linden (2021, PNAS 118(26), 8 studies, N=2,951,322) - identifies OUT-GROUP ANIMOSITY as the driver of engagement. So the underlying engine is: naming a shared enemy or a shared violation lets your reader declare which side they are on.

WHY THE REACH CEILING IS STILL LOW. A 13% multiplier on expected shares is applied to a base rate that is, for almost every post, near zero. Per Goel, Anderson, Hofman & Watts (Management Science 2016, sibling item 'Limits of virality prediction'), the average cascade size across a billion Twitter diffusion events is 1.3 and over 99% of adoptions come from the root node or its immediate followers. Multiplying a near-zero probability by 1.13 leaves it near zero. This item raises a rate; it does not create a cascade, and it cannot rescue a post nobody sees.

WHERE IT MAPS ONTO THE BERGER FRAMEWORK: in the sibling item 'Berger word-of-mouth synthesis', this sits at the intersection of EMOTION REGULATION (high-arousal anger and anxiety transmit; the venting and vengeance sub-functions specifically) and IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT (resharing a moral position signals identity). It is one narrow, well-quantified slice of a much larger motivational picture - which is exactly the right way to hold it.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Three roles, and one of them is unusually well-licensed because the anchor paper itself validated it.

1. MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT (the licensed use). The paper re-ran its entire analysis with GPT-3.5 scoring moral-emotional content and recovered the effect (mean IRR 1.16 per SD versus 1.08 per SD for the dictionary), and it leans on Rathje et al. (2024, PNAS 121(34):e2308950121, 'GPT is an effective tool for multilingual psychological text analysis'). So 'ask an LLM to rate the moral-emotional density of this draft on a 0-10 scale' is a peer-reviewed-validated measurement operation, not a vibe check. It is also validated MULTILINGUALLY, which matters for Polish-language drafting where no moral-emotional dictionary exists.

2. AUDITOR / BRAKE (the use I would actually deploy). Run the score to find out whether a draft has DRIFTED into outrage register without you noticing. For a professional B2B account the useful direction of this item is usually downward, not upward - you are checking you have not written something that will recruit mutes. Set a ceiling, not a floor.

3. CORPUS ANALYST. Score your last 100 posts for moral-emotional density and cross it against reshares, comment sentiment and follower churn. This is the only way to find out whether the effect exists for YOUR audience, because no published study has measured it on professional content.

NOT an AI role: generating moral-emotional content. Asking a model to 'make this more emotionally charged' produces exactly the outrage-bait register the model has seen most of, with none of the standing that makes a moral claim land. The sibling item 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes' covers why a moral position without personal exposure reads as manufactured.

**automation level**

L1 - AI-assisted, and an L2 gate is defensible only in the SUPPRESSIVE direction. L1 use: score the draft, read the score, decide. A legitimate L2 'autonomous with guardrails' implementation is a publication gate that blocks any draft scoring above a moral-emotional ceiling you set for your account - that is a safety rail and needs no human in the loop to be correct. What must never be automated is the opposite: a rewrite loop that maximises moral-emotional density. That optimises directly against the negative-action weights that get accounts muted and reported, and it is the mechanical definition of outrage-farming. Nothing here belongs at L3. No commercial tool implements moral-emotional scoring as a product feature as of 2026-09-11; you are building this from a prompt or from the open Moral Foundations Dictionary lineage.

**prompt patterns**

1. DENSITY MEASUREMENT (mirrors what the paper actually validated with GPT-3.5):
'Rate this text on moral-emotional content: language that is simultaneously MORAL (about right and wrong, harm, fairness, betrayal, cheating, loyalty) and EMOTIONAL (carrying affect). Reference examples of moral-emotional words: hate, disgust, greed, shame, outrage. Give (a) a 0-10 score, (b) every moral-emotional word or phrase, quoted verbatim, (c) whether the moral frame targets a PERSON, a GROUP, or a PRACTICE. Do not rewrite anything.'
The (c) clause is the one that earns its place - see the B2B translation in how_to_apply.

2. THE CEILING CHECK (suppressive, the direction that actually matters for a professional account):
'On a scale where 0 is a neutral technical note and 10 is political outrage content, score this draft. If it scores above 4, quote the three phrases pushing it up and say, for each, whether removing it would weaken the argument or only weaken the heat. Do not soften anything yourself.'

3. THE MUTE TEST (targets the real X mechanism, not the folklore):
'A reader who disagrees with this post has four options: ignore, reply, mute me, report me. Which is most likely, and quote the sentence that decides it. Do not tell me the post is balanced - tell me what the disagreeing reader does with their thumb.'

4. TARGET RELOCATION (the B2B-safe transform):
'This draft makes a moral claim. Identify its target. If the target is a person or an identifiable group, rewrite so the target is a PRACTICE or an INCENTIVE STRUCTURE instead, keeping the moral stakes and the specific harm intact. Name who is harmed and how. Do not make it neutral - make it about the practice.'

5. CORPUS AUDIT (over an exported archive):
'For each of these posts, output: post id, moral-emotional score 0-10, moral target (person/group/practice/none). Return as CSV. No commentary.' Then cross it against your own reshare and follower-churn data.

ANTI-PATTERN: 'make this post more emotionally compelling.' It reliably produces generic outrage register - superlatives, villains, 'it's time we talked about' - which is both slop and risk. Always measure; never ask for more.

**tool examples**

PRIMARY SOURCE, free and complete: the paper is CC-BY-NC 4.0. Full text at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12578369/ or https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12578369, DOI https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf327. Machine-readable full text (what I used) at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12578369/fullTextXML.

REPLICATION MATERIALS, all open: data and analysis scripts at https://osf.io/96fwc/; the pre-registration at https://osf.io/gd734; the preprint at https://osf.io/preprints/osf/s4w2x_v2; the ORIGINAL 2017 study's analysis pipeline, which this replication reused directly, at https://osf.io/59uyz/. If you want to check any number in this entry, those four links are sufficient.

MEASUREMENT TOOLING: the Moral Foundations Dictionary lineage (freely available) for the dictionary method; any frontier LLM for the GPT-equivalent method, validated for this purpose in the anchor paper and in Rathje et al. (2024, PNAS 121(34):e2308950121). Statistical replication requires negative-binomial regression - the R `MASS::glm.nb` family - and the meta-analysis used the R `meta` package with HKSJ.

NO commercial content tool scores moral-emotional language. Any vendor claiming to 'optimise emotional resonance' is running sentiment analysis, which is a different and weaker construct - the paper explicitly shows that adding sentiment and discrete emotions to the model leaves the moral-emotional coefficient unchanged, i.e. sentiment does not capture this.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

STRONG for the narrow claim; UNVERIFIED for the claim anyone actually wants to make. Split this deliberately.

(a) 'Moral-emotional language is associated with more retweets on US political Twitter, 2017-2020': STRONG. Pre-registered direct replication with a larger sample than the original, a meta-analysis of all locatable data, a publication-bias check that comes back clean, a p-curve showing evidential value, and a successful conceptual replication with a completely different measurement method (LLM instead of dictionary). This is about as good as observational social-media research gets.

(b) 'Moral-emotional language CAUSES more sharing': MODERATE. The authors state plainly that their own data are correlational and cannot establish causality. They point to Brady & Van Bavel (2025, J. Exp. Psychol. General 154(6):1505-1522) for controlled behavioural experiments showing a causal effect - but again on political message sharing.

(c) 'The effect is +17% per word': WEAK AS STATED, and this is where most secondary reporting goes wrong. 1.17 is the unweighted mean of five datasets in one replication; the median dataset is 1.07; the inverse-variance-weighted population estimate is 1.13 [1.06, 1.20]; and on a standardized scale the dictionary effect is +8% per SD. All four numbers are in the same paper and they are not interchangeable.

(d) 'This applies to professional B2B content': UNVERIFIED, bordering on unsupported. Zero LinkedIn data. Zero professional or commercial content. Zero non-political topics - all five replication datasets and effectively all 27 meta-analysed studies are political controversies. The construct being measured is moral outrage about public affairs. There is no evidence base for transferring it to a consultant writing about automation pipelines, and the burden of proof is on anyone who wants to.

(e) INTERNAL CONSISTENCY OF THE SOURCE: the published paper contains several sign/value mismatches in its results prose - the abstract gives the replication mean as IRR = 1.17 while the Results section gives 1.15 for the same quantity; a paragraph describes 'significant negative associations' for a dataset it reports at IRR = 1.19; another describes a 'nonsignificant' association at p = 0.001; another lists IRR = 0.80 among positive associations. None of these affect the headline meta-analytic estimate, which is computed from data rather than prose, but they mean you should take per-dataset numbers from the tables and the OSF data, not from the narrative text.

**evidence provenance**

PEER-REVIEWED, and specifically a pre-registered replication - the strongest design class in this research set. PNAS Nexus is the open-access companion to PNAS; the handling editor is named in the record (David Rand). Authors: William J. Brady (Northwestern, Kellogg), Steve Rathje, Laura K. Globig and Jay J. Van Bavel (NYU; Van Bavel also Norwegian School of Economics). No competing interests and no funding declared. Data and code fully open on OSF. Pre-registered before collection.

THE PROVENANCE CAVEAT THAT MATTERS, AND IT IS NOT SMALL. The paper is by the ORIGINAL AUTHORS replicating their own finding, and the meta-analysis is dominated by their own group's data. From the paper's own Table 2: Rathje et al. (2021, PNAS) contributes 2,951,322 messages; the current replication 849,266; Brady et al. (2017, PNAS) 313,003; Brady et al. (J. Exp. Psychol. General) 286,255. That is 4,399,846 of the stated 4,821,006 total - approximately 91% of the meta-analytic sample comes from the authoring group. The genuinely independent contributions are Burton et al. (207,622), Jordan (188,129, an unpublished Oxford master's thesis) and Ariztia (25,560, unpublished) - together about 9%. '5 labs, 27 studies, N = 4.8 million' reads as broad independent convergence; the weighted reality is one research programme confirming itself, with the largest independent contributor being the very critique the paper is rebutting. This does not make the finding wrong - the design is strong and the data are open - but 'independently replicated' is not the right phrase for it.

(Arithmetic note: summing Table 2's per-paper Ns gives 4,821,157 against a stated total of 4,821,006, a 151-message discrepancy. Trivial in effect, but it is the kind of thing to notice before quoting a figure to seven digits.)

DOWNSTREAM: every marketing blog that cites 'science says emotional content gets 17% more shares' is quoting a number from this paper without the political-Twitter scope condition, without the weighting caveat and usually without the meta-analytic estimate that supersedes it. That is vendor-grade provenance regardless of the peer-reviewed origin.

**effect size and n**

- HEADLINE, THE ONE TO QUOTE: meta-analytic IRR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.06, 1.20]. Random-effects model, generic inverse-variance weighting, Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman between-study variance, Q-profile CI on tau-squared. 5 labs, 27 studies, N = 4,821,006 messages. Interpretation: each additional moral-emotional word in a post is associated with roughly 13% more expected shares, with a plausible range of 6-20%.
- PRE-REGISTERED REPLICATION: N = 849,266 tweets across 5 US political topics. Mean IRR across datasets = 1.17 (this is the '+17%' figure). Note the paper reports this same quantity as 1.15 in its Results/Discussion narrative while the abstract says 1.17 - an internal inconsistency in the published text.
- PER-DATASET (dictionary method, moral-emotional predictor, all p < 0.001): Kavanaugh hearings 1.05 (N=195,567); border-wall shutdown 1.07 (N=200,000); transgender military ban 1.66 (N=53,649); COVID mask-wearing 1.12 (N=200,000); George Floyd killing 0.97 - SIGNIFICANTLY NEGATIVE (N=200,000). Four of five positive, one negative.
- THE WEIGHTING CAVEAT (my arithmetic on the paper's numbers): the 1.17 mean is UNWEIGHTED across the five datasets, so the 1.66 outlier - which comes from the SMALLEST sample, 53,649 tweets or 6.3% of the replication N - carries the same weight as datasets four times its size. The MEDIAN of the five is 1.07 and four of five fall between 0.97 and 1.12. The inverse-variance-weighted meta-analytic estimate of 1.13 is the statistically correct handling of exactly this problem, which is the technical reason to prefer it over 1.17.
- ORIGINAL STUDY for comparison: Brady, Wills, Jost, Tucker & Van Bavel (2017), PNAS 114(28):7313-7318, mean IRR = 1.20 (+20%), on gun control, same-sex marriage and climate change; N = 313,003 across 3 studies. The replication's estimate is slightly smaller than the original and the meta-analytic estimate smaller still - the classic decline pattern, here modest and well-behaved.
- STANDARDIZED EFFECT - the honest magnitude for practical use, because it removes the unit ambiguity: dictionary method, +8% in sharing per one standard deviation increase in moral-emotional word count. GPT-3.5 method, +16% per SD (mean IRR 1.16 across datasets). Note that '+17% per additional word' and '+8% per SD' are two framings of the same data and the per-SD one is what you should reason with when asking 'how much more moral-emotional should this post be'.
- LLM MEASUREMENT REPLICATION: consistent with the dictionary method on four of five datasets (the Trump-wall dataset was the exception). Adding sentiment and discrete emotions (sadness, anger, fear, joy, negativity) to the model left the moral-emotional coefficient unchanged, supporting it as a unique predictor rather than a proxy for general emotionality.
- META-ANALYSIS COMPOSITION (Table 2): Rathje et al. 2021 (PNAS), 8 studies, N=2,951,322; the current pre-registered replication, 5 studies, N=849,266; Brady et al. 2017 (PNAS), 3 studies, N=313,003; Brady et al. (J. Exp. Psychol. General), 2 studies, N=286,255; Burton et al. (Cognitive Science Society Proceedings / Nature Human Behaviour), 5 studies, N=207,622 - flagged by the authors as lacking the covariates used everywhere else; Jordan (unpublished Oxford master's thesis), 3 studies, N=188,129; Ariztia (unpublished), 1 study, N=25,560.
- PUBLICATION BIAS: Egger's intercept test = 3.049, p = 0.171 - no evidence of asymmetry. P-curve analysis indicates evidential value. The authors note that the studies with the LARGEST samples were most likely to replicate the effect, which is the pattern you want to see.
- NO EFFECT SIZE EXISTS FOR: LinkedIn, any professional or B2B content, any non-political topic, any non-English language, or any post-2020 platform. Write 'no effect size found' for those; do not transfer 1.13.

**conflicting evidence**

1. THE GEORGE FLOYD EXCEPTION - a genuine negative inside the replication itself. IRR = 0.97, p < 0.001, on a 200,000-tweet dataset. In the discussion set of a topic that precipitated the largest protest wave in recent US history, MORE moral-emotional language predicted FEWER retweets. The authors offer three candidate explanations without choosing: sampling error, real contextual moderators of moral contagion, or analytic decisions. The honest reading is that the effect has boundary conditions nobody has mapped, and that the conditions under which it reverses are exactly the high-salience, high-consensus ones where you would most expect it to fire. Do not treat 1.13 as a law.

2. BURTON, CRUZ & HAHN (2021), Nature Human Behaviour 5(12):1629-1635, 'Reconsidering evidence of moral contagion in online social networks' (with an earlier version at Proc. Annu. Meet. Cogn. Sci. 41:175-181, 2019). The substantive critique: the effect does not replicate well out of the original sample, and the moral-contagion model performs 'no better' than a nonsense 'XYZ contagion' model - i.e. arbitrary word categories predict retweets about as well, which would make the moral framing decorative. THE 2025 REBUTTAL: the moral-contagion model substantially outperforms the XYZ nonsense model in the new data; Burton et al. used smaller samples, did not pre-register collection or analysis, and omitted the covariates (follower count, media, verification) that everyone else includes, which matters enormously with data this skewed. THE HONEST SCORE: the 2025 paper wins on design - pre-registered, larger, open data, covariate-controlled. But note who is refereeing: Burton et al. is the largest genuinely independent dataset in the meta-analysis (207,622 messages, ~4% of N), and it is being down-weighted by the authors of the finding it challenges. The rebuttal is methodologically sound and I would take it; it is not disinterested.

3. CORRELATIONAL vs CAUSAL. The authors concede: 'our present analysis cannot establish a causal link... messages with moral-emotional language may differ from messages without it on other aspects not controlled for'. They cite Brady & Van Bavel (2025, J. Exp. Psychol. General 154(6):1505-1522) for controlled experiments showing causation. So causality is supported, but by a different study, on political messages, in an experimental setting rather than a live feed.

4. THE MEASUREMENT CRITIQUE the authors raise against themselves: 'word-count methods can produce noisy results'. Dictionary counting cannot see negation, irony, quotation or context - a post CRITICISING outrage scores as outrage. The GPT replication partly addresses this and partly does not, since the LLM was scoring the same short texts.

5. THE OPPOSING PLATFORM MECHANIC - the most important conflict for actually using this, and it comes from outside this literature. Moral-emotional language maximises the probability of a reshare AND the probability of a mute or report. X's ranker weights the second class an order of magnitude harder (ReportWeight -234.0, MuteAuthorWeight -58.8 against FavoriteWeight 0.5), and Agatha labels ACCOUNTS by blocks and reports relative to favorites - so the damage is persistent and account-level, not per-post. No paper in the moral-contagion literature measures mutes, blocks or reports, because the Twitter API never exposed them. The published effect size is therefore a measurement of the upside only, with the downside structurally invisible. This is the single strongest reason a professional account should treat +13% as not worth collecting.

6. BERGER'S WEAK-TIE FINDING, pulling the other way for B2B. Word of mouth is more POSITIVE with weak ties and people are less willing to raise controversial topics with acquaintances (Dubois et al. 2016; Chen & Berger 2013, both in the sibling item 'Berger word-of-mouth synthesis'). A professional feed is almost entirely weak ties. The moral-contagion data comes from political Twitter, where users self-select into ideological in-groups - a strong-tie-like structure for these purposes. The two literatures are describing different audience structures, and the B2B one is the structure where moral language travels worst.
