#### fit

**platform and format fit**

MEASURED ON: Twitter, 2018-2020, US political topics, text posts, retweet count as the outcome. The meta-analysis adds Facebook. That is the complete list of platforms where this has been tested.

X / TWITTER: the effect was measured here, so it transfers best - but this is also the platform where the downside is documented and severe. The open-sourced ranker (github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm, Apache-2.0) weights ReportWeight -234.0, MuteAuthorWeight -58.8, NotInterestedWeight -43.2 and BlockAuthorWeight -31.2 against FavoriteWeight 0.5, and Agatha labels ACCOUNTS by blocks and reports relative to favorites. Moral-emotional language is the most reliable way to trigger those negative actions. You are trading a +13% per-word reshare multiplier against an account-level penalty term hundreds of times heavier per event. Verified in the sibling item 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes'; do not re-derive it.

LINKEDIN: NO EVIDENCE. Zero studies. And the structural reasons to expect a weaker or reversed effect are real: identity is non-pseudonymous and career-linked, so resharing a moral claim carries employment risk; the audience is weak ties, where sharing skews positive (Dubois et al. 2016); and the 2026 ranking mix weights dwell time and comment depth rather than raw reshares. Treat any 'LinkedIn posts with emotional language get X% more reach' claim as vendor content with no basis in this literature.

FORMAT: the entire literature is SHORT TEXT - tweets. Nothing measured on carousels, video, long-form, or images. The dictionary method is length-sensitive in a way that does not obviously generalise: counting moral-emotional words in a 280-character tweet and in a 1,800-character LinkedIn post are not the same measurement, and neither paper addresses normalisation by length.

WHERE IT BACKFIRES OUTRIGHT: any context where your reader's reshare is professionally costly, any B2B account whose pipeline depends on being seen as level-headed, and any audience containing your prospects and your competitors simultaneously - which is every professional feed.

**scales with**

Scales with STANDING, not with account size, corpus size or budget - and standing is the input nobody can buy.

(1) The binding constraint is whether you have earned the right to make a moral claim in your niche. A moral position from someone with visible skin in the game reads as conviction; the identical sentence from someone without it reads as posturing. This is the same cap as the sibling items 'Proof-of-work receipts' and 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes'.

(2) It scales INVERSELY with audience heterogeneity. In a tight ideological or professional in-group, a moral frame recruits reshares cheaply. In a mixed audience - which is what a growing professional following becomes - the same frame splits the room, and the mute side costs more per head than the reshare side gains. So this tactic gets WORSE as your account grows, which is the opposite of most items in this set.

(3) It does not scale with volume. Repeated moral framing converts an account's perceived identity from 'expert who occasionally takes a position' to 'person who is angry about things', which is a positioning change, not a content change, and it is slow to reverse.

(4) NOT capped by: tooling (a prompt), cost (near zero), or team size. The constraint is entirely reputational.

CEILING NOTE: even where it works, the effect is a ~13% multiplier on the expected share count. Per the sibling item 'Limits of virality prediction', the base rate is so low that this cannot produce a cascade - it improves the odds on a lottery ticket rather than changing the game.

**decay and saturation**

THE FINDING: stable for 5-10 years. It is basic social psychology with an open, replicated, pre-registered evidence base, and moral signalling is not a platform feature that can be switched off.

THE TACTIC: ALREADY HEAVILY SATURATED, and this is the practical point. The finding has been public since 2017 and heavily popularised; outrage-framed content is now the default register of political and much commercial social media. Saturation cuts two ways here: (a) readers have become fluent at recognising manufactured moral framing, and recognition kills the identity-signalling value that made the reshare worthwhile; (b) platforms have spent the same period building exactly the countermeasures - LinkedIn's May-2026 low-quality-AI change and March-2026 authenticity update, X's negative-action weighting and Agatha account labelling. The tactic is decaying not because the psychology changed but because the environment adapted around it.

THE MEASUREMENT is also decaying: dictionary-based moral-emotional scoring was built for 2013-2020 English Twitter and degrades on longer, more professional, non-English text. The LLM method supersedes it and is itself version-dependent - the paper used GPT-3.5, and there is no guarantee a 2026 model scores the same construct the same way, which is a real reproducibility issue for anyone building a threshold on it.

SHELF-LIFE for the B2B translation ('moral stakes, not moral outrage'): unknown, because it has never been measured. Reason about it as positioning, which rots in 12-24 months, rather than as psychology, which does not.

#### risk

**failure modes**

1. QUOTING 1.17 AS THE ESTIMATE. The population estimate is 1.13 [1.06, 1.20]; 1.17 is one replication's unweighted mean, inflated by a 1.66 outlier on its smallest dataset. If someone checks the paper - which is free and open-access - the correction is embarrassing and immediate.

2. TRANSFERRING THE NUMBER TO LINKEDIN OR TO B2B. The most common failure and the least defensible. Every dataset is political Twitter. There is no professional-content estimate at all.

3. CONFUSING THE UNITS. '+17% per additional word' and '+8% per standard deviation' describe the same data. Reasoning about how much moral-emotional language to add requires the per-SD figure; the per-word figure invites the arithmetic error of assuming that ten such words multiply shares by 1.13^10 (which would be 3.4x, and is not what a negative-binomial coefficient licenses over that range).

4. MEASURING THE UPSIDE AND NOT THE DOWNSIDE. No paper in this literature measures mutes, blocks, reports or follower churn, because the API never exposed them. So the published effect is one side of a two-sided trade, and the invisible side is the one weighted -234.0 on X. Acting on a one-sided measurement is the structural failure here.

5. THE DICTIONARY'S BLINDNESS TO STANCE. Word counting cannot distinguish expressing outrage from criticising outrage. A post ABOUT moral grandstanding scores as moral grandstanding. If you build an automated gate on this, it will flag your most thoughtful posts.

6. ASSUMING MONOTONICITY. The George Floyd dataset - 200,000 tweets, on the highest-salience moral event in the sample - shows a SIGNIFICANTLY NEGATIVE association. Whatever governs that reversal is unmapped. 'More moral-emotional language is always better' is contradicted inside the anchor paper itself.

7. IDENTITY DRIFT. The slowest and most expensive failure: each individual post is defensible, and after six months the account's perceived identity has changed from practitioner to commentator. Nobody notices it happening, including the author.

**ai slop risk**

HIGH, and with a distinctive signature - this is one of the easiest things for a model to fake badly, because outrage register is overrepresented in training data.

THE TELLS. (a) THE UNNAMED VILLAIN: 'too many companies', 'the industry', 'certain consultants' - moral condemnation aimed at a target specific enough to feel pointed and vague enough to be unfalsifiable. A real moral claim names something. (b) BORROWED STAKES: harm asserted without a victim - 'this is costing businesses millions' with no business, no figure and no source. (c) ESCALATION WITHOUT EVIDENCE: the draft's temperature rises paragraph by paragraph while its evidence does not. (d) THE MORAL PIVOT: a technical post that suddenly acquires a moral frame in its final third, because the model was asked to make it more compelling. (e) SAFE OUTRAGE: indignation about something nobody defends ('AI slop is bad', 'meetings waste time'), which costs nothing and signals nothing - the giveaway is that no reader could possibly disagree. (f) MORALISED VOCABULARY WITH NEUTRAL CONTENT: 'betrayal', 'shameful', 'broken promise' attached to a product decision.

WHY IT IS WORSE HERE THAN ELSEWHERE: the mechanism requires the reader to believe the writer actually holds the position. Models produce the LANGUAGE of moral conviction at zero cost and without the standing that makes it credible, so the failure is not merely bland output - it is output that actively damages credibility. Generic advice slop is ignored; fake moral conviction is resented.

THE TEST: for every moral claim in the draft, ask 'who specifically is harmed, how, and how do I know?'. If the answer is not in the post, delete the claim rather than softening it. A removed moral frame costs you a hypothetical 13%; a hollow one costs you standing.

**human input required**

THE STANDING TO MAKE THE CLAIM. This is the least substitutable input in the entire research set, because the effect depends on the reader believing the position is real.

Concretely, at minimum one of:
- A first-hand instance of the harm: you watched this practice damage a named client, a named project, or your own business, and you can say when.
- A number you produced showing the cost of the thing you are condemning.
- Personal exposure: you are arguing against something that would be convenient for you, or you are naming a practice you yourself used to follow.
- A position you will defend in the replies when someone who disagrees turns up - because on a moral post, someone will.

THE CHECKABLE GATE: quote the sentence that names WHO is harmed and HOW YOU KNOW. If that sentence does not exist, the post has no moral standing and the moral framing should come out entirely. This is a harder gate than the general anti-slop one, and deliberately so: for most items in this set the cost of a hollow post is that it underperforms, whereas here the cost is that it is read as posturing and remembered.

WHAT THE MODEL MAY DO: measure density, find the target of the moral frame, flag escalation, run the mute test. What it may not do: supply the conviction, the harmed party or the evidence.

**detectability and disclosure**

TWO SEPARATE DETECTION QUESTIONS, and only one of them is about AI.

(1) IS THE TEXT DETECTABLE AS AI-GENERATED? The standard question, covered in the sibling items 'AI slop and the authenticity penalty' and 'Platform AI labeling and C2PA provenance'. Moral-emotional text drafted by a model carries the usual signature plus the specific tells in ai_slop_risk. Text is not watermarked the way images are - no C2PA manifest and no SynthID payload attaches to a pasted post - so detection here is classifier-based and probabilistic, not cryptographic.

(2) IS THE MORAL-EMOTIONAL CONTENT ITSELF DETECTABLE? YES, trivially, and this is the more consequential answer. The anchor paper demonstrates that both dictionary methods and a commodity LLM score moral-emotional density accurately at scale on short social text. Platforms run far more sophisticated classifiers than GPT-3.5. So assume that your moral-emotional density is a measured quantity on the platform side, whatever the ranking consequence turns out to be. X's published ranker carries no valence or tone score - verified from the open source in the sibling item 'Contrarian / pattern-interrupt takes', where the widely-repeated claim that X throttles combative tone was found to be false - but it does carry the negative-action weights that moral-emotional content reliably triggers. The measurement is cheap and available; assuming it is not being made is not a safe assumption.

DISCLOSURE TRIGGERED: none specific to this item. Writing with moral-emotional language is not a disclosable act. If a model drafted the text, ordinary AI-drafting disclosure considerations apply - see policy_and_legal.

AN IRONY WORTH NOTING: the same LLM-as-measurement-instrument capability that the paper validated for research is available to you, to platforms, and to anyone auditing your corpus. Your account's moral-emotional trajectory over three years is a computable quantity from public data.

**reversibility and blast radius**

THE HIGHEST BLAST RADIUS OF ANY COPY ITEM IN THIS RESEARCH SET, and the least reversible.

PER POST: recoverable. A post that lands wrong can be deleted; the reach cost is bounded.

PER ACCOUNT: NOT cleanly recoverable, and this is the part that matters. Mutes and blocks are permanent per user - nobody un-mutes you - and X's Agatha system labels ACCOUNTS by blocks and reports relative to favorites, so the penalty attaches to the account rather than the post and persists after deletion. You cannot delete your way out of having been muted.

PER BRAND: the slowest and most expensive. For a B2B consultant whose pipeline depends on being perceived as measured, a reputation as someone who posts angry takes changes who is willing to make an introduction. That is not a metric, it is not visible in analytics, and it does not recover on a posting-behaviour change - it recovers, if at all, over quarters.

SUSPENSION RISK: low for practice-targeted moral language; real for person- or group-targeted language, which crosses into hateful-conduct and harassment policy on every platform.

ASYMMETRY, stated plainly: the measured upside is a ~13% multiplier on expected shares (CI 6-20%) on a base rate that is near zero for most posts. The unmeasured downside is a permanent per-user mute, an account-level negative label, and a positioning change. For a professional account this is a bad trade, and the fact that only the upside has a published number is the reason it keeps getting taken.

#### practice

**how to apply**

READ THIS SECTION AS A CONSTRAINT, NOT A TACTIC. For a B2B professional audience the defensible application of this finding is a CEILING and a TRANSLATION, not an optimisation. The steps below implement that.

STEP 0 (once, 45 minutes). Read the paper. It is free: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12578369/. Read the per-dataset IRRs in the replication section and the meta-analysis section. You are looking for two things: the spread (0.97 to 1.66 across five datasets) and the scope (every dataset is US political Twitter). Those two facts do more work than the headline number.

STEP 1 (once, 20 minutes). Fix the numbers you will use. Population estimate: IRR 1.13, 95% CI [1.06, 1.20], 5 labs / 27 studies / N=4,821,006. This replication's mean: 1.17, N=849,266. Standardized: +8% per SD (dictionary), +16% per SD (LLM). Original 2017: 1.20. Write these down once so you never quote 1.17 as the estimate.

STEP 2 (once, 30 minutes). Set your account's moral-emotional CEILING. Run prompt pattern 1 over your twenty best-performing past posts and your twenty worst. If your good posts cluster at 2-4 on the 0-10 scale, that is your band; going above it is a deliberate decision, not a default.

STEP 3 (per post, 2 minutes). Score the draft with prompt pattern 1. Read the quoted words, not the number - the word list tells you whether the moral content is load-bearing or decorative.

STEP 4 (per post, 2 minutes). TARGET CHECK, the single highest-value step. Identify what the moral frame is aimed at. PERSON or GROUP -> rewrite or cut; this is where mutes, reports, defamation exposure and hateful-conduct policy all live. PRACTICE or INCENTIVE STRUCTURE -> keep. This is the whole B2B translation: 'this vendor lies' becomes 'this pricing pattern makes it impossible for a buyer to compare offers, and here is the quote that proves it'. Same moral stakes, no target.

STEP 5 (per post, 1 minute). EVIDENCE GATE. For each surviving moral claim, quote the sentence naming who is harmed and how you know. No such sentence -> delete the claim. Do not soften it; softening produces safe outrage, which is the worst of both.

STEP 6 (per post, 1 minute). MUTE TEST (prompt pattern 3). Ask what the DISAGREEING reader does with their thumb. If the answer is mute or report, weigh it against the X negative-action weights: a mute is -58.8 against a favourite's 0.5, and it is permanent.

STEP 7 (per post, 30 seconds). EXPECTATION SETTING. Write down what you expect before publishing. Moral-framed posts reliably produce comments (cheap for the reader) and unreliably produce reshares (expensive for the reader), particularly in a weak-tie professional feed. Predicting that in advance stops you drawing the wrong lesson from the result.

STEP 8 (quarterly, 60 minutes). Score your whole quarter's posts (prompt pattern 5) and plot moral-emotional density against reshares, comment sentiment and follower churn. This is the only way to get an effect size for YOUR audience, and it is the honest replacement for borrowing 1.13. Expect it to be smaller. If follower churn correlates with density, you have found your ceiling empirically.

**checklist**

PASS/FAIL GATE - all seven before publishing anything with a moral frame.
1. TARGET. The moral claim is aimed at a PRACTICE or an INCENTIVE, not at a person, a company or a group. FAIL on any identifiable target.
2. HARMED PARTY. I can quote the sentence naming who is harmed and how I know it. FAIL if that sentence does not exist in the post.
3. STANDING. I have first-hand exposure to this harm - a client, a project, my own past practice. FAIL if my only basis is that the position is popular in my niche.
4. CEILING. The draft scores within my account's established moral-emotional band, or I have consciously decided to exceed it for this specific post. FAIL on unexamined escalation.
5. MUTE TEST. A reader who disagrees would reply or ignore, not mute or report. FAIL if the most likely thumb action is mute.
6. NUMBERS. If I cite the research, I cite IRR 1.13 [1.06, 1.20] as the estimate, note the political-Twitter scope, and do not present 1.17 as the population effect. FAIL on any unscoped percentage.
7. DEFENCE. I will be in the replies, and I have a real answer for the strongest objection. FAIL if I am publishing and leaving.

**cost and time to execute**

ONE-OFF: 45 minutes to read the paper (free, CC-BY-NC, no paywall), 20 minutes to fix the correct numbers, 30 minutes to establish your account's moral-emotional baseline across 40 past posts. EUR 0 in tooling.

PER POST: 6-7 minutes - 2 min scoring, 2 min target check, 1 min evidence gate, 1 min mute test, 30 sec expectation setting. Note this is a SUPPRESSIVE cost: it is time spent not publishing something, which is the correct shape for this item.

PER QUARTER: 60 minutes for the corpus audit. LLM cost for scoring 100 posts is a few cents on API pricing, or free inside an existing subscription.

TOOL SUBSCRIPTIONS: none. No commercial tool does this; you are running a prompt.

THE REAL COST IS NOT TIME. It is the reply-thread obligation. Publishing a genuine moral position commits you to defending it, which is 30-90 minutes of comment engagement over the following two days, and it is not optional - a moral post you abandon reads worse than one you never published. That is the cost to weigh against a 13% share multiplier, and against a 4-hour original-data post it is a poor use of the same attention.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

THE CRITICAL POINT: the standard KPI set measures only the upside of this item, which is precisely how it keeps getting over-adopted. Track both sides or do not track it.

UPSIDE METRICS (all natively available): reshare/repost rate per impression - the outcome the literature actually measured, so the only one comparable to IRR 1.13; comment volume, which rises faster than reshares on moral content because commenting is cheap and resharing is not; reply depth.

DOWNSIDE METRICS - track these or the exercise is worthless: FOLLOWER CHURN in the 48 hours after a moral post, which is the only natively-visible proxy for mutes and blocks and which almost nobody watches; the ratio of reshares to net follower change, which is the actual trade this item makes; comment SENTIMENT COMPOSITION, distinguishing people arguing with the idea from people objecting to you; and reach on your NEXT post, which is the most sensitive available indicator of an account-level penalty having been applied.

LEADING INDICATORS, first 60-90 minutes: whether the first three comments engage the argument or the framing - if they are about your tone, the post has recruited the wrong reaction and the mute count is already rising; and first-hour reshare rate against your own baseline.

THE ONE METRIC THAT ACTUALLY TESTS THIS ITEM FOR YOU: over a quarter, regress moral-emotional density (prompt pattern 5) against reshare rate on your own posts, with follower churn as a second outcome. That gives you a personal effect size, which is the only one that applies to your audience. Expect something well below 1.13, and expect the churn coefficient to be the one that changes your behaviour.

NOT A KPI: impressions and reach. Moral content reliably produces comment-driven activity that inflates engagement rate while telling you nothing about whether the post helped you.

**measurement feasibility**

PARTIALLY FEASIBLE, with the decisive variable structurally invisible - and that invisibility is not incidental, it is the reason the published literature is one-sided.

FEASIBLE: the PREDICTOR is genuinely easy to measure. Moral-emotional density can be scored on any draft or archive with a single LLM call, validated for exactly this purpose in the anchor paper (GPT-3.5) and multilingually in Rathje et al. (2024). This is unusual - most items in this set have an unmeasurable predictor and a measurable outcome; here it is the reverse.

FEASIBLE: reshare counts, comment counts and comment text are native on every platform. Follower count over time is native and, differenced daily, is your churn proxy.

NOT FEASIBLE - and this is the whole problem: MUTES, BLOCKS, REPORTS and NOT-INTERESTED signals. No platform exposes any of them to the creator. Twitter's API never did, which is why no paper in this literature - including the anchor - measures them. So the published effect size is an estimate of the benefit with the cost term structurally absent, and no amount of your own analytics will recover it either. PROXIES, in descending quality: (1) follower churn in the 48h window, which catches unfollows but not mutes, and mutes are the commoner and quieter action; (2) reach decay on subsequent posts, which is confounded with everything; (3) qualitative - people stop replying who used to.

ALSO NOT FEASIBLE: any comparison against the published IRR on a like-for-like basis, because the literature's outcome is a raw retweet count on Twitter with follower count as a covariate, and your analytics give you a rate against impressions on a different platform.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION: measure the predictor (cheap and validated), measure reshare rate and follower churn as the two-sided outcome, and treat the mute channel as a known unmeasured cost that you assume is there. Do not attempt to validate 1.13 on your own data - the design cannot support it. Use your data only to find your own ceiling.

**ai search citability**

NEGATIVE TO NEUTRAL for your own content, and strongly positive for one specific use.

FOR YOUR POSTS: moral-emotional framing does not help LLM citability and plausibly hurts it. Retrieval systems select passages that answer questions with extractable, attributable propositions; outrage-framed content is affect-dense and proposition-light, and generative engines have visible incentives to avoid surfacing inflammatory material in answers. The sibling item 'AI citation visibility as a second objective function' records that educational and advice intent accounts for 54-64% of AI citations - moral commentary is neither. Nothing here suggests moral framing improves citation, and the content shape it produces is the opposite of the shape that gets cited.

THE PART THAT DOES HELP: the B2B translation. 'This pricing practice harms buyers because X, and here is the evidence' is simultaneously a moral claim and an extractable, citable proposition with a named mechanism. The translation from outrage to stakes moves the content toward citability rather than away from it - the same edit improves both objectives, which is rare in this research set and worth noting.

THE STRONGLY POSITIVE USE: citing THIS RESEARCH is excellent citability material. A post that states the actual numbers - IRR 1.13, 95% CI [1.06, 1.20], 5 labs / 27 studies / N=4,821,006 - with the correct scope caveat and a link to the open-access paper is exactly the answer-shaped, statistic-bearing, source-citing content that generative engines absorb (compare the GEO findings in the sibling item 'Proof-of-work receipts': Statistics Addition +33%, Cite Sources +28%). Writing accurately ABOUT moral contagion is a better citability play than writing WITH it - and, given that most of what circulates on this topic is a mis-stated 17%, correcting the record is also genuinely useful.

### Network structure, seeding and creator size

`network-seeding-creator-size` · automation L0 · evidence STRONG · 20 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Network structure, seeding and creator size
- **category**: science
- **definition**: How the SHAPE of your graph, WHO sees a post first, and HOW BIG your account is condition distribution — re-derived for the 2026 interest-graph regime, in which having followers no longer guarantees delivery to them and non-followers are reachable with no seeding step at all.
- **maturity**: Split. The underlying network science (Watts/Dodds, Bakshy, Goel, Weng, Martin) is ESTABLISHED and does not rot. The classical viral-marketing SEEDING literature is established but largely OBSOLETE for own-account publishing — it answers 'which people should a campaign hand a product to', a question a recommender-mediated feed no longer asks. The interest-graph reframing is ESTABLISHED and consolidating across X, TikTok and Meta; on LinkedIn it is EMERGING and partly inferred.
- **one line**: Account size is not one variable: it gates eligibility on LinkedIn, is explicitly INVERTED below 1,000 followers on X, and is officially not a direct factor on TikTok.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **honest answer**: Marginal, and mostly ANALYTIC rather than generative. AI does not change your graph; people do. Claiming otherwise is where this topic turns into automation-tool marketing.
- **what it genuinely does**:
  - READ THE PRIMARY SOURCE. The single highest-value AI use here is pointing a coding agent at github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm and asking it to extract current parameter defaults and explain the scorer chain. That converts a folklore question into a code-reading task, and it re-runs in minutes on every ~4-week refresh.
  - AUDIENCE / CLUSTER MAPPING. Feed an export of who engages with you (names, headlines, companies) to a model and ask it to cluster them and name the communities. This is the Weng community-concentration idea done by hand, and it is the only way a creator observes their own graph's modularity.
  - BRIDGE IDENTIFICATION. Ask for the communities ADJACENT to your named clusters that you have near-zero presence in, and what would legitimately interest them.
  - TOPIC-AUTHORITY CONSISTENCY. Under a semantic ranker, retrieval fires on coherent topical identity. A model checking 'do my last 20 posts read as one expertise or five?' targets the gate directly.
  - NARROWCAST PAYLOAD DRAFTING. Writing the forwardable block — covered properly in the sibling share-to-DM entry.
- **what it must not do**: Generate connection requests, DMs or comments at volume. That is the automation path, it is against LinkedIn's User Agreement, and the downside is loss of the account — i.e. loss of the graph this whole item is about.

**automation level**

- **taxonomy placement**: L0-L1 for everything legitimate.
- **L0 manual**: Building bridging ties, replying to people, choosing who to connect with. Non-substitutable.
- **L1 ai assisted**: Cluster analysis of your audience export, parameter extraction from the X repo, topic-coherence review, drafting outreach you then personalise and send yourself. This is where the real value sits.
- **L2 autonomous with guardrails**: Nothing here should be L2. The only candidates are scheduled outreach and auto-engagement, which are exactly what platform enforcement targets.
- **L3**: Nothing. Tools marketed as 'AI growth agents' or 'AI networking agents' for LinkedIn are L1 schedulers plus a generation step, operating a browser automation layer against the User Agreement. The 'agent' framing describes the pricing page, not the architecture.

**prompt patterns**

- **1 primary source extraction**: Use on a coding agent with repo access, not a chat model: 'Clone github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm. From home-mixer/params/param.rs extract the current DEFAULT values of: ColdStartFollowerCap, ColdStartImpressionThreshold, ColdStartMaxPostAgeSecs, ColdStartSlotMin, ColdStartSlotMax, LowImpressionsMaxPositionRatio, EnableViewerColdStart, EnableColdStartThompsonSampling, ColdStartBetaAlpha0, ColdStartBetaBeta0, OonWeightFactor, TopicOonWeightFactor, AuthorDiversityDecay, AuthorDiversityFloor. Then read home-mixer/scorers/author_cold_start.rs and state the exact eligibility predicate and what the boost does to the score. Quote line numbers. Do not infer anything the code does not say.' Re-run monthly.
- **2 community concentration audit**: 'Here is a list of the 150 people who engaged with my last 30 posts, with their headlines and employers. Cluster them into communities and name each one. For each cluster give: size, how much it overlaps the others, and one sentence on what that cluster actually cares about. Then tell me which SINGLE cluster is over-represented, and name three adjacent communities I have almost no presence in. Do not suggest content yet.'
- **3 bridge brief**: 'Community X (named above) is adjacent to my strongest cluster but I have no presence there. What does that community argue about internally? Which of my existing, already-published posts would land there UNCHANGED, and which would need a different frame? Name the specific people or venues where that community actually talks.'
- **4 topic coherence gate**: 'Here are my last 20 posts, text only. If you were a semantic ranker deciding what this account is an authority on, what would you conclude — give me the top three topics with a confidence each. Then tell me which posts pulled the estimate away from my intended topic.' The test is whether the model returns ONE topic at high confidence. Three at 33% each means retrieval has nothing to fire on.
- **5 the size reality check**: 'My account has N followers on platform P. Given only what platform P has OFFICIALLY published about follower count as a ranking input, what does N change? Cite the official statement. If there is no official statement, say so and stop — do not fill the gap with marketing blogs.' This prompt exists to stop the model laundering vendor claims, which is its default behaviour on this topic.
- **anti pattern**: 'How do I grow my LinkedIn network fast?' — returns the automation playbook every time, because that is what the training corpus contains on this query.

**tool examples**

- **primary source**: github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm (Apache-2.0, ~33k stars, last push 2026-09-10) — strictly better than any 'X algorithm 2026' article. No other major platform offers this.
- **analytics**: LinkedIn native analytics (audience demographics by job title/industry/company — the closest thing to observing your own cluster structure); Shield Analytics and AuthoredUp (LinkedIn post-level history, vendor); Metricool (cross-platform, vendor, publishes a 1M-account annual study).
- **citation side**: Semrush AI-visibility tooling and Profound — both vendors with a product to sell, both the only sources of LinkedIn AI-citation data.
- **avoid**: Taplio, Dripify, Expandi, PhantomBuster and the LinkedIn automation category generally — browser automation against the User Agreement. Named here so the category is recognisable, not as a recommendation.
- **dates**: All tool statements as of 2026-09-11. The x-algorithm repo updates roughly every four weeks.

#### fit

**audience fit**

- **b2b**: Network structure dominates, because B2B distribution is LinkedIn-shaped and LinkedIn is the platform where the graph IS the test pool. A 2,000-connection network of actual practitioners in your niche beats an 8,000-connection network assembled from accepting everything.
- **b2c**: Network structure barely matters; TikTok and Reels are content-gated. The classical seeding literature is furthest from applicable here.
- **technical vs general**: Technical niches are dense and small, which is exactly the Weng failure case: high early engagement, hard ceiling, because the whole community saturates in two days. A technical creator's growth constraint is bridging into adjacent non-identical communities (e.g. from 'AI agents' into 'engineering management'), not posting more inside the same one.
- **pl vs en**: Language is a hard cluster boundary on an interest-graph platform. A Polish-language post is retrieved into a much smaller candidate space: lower ceiling, but higher relevance density and far less competition — the saturation Metricool measures is overwhelmingly an English-language phenomenon. English gives access to the sub-1000-follower X subsidy in a market where it matters; Polish gives a defensible niche where a 500-person first degree can be nearly the entire relevant audience. These are different games, not the same game at different scales.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- GENERALISING ACROSS PLATFORMS. The single most common and most expensive error. 'Followers don't matter any more' is officially true on TikTok, inverted on X, and close to false on LinkedIn. A tactic imported from a TikTok-shaped mental model into LinkedIn fails silently.
- OPTIMISING SIZE INSTEAD OF COMPOSITION. Accepting every connection request grows the number and degrades the test pool: a first degree full of recruiters and lead-gen agencies produces a weak, off-topic early signal under a semantic ranker, which caps escalation on every future post. This damage is cumulative and slow to undo.
- THE DENSE-CLUSTER PLATEAU. Strong early engagement, then a hard stop, post after post — the Weng complex-contagion signature. It reads like a content problem and gets treated with hook rewrites, which do nothing. The fix is structural: bridge into a community that does not already know you.
- BUILDING ON THE X SUBSIDY. It is one candidate per request, capped at 1,000 impressions, expires at 1,000 followers, excludes replies and retweets, and is a config default.
- REACHING FOR AUTOMATION WHEN ORGANIC GRAPH-BUILDING IS SLOW. The predictable end-state of this item, and the one with a catastrophic downside (see reversibility).
- MISTAKING BROADCAST FOR VIRALITY. Goel et al.: large cascades are mostly one big broadcast. A post that 'went viral' usually got picked up by one large node or one recommender push. Attributing it to network design and trying to reproduce the design reproduces nothing.
- EXPECTING PREDICTABILITY. Martin et al. cap explainable variance below 50% with a feature set no creator will ever have. Treat every outcome here as a distribution, never as a plan.

**human input required**

- **the non substitutable minimum**: A true, specific, verifiable reason why THIS person should connect with YOU — something that could only be written by someone who read their work. One sentence is enough; it cannot be generated without the reading.
- **concretely**:
  - A reference to a specific thing they published, with what you disagreed with or took from it.
  - A shared context that actually exists: a conference you both attended, a project you both touched, a client in common, a repo you contributed to.
  - A judgement call about who is worth knowing — which requires knowing the field, and is exactly what an automated targeting filter cannot supply.
  - For bridging: months of genuine presence in a community before asking it for anything. There is no AI substitute because the thing being built is other people's memory of you.
- **the checkable gate**: Could this message have been sent, unchanged, to 200 other people? If yes, do not send it. That is the whole test, and it is the same test platform classifiers are effectively applying.
- **why it is load bearing here**: Elsewhere in this research set the human input improves the content. Here it IS the asset: a graph of people who remember you is the only thing in this entry that neither decays on a four-week refresh nor can be bought.

#### practice

**how to apply**

A four-week sequence. Steps 1-2 are analysis, 3-4 change the graph, 5 is maintenance. Nothing here is fast, and any version that is fast is the automation version.

STEP 1 — READ THE ONE PRIMARY SOURCE (45 minutes, once, then 10 minutes monthly).
Point a coding agent at github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm with prompt pattern 1. Extract the current defaults and the cold-start eligibility predicate. Record the values and the date in a file you can diff. If you publish on X and are under 1,000 followers, this single step tells you something no blog can: you have a reserved slot, it applies only to original posts, only under 1,000 impressions, only in the first 24 hours, and only if the post is already competitive. If you are over 1,000, it tells you that consecutive posts competing in the same viewer's candidate pool decay at 0.5^k toward a 0.25 floor.

STEP 2 — AUDIT YOUR ACTUAL GRAPH (90 minutes, once per quarter).
Export the list of people who engaged with your last 30 posts (LinkedIn analytics gives demographics; Shield or AuthoredUp give per-post detail). Run prompt pattern 2. You want three outputs: the named clusters, the over-represented one, and three adjacent communities you are absent from. The diagnostic you are looking for: if one cluster is more than roughly half your engagement, you are in the complex-contagion trap and your ceiling is structural, not editorial.

STEP 3 — FIX COMPOSITION BEFORE VOLUME (ongoing, the slow part).
Stop accepting connections indiscriminately; on LinkedIn each accepted connection changes the test pool that will judge every future post. For each of the three adjacent communities from step 2, pick FIVE named people who are central in that community and spend four weeks reading and responding to their work substantively before any connection request. Then connect with a one-sentence, unrepeatable reason. Twenty bridging ties built this way move your ceiling more than two thousand accepted requests.

STEP 4 — RUN THE TOPIC-COHERENCE GATE (20 minutes, monthly).
Prompt pattern 4 on your last 20 posts. One topic at high confidence means semantic retrieval has something to fire on. Three at 33% means it does not, and no amount of network work will compensate — under a semantic ranker, topical incoherence is a retrieval problem, not a branding problem.

STEP 5 — PICK THE OBJECTIVE YOUR GRAPH CAN ACTUALLY SERVE (a decision, not a task).
If your network is small and dense, the virality ceiling is low and will stay low for months. The flat-ceiling objective is AI-engine citation: sub-500-follower creators are cited comparably to large ones, ~75% of cited authors simply posted 5+ times in the prior four weeks, and the median cited post carried 15-25 reactions. Choosing that target is the single highest-expected-value move available to a small account, and it is orthogonal to everything in steps 1-4.

WHAT NOT TO DO: buy a tool that automates step 3. The step is slow because the asset is other people's genuine attention, and that is not a throughput problem.

**checklist**

PASS/FAIL before acting on anything in this entry:
[ ] I have named the PLATFORM before applying any claim about follower count. (Fail if I am about to generalise.)
[ ] If X: I re-read param.rs within the last 30 days and the defaults still match what is recorded here.
[ ] If X and under 1,000 followers: this is an ORIGINAL post (not a reply, not a retweet), so it is cold-start eligible.
[ ] If X and posting more than once: I have accepted that my 2nd post in the same candidate pool scores at 0.625 and my 3rd at 0.4375.
[ ] If LinkedIn: the last 20 people I connected with are people whose reaction to my topic I would actually want in a test pool.
[ ] Any outreach message I am about to send could NOT be sent unchanged to 200 other people.
[ ] I have not quoted a number about Instagram's test pool or LinkedIn's 2-5% slice as if it were established.
[ ] I know which of my engagement clusters is over-represented, and I checked it within the last quarter.
[ ] Nothing in my plan depends on a tool that logs into a platform on my behalf.
[ ] My last 20 posts read as ONE topic to a semantic ranker.
[ ] I have decided, explicitly, whether I am optimising for virality (steep ceiling) or citability (flat ceiling) — and I am not pretending one plan serves both.
[ ] I am treating every outcome as a draw from a heavy-tailed distribution whose variance is more than half unexplainable.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **the one that matters**: SHARE OF ENGAGEMENT FROM YOUR LARGEST CLUSTER, quarter over quarter. Falling means you are bridging successfully. This is the Weng result operationalised, and almost nobody measures it.
- **leading indicators fast**:
  - Non-follower / out-of-network share of impressions (LinkedIn shows 'non-connections'; Instagram shows follower vs non-follower; TikTok shows traffic source). Moves within days and is the most direct read on whether interest-graph retrieval is firing for you.
  - Number of NEW named individuals engaging per post — distinct from total engagement, and the early sign of cluster expansion.
  - On X under 1,000 followers: whether posts cross ~1,000 impressions at all, since that is the threshold at which the subsidy stops applying.
- **lagging**:
  - Impressions per post (noisy, heavy-tailed, near-useless below ~30 posts).
  - Follower count — the worst metric here, since on X it is inverted below 1,000 and on TikTok it is officially not an input.
  - Engagement rate — denominator differences between tools make cross-source comparison meaningless (Socialinsider ~5.20% average LinkedIn ER vs Buffer's 21.77% median for carousels: a 4x gap in the same headline metric).
- **what moves first**: Non-follower share moves first (days). New-individuals-per-post moves second (weeks). Cluster share moves third (a quarter). Impressions move last and most noisily.

### Platform AI labeling and C2PA provenance

`platform-ai-labeling-and-provenance` · automation L2 · evidence SPLIT · 12 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Platform AI labeling and C2PA provenance
- **category**: science
- **definition**: The cryptographic-metadata layer (C2PA Content Credentials) plus invisible watermarking (SynthID) plus platform-side NLP/pixel classifiers that together decide whether a post's assets get auto-labeled as AI-generated — independently of what the creator chooses to disclose.
- **maturity**: established as a standard and as platform policy; emerging and unreliable as an end-to-end working chain. The specification, the steering committee and the platform label surfaces all exist and are stable; what does NOT exist is a dependable guarantee that a credential survives an upload-download round trip on any given platform.
- **one line takeaway**: You do not control the label. You control whether the label, when it appears, is consistent with what you already said.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

- **the chain in order**:
  - 1. SIGNING. A generating or editing tool (Adobe Firefly/Photoshop, OpenAI image models, Google Gemini/Imagen, Truepic-enabled capture devices) writes a C2PA manifest into the asset. The manifest is a cryptographically signed claim set: what tool made it, what actions were applied (generated / edited / composited), an optional identity assertion, and a hash binding the manifest to the pixels. It is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof: you cannot silently ALTER it, you can trivially DELETE it.
  - 2. UPLOAD. The platform's ingest pipeline re-encodes the asset (resize, transcode, strip EXIF for privacy, generate derivatives). Any of those steps can drop the manifest. Preservation is a deliberate engineering choice per pipeline, not a default.
  - 3. READ AND LABEL. Platforms that implement the reading side parse the manifest and, if it asserts AI generation, attach a visible label — Meta's 'AI Info' across Facebook/Instagram/Threads, TikTok's 'AI-generated' tag, YouTube's 'altered or synthetic content' disclosure. Meta's own description: the label fires on industry-standard indicators embedded by the AI tool, OR on voluntary creator self-disclosure.
  - 4. DISPLAY. Some platforms show the credential to viewers (a 'CR' pin or a menu entry) rather than only consuming it internally. Meta moved the label for merely AI-EDITED content into the post's overflow menu, keeping the prominent label for fully AI-generated content — a deliberate de-escalation after the 2024 'Made with AI' over-labeling backlash.
  - 5. DOWNLOAD. A viewer saves the asset. Whether the manifest comes back out is a separate pipeline decision from step 2 and is frequently different. TikTok explicitly claimed at launch that credentials it attaches 'will remain on content when downloaded'. Other platforms make no such claim.
  - 6. RECOVERY (durable credentials). Because steps 2-5 leak, the C2PA/CAI answer is a three-part fallback: embedded metadata FIRST, then an invisible watermark carrying an identifier that resolves the manifest from cloud storage, then a perceptual fingerprint that matches the content against a provenance store with no embedded data at all. CAI's framing: 'fingerprints are immune to information removal because there is no information to remove.' Adobe + Digimarc demonstrated the first interoperable durable Content Credentials via watermarking on 2025-06-02; Cloudflare became the first major CDN to preserve credentials across its network on 2025-02-03.
- **the parallel text track**: Text has no equivalent chain. There is no C2PA manifest for a LinkedIn post body. The three mechanisms that exist are: (a) statistical watermarking at generation time (Google SynthID adjusts token probability scores during sampling — works only for text produced by an instrumented model, and only Google's); (b) post-hoc classifiers (platform-internal 'AI slop' NLP models, commercial detectors like Pangram, GPTZero); (c) behavioural signals (posting cadence, template repetition, near-duplicate embedding distance across accounts). None of these produce a cryptographic label, and (b) is provably unreliable.
- **why the asymmetry exists**: Imagery is produced by a small number of instrumented pipelines that can be made to sign at the point of generation. Text is produced by thousands of models, many open-weight and uninstrumented, and then EDITED by a human — and editing destroys any statistical watermark long before it destroys meaning. The C2PA model assumes a bounded set of cooperating generators. That assumption holds for Firefly and Imagen; it does not hold for a local Llama running on a laptop.
- **what actually happens to your post**: For a text-only LinkedIn post drafted with an LLM and edited by you: nothing. No manifest exists, no watermark survives the edit, and the only detection surface is the platform's own slop classifier reading the text as text. For the same post with an AI-generated header image or carousel: the image may carry a manifest, the platform may read it, and the AI label may appear on your post regardless of your intent — and it will appear on the POST, not just the image.

**why it drives reach**

- **it mostly does not**: This is the rare entry in the table where the tactic is DEFENSIVE. Provenance hygiene does not add distribution; it prevents a category of distribution loss and a category of credibility loss. Rank it by downside avoided, not upside gained.
- **the three causal paths that do exist**:
  - MISMATCH PENALTY. If the platform auto-labels an asset as AI while your caption implies you shot/made it, the mismatch is visible to every reader who opens the overflow menu. The reach cost is social (comment-section challenge, reduced reshares), not algorithmic — but on LinkedIn, where comment quality and dwell drive Stage-1 escalation, a derailed comment section in the first 60-90 minutes is a real distribution cost.
  - CONSISTENCY DIVIDEND. Disclosing before the platform does converts an auto-label from a gotcha into a corroboration. This is the only mechanism here with a plausible positive sign, and it is unmeasured.
  - ENFORCEMENT AVOIDANCE. Undisclosed synthetic media is a policy violation on X ('Manipulated Media'), YouTube (mandatory realistic-synthetic disclosure) and TikTok. Strikes compound; channel-level enforcement on YouTube wiped ~16 AI-slop channels (~35M subs, ~4.7B views) in 2026 per the vault note. Avoiding a strike is worth more than any hook optimization.
- **the counterintuitive part**: The provenance layer is most valuable to creators who are NOT using much AI — because it gives them a way to prove it. A C2PA-signed camera original or a signed screen recording of real work is a positive credential in a feed where everyone claims authenticity and nobody can demonstrate it. That use is currently almost unexploited on professional social platforms.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **primary**: None in the classic sense — the model is the SUBJECT of this entry, not the operator. The AI's role is that it leaves (or fails to leave) a mark.
- **where a model genuinely helps**:
  - AUDIT / RETRIEVE. Run a pre-publish check over every asset in a post: does it carry a manifest, what does the manifest assert, does the assertion contradict the caption. This is a scripted check (c2patool) with an LLM only writing the human-readable verdict.
  - DRAFT the disclosure line so it is accurate and specific rather than boilerplate ('image generated with Gemini, text drafted with Claude and rewritten by me' beats 'made with AI').
  - CRITIQUE the caption against the manifest — the one genuinely useful LLM task here: 'this manifest says c2pa.created by a generative model; the caption says I photographed this; flag the contradiction.'
  - VARY nothing. Do not let a model near the manifest itself.
- **what the model must not do**: Generate, edit or remove provenance assertions. Stripping a C2PA manifest to avoid a label is technically trivial (exiftool, a re-encode) and is the single action in this entry that converts a compliance posture into a deception. Under EU AI Act Art. 50 the DEPLOYER disclosure duty for deepfakes survives the removal of the provider's mark, so stripping buys nothing legally and costs everything if noticed.

**automation level**

- **level**: L2 — autonomous with guardrails, for the verification half only.
- **detail**: The check ('does every asset in this post carry a manifest, and does it contradict the caption?') is a deterministic CI step: c2patool over the asset directory, exit non-zero on contradiction. That is safely autonomous. The DECISION ('do we disclose, and in what words?') is L1 at most — it is an editorial and legal judgement under Art. 50(4), and the whole value of the human-editorial-review exemption is that a human actually made it.
- **vendor label warning**: Nothing marketed as an 'AI provenance agent' in 2026 does more than wrap c2patool plus a verify API call. Treat any L3 claim here as false: no autonomous system can decide your disclosure posture, because the exemption you are relying on is defined by a human having decided it.
- **existing precedent in this vault**: content/_raw/research-workspaces/marketing-agent-research/report.md item F3 ('PR jako bramka + draft w Publerze + podpisywanie C2PA') already scopes C2PA signing as a pull-request gate — the same shape, one step further (sign, not just verify).

**prompt patterns**

- **note**: This entry is 80% tooling and 20% prompting. The prompts that matter are contradiction-detection and disclosure-drafting, not generation.
- **patterns**:
  - **name**: Manifest-vs-caption contradiction check | **shape**: Here is the c2patool JSON for each asset in this post: <json>. Here is the caption: <text>. For each asset, answer: (a) what does the manifest assert about how it was made; (b) does the caption state or imply something incompatible with that assertion; (c) if yes, quote the exact caption clause that conflicts. Answer NO CONTRADICTION or list them. Do not soften. | **why**: Turns the audit into a single deterministic-ish call with quotable output. The 'quote the exact clause' instruction is what stops the model from producing a vague 'seems fine'.
  - **name**: Specific-disclosure drafting | **shape**: Write a one-line disclosure for this post. Constraints: name the specific tool and the specific step it performed; state what I did myself; maximum 15 words; no hedging, no 'AI-assisted' as a standalone phrase. Inputs: <manifest assertions>, <my actual workflow>. | **why**: Generic disclosure ('made with AI') reads as either boilerplate or confession. A specific one reads as craft description and tends not to depress engagement the way a vague one does. Unmeasured but low-risk.
  - **name**: Art. 50 applicability triage | **shape**: Given this post: (1) Is it published to inform the public on a matter of public interest (politics, justice, health, environment, migration, consumer safety)? (2) Does it contain a deepfake — realistic synthetic image/audio/video of a real person, place or event? (3) Was the text substantively reviewed by a named human who can approve, alter or reject it? Return a 3-line verdict plus the resulting obligation. | **why**: The three questions ARE the statute. Most marketing posts answer no/no/yes and carry no Art. 50 labeling duty. Making that an explicit triage stops both over-disclosure and the assumption that nothing applies.
  - **name**: Round-trip test log | **shape**: I uploaded <asset> with a signed manifest to <platform> as <format>. I then downloaded it via <path>. c2patool on the downloaded file returns: <output>. Record this as a test result with date, platform, format, upload path, download path, verdict (PRESERVED / STRIPPED / RE-SIGNED / PARTIAL). Then state what this implies for the other formats on the same platform, and mark that implication as inference not evidence. | **why**: The per-platform preservation table is the fastest-rotting fact in this entry. The only way to own a true one is to keep a dated log of your own round trips, and the separation of 'tested' from 'inferred' is what keeps the log honest.

**tool examples**

- **verification and signing**:
  - c2patool (Content Authenticity Initiative, open source) — read/validate/sign manifests from the CLI; the only tool in this list you should put in CI.
  - Content Credentials Verify — https://contentcredentials.org/verify — browser drop-target for a one-off human check.
  - exiftool — to see what metadata actually survived a round trip, including the non-C2PA layers (IPTC, XMP, EXIF) that platforms strip for different reasons.
- **signing at source**:
  - Adobe Firefly / Photoshop / Lightroom — Content Credentials on by default for generated content.
  - Google Gemini app and web, Imagen, Veo — SynthID watermark across text, image, audio and video per DeepMind's own description; SynthID Detector portal in limited/tester access as of the last public description.
  - OpenAI image generation — C2PA metadata attached to generated images.
  - Truepic — capture-time signing (the provenance-first vendor; also a C2PA steering committee member).
  - Digimarc — watermarking half of the durable-credentials demonstration with Adobe (2025-06-02).
- **platform read side**:
  - TikTok — first video platform to implement Content Credentials (announced 2024-05-09); auto-labels AIGC, reads incoming credentials, and stated credentials it attaches remain on downloaded content. C2PA steering committee member as of 2026-09-11.
  - Meta (Facebook / Instagram / Threads) — 'AI Info' label, fired by industry-standard embedded indicators or by voluntary creator disclosure; prominent for fully AI-generated, moved into the post menu for merely AI-edited.
  - YouTube — SynthID detection plus expanding C2PA checks, mandatory altered/synthetic disclosure for realistic media (per vault note, section 3).
  - X — voluntary 'Made with AI' label plus an automatic 'Manipulated Media' tag (Jan 2026); leans on its own classifiers because it does not guarantee C2PA passthrough (per vault note, section 4).
  - Cloudflare — first major CDN to preserve Content Credentials across its network (2025-02-03); relevant if you self-host assets behind it.
- **infrastructure you will want**: A private asset store holding the ORIGINAL signed files, because once a platform strips a manifest the only recoverable copy is yours. Object storage plus a manifest sidecar is sufficient; no product needed.
