#### fit

**scales with**

- **caps**:
  - ASSET VOLUME, not account size. This entry costs you nothing until you publish images; it costs you proportionally once you do. A text-first creator at any follower count has near-zero exposure.
  - PIPELINE COMPLEXITY. One tool making one image is auditable. A five-tool chain (generate → upscale → composite → export → platform-resize) breaks the manifest somewhere in the middle and you will not know where without testing each hop.
  - TEAM SIZE, inverted. A solo creator can hold the whole provenance story in their head. The moment a second person or a scheduling tool touches the assets, the chain needs to be a written gate, because 'I know what I made' stops being true.
  - REGULATORY SURFACE, by topic not by size. Art. 50's text obligation triggers on matters of PUBLIC INTEREST (politics, justice, health, environment, migration, consumer safety). A creator posting on health or AI policy carries an obligation that a creator posting on B2B SaaS pricing does not — at identical follower counts.
- **the objective asymmetry that matters here**: Sub-500-follower accounts are cited by AI engines comparably to large ones (Semrush) but do not go viral comparably. Provenance exposure follows the VIRALITY curve, not the citability curve: a label on a post seen by 300 people is a non-event; the same label on a post that breaks out is the thing the quote-tweets are about. So the risk is concentrated precisely in the outcomes you are optimizing for, and it is asymmetric in the bad direction.
- **does not scale with**: Budget. Nothing here gets better by spending more. The expensive commercial provenance products solve institutional verification problems (newsroom ingest, insurance claims), not creator problems.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- **silent strip**: You publish a signed asset; the platform strips the manifest; you believe you have a verifiable chain and you have a JPEG. Detected only by a download-and-check round trip, which nobody does.
- **false positive label**: The label fires on an asset that was only lightly AI-edited (a generative fill, an upscale), your caption says nothing about AI, and readers infer the whole thing was synthetic. Meta's 2024 'Made with AI' backlash was exactly this failure at platform scale, and their fix — demoting the edited-content label into the overflow menu — was an admission of it. You cannot appeal a label into the shape you wanted.
- **false negative complacency**: No label appears, so you assume no one can tell. Platform slop classifiers operate on text and behaviour, entirely outside the provenance layer. The absence of a C2PA label says nothing about whether LinkedIn's classifier has read your post as machine-written.
- **caption manifest drift**: You write the caption days after making the asset and misremember your own workflow. The manifest does not misremember. This is the most common realistic failure for an honest creator.
- **over disclosure**: Disclosing on every post, including ones where AI touched nothing material, trains the audience to discount the disclosure and makes the genuinely AI-heavy posts indistinguishable. Disclosure inflation destroys the signal it was meant to carry.
- **the pdf carousel blind spot**: You build a provenance discipline for images and video, then publish your highest-reach format — the LinkedIn document carousel — through a server-side PDF-to-slides conversion that was never tested. Most likely place for the chain to break unnoticed.
- **tooling drift**: c2patool validates against a spec version. A manifest written by a tool on an older spec can read as invalid rather than as absent, which looks worse than no manifest at all.

**ai slop risk**

- **risk level**: Low for the entry itself — provenance work produces no content. High for what it is DOWNSTREAM of.
- **the real relationship**: An AI label is a symptom; slop is the disease. Platforms did not build slop classifiers because content carried manifests — they built them because mass-produced, templated, low-variation content degraded the feed. YouTube's Inauthentic Content Policy names exactly that: mass-produced, templated, repetitive, low-variation. The provenance layer catches a narrow, honest slice of AI use (a generated illustration) while missing the thing that actually gets punished (a hundred near-identical posts).
- **the specific tell this entry creates**: Boilerplate disclosure. 'This post was created with the help of AI' appended to every post is itself an AI-slop tell — it is the sentence a compliance-anxious LLM writes when asked to add a disclosure, and readers have learned to read it as 'nobody was home for this one'. The non-slop version names the tool, the step and what the human did: 'chart generated from my own 2026 booking data, written by me, cleaned up with Claude.'
- **second tell**: AI-generated header images on B2B text posts. The single most reliable visual marker of an automated content pipeline in 2026, immediately legible to the exact professional audience being courted, and it converts a text post (zero provenance exposure, high citability) into a labeled one (label exposure, no citability gain). It is a pure cost.

**human input required**

- **the non substitutable contribution**: A truthful, specific account of what you actually did — which no system can reconstruct, because the manifest records what the TOOL did, not what the person did around it. The manifest says 'generated by model X'. Only you can say 'from my own client data, after three failed versions, and I rewrote the conclusion because the model's was wrong.'
- **the editorial decision that carries legal weight**: Under Art. 50(4), AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest is EXEMPT from the labeling duty where it has undergone human review or editorial control — and the Commission's FAQ is explicit that this means substantive examination by a knowledgeable person and a responsible entity with authority to approve, alter or reject; superficial checks such as spell-checking do not count. The human contribution is therefore not decorative: it is the legal basis of the exemption you are relying on. A reviewer who cannot explain why a claim in the post is true has not performed the review.
- **the checkable gate**: For every post: name the human who can approve, alter or reject it, and record one specific thing that human changed or verified. If the answer is 'nothing, it was fine', the review did not happen.
- **what platform classifiers are probing for**: Exactly this. Not vocabulary — specificity. A proprietary number, a named client, a date, a failure, a judgement call with a stated reason. Those are cheap for a human with real experience and expensive for a model with none, which is why they are the discriminating feature.

**detectability and disclosure**

- **the asymmetry stated precisely**: AI-assisted TEXT that a human has edited is, for practical purposes, not reliably machine-detectable — and this is a theoretical result, not a tooling gap. AI-generated IMAGERY from a mainstream instrumented tool is both watermarked (SynthID, for Google models) and provenance-signed (C2PA), and is auto-labeled by Meta and TikTok without your involvement. Same post, two completely different detection regimes.
- **text side detail**: Sadasivan et al. (TMLR) prove detector AUROC is bounded by the total-variation distance between the human and AI text distributions — as models get better at imitating human text, that distance shrinks and every detector converges toward chance. They further show recursive paraphrasing defeats watermarking, neural-classifier, zero-shot and retrieval-based detection alike on 300-token passages, and that watermarks can be SPOOFED, exposing model developers to false accusations against human text. The practical consequence for a creator: a human editing pass over an LLM draft removes whatever statistical signal existed, and the remaining detection is behavioural (cadence, templating, cross-account duplication), not textual.
- **text side caveat do not overstate**: 'Undetectable' is wrong. Platform classifiers are not text-only detectors — they see posting cadence, near-duplicate embeddings across accounts, engagement-pattern anomalies and account history. LinkedIn's reported ~97% accuracy on engagement-pod detection is the shape of what a graph-aware classifier can do. Text that is genuinely specific and genuinely yours survives; text that is generic AND mass-produced gets caught by the behavioural half regardless of how clean the prose is.
- **image side detail**: Two independent marks. (1) C2PA manifest — cryptographic, removable, tamper-evident. (2) SynthID — invisible watermark across text, image, audio and video for Google-generated content, surviving cropping, compression and speed changes; detection via the SynthID Detector portal. Removing (1) does not remove (2). Meta's label fires on either an embedded indicator or your own voluntary disclosure. So for a Gemini- or Firefly-generated image, auto-labeling on Meta and TikTok should be your DEFAULT assumption, not your risk case.
- **what disclosure this triggers for you**:
  - PLATFORM: the label appears whether or not you disclose; disclosing first costs nothing and removes the mismatch risk. On YouTube and TikTok, disclosure of realistic synthetic media is a policy DUTY, not a courtesy.
  - LEGAL (EU, deployer): a deepfake — realistic synthetic image/audio/video of a real person, place or event — must be disclosed to the viewer at first exposure, in a clear and distinguishable, perceivable way. The Commission FAQ is explicit that a machine-readable mark alone does NOT satisfy this: you need a visible or audible label.
  - LEGAL (EU, text): AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be labeled UNLESS it underwent human review with editorial responsibility. Ordinary B2B marketing content is largely outside this — the obligation attaches to public-interest subject matter, not to commercial text as such.
- **the operational rule**: Disclose per ASSET, not per post, and name the step. 'Header image: Gemini. Text: mine, drafted with Claude and rewritten.' This survives an auto-label appearing later, satisfies the deployer duty where it applies, and reads as craft rather than confession.
- **what not to do**: Do not strip manifests. It is mechanically easy, it does not remove SynthID, it does not extinguish the Art. 50 deployer duty, and if discovered it reframes an ordinary tool-use disclosure as a deliberate concealment — a category change in how the audience reads everything else you publish.

**policy and legal**

- **jurisdiction assumed**: Poland / EU. Art. 50 is directly applicable; no national transposition needed for these obligations.
- **eu ai act article 50**:
  - **applies from**: 2026-08-02, with a limited grace period to 2026-12-02 for marking obligations on systems placed on the market before August. No retroactive labeling of content produced before that date.
  - **provider duty**: Providers of generative systems must mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable format, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible. Exemptions for assistive/basic editing functions that do not substantially alter the input or its meaning. This is the duty that lands on OpenAI, Google and Adobe — not on you.
  - **deployer duty deepfakes**: If you deploy an AI system to generate or manipulate image, audio or video constituting a deepfake, you must disclose it. Clear, distinguishable, perceivable, at first exposure. Artistic/satirical/fictional works need only appropriate disclosure that does not hamper enjoyment.
  - **deployer duty text**: AI-generated or manipulated text PUBLISHED TO INFORM THE PUBLIC ON MATTERS OF PUBLIC INTEREST must be labeled — unless it underwent human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person holding editorial responsibility. The Commission FAQ defines human review as substantive examination by a knowledgeable person and editorial control as authority to approve, alter or reject; spell-checking does not qualify.
  - **who counts as a deployer**: Natural persons using AI personally and non-professionally are EXCLUDED. But the FAQ states that where the activity generates economic benefit on a regular basis, or is business/freelance work, the person is a deployer. A consultant posting to generate leads is a deployer. This is the sentence that catches most creators who assume the Act is about big labs.
  - **penalties**: Up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of total worldwide turnover for the preceding financial year, with proportionality for SMEs and small mid-caps — for SMEs it is the LOWER of the two figures, a detail frequently reported backwards.
  - **code of practice**: The European AI Office released a Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content (2026-06-10). It sets out approved marking techniques and offers signatories legal certainty. It is the operative document for WHICH technical marking counts — watch it rather than the Article text for the technique list.
- **platform terms**:
  - **youtube**: Mandatory disclosure for realistic altered/synthetic content; Inauthentic Content Policy enforces channel-level against mass-produced/templated content; enforcement is monetization-linked.
  - **tiktok**: AI-content labels required; branded/AI ad-disclosure enforcement tightened in 2026; undisclosed AI promo risks strikes.
  - **meta**: AI Info labeling; content stays up unless it violates other Community Standards.
  - **x**: Voluntary 'Made with AI' label; automatic 'Manipulated Media' tag; unlabeled synthetic media may be treated as a violation.
  - **linkedin**: No published C2PA regime found. The operative LinkedIn rule for a text-first creator is the authenticity/inauthentic-behaviour policy and the 2026 reach suppression of AI-classified content, not a labeling duty.
- **other jurisdictions worth knowing**: California SB 942 (AI transparency, effective Jan 2026) and the US state disclosure patchwork matter if your audience or entity touches the US. FTC rules on endorsements and deceptive advertising apply independently of the AI question and are the more likely enforcement route for a marketing post.
- **the practical legal position for this use case**: A Poland-based consultant writing B2B LinkedIn posts with LLM assistance, reviewed and rewritten by themselves, publishing on non-public-interest commercial topics, with no synthetic media of real people: no Art. 50 labeling duty attaches. The duty attaches the moment you (a) post a realistic synthetic image/video of a real person, place or event, or (b) write on health, politics, justice, environment or consumer safety without substantive human review. Those two lines are the whole compliance question.

**reversibility and blast radius**

- **best case failure**: An unexpected AI label appears on a post. Reversible in practice: acknowledge it in the comments within the hour, name what the tool did. Cost is one awkward thread.
- **middle case**: A caption-manifest contradiction is spotted publicly. Not reversible by editing — the screenshot precedes the edit. Cost is a credibility hit scoped to that post plus whatever the quote-posts do. Recovery is a post that explains the actual workflow, which usually performs well.
- **worst case platform**: A strike for undisclosed synthetic media on YouTube or TikTok. Strikes compound; on YouTube the enforcement is channel-level and monetization-linked, and the 2026 wave removed channels outright. This is the only path in this entry that ends with losing an account.
- **worst case legal**: An Art. 50 enforcement action. Very low probability for an individual creator — enforcement capacity is going to providers and large deployers first — but the exposure is defined by SUBJECT MATTER, not size, so a health or policy creator carries real risk that a SaaS creator does not.
- **worst case reputational**: Being shown to have stripped provenance metadata. This is the asymmetric one: the act itself is minor, but it is unambiguous evidence of intent, and it retroactively recolours every prior disclosure. Unrecoverable in a professional niche where trust is the product.
- **blast radius summary**: Small and local for labeling accidents. Account-ending only on YouTube/TikTok for undisclosed realistic synthetic media. Career-shaped only for deliberate concealment. The distribution of outcomes is heavily skewed by intent, which is why the discipline is 'never strip' rather than 'always disclose'.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **step 0 scope**: Decide which of your formats carry assets at all. For a text-first B2B creator the honest answer is often 'only the carousel', which reduces this entire entry to one test and one habit.
- **step 1 build the round trip test harness**:
  - Install c2patool. Prepare three test assets with known-good manifests: (a) a PNG exported from Photoshop/Firefly with Content Credentials on, (b) a JPEG generated by Gemini or an OpenAI image model, (c) a short MP4 from an instrumented tool.
  - Record the baseline: `c2patool <file>` for each; save the JSON. This is your control.
  - For each platform and each ingest path, upload, publish (to a connections-only or unlisted audience where possible), then download by every route a real viewer would use: browser right-click save, mobile app save, and — for LinkedIn documents — the viewer's download button.
  - Run c2patool on each downloaded artifact. Record PRESERVED / STRIPPED / RE-SIGNED / PARTIAL with the date, platform, format and both paths.
  - Log results in an append-only file. Re-run quarterly. Nothing else in this entry produces a fact you can rely on.
- **step 2 the linkedin pdf document test specifically**:
  - This is the test the brief asks for and the one with no published answer. Protocol, precisely:
  - (a) Build a 5-page carousel in your normal tool. Export to PDF. Before upload, embed or confirm a manifest — either by exporting pages from an app that signs, or by signing the PDF's page images with c2patool and reassembling. Record the baseline manifest JSON.
  - (b) Upload as a LinkedIn DOCUMENT post (not as images). Publish to a restricted audience.
  - (c) Download via the document viewer's own download control. Run c2patool on the returned PDF. Record.
  - (d) Separately, screenshot/extract one rendered slide from the in-feed viewer and run c2patool on it. Record.
  - (e) Repeat the same content as five individual IMAGES in a multi-image post, and as a single image. Three ingest paths, one comparison table.
  - EXPECTED RESULT, stated in advance so the test can falsify it: STRIPPED on the document path. LinkedIn's document viewer re-renders pages server-side into a paged image format; server-side re-rendering is precisely the operation CAI names as destroying embedded metadata. Predicted PARTIAL-to-STRIPPED on the multi-image path. This prediction is currently UNTESTED — do not cite it as a finding until the log has a dated row.
  - (f) Whatever the result, it changes nothing about what you publish. It changes only whether you can claim a verifiable chain. Run it once, write it down, stop thinking about it.
- **step 3 the publication gate**:
  - Add a pre-publish check with three questions. (1) Does any asset in this post carry a manifest asserting AI generation? (2) Does the caption state or imply anything incompatible with that assertion? (3) Is this post public-interest subject matter, or does it contain a realistic synthetic depiction of a real person, place or event?
  - Question (1) is c2patool. Question (2) is the contradiction-check prompt. Question (3) is the Art. 50 triage prompt. Total runtime: under a minute.
  - Fail-closed on (2). Fail-to-human on (3).
- **step 4 the disclosure habit**:
  - Write disclosure per asset, naming tool and step. Put it in the post body for image-bearing posts, not in the first comment — a disclosure in the first comment is invisible to anyone who reads the label in the overflow menu first, which inverts the entire point.
  - Do not disclose on text-only posts you wrote and edited. Over-disclosure destroys the signal.
  - Keep the wording specific and unapologetic. 'Chart built from my own booking data; visual generated with Gemini' is a craft note. 'Created with the help of AI' is an apology and an AI-slop tell.
- **step 5 archive the originals**: Keep the signed originals in your own storage, organised by post. Once a platform strips a manifest, your copy is the only remaining proof, and the one occasion you will need it — a challenge to the authenticity of something you genuinely made — is unforecastable.
- **step 6 prefer the format that sidesteps all of this**: Text-first posting with real screenshots of your own work has zero auto-label exposure and the highest AI-citation value. The cheapest provenance strategy is usually a format choice, not a tooling choice.

**checklist**

- **gate type**: Pass/fail before publishing. Any FAIL blocks.
- **items**:
  - [ ] Every image/video/document asset in this post has been run through c2patool and the result recorded. (FAIL if unchecked.)
  - [ ] No caption clause contradicts any manifest assertion. (FAIL on any contradiction — rewrite the caption, do not strip the manifest.)
  - [ ] No manifest was removed, edited or suppressed at any point in this post's production. (FAIL is terminal; this is the one non-negotiable line.)
  - [ ] If any asset is a realistic synthetic depiction of a real person, place or event: a visible, perceivable disclosure is present in the post body itself, not in a comment. (FAIL otherwise — this is the Art. 50 deployer duty and a machine-readable mark does not satisfy it.)
  - [ ] If the post is on a matter of public interest (politics, justice, health, environment, migration, consumer safety) AND the text is AI-generated: either a label is present, or a named human performed substantive review with authority to alter or reject, and that person is recorded. (FAIL if neither.)
  - [ ] The disclosure, if present, names the specific tool and the specific step. (FAIL on 'created with the help of AI'.)
  - [ ] The disclosure is absent on text-only posts I wrote and edited myself. (FAIL on reflexive disclosure — it is inflation.)
  - [ ] Signed originals are archived outside the platform. (FAIL if the only copy is the uploaded one.)
  - [ ] The round-trip preservation log for this platform+format has a row dated within the last 90 days. (WARN, not FAIL — but a stale log means you do not actually know what happens.)

**cost and time to execute**

- **setup one time**: 3-5 hours. c2patool install and baseline (30 min); the round-trip test harness across your two or three real platforms and formats (2-3 h, most of it waiting on uploads and downloads); the LinkedIn PDF document test specifically (45 min); writing the gate into whatever your publish routine is (30 min).
- **per post**: Under 2 minutes for an image-bearing post — one CLI run, one contradiction check, one disclosure line. ZERO for a text-only post, which is the majority of B2B output. This is among the cheapest gates in the whole table.
- **per quarter**: 60-90 minutes to re-run the round-trip tests and update the log. Non-negotiable if you intend to make claims about preservation.
- **tool subscriptions**: EUR 0. c2patool is open source; Verify is free; exiftool is free. Nothing in the recommended path requires a paid service.
- **hidden cost**: The real cost is FORMAT DISCIPLINE, not tooling: giving up generative header images and rendering charts from actual data takes ten to thirty minutes more per visual than prompting one. That time buys a better chart and removes the label exposure, so it is not really a cost — but it is the part people resist.
- **comparison anchor**: Against a 4-hour original-data post, this gate is rounding error (2 min). Against a 10-minute repurpose, it is 20% overhead on image-bearing posts and 0% on text ones — which is another reason the repurposing pipeline should default to text.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **primary kpi**: Number of posts published with an UNEXPECTED AI label. Target: zero. This is the only metric that directly measures whether the gate works.
- **secondary**:
  - Preservation-log coverage: platforms × formats tested within the last 90 days. Target: 100% of formats you actually publish.
  - Contradiction-check failure rate at the gate. A rate that is non-zero but low means the gate is catching real drift. Zero forever means nobody is running it.
  - Comment-section provenance challenges per month ('is this AI?'). A lagging trust indicator — and the cheapest early warning that your visual style has drifted into the generic.
- **leading indicators**:
  - The FORMAT MIX is the true leading indicator: share of posts carrying generatively-created imagery. It moves weeks before any label problem appears, and you control it directly.
  - Platform policy-page diffs. Set a change-watcher on the AI-content help pages for your two or three platforms; a policy change precedes an enforcement wave by weeks.
  - The Code of Practice signatory list and technique annex — the leading indicator for the whole EU marking regime.
  - Whether your generation tools have started signing by default. A tool that silently turns on Content Credentials changes your exposure with no action on your part; the first sign is a manifest appearing in the gate output where there was none last month.
- **what not to track**: Reach deltas attributed to labels. You cannot isolate the label's effect from everything else moving in the same post, and there is no published effect size to compare against. Tracking it will manufacture a false causal story.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- as of date and volatility
- audience fit
- conflicting evidence
- decay and saturation
- effect size and n
- evidence strength

### The AI disclosure paradox

`ai-disclosure-penalty-paradox` · automation L0 · evidence STRONG · 9 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: The AI disclosure paradox. Category: science. Definition: telling your audience you used AI reliably costs you trust, perceived authenticity, competence and likability — even when the disclosure is voluntary, honest and the work is good — which means disclosure is a PERSUASION VARIABLE with a measurable price, not merely a compliance checkbox. The paradox is that transparency, which is supposed to build trust, measurably reduces it. Maturity: ESTABLISHED as a finding and unusually well-evidenced for something this new — thirteen preregistered-style experiments in a top organisational-behaviour journal (2025), eight preregistered experiments plus platform field data in a top consumer-research journal (2026), and a growing replication and mechanism literature through 2026. The second-order finding, which is the actionable one: the penalty is mediated by PERCEIVED EFFORT and legitimacy, not by AI aversion — so a disclosure that reveals effort can be neutral or even positive, while a disclosure that reveals a shortcut is maximally damaging.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. Three clocks, and unusually for this research the core finding sits on the slowest one. (1) STABLE, multi-year: the psychology. Schilke and Reimann's trust penalty (Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 2025, 13 experiments, 177 citations by September 2026) and the Carney, Riveros and Tully effort/parasocial mechanism (Journal of Consumer Research 2026, 8 preregistered experiments plus TikTok field data) are the kind of findings that get refined rather than reversed. Treat the DIRECTION as durable. (2) 12-24 MONTHS AND GENUINELY UNCERTAIN: the MAGNITUDE, because the penalty is by construction a function of how unusual AI use appears. Schilke and Reimann locate the mechanism in LEGITIMACY — a departure from a human-centric norm — and norms move. As AI assistance becomes universal (40.5% of LinkedIn long-form posts were fully machine-written by mid-2026), the typicality component of legitimacy should erode, which predicts the penalty shrinking or inverting for some audiences within a couple of years. Nobody has measured that drift yet; it is the single most important thing to re-check. (3) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER: the legal and platform layer. EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations became applicable 2026-08-02; TikTok and Meta auto-label synthetic media via C2PA (TikTok joined the C2PA steering committee 2026-07-27); LinkedIn added a reader-facing 'seems like AI slop' report button 2026-07-30 while continuing to permit AI assistance. None of these currently mandates disclosure for AI-assisted text by an individual creator, but the direction of travel means today's voluntary choice may become tomorrow's default label — which changes the calculation entirely, because an imposed label carries no effort signal.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

THE CORE EFFECT. Across thirteen experiments spanning task types (communication, analytical, creative) and roles (supervisors, subordinates, professors, analysts, creatives, investment fund managers), actors who disclosed using AI were trusted LESS than those who did not (Schilke and Reimann 2025). The effect held whether AI use was voluntary or mandated, and — importantly for anyone hoping to prompt their way out of it — it PERSISTED ACROSS DIFFERENT DISCLOSURE FRAMINGS. An internal meta-analysis found it attenuated, but not eliminated, among evaluators with favourable attitudes toward technology and where AI accuracy was high. THE MECHANISM, first pass: LEGITIMACY. Drawing on micro-institutional theory, the authors argue disclosure signals a departure from a taken-for-granted human-centric norm, and it is the resulting legitimacy deficit — not a judgement about quality — that produces the trust loss. Their 2026 follow-up in Social Psychology Quarterly decomposes legitimacy into three sequential pathways: perceived TYPICALITY (is this how things are normally done), COMMITMENT (did you invest yourself), and AUTHENTICITY (is this really you), each mediating the drop. THE MECHANISM, second pass and the one that makes this actionable for social media: EFFORT. Carney, Riveros and Tully (Journal of Consumer Research 2026) studied TikTok engagement after the platform's AI-disclosure policy took effect, plus eight preregistered experiments, and found disclosures reduce engagement through reduced PARASOCIAL CONNECTION — the one-sided bond between viewer and creator — mediated by PERCEIVED CREATOR EFFORT. They explicitly ruled out three intuitive explanations: it is not concern about content quality, not AI skepticism, and not general AI aversion. The audience is not punishing machine involvement; it is punishing the inference that you did not bother. THE MITIGATION FALLS OUT OF THE MECHANISM, and this is the finding that converts the paradox from a trap into a lever: the same paper reports that GREATER-EFFORT DISCLOSURES can mitigate the engagement reduction. If effort is the mediator, then a disclosure that makes effort VISIBLE — what you did, what you checked, what you decided, what you rejected — restores the signal the bare label destroyed. Independent support from a different domain: Waddell (Mass Communication and Society 2026, N=675, US, between-subjects) found that a rich 'how and why' AI ethics disclosure policy, written to Poynter best-practice, significantly INCREASED perceived transparency, supervision, ethicality, helpfulness and trustworthiness of AI-assisted news, and raised willingness to subscribe, relative to no disclosure. Note the scope difference carefully — that is an ORGANISATIONAL POLICY explaining process, not a per-item 'made with AI' label. WHY THE TWO FAMILIES OF RESULT ARE COMPATIBLE: a bare label communicates only the fact of AI involvement, which reads as reduced effort and atypical practice; a process disclosure communicates the human labour around the AI, which reads as more effort and editorial responsibility. The variable that moves is not honesty, it is what the disclosure lets the reader infer about you.

**ranking signal targeted**

No algorithmic ranking signal is directly targeted — no platform has stated that disclosing AI assistance in text changes distribution, and LinkedIn explicitly permits AI assistance. The signals this moves are AUDIENCE-SIDE and then feed ranking second-hand, in this order of sensitivity: PARASOCIAL CONNECTION (not measurable, but the proximate cause), then the effortful engagement acts it licenses — COMMENTS, SHARES, SAVES and DM SENDS — then dwell time, then passive likes and impressions, which barely move. That ordering is the practically useful part: if a disclosure costs you something, it shows up in comments per impression long before it shows up in reach. TWO IMPORTANT EXCEPTIONS where disclosure DOES touch the algorithm. First, on platforms with mandatory synthetic-media labelling (TikTok, Meta via C2PA), an AI-generated IMAGE or VIDEO gets an automatic platform label regardless of your choice, and the JCR 2026 field data is precisely about engagement under that regime — so for visual content the label is a distribution-adjacent fact, not a voluntary one. Second, on LinkedIn since 2026-07-30, readers who conclude you used AI can tap 'seems like AI slop', and those reports feed the classifier — which means concealment has its own algorithmic downside if the concealment fails. 'Unknown' is the honest answer for whether any ranker reads a disclosure string itself; there is no evidence either way.

**why it drives reach**

This item mostly explains reach LOST, and the causal chain is unusually well-identified for social-media research because the mediator was measured rather than assumed. Chain: a disclosure (or a reader's inference of AI use) lowers perceived creator effort; lower perceived effort weakens the parasocial bond; a weakened bond suppresses the effortful engagement acts — commenting, sharing, saving, sending — because those are social acts directed at a person and they are only worth performing if there is a person there; suppressed effortful engagement lowers the quality signals that drive out-of-network distribution; distribution falls. Separately and in parallel, disclosure lowers perceived legitimacy and therefore trust, which affects conversion rather than reach — fewer DMs, fewer meetings, less willingness to hire — and that cost is invisible in every dashboard. THE INVERTED CHAIN IS THE OPPORTUNITY: if effort is the mediator, then the same disclosure act, written to reveal process rather than to confess shortcut, RAISES perceived effort above the no-disclosure baseline. You are not choosing between honesty and performance; you are choosing what your honesty lets the reader infer. The strongest version of this in practice is a disclosure that is indistinguishable from proof of work — 'I pulled 41 pull requests from our repo, had Claude compute the review-comment ratio, checked the outliers by hand, and here is what I found' both discloses and demonstrates. Caveat on strength of evidence: the effort-mitigation result is reported at abstract level in a top journal; I did not read the per-experiment magnitudes, so the DIRECTION of the mitigation is well-sourced and its SIZE is not.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

Two distinct roles, and confusing them is what produces bad disclosure practice. (1) THE ROLE BEING DISCLOSED — the thing your statement is about. Accuracy here is the whole point: 'I used Claude to restructure my own draft' and 'I asked ChatGPT to write a post about leadership' describe wildly different effort profiles, and the research says the audience is reading exactly that difference. A disclosure that is vaguer than the truth reads as worse than the truth, because readers default to assuming FULL automation when told 'AI-generated' (Altay and Gilardi, PNAS Nexus 2024, found people discount AI-labelled headlines even when true or human-made, precisely because they assume complete automation). Specificity is therefore not pedantry, it is damage control. (2) THE ROLE OF THE MODEL IN MANAGING DISCLOSURE — narrow and mostly editorial. A model can draft alternative disclosure phrasings for you to choose between, can check that a claimed process description matches what you actually did (given your own log), and can flag where a post's claims exceed what your disclosure covers. What it must NOT do: write the disclosure unsupervised, since a fabricated process description is straightforwardly a lie about your own labour and is the one failure in this item with real reputational and, in commercial contexts, legal exposure. Note the reflexive trap worth naming: asking a model to write your AI-disclosure is the most on-the-nose version of the thing the disclosure is about.

**automation level**

L0 for the disclosure decision itself, and that is not negotiable — deciding what to tell your audience about your own labour is a judgement call about your own conduct and cannot be delegated. L1 is appropriate for the WORDING (generate three phrasings, pick one, edit it). L2 and above are actively dangerous here: a system that auto-appends a standing 'created with AI assistance' line to every post produces exactly the bare, effort-free label the research shows is maximally costly, applied indiscriminately to posts where it is true and posts where it is barely true. If you want a standing disclosure, put it in your profile or a footer where it is a stable statement of practice rather than a per-post signal, and make it a process description rather than a label. Relevant taxonomy note for this whole research: the disclosure question changes shape by automation level. At L0 there is nothing to disclose. At L1 (AI-assisted draft, human substance, human edit) the EU AI Act human-review carve-out normally applies and no platform requires anything, so disclosure is purely strategic. At L2/L3 the honest disclosure becomes materially harder to write without revealing low effort — which is itself a useful signal that you are operating above the level your audience will forgive.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

STRONG by the standards of this entire research area, and notably stronger than anything in the platform-mechanics items — which is worth saying explicitly, because the best-evidenced finding in this workspace is a psychological one, not an algorithmic one. STRONG / PEER-REVIEWED: that disclosing AI use reduces trust (Schilke and Reimann, OBHDP 2025 — 13 experiments across task types and roles, 177 citations, effect robust across framings and across voluntary vs mandated use). STRONG / PEER-REVIEWED: that AI disclosure reduces social-media engagement, and that the mechanism is reduced parasocial connection mediated by perceived creator effort rather than quality concerns or AI aversion (Carney, Riveros and Tully, Journal of Consumer Research 2026 — 8 preregistered experiments plus TikTok field data). MODERATE / PEER-REVIEWED: the legitimacy decomposition into typicality, commitment and authenticity (Schilke and Reimann, Social Psychology Quarterly 2026 — content analysis plus vignette experiment plus replication). MODERATE: that rich process-level disclosure mitigates or reverses the penalty — supported from two independent directions (the effort-mitigation result in JCR 2026, and Waddell's N=675 news experiment in Mass Communication and Society 2026 showing a 'how and why' policy RAISED trustworthiness), but the two operate at different levels (per-item label vs organisational policy) and no study located tests the effort-visible per-post disclosure format directly on social media. MODERATE-TO-WEAK: that AI literacy moderates the effect — a plausible and frequently asserted claim with thin located sourcing (one 2026 paper in a low-profile venue whose abstract I did not read). ANECDOTAL: everything about what specific wording works best.

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

LINKEDIN: highest stakes for the TRUST half of the penalty, because the audience is evaluating you professionally and the trust loss converts directly into fewer inbound conversations. No disclosure is required for AI-assisted text and the platform explicitly permits assistance, so this is a pure strategy decision — and the effort-visible format fits LinkedIn unusually well, because the platform's own stated standard (posts should represent your voice and your perspectives) is satisfied by the same sentence that discloses. TIKTOK AND INSTAGRAM: the setting where the JCR engagement penalty was actually measured, and the setting where you often have no choice — synthetic media carries C2PA-driven platform labels automatically, so the question shifts from whether to disclose to whether to pre-empt the label with context. X: no disclosure regime, fast-scrolling format that punishes any added line, and the lowest return on a nuanced process statement — if you disclose here, do it in the profile, not the post. NEWSLETTER, BLOG, LONG-FORM: the best fit for rich process disclosure by a wide margin, because there is room for a real methods note and because the Waddell result (an organisational 'how and why' policy raising trustworthiness) is closest in kind to an about-page or a standing editorial-practice note. This is where the positive version of the finding lives. REDDIT: disclose or do not post. Norm enforcement is human and permanent, and the community reaction to undisclosed AI writing is categorically harsher than any algorithmic penalty. FORMAT NOTE: the cost scales with how INTERPERSONAL the writing is — a personal story, a condolence, a recommendation, a DM, a comment on someone's post are the formats where disclosed AI involvement is most damaging, because the whole value of the artefact is that a person bothered. A market analysis or a technical explainer carries far less of this exposure. Cross-reference [[Social Media Algorithms — Maximizing Reach in 2026]] for ranking mechanics rather than re-deriving them.

**scales with**

(1) RELATIONSHIP DEPTH, in both directions and this is the dominant factor: the more parasocial the bond, the more there is to lose from an effort-inference drop — and the more credit you have banked to absorb it. An established creator disclosing once, in context, with evident process, is in a very different position from an unknown account whose first signal is a label. (2) HOW MUCH OF YOUR VALUE IS 'BEING A PERSON': a creator whose product is judgement, taste or relationship carries maximal exposure; a creator whose product is information or utility carries much less, because the reader wants the answer rather than the author. (3) VERIFIABILITY OF YOUR PROCESS: the effort-visible disclosure only works if you actually have process to describe — a proprietary dataset, a client engagement, a real workflow. This is the binding constraint, and it is the same constraint as the anti-slop item: you cannot disclose effort you did not expend. (4) AUDIENCE NORM DRIFT, the slow variable: as AI assistance becomes typical, the typicality component of legitimacy weakens and the penalty should shrink — meaning the cost of disclosure is probably at its historical peak right now and declining. (5) WHAT IT DOES NOT SCALE WITH: follower count and reach. This is a per-reader inference, not an audience-size effect. (6) CEILING WORTH NAMING: there is no volume of disclosure that converts into trust. Over-disclosing — a label on every post, an AI footnote on a two-line comment — raises salience without raising perceived effort, which is the worst of both.

**decay and saturation**

The MECHANISM does not decay; the MAGNITUDE probably does, and unusually the decay is in your favour. Legitimacy has a typicality component, and typicality is a function of prevalence — at 40.5% of LinkedIn long-form public posts already fully machine-written by mid-2026, 'used AI' is on a fast path from deviant to normal, and Schilke and Reimann's own theory predicts the penalty shrinks as that happens. Expect the trust penalty to be materially smaller in 2028 than in 2026, and plan for a world where the differentiating disclosure is not 'I used AI' but 'here is what I did that a model could not'. WHAT DECAYS FAST, within about a quarter: any specific disclosure WORDING. Phrases like 'AI-assisted' acquire connotations quickly, and a formulation that reads as candid this quarter reads as boilerplate the next — boilerplate being exactly the effort-free label the research says is costly. WHAT DECAYS IN 12-24 MONTHS: the strategic calculus itself, if regulation or platforms make labelling mandatory and automatic. An imposed label carries no effort signal and no editorial credit, which would collapse the mitigation strategy in this entry — the counter-move then becomes attaching your process statement to the imposed label rather than choosing whether to have one. WHAT DOES NOT DECAY: the effort inference. Readers will still be asking whether a human bothered, in any norm regime and under any labelling rule, which is why the durable investment is a describable process rather than a good sentence.

#### risk

**failure modes**

(1) THE BARE LABEL — appending 'written with AI' and nothing else. It is the exact stimulus the research shows is costly: it supplies the fact without the effort, and readers fill the gap by assuming full automation (Altay and Gilardi). This is the most common failure and it is worse than either silence or a full process note. (2) VAGUENESS READ AS MAXIMUM: 'AI-generated' applied to a post you drafted, edited and fact-checked yourself understates your labour and is punished accordingly. Under-claiming your own work is not humility here, it is self-harm. (3) OVERCLAIMING PROCESS: describing verification you did not do. This is the one failure mode in this item with real downside — it is a lie about your own conduct, it is checkable, and in commercial material it moves from reputational to legal exposure. (4) DISCLOSURE INFLATION: labelling everything, including trivial assistance, which raises AI salience on every post without ever raising perceived effort. (5) WRONG LEVEL: putting an organisational-style policy statement in every post, or a per-item confession in a profile bio. The Waddell result is about a stable policy; the JCR penalty is about per-item labels; mixing them up wastes the mitigation. (6) CONCEALMENT THAT FAILS: staying silent on a post that visibly reads as machine-written, in a 2026 environment where readers have a report button and detectors are one paste away. The exposure is worse than the disclosure would have been, and it is unrecoverable in a way the trust penalty is not. (7) ASSUMING A LITERATE AUDIENCE IS IMMUNE: the moderators attenuate, they do not eliminate. (8) TREATING IT AS A COMPLIANCE TASK: filing the decision under legal, applying one template forever, and never noticing that the persuasion cost differs by format, platform and how interpersonal the post is.

**ai slop risk**

Moderate, and specific. THE SLOP RISK IN THE DISCLOSURE ITSELF: generated disclosure language is unmistakable and self-defeating — 'This post was crafted with the assistance of advanced AI tools to bring you the best possible insights' announces simultaneously that a model was involved and that you did not care enough to write one sentence about it yourself. Tells: passive voice, 'leveraged', 'to enhance', 'cutting-edge', no named tool, no named step, no named human decision. THE DEEPER RISK: using disclosure as a substitute for substance. A post with nothing in it does not become acceptable because it is honestly labelled; it becomes an honestly labelled empty post, and the reader's effort inference — which is what the research says drives the damage — lands in exactly the same place. Disclosure is not absolution. THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it doubles as the quality test: does the disclosure name a specific tool, a specific step, and a specific thing YOU did or decided? 'Claude computed the ratios, I checked the outliers and dropped one' passes. 'AI-assisted' does not. Note the reflexive tell worth watching for in your own workflow: if you asked a model to write your AI disclosure, you have demonstrated the exact disposition the disclosure is meant to reassure the reader about.

**human input required**

Two non-substitutable contributions, and they are different in kind. FIRST, THE DECISION: whether to disclose is a judgement about your own conduct and your own audience, and it cannot be delegated to a model, a template or a policy engine without becoming the bare label that costs the most. SECOND, AND THE ONE THE MECHANISM DEMANDS: something true to disclose about your own labour. The research is unambiguous that perceived effort is the mediator, which means the minimum viable disclosure requires a real human act to point at — a dataset you collected, a source you verified, an outlier you checked by hand, a model output you rejected and why, a judgement you made that the model argued against. If you cannot name one, the honest disclosure is a confession of low effort and the correct response is not better wording but a better post. THE CHECKABLE GATE, phrased as a rule: your disclosure must contain at least one verb whose subject is YOU and whose object is the substance. 'I pulled', 'I verified', 'I dropped', 'I decided against' — not 'AI was used to assist'. That single grammatical test operationalises the entire finding, and it also happens to be the test that distinguishes a disclosure that helps you from one that hurts you.

**detectability and disclosure**

This field is the item's own subject, so the useful content is the DECISION RULE, stated against what is detectable. WHAT IS DETECTABLE: AI-assisted TEXT has no cryptographic provenance — C2PA is signed metadata on media files and does not survive typing or pasting into a composer, and SynthID-Text covers participating Google models only. Third-party detectors are probabilistic, degrade sharply once text is edited, and carry documented false-positive bias against non-native English writers, so 'passes a detector' and 'is human' are not the same claim in either direction. What IS reliably detectable is genericness, by readers and by LinkedIn's classifier — and since 2026-07-30 readers can act on it with a 'seems like AI slop' report. AI-generated IMAGES are different: C2PA Content Credentials can trigger automatic platform labels on TikTok, Meta and elsewhere, so for visual content disclosure is frequently involuntary. THE DECISION RULE I would defend from the evidence. DISCLOSE, in effort-visible form, when: the model materially shaped the SUBSTANCE or the argument; the output is an image, video or voice that a platform may label anyway; the content is commercial or advisory and a reader's decision depends on who produced the analysis; or the post makes any claim about your own process. DO NOT DISCLOSE per-post when: the model acted as a spell-checker, formatter or thesaurus — labelling that is disclosure inflation, and it overstates AI involvement in a way readers will read as maximal. PUT IT IN THE PROFILE, not the post, when you want a standing statement of practice — that is the level at which the positive result (Waddell 2026) was observed. ALWAYS, regardless of disclosure: keep the human-input gate from the anti-slop item, because the disclosure decision only has good options when there is real work to point at.

**policy and legal**

Assuming a Poland/EU-based creator. EU AI ACT ARTICLE 50(4), applicable since 2026-08-02: deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate TEXT published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text is artificially generated. TWO CARVE-OUTS DECIDE almost every ordinary case. First, human review and editorial responsibility: the obligation does not apply where the content underwent human review or editorial control AND a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication — with Commission guidance indicating that review means a knowledgeable person deliberately examining the substance, including fact-checking, and that a spelling or grammar pass does NOT qualify. Second, the 'matters of public interest' threshold, which ordinary professional or personal-brand posting does not obviously cross. A creator who writes the brief, supplies the substance and edits materially normally sits inside both. NOTE THE ELEGANT ALIGNMENT, which is the most useful legal observation in this entry: the conduct that satisfies the AI Act carve-out (deliberate substantive human review with named editorial responsibility) is the SAME conduct that the effort-visible disclosure describes and that the trust literature says mitigates the penalty. Compliance and persuasion point at the same behaviour, so you can write one sentence that serves both. SYNTHETIC MEDIA is a different regime: Art. 50(2) and the deepfake provisions target AI-generated or manipulated image, audio and video, and an AI avatar or cloned voice triggers duties that AI-assisted text does not. PLATFORM RULES: no major platform requires labelling AI-assisted text as of 2026-09-11; LinkedIn explicitly permits AI assistance; TikTok and Meta require or auto-apply labels for synthetic media. COMMERCIAL SPEECH: if AI-assisted content promotes a product or service, Polish/EU unfair-commercial-practices law (UOKiK enforcement of the UCPD implementation) governs misleading impressions — including a false impression about who produced an analysis you are selling. US FTC endorsement rules concern material connections and do not govern drafting method, but apply if you are addressing a US audience commercially. GDPR is engaged not by drafting but by what goes INTO the prompt: client transcripts and third-party personal data need a lawful basis, which matters precisely because the anti-slop and pro-disclosure advice both push you toward using real client material.

**reversibility and blast radius**

ASYMMETRIC, and the asymmetry is the whole argument for erring toward disclosure. THE COST OF DISCLOSING is real but bounded and reversible: a trust and engagement penalty measured per-item, which decays as the post ages out of the feed, leaves no account-level mark, triggers no platform action (LinkedIn explicitly permits AI assistance), and — per the theory's own typicality mechanism — is shrinking year over year as AI use becomes normal. If a disclosure format underperforms, you change the format next week and nothing is lost but a few posts' engagement. THE COST OF BEING EXPOSED is unbounded and largely irreversible: being publicly identified as having passed off machine output as your own is a character judgement rather than a quality judgement, it is screenshot-portable, it outlives any algorithm change, and since 2026-07-30 LinkedIn readers have a one-tap, platform-sanctioned mechanism for making the accusation in public. In B2B the audience that matters is small, repeated and long-memoried. THE COST OF OVERCLAIMING PROCESS sits in between and is the sharpest trap: a disclosure that describes verification you did not perform is a checkable false statement about your own conduct, which converts a recoverable trust dip into a credibility event, and in commercial material moves from reputational into unfair-commercial-practices territory. BLAST RADIUS is capped at one identity in every case — no scenario here reaches account suspension, since disclosure is not a policy violation anywhere and AI assistance is permitted. PRACTICAL POSTURE that follows: treat the disclosure penalty as a manageable operating cost, treat exposure as the tail risk to insure against, and treat accuracy in the disclosure as non-negotiable, because it is the only one of the three that can turn a bad week into a lasting problem.

#### practice

**how to apply**

SET THE POLICY ONCE (30-45 minutes) — this is the whole job, and doing it once removes a recurring judgement. 1. Write a standing PROCESS statement for your profile or site footer, in the Waddell 'how and why' shape rather than as a label. Example structure: what you use models for, what you never use them for, what you verify before publishing, and who is responsible for errors. One short paragraph. 2. Write the PER-POST rule, and write it as a binary you can apply in five seconds: disclose in effort-visible form when the model shaped the substance or the argument, or when the artefact is synthetic media; do not disclose per-post when the model acted as a spell-checker or formatter. 3. Save both to a vault note (content/BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/INFO/AI Disclosure Policy.md) so the decision is a lookup rather than a re-derivation at publish time. PER POST (2 minutes when triggered). 4. Apply the rule. If it says disclose, use the effort-visible template: what you produced or gathered yourself, what the model did (named specifically), what you verified or rejected, what you are responsible for. 5. Apply the grammatical gate: the disclosure must contain at least one verb whose subject is you and whose object is the substance. If it does not, either rewrite it or reconsider the post. 6. Apply the inference test — read only the disclosure line and ask what effort it implies. If the implied effort is low, the disclosure is doing damage that the post does not deserve. 7. Place it where it does not cost you the opening: at the end, or in the first comment on LinkedIn, never in the hook — the first two lines are the scarcest real estate you have and should carry the substance, not the meta-commentary. 8. For synthetic imagery, assume the platform may label it anyway and write your context line in advance rather than reacting to a label you did not choose. MAINTENANCE. 9. Re-read the wording quarterly; formulations go stale into boilerplate faster than almost anything else in this research. 10. Re-check the regulatory layer at least twice a year (Art. 50 guidance is still evolving) and the platform labelling behaviour whenever you change how you produce visuals. 11. Watch the norm drift: as AI use becomes typical, revisit whether disclosure still costs anything — the honest expectation is that this entry's penalty shrinks over the next two years.

**checklist**

Pass/fail gate before publishing a disclosure — and before deciding to omit one. Any FAIL means stop. 1. I have applied my written per-post rule rather than deciding ad hoc. PASS/FAIL. 2. If disclosing: the disclosure names a specific tool and a specific step, not 'AI-assisted'. PASS/FAIL. 3. If disclosing: it contains at least one verb whose subject is me and whose object is the substance ('I pulled', 'I verified', 'I rejected'). PASS/FAIL. 4. Everything the disclosure claims about my process is true and I could evidence it. PASS/FAIL. 5. Reading ONLY the disclosure line, a stranger would infer high rather than low effort. PASS/FAIL. 6. The disclosure is not in the first two lines. PASS/FAIL. 7. If omitting: the model's role was genuinely mechanical (spelling, formatting), not substantive. PASS/FAIL. 8. If omitting: nothing in the post would look like concealment if the full process were later known. PASS/FAIL. 9. If the post contains a generated image, video or voice: I have accounted for the platform labelling it without my involvement. PASS/FAIL. 10. If the content is commercial or advisory: I have considered misleading-practice exposure, not just the AI Act. PASS/FAIL. 11. The post would still be worth publishing if the disclosure were read first. PASS/FAIL — this is the real test, because if the answer is no, the problem is the post.

**cost and time to execute**

SETUP, one-off: 30-45 minutes to write the standing process statement and the per-post rule, plus about 10 minutes to save them as a vault note. This is the entire fixed cost and it is the highest-leverage half-hour in this research area, because it converts a recurring, high-stakes judgement into a lookup. PER POST: zero for most posts (the rule says nothing is needed), and 2-4 minutes when triggered — one to two sentences plus the inference test. MAINTENANCE: about 15 minutes per quarter to re-read the wording for staleness, plus roughly 30 minutes twice a year to re-check EU Art. 50 guidance and platform labelling behaviour. TOOL COST: zero. Nothing in this item requires a subscription, a detector or a compliance product, and any vendor selling an 'AI disclosure compliance' SaaS to an individual creator is selling you a template you can write in fifteen minutes. THE REAL COST IS NOT TIME: it is the engagement and trust penalty itself, which is measured in two top journals and not quantified in any way I could extract — expect it to be non-trivial for interpersonal content on personal accounts and small for utility content, and expect it to shrink over the next two years as AI use becomes typical. THE COST OF THE MITIGATION is also not time: an effort-visible disclosure requires real effort to describe, so the honest accounting is that this item's price is paid upstream, in the anti-slop item's substance gate.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

Measuring this on your own account is genuinely hard, and pretending otherwise is how people talk themselves into conclusions. LEADING, fully under your control: (1) POLICY ADHERENCE — share of posts where the written rule was applied rather than an ad-hoc call; (2) DISCLOSURE SPECIFICITY — share of disclosures naming a tool, a step and a human act (target 100%; a bare label is a defect, not a variant); (3) the grammatical gate pass rate from human_input_required. MIDDLE, days to a week, and the metrics the mechanism predicts will move FIRST if a disclosure is costing you: (4) COMMENTS PER IMPRESSION and (5) SHARES OR SAVES PER IMPRESSION — effortful acts are downstream of the parasocial bond and are the sensitive instruments here; likes and impressions are not and should be ignored for this purpose. LAGGING, weeks to months, and the metrics that actually matter commercially: (6) INBOUND DMs, enquiries and meetings per post — the trust penalty lands on conversion, not reach, and this is the only place you will see it; (7) profile views per impression. ORDER OF MOVEMENT: specificity and adherence immediately, comments per impression within a week, inbound conversations over a month or more. THE HONEST CAVEAT: to detect a disclosure effect on your own account you would need to randomise disclosure across otherwise-matched posts and have enough of them to beat within-author variance — which for most individual creators means low hundreds of posts and is therefore not feasible. Treat the peer-reviewed effect as your prior, instrument the inputs, and do not try to re-derive the science from a dozen posts.

**measurement feasibility**

Poor for the outcome, good for the inputs, and the gap is unusually wide here. NOT OBSERVABLE AT ALL: perceived effort, parasocial connection, trust and legitimacy — the entire causal chain the research identifies is invisible in creator analytics. You cannot see the mechanism; you can only see a slightly quieter comment section and never know why. NOT NATIVELY OBSERVABLE: dwell time; DM and dark-social forwarding, which is where a trust effect would plausibly show up first and which no platform exposes; and, for LinkedIn, whether any classifier touched the post. PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE: comments per impression and shares per impression, which are the best available proxies because the mechanism predicts they move before reach does — read as a trend across 8-10 posts against your own rolling median, never per post. FULLY OBSERVABLE BECAUSE YOU OWN IT: whether you applied the rule, whether the disclosure was specific, whether it passed the grammatical gate, and where you placed it. USABLE QUALITATIVE PROXIES, and in this item they beat the quantitative ones: ask three readers who know you to read a disclosed post and say what they infer about how it was made; and watch for the specific comment types that indicate the effort inference landed badly ('so did you even write this?'). ONE MEASUREMENT THAT IS FEASIBLE AND WORTH DOING: keep a simple log of disclosed vs undisclosed posts with comments per impression, not to run an experiment but to notice a large, sustained divergence if one appears. Anything smaller than large and sustained is noise at individual-creator volumes.

#### omitted as uncertain

- ai search citability
- audience fit
- conflicting evidence
- effect size and n
- evidence provenance
