### Anti-pattern — inauthentic amplification

`anti-pattern-inauthentic-amplification` · automation L2 · evidence SPLIT · 13 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Anti-pattern - inauthentic amplification
- **category**: system
- **definition**: Manufacturing early engagement rather than earning it: engagement pods and comment rings, reciprocal like/reshare agreements, bought likes, followers or views, automated commenting bots, and coordinated voting. The shared mechanic is a pre-arranged or purchased burst of interaction intended to fake the early-velocity signal that rankers historically used as a quality proxy.
- **maturity**: Decayed, and now actively enforced against. It is listed here not as a tactic but as a named anti-pattern with a sanctioned replacement, because it remains widely sold and widely practised on LinkedIn in particular. The prohibition itself is stable and explicit in platform policy; what changes quarter to quarter is the detection and the consequence.

#### mechanism

**ranking signal targeted**

INTENDED: first-hour engagement velocity, early comment count, and comment-thread position - the cold-start escalation decision. ACTUALLY MOVED, in practice: (a) on LinkedIn, a burst of in-network, low-dwell, low-substance engagement from a repeating account set, which a per-viewer semantic ranker reads as information about those viewers rather than as a quality signal about the post, and which NLP comment scoring discounts on top; (b) on X, nothing at all at ranking time, because engagement reached by direct navigation from a group chat is outside the recommendation system's accounting entirely; (c) on every platform, account-level integrity scores - on X explicitly so, via agatha's blocks-per-favourite, reports-per-favourite and spam-reports-per-favourite user labels, which feed visibility filtering and enforcement rather than the per-post ranking score. The single most important structural point: the intended signal is per-post and recoverable, while the signal actually moved is per-ACCOUNT, cumulative, long-memoried (reports aggregate over 180 days in the published code) and invisible in any dashboard. You cannot see the cost, you cannot attribute it to a post, and deleting the post does not undo it.

**why it drives reach**

It no longer does, and the honest causal story is that it used to. When cold-start decisions were driven by crude velocity thresholds, a synchronised burst genuinely could clear the bar, and the tactic spread because it worked. Three things removed the mechanism. First, rankers moved from threshold heuristics to per-viewer learned relevance, so engagement is interpreted relative to WHO produced it rather than counted; forty likes from the same forty accounts every time carries almost no information about a new viewer. Second, engagement quality became explicitly scored - substantive comments are weighted far above generic ones, and pod comments are by construction generic. Third, the negative side of the ledger became account-scoped: a post that draws mutes, blocks, reports or 'not interested' is priced sharply against the author, and low-relevance content pushed to uninterested people is exactly what generates those. The residual belief that pods work persists because their failure is silent - a suppressed post looks identical to a post that was not very good, and the pod members keep supplying visible likes the whole time, so the tactic produces continuous positive feedback while delivering nothing.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **on the offence side this is where ai made it worse**: The 2026 form of this anti-pattern is not a Telegram pod but an auto-commenter: an LLM generating plausible comments at volume on a target list. This is strictly more detectable than a human pod, because it adds a text signature to the graph signature - generic, on-topic-but-contentless comments in a recognisable register, at machine timing, at machine volume. Pangram Labs' analysis of roughly 57,000 public LinkedIn items (Apr-Jun 2026) found around 30% of comments fully AI-generated; a detector vendor's own number and therefore to be read with the obvious bias, but the direction is corroborated by LinkedIn shipping a member-facing 'seems like AI' report control that Fortune reported had been used a million times by 2026-08-25.
- **on the defence side**: Detection is the easy half of this problem and always was. Coordinated engagement is a graph problem before it is an NLP problem - repeated engager sets, synchronised timing, reciprocity closure - and none of it needs a large model. The NLP layer adds comment-quality scoring and AI-text classification on top.
- **on the sanctioned replacement**: A model can legitimately help you comment better, and this is a narrow, high-value use: summarise the day's posts from your curated list, identify the two or three where you have something genuinely non-substitutable to add, and draft a first version that you then rewrite. What it must NOT do is post. The value of the comment is that it contains something only you know; a model cannot supply that, and a model posting on your behalf converts the sanctioned practice into the prohibited one.
- **the uncomfortable symmetry**: An AI-drafted comment on a curated list and an AI-generated pod comment can be textually indistinguishable. If your commenting workflow would look identical to an auto-commenter in a log, the fact that you pressed the button yourself will not save the account. Make the comments specific enough that no classifier would group them with the slop.

**automation level**

The anti-pattern lives at L2 and that is precisely what makes it fatal. L0 (a human manually liking a friend's post) is unremarkable and undetectable; L1 (an AI drafting a comment a human reads, edits and posts) is defensible; L2 (autonomous commenting or liking against a target list, on a schedule, with guardrails) is the configuration that produces the machine-timing and machine-volume fingerprints, and it is explicitly banned by LinkedIn's prohibited-software policy regardless of output quality. Nothing here is L3 and nothing needs to be. Note the marketing inversion: pod tools and 'AI engagement agents' present the L2 configuration as the product benefit ('engage with 200 accounts a day automatically'), i.e. the feature being sold IS the violation. For the sanctioned replacement, hold the workflow at L1 with a hard human gate at the post step - and keep the volume human-plausible, because 15 substantive comments a day is credible and 200 is not, whoever typed them.

**prompt patterns**

- **curated list triage**: Here are today's posts from my 40-account list, with author and full text. For EACH, answer only: do I have a specific, non-substitutable contribution - a number from my own work, a case I ran, a technical correction, a counter-example? Output only the posts where the answer is yes, with one line naming the specific thing I know. If the answer is yes for more than 5 posts, you are being generous; re-run with a stricter bar. Never suggest a comment for a post where my only contribution would be agreement.
- **comment draft with a substance gate**: Draft a comment on the post below. Hard constraints: (1) it must contain at least one concrete particular from MY experience that I supply here: [paste the specific fact]. (2) It must not restate the post. (3) It must not open with praise, with the author's name, or with 'This is so true'. (4) No em-dashes, no 'I'd argue', no 'great point'. (5) 25-60 words. (6) If the specific fact I supplied does not actually bear on the post, reply only: 'No comment warranted.'
- **self audit against the policy line**: Review my engagement routine described below against this verbatim policy text: 'Don't do things to artificially increase engagement with your content. Respond authentically to others' content and don't agree with others ahead of time to like or re-share each other's content.' For each element of my routine, classify: CLEARLY PERMITTED / PROHIBITED / AMBIGUOUS. For anything ambiguous, state precisely which fact would move it to prohibited. Do not reassure me.
- **slop tell check before posting**: Score this comment 0-10 on: could any of the 500 people following this author have written it without knowing what I know? A score above 3 means do not post. Then list every phrase in it that appears in the generic-LinkedIn-comment register.
- **what not to prompt**: There is no legitimate prompt for 'generate 40 varied comments so they do not look templated'. If a prompt's purpose is to defeat detection, the practice it serves is the violation, and prompt-level variation does not defeat graph-level detection anyway - varying the text does nothing about the fact that the same account commented on the same 40 people within the same eight minutes every weekday.

**prompt artifact link**

No artifact exists in this vault yet. Recommended: a single note at 'content/BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/HOWTO/Curated Commenting Routine.md' holding the curated list (30-50 accounts with the reason each is on it), the triage and substance-gate prompts above, and the self-audit prompt to be re-run whenever the routine changes. Do NOT build this as an automated skill with posting capability - the whole point of the item is that the automation IS the violation, so the artifact should deliberately stop at draft. Cross-reference the anti-slop gate and HITL approval patterns already researched in 'content/PROJECTS/AGENTIC-SYSTEMS/Marketing Agent Research.md' rather than rebuilding them. [uncertain - recommendation, not an existing path]

**tool examples**

- **the anti pattern tooling named so it can be recognised**: Telegram and WhatsApp pod groups (the dominant form, tool-free and therefore harder to detect by software fingerprint but trivially detectable by graph pattern); browser-extension pod platforms of the Lempod/Podawaa lineage, which inject engagement from a shared account pool; 'AI engagement agent' products that auto-comment against a target list; follower, like and view marketplaces. Naming specific current vendors is deliberately avoided here - the category is what matters, the vendors churn, and any current list would be a shopping list.
- **detection side**: Platform-internal graph and timing analysis (not documented publicly by any platform); Pangram Labs for AI-text detection at corpus scale; LinkedIn's member-facing 'seems like AI' reporting control shipped in 2026.
- **sanctioned replacement tooling**: A spreadsheet or Obsidian note holding the 30-50 account list is genuinely sufficient. Feed-surfacing features in AuthoredUp, Taplio or Shield reduce the time cost of finding the day's posts from your list; use them for surfacing only, and never enable any auto-engagement feature they ship, which is the same product boundary that decides whether you are inside or outside the prohibited-software policy.
- **cross reference**: The X ranking and integrity stack referenced throughout is public: github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm (Apache-2.0), specifically home-mixer/params/param.rs, agatha/ and visibility-filtering/rules/registry.rs.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

Sharply split. STRONG, verified in this session against primary sources: that pre-arranged reciprocal engagement is explicitly prohibited by LinkedIn policy in near-verbatim terms; that LinkedIn separately prohibits automated engagement tooling and states accounts may be 'restricted or shut down'; that X operates account-level integrity scoring derived from blocks, reports and spam reports relative to favourites, that these are per-user labels feeding visibility filtering and enforcement, and that reports are aggregated over a 180-day window; that X's own ranker documentation states engagement reached by direct navigation after group-chat coordination has no ranking impact. All of these are readable in platform policy text or in Apache-2.0 licensed source code. MODERATE: that pods are ineffective in practice on LinkedIn - strongly implied by the ranking architecture and by policy, but LinkedIn publishes no data and the inference is ours. ANECDOTAL to VENDOR-CLAIM, and explicitly flagged as such: the 45% reach penalty, the ~97% account drops, the ~97% pod-detection accuracy, and the specific Feb-Mar 2026 enforcement mechanics (automated comments hidden, comments limited to direct connections, out-of-network reach penalty) - all trade-press or agency-blog sourced, none platform-confirmed, and the primary Forbes piece was inaccessible in this session. UNVERIFIED: Reddit's ~2M fake votes removed per day; Reddit's own domains were not reachable here. NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY: the effectiveness of the sanctioned replacement, which is recommended on mechanism and policy grounds, not measured ones.

**evidence provenance**

PLATFORM-OFFICIAL, POLICY TEXT: LinkedIn Professional Community Policies (the 'don't agree with others ahead of time' sentence quoted verbatim) and LinkedIn Help - Prohibited Software and Extensions. These are the only sources here that state a rule with a stated consequence. PLATFORM-OFFICIAL, SOURCE CODE AND ENGINEERING DOCUMENTATION: xai-org/x-algorithm, Apache-2.0 - the repository README's own descriptions of agatha/ and abuse-enforcement-service/, the AgathaLabelManager and RateBasedLabels sources, and the comment block in home-mixer/params/param.rs. This is an unusual and valuable provenance class: it is a platform describing its own mechanism in code rather than in marketing, but it is a published snapshot and may diverge from production. INDEPENDENT LARGE-N, VENDOR-OPERATED: Pangram Labs' ~57,000-item LinkedIn corpus (Apr-Jun 2026) for AI-comment prevalence - the vendor sells detection. TRADE PRESS, NO PRIMARY DATA: Forbes/Jodie Cook, 'LinkedIn Just Killed Engagement Pods' (2026-03-18) - the most-cited source for the 2026 enforcement narrative, inaccessible in this session (HTTP 403), so its contents are reported second-hand from sibling research and must not be treated as verified. Fortune (2026-08-25) reporting LinkedIn's one-million 'seems like AI' clicks - trade press relaying a platform figure. VENDOR-WITH-PRODUCT-TO-SELL / UNTRACEABLE: every percentage penalty in circulation. Note the structural conflict of interest: much of the 'pods are dead' content is published by agencies and SaaS vendors selling the authentic-engagement alternative, which is the same commercial incentive that produced the pod-effectiveness claims a few years earlier, pointed the other way. SINGLE-CREATOR ANECDOTE: all reports of specific accounts dropping 97%.

#### fit

**audience fit**

Overwhelmingly a B2B/LinkedIn phenomenon, and the audience is precisely why it backfires. A professional audience that recognises the same twelve names in the comments of every one of your posts reads it as social proof of the wrong thing, and in a dense niche the overlap is obvious without any analysis. The reputational cost is concentrated exactly where the commercial value is: the senior people you want as clients are the ones most likely to notice. For technical audiences the effect is sharper still, because the comments themselves are content-free and a technical reader notices immediately. PL vs EN matters here in a specific way: the Polish professional network is small and dense, so a pod's engager set is recognisable to a much larger fraction of the addressable audience than the same pod would be in English - the anonymity that makes pods survivable in a large market does not exist in a small one. For B2C creator accounts the calculation differs slightly (audiences are larger and less interconnected, so recognition is lower) but the platform-side enforcement is identical, and the account risk does not scale down.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- **the silent failure is the whole problem**: A pod-suppressed post is indistinguishable from a mediocre post, and pod members keep supplying visible likes throughout. The practice therefore generates continuous positive feedback while delivering nothing, and there is no dashboard state, notification or appeal that would tell you otherwise. This is the failure mode that keeps the tactic alive.
- **relevance mismatch**: Pods assemble on reciprocity, not on topic. The resulting engagement is off-niche by construction, which a per-viewer semantic ranker reads as evidence your content is for people unlike your actual audience - potentially steering future distribution AWAY from the right readers. The tactic can be worse than doing nothing, not merely equal to it.
- **negative feedback accumulation**: Pushing content to uninterested people generates the exact actions that are priced hardest - mute, block, report, not-interested - and on X those roll up into account-level labels over windows as long as 180 days. The cost is cumulative, delayed, unattributable and survives deletion of the content that caused it.
- **the ai comment double fault**: Automating the pod adds a text fingerprint to the graph fingerprint and puts you in the population a member-facing 'seems like AI' control is pointed at. Two independent detection surfaces, one action.
- **reputational failure is the uninsured one**: Platform enforcement is at least bounded and occasionally reversible. Being known in a small professional market as the person with the pod is neither. In a dense Polish-language niche this is the dominant risk and it is not on anyone's risk register.
- **replacement failure by hollowness**: The curated-commenting routine fails the same way the pod does if the comments are contentless. 'Great post, totally agree' at scale from a fixed list of 40 accounts every morning is a pod with extra steps and no agreement - it produces the same pattern, the same low-substance text, and the same discount.
- **replacement failure by conversion**: The routine is one message away from becoming the violation. Proposing mutual support to your list converts a permitted practice into a prohibited one instantly, and the resulting data pattern is identical to a pod whether or not anyone ever replies.

**ai slop risk**

Very high, and here the slop IS the anti-pattern rather than a side effect of it. The specific tell in generated pod or auto-comments: it restates the post's thesis in different words and adds nothing, it opens with the author's first name plus praise, it agrees without a position, it is uniformly 20-40 words, it arrives within minutes of publication, and it appears from the same set of accounts across many authors. Any two of those together is diagnostic. Register tells commonly cited: 'This is so true', 'Couldn't agree more', 'Great insights, [Name]!', 'This resonates', heavy em-dash use, and a tidy three-clause rhythm. The corpus-level evidence is that roughly 30% of LinkedIn comments were assessed as fully AI-generated in a ~57,000-item sample (Apr-Jun 2026, vendor-operated), which means the generic register is now the majority background and standing out from it requires specificity rather than polish. The mitigation is a single hard gate: a comment must contain at least one particular that only you could supply - a number from your own work, a case you ran, a technical correction, a named counter-example. If it does not, do not post it. That gate is also what makes the sanctioned replacement work at all, since a comment's entire value is being worth reading by the author's audience.

**human input required**

Two non-substitutable contributions, and they are small but load-bearing. (1) THE SPECIFIC PARTICULAR IN EVERY COMMENT. The model can find the right posts, summarise them and shape a sentence; it cannot supply the number from your own project, the client situation you actually handled, the thing that broke in production last month, or the technical objection only someone who has implemented it would raise. That particular is the entire payload - without it you have produced background noise, with it you have produced the only kind of comment that earns a profile visit from a stranger. (2) THE CURATION DECISION. Which 30-50 accounts, and why each one is on the list, is a judgement about where your audience actually overlaps - it is a positioning decision wearing an engagement costume, and delegating it to follower-count sorting is how people end up commenting on celebrities whose audience will never buy anything from them. A third, narrower item: the decision to stay out. Everyone in a dense niche gets invited to a pod eventually, and the invitation arrives framed as normal professional reciprocity from people you like. Deciding in advance, in writing, that the answer is no is cheaper than deciding in the moment.

**detectability and disclosure**

DETECTABILITY: high, by several independent routes, and this is not a close call. GRAPH: a repeated engager set hitting the same author within minutes, with reciprocity closure across the group - detectable without any machine learning, and strengthening with every cycle. TIMING: machine-regular intervals, engagement volumes outside human plausibility. TEXT: NLP comment-quality scoring discounts contentless comments regardless of who wrote them, and AI-text classification identifies generated ones; LinkedIn also ships a member-facing 'seems like AI' report control, reported at a million uses by 2026-08-25, which means detection is partly crowdsourced to your own audience. CLIENT-SIDE: pod browser extensions and automation tools touch the product in ways the prohibited-software policy is specifically written about. ACCOUNT-LEVEL: on X, explicitly - agatha computes blocks-, reports- and spam-reports-per-favourite as per-user labels feeding visibility filtering. DISCLOSURE: none available and none relevant, and this is an important distinction from the AI-content items elsewhere in this table. Inauthentic amplification is a CONDUCT rule, not a transparency rule; there is no label that makes a pod compliant, disclosing that your engagement is coordinated does not cure the violation, and the EU AI Act's Article 50 has nothing to say about it. The only compliant state is not doing it.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **framing**: This is an anti-pattern, so 'apply' means two things: remove the practice if it is present, and stand up the replacement.
- **part 1 exit if you are in**:
  - Leave the pod groups. Do not announce it, do not negotiate a wind-down, just leave - continuing at reduced volume preserves the pattern that is the detectable thing.
  - Uninstall any extension or tool that engages on your behalf. This is the highest-priority step because it is the clearest policy breach and the one with an explicit stated consequence.
  - Cancel any purchased engagement, followers or views. Do not attempt to remove bought followers manually at speed; the removal pattern is itself anomalous. Let them decay.
  - Do not delete your historical posts. Deletion does not remove account-level signals and costs you the analytics history you need for the measurement loop.
  - Re-baseline: from the date you stopped, start a fresh 30-day rolling median of ln(impressions). Expect a drop as the manufactured engagement disappears and DO NOT interpret it as a penalty. You will not be able to distinguish the two, which is itself the lesson.
- **part 2 build the curated list ninety minutes once**:
  - List every account whose audience genuinely overlaps the buyers or peers you want. Sort by audience overlap and topical adjacency, NOT by follower count.
  - Cut to 30-50. Write one line per account saying why it is on the list. If you cannot write the line, it is not on the list.
  - Mark 5-10 as tier one (comment whenever they post) and the rest as tier two (comment when you have something specific).
  - Re-cut the list quarterly. Accounts drift off-topic and so do you.
- **part 3 the daily routine twenty to forty minutes**:
  - Once a day, at a time that suits you rather than at publication o'clock, read the day's posts from the list.
  - Run the triage prompt: which of these do I have a specific, non-substitutable contribution to? Expect the honest answer to be 3-8, not 40.
  - Write those comments yourself, 25-60 words, each containing one concrete particular from your own work. Use the model to draft if you like, and rewrite every one.
  - Reply to any response you get. The reply thread is where the actual relationship forms, and reply depth is weighted well above a like in every ranking system with public weights.
  - Never post a comment you would be embarrassed to have quoted next to your name in a screenshot. That is the whole standard and it is sufficient.
- **part 4 hard rules**:
  - Never agree with anyone, explicitly or implicitly, to engage with each other's content. This single rule is the entire legal boundary and it is quoted verbatim in platform policy.
  - Never automate the posting step. Drafting is fine; posting is the line.
  - Never buy engagement, followers, views or votes, in any amount, for any reason, including 'just to seed the account'.
  - Keep daily comment volume human-plausible. If your routine would look identical to a bot in a log, the fact that you typed it will not help you.
- **part 5 how to refuse an invitation**: You will be invited, by people you like, in terms that sound like normal reciprocity. A usable answer that does not cost the relationship: 'I'll read and comment when I've actually got something to add - I'd rather do that than agree to it in advance.' It is true, it is compliant, and it commits you to the better practice.

**checklist**

- **the single question gate**: Did I, or anyone acting for me, arrange in advance for someone to engage with my content, or pay for engagement, or automate engagement? If yes to any part: stop. There is no disclosure, threshold or justification that makes it compliant.
- **pre publish gate**:
  - No pod, group chat or DM thread will be notified when this goes live.
  - No tool will like, comment or view on my behalf.
  - No engagement has been purchased for this post or this account, ever.
  - The first comment on my own post, if any, adds substance rather than occupying a position.
- **commenting gate per comment**:
  - Does this comment contain at least one concrete particular only I could supply? (no -> do not post)
  - Would it read as valuable to the author's audience, who do not know me? (no -> do not post)
  - Am I posting it because I have something to say, or because it is this account's turn? (the latter -> do not post)
  - Did a human write or materially rewrite it and press the button? (no -> policy violation)
  - Is today's total volume something a person could plausibly have produced by reading? (no -> cut it)
- **quarterly audit**:
  - Look at the engager set across my last 20 posts. Do the same names appear on most of them? If yes, that is a pattern whether or not I arranged it - understand why before a classifier does.
  - Re-run the self-audit prompt against the verbatim policy sentence.
  - Re-cut the 30-50 list.
  - Check whether reported out-of-network comment restrictions have changed, since they are the one thing that would invalidate the replacement.

**worked example**

- **the policy sentence that decides everything**: LinkedIn Professional Community Policies, verbatim: 'Don't do things to artificially increase engagement with your content. Respond authentically to others' content and don't agree with others ahead of time to like or re-share each other's content.' Read it as an operational test rather than as boilerplate: the prohibited element is the PRIOR AGREEMENT, which means regularity is permitted and reciprocity is not.
- **case a prohibited**: A 35-member Telegram group of Polish B2B consultants. Each member drops their post link on publication; members like and comment within 20 minutes. Comments are drafted by an LLM from the post text. Result pattern: the same 35 names in the first 20 minutes of every post, 20-40-word contentless comments, machine-regular timing, and a closed reciprocity graph. This fails on the policy sentence (prior agreement), on the automation policy (LLM posting), and on substance (NLP comment scoring). It is also, on X, simply inert - members navigate directly from the group chat, and X's own ranker documentation states that engagement not occurring on a post served in Home Timeline 'has no ranking impact'.
- **case b permitted same regularity**: The same person, instead, keeps a list of 40 accounts: 12 Polish CTOs and heads of engineering, 15 EU automation consultants, 8 AI-tooling builders, 5 journalists covering the space. Every morning they read the day's posts from that list, find the three where they have something specific, and write those three comments by hand. Nobody has agreed to anything, nothing is expected back, nothing posts automatically. The daily regularity is identical; the policy status is not.
- **the two comments side by side**:
  - **pod comment**: 'Great breakdown, Marek - couldn't agree more. This is exactly what most teams get wrong. Saving this one!' - 19 words, restates nothing, adds nothing, works for literally any post, and sits squarely in the register a detector and a reader both recognise.
  - **curated comment**: 'We hit this on a Make-to-n8n migration in June - the retry semantics differ, so idempotency keys that were decorative in Make became load-bearing. Cost us two days of duplicate invoices before we caught it. Did you see the same on the webhook side?' - 44 words, contains a specific project, a specific failure, a specific cost, and a question that invites the author to reply. Nobody else could have written it.
  - **the difference that matters**: The second one earns a profile visit from strangers reading the thread, which is the actual mechanism. The first one earns nothing and contributes to a pattern.
- **what the numbers are not**: Note what this example does NOT contain: a claimed reach lift. The circulating figures - 45% pod penalty, 97% account drops, 97% detection accuracy - are untraceable, and the sanctioned replacement has no measured effect size at all. The case for it is the policy text and the mechanism, and dressing that up with a percentage would repeat exactly the error this table exists to avoid.

#### measurement

**measurement feasibility**

Poor in the specific ways that make this anti-pattern persistent, and it is worth being blunt about it. NOT OBSERVABLE: whether you have been penalised; the magnitude of any penalty; your account-level integrity labels (agatha scores are internal and no thresholds are published); which classifier, if any, flagged you; whether a competitor's pod is working; and any counterfactual reach. There is no notification, no flag, no score and no appeal for a ranking demotion. OBSERVABLE: profile views, inbound connection requests, follows, replies from authors, comment threads you participated in, and out-of-network reach share on your own posts where the platform exposes it. PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE BY HAND: your own engager-set overlap - export the reactor and commenter lists from your last 20 posts and count how many names appear on most of them. That is the one piece of the detection signal you can compute about yourself, it takes an hour, and it is worth doing once. THE STRUCTURAL PROBLEM: the practice is a bet whose payoff you cannot observe and whose cost you cannot observe either, which means it can never be evaluated empirically by the person doing it - and it will therefore be sustained indefinitely by the visible likes it does produce. That asymmetry, not any penalty figure, is the actual argument against it. Decide this one on policy text and mechanism, because measurement will never arrive.

### Compliance layer — EU AI Act Article 50

`compliance-layer-eu-ai-act` · automation L2 · evidence STRONG · 11 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

- **name**: Compliance layer - EU AI Act Article 50
- **category**: system
- **definition**: The transparency gate that sits between draft and publish for an EU-based creator: Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 imposes a machine-readable MARKING duty on providers of generative systems (Art 50(2)) and a human-readable DISCLOSURE duty on deployers for deepfakes and for AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest (Art 50(4)), with an exemption for text that underwent human review or editorial control where a named person or organisation holds editorial responsibility.
- **maturity**: Established and in force since 2026-08-02, with a first-generation interpretive layer already published (Commission Guidelines applicable from the same date, plus a voluntary Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content). Enforcement practice is emerging: the penalty framework has been live since 2025-08-02, but no Article 50 enforcement decisions against a solo creator are known.

#### mechanism

**ranking signal targeted**

None - this item targets no ranking signal and claiming otherwise would be dishonest. It is a gate, not a tactic. Two adjacent effects are worth recording, though, because they are what make compliance interact with reach rather than sit beside it. First, the disclosure DECISION is a persuasion variable: research summarised in the sibling item 'The AI disclosure paradox' finds that disclosing AI involvement erodes perceived trustworthiness, authenticity, competence and likability, sharpest in social and interpersonal writing - so an unnecessary disclosure has a real cost in exactly the currency the rest of this table optimises. Second, the human-review process the exemption demands is substantively the same work that platform NLP classifiers are probing for when they reach-limit generic AI content: substantive examination by someone with relevant knowledge, who adds judgement the model could not. The compliance gate and the anti-slop gate are, in practice, one gate. That is the only sense in which this item touches distribution.

**why it drives reach**

It does not drive reach, and it can cost reach. The honest causal story runs the other way: an over-cautious reading of Article 50 leads a creator to stamp 'written with AI' on every post, which the disclosure-penalty literature says degrades perceived authenticity and competence, and which the law did not require. A correct reading produces a narrow, well-understood duty - synthetic media and civic-affairs text without editorial review - and leaves ordinary AI-assisted professional writing untouched and unlabelled. The reach-relevant contribution of getting this right is therefore avoided self-harm plus one genuine asset: an explicit, written editorial-review step that you can point to. That step is simultaneously the legal exemption, the anti-slop gate, and the source of the non-substitutable human content that the rest of this research says actually drives sharing. Where disclosure IS required, rich process-level disclosure - naming the tool, the verification performed, and the sources - measurably mitigates the trust penalty relative to a bare label, so the compliant move and the persuasive move coincide.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

- **as the thing being regulated**: The model is the regulated artefact, not a participant in compliance. Its role determines which duty applies: drafting and editing text under human review triggers nothing; generating a photoreal image of a real person or a cloned voice triggers the deepfake duty unconditionally; conversing with your audience triggers the Art 50(1) chatbot duty.
- **as a classifier in the gate**: A legitimate and narrow use: run every draft through a deterministic pre-publish classifier that answers three questions - does this contain synthetic media depicting anything real? is this text on a matter of public interest as the Commission enumerates them? has a substantive human review been logged? That is a rules-and-prompt job, it is cheap, and it removes the failure mode of deciding case by case under time pressure.
- **as the reason the exemption needs evidence**: The exemption is about a PROCESS, and a process you cannot evidence is a process you did not have. The practical artefact is a short review log - what you changed, what you verified, what you added that the model could not know - produced as a by-product of editing rather than as paperwork.
- **what ai must not do here**: Determine your legal position. An LLM asked 'does Article 50 apply to my post' will produce a confident answer, frequently the over-cautious one, and frequently citing the deepfake rule for a text post or importing a US FTC framing. Use a model to run the decision tree you wrote from the primary text; do not use it to write the decision tree from memory. Every operative sentence in this entry is quoted or paraphrased from the Regulation, the Commission FAQ or the Commission Guidelines for exactly that reason.

**automation level**

L2 (autonomous with guardrails) for the gate, L0 for the judgement. The screening questions are deterministic and belong in a pre-publish hook that blocks on a fail: does the asset contain synthetic audio, image or video depicting something real? does the text concern one of the eight enumerated public-interest domains? is there a logged substantive review by a named human? Automating that is safe because a false positive costs a human 30 seconds and a false negative is what you are trying to prevent. What stays L0: the borderline call on whether a given topic is a matter of public interest, the decision on how to word a disclosure, and - critically - the human review itself, which cannot be delegated to a model without destroying the very exemption it exists to secure. Note the recursion: an L2 or L3 autonomous posting agent publishing without human review forfeits the Art 50(4) text exemption by construction, and if it also converses with readers it picks up the Art 50(1) duty. Full autonomy is not merely risky here; it changes your legal position. That is a stronger argument against L3 publishing than any of the quality arguments elsewhere in this table.

**prompt patterns**

- **the pre publish gate**: You are a compliance screen for the EU AI Act Article 50. Given the draft below, answer ONLY these questions, each Yes/No plus one line of reasoning. 1) Does this post include AI-generated or AI-manipulated IMAGE, AUDIO or VIDEO that resembles a real person, object, place, entity or event and could be taken as authentic? 2) Is the TEXT published with the purpose of informing the public on a matter of public interest, using the Commission's list ONLY: politics and democratic processes; public administration and services; administration of justice and law enforcement; fundamental rights; public security; public health; environmental protection; consumer safety? 3) Has a named human substantively reviewed the content - examined the substance, not spelling - and is that logged? 4) Does the post involve an AI system that will interact directly with readers (auto-replies, DM agent)? Then output one verdict: NO DISCLOSURE REQUIRED / DEEPFAKE DISCLOSURE REQUIRED / TEXT DISCLOSURE REQUIRED / CHATBOT DISCLOSURE REQUIRED / BLOCKED - NO HUMAN REVIEW LOGGED. Do not hedge. Do not mention the FTC or any non-EU rule.
- **the public interest borderline test**: The draft is about [topic]. Using ONLY the Commission's enumerated domains, argue the strongest case that this IS a matter of public interest, then the strongest case that it is NOT, then state which is more persuasive and why. Do not default to caution: an unnecessary disclosure has a measurable trust cost, so 'label it anyway' is not a free answer.
- **the review log generator**: I have just edited an AI draft. Produce a three-line review record: (1) what I materially changed or added that the model could not have known; (2) what factual claims I verified and against what; (3) confirmation that I, [full name], hold editorial responsibility for this publication. If my edits were only stylistic, say so plainly - that is not substantive review and it does not support the Article 50(4) exemption.
- **the disclosure line writer**: Write a disclosure for a post that requires one. Constraints: clear and distinguishable, perceivable at first exposure without special tools, placed where a reader sees it before or with the content. Prefer process-level disclosure over a bare label - name the tool, name the human verification performed, and name who holds editorial responsibility - because rich disclosure mitigates the trust penalty that a bare label carries. 20-35 words. No hedging, no apology, no 'partially'.
- **anti pattern prompt to avoid**: Do not use prompts of the form 'is this legal?' or 'write me an AI disclaimer'. The first invites a fabricated legal conclusion; the second produces boilerplate that either over-discloses (trust cost, no legal benefit) or under-specifies (no compliance benefit).

**tool examples**

- **primary legal texts and guidance**: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 3(3), 3(4), 3(60), 50, 99(4) and (6), 111(4), 113, and Recitals 133-135. European Commission Guidelines on transparency obligations under Article 50, applicable from 2026-08-02 (non-binding). European Commission FAQ on transparency obligations under Article 50. Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (voluntary, assessed adequate by the Commission and the AI Board).
- **provider side marking technologies**: Google SynthID (watermarking across Gemini/Imagen outputs); C2PA Content Credentials, adopted across the Adobe/Microsoft/OpenAI ecosystem; metadata and cryptographic provenance methods generally. These are how providers discharge Art 50(2). Relevant to a creator only as context - and as a caution, since credentials survive some platform pipelines and are stripped by others.
- **deployer side in practice**: There is no compliance product a solo creator needs, and this is worth saying plainly against the market noise. The entire deployer-side toolkit is: a screening checklist, a disclosure line, and a review log. Platform-native labels (Meta 'AI Info', TikTok AI-generated labels, LinkedIn's handling of C2PA credentials) are an ADJACENT mechanism that may label your content automatically - they do not discharge your Article 50(4) duty, and their absence does not mean you had no duty.
- **cross reference**: The provenance and auto-labelling landscape is researched separately in the sibling item 'Platform AI labeling and C2PA provenance'; the trust cost of disclosing is in 'The AI disclosure paradox'. Do not re-derive either here.

#### evidence

**evidence provenance**

REGULATORY-OFFICIAL, PRIMARY LEGISLATION: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as reproduced by the artificialintelligenceact.eu consolidated text (Articles 3, 50, 99, 111, 113 and Recitals 133-135). Note the provenance caveat this deserves: that site is a widely used, well-maintained consolidation and NOT the Official Journal, and it renders amendment markers inline - direct EUR-Lex access failed from this session, so for anything load-bearing, verify against the Official Journal text before relying on it. REGULATOR-OFFICIAL GUIDANCE: the European Commission's FAQ on transparency obligations under Article 50 and the Guidelines on AI transparency obligations applicable from 2026-08-02. These are the source of the public-interest enumeration, the personal-versus-professional test, and the definitions of human review and editorial responsibility. They are authoritative as to the Commission's interpretation and are expressly non-binding on courts. LAW-FIRM ANALYSIS OF BINDING LAW: Orrick's August 2026 note on Article 50 - useful for the practical framing (identifiable responsible entity with public contact details; disclosure via EU icons or equivalent) and for the 2 February 2027 interoperability date, which was not independently verified. NOT PRESENT AND DELIBERATELY SO: vendor compliance content, LinkedIn-guru summaries of the AI Act, and US FTC framings. Where this entry states a rule, it states it from the statute or the Commission; where it applies the rule to a creator's situation, it says so.

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

- **the law is platform neutral the exposure is not**: Article 50 attaches to the act of publishing, not to the channel. What varies by platform and format is how much synthetic media you are tempted to use and whether the platform labels it for you.
- **text posts linkedin x threads**: Lowest exposure of anything in this table. AI-assisted text under your own name with substantive review triggers no disclosure duty, on any platform, in almost every topic a professional creator writes about. The correct output of the gate here is usually 'no disclosure required', and a creator adding a disclaimer anyway is paying a trust cost for nothing.
- **images and carousels**: The boundary runs through photorealism and reference to something real. A generated abstract illustration or a clearly stylised diagram is not a deep fake; a generated 'photo' of a conference, a team, a product in use, or any identifiable person is. Carousel and document posts are a quiet risk because generated stock-style imagery accumulates across slides without anyone deciding to use a deepfake.
- **video and avatars**: Highest exposure by a wide margin. AI avatars, cloned voices and lip-synced talking heads are squarely within the Article 3(60) definition, the duty is unconditional, and no editorial process removes it. For an EU creator this is the single decision in the whole table with a legal consequence attached, and 'I reviewed it carefully' is not a defence.
- **auto reply agents and dms**: The overlooked one. An agent answering comments or DMs in your name engages Article 50(1) and must inform the person that they are interacting with AI unless it is obvious. This is a format question disguised as a workflow question.
- **where it backfires**: Reflexive disclosure on ordinary AI-assisted text. It has no legal benefit, it carries a documented trust cost, and it publicly mislabels the work of a human who actually did the substantive thinking. The Act does not ask for it.

**scales with**

Compliance effort scales with the SYNTHETIC-MEDIA share of your output and with the civic-affairs share of your topics - not with account size, follower count or posting volume. A creator publishing twenty AI-assisted text posts a month on consulting topics has essentially the same (near-zero) obligation as one publishing two. Add one AI avatar video and the obligation appears immediately, regardless of scale. Two things do scale. (1) Evidence burden: the review log is per post, so the marginal cost of the exemption grows linearly with volume - which is a real argument for making the log a by-product of editing rather than a separate task. (2) Enforcement salience: Article 99(7) proportionality criteria include the size of the operator, and the SME rule caps a micro-enterprise at the lower of 3% or EUR 15M, so exposure genuinely scales down for an individual. The ceiling that does NOT scale down is reputational and platform-side: being publicly wrong about an AI avatar costs the same whatever your turnover. One threshold effect worth naming: publishing a branded AI tool or custom GPT flips you from deployer to provider and adds the Article 50(2) marking duty, which is an obligation of a different character and cost entirely.

#### risk

**failure modes**

- **over disclosure**: The most common and most costly failure for this profile. Labelling ordinary AI-assisted text 'AI-generated' buys no legal protection you did not already have via the editorial exemption, and costs measurable perceived trustworthiness, authenticity and competence. It also trains your audience to discount work you actually did.
- **under disclosure on synthetic media**: The mirror failure and the one with legal teeth. An AI avatar, a cloned voice or a photoreal generated image of something real requires disclosure unconditionally, and editorial review does not cure it. Creators who have correctly concluded that their text is exempt frequently generalise that conclusion to their visuals.
- **confusing provider and deployer duties**: Assuming the provider's watermark discharges your disclosure duty. The Commission states explicitly that a deployer cannot rely solely on machine-readable markings; the two obligations are separate acts with separate audiences - one for machines, one for people.
- **misreading the grace period**: Treating 2 December 2026 as a general postponement of Article 50. It is a provider-side, Art 50(2)-only, pre-existing-systems-only transition and it gives a deployer nothing.
- **ceremonial review**: Running a spell-check or a skim and calling it human review. The Commission's definition - deliberate examination of the substance by a person with relevant knowledge - excludes superficial checks explicitly. A review you cannot describe afterwards is a review you cannot evidence.
- **autonomous publishing that silently forfeits the exemption**: An L3 agent that drafts and posts without a human in the loop removes the factual basis for the exemption. Nobody notices, because nothing changes visibly until the day the question is asked.
- **importing the wrong jurisdiction**: Applying US FTC endorsement rules, platform ToS or general 'AI ethics' advice as though they were the EU duty. These diverge in both directions - platform policy can require a label where the Act does not, and the Act can require one where no platform asks.
- **forgetting the chatbot limb**: Building an auto-reply or DM agent and never considering Article 50(1). This is the fastest-growing exposure for exactly the agentic-creator profile this vault serves.

**ai slop risk**

Low as to the output of this item - a compliance gate produces a verdict, not content - but the item is where the anti-slop discipline is enforced, so the risk it MANAGES is high. Two specific slop risks attach here rather than elsewhere. (1) SLOPPY LEGAL PROSE. AI-written compliance text is a recognisable genre and a dangerous one: the tells are the EUR 15M figure quoted without the SME rule that halves it to a fraction of turnover, the deepfake rule cited for a text post, the 2 December date presented as a general deadline, an FTC reference in an EU analysis, and a confident conclusion with no article number attached. Any 'AI Act summary' exhibiting two of those was generated without reading the statute. (2) CEREMONIAL REVIEW AS SLOP LAUNDERING. The Article 50(4) exemption and the platform anti-slop classifiers are probing for the same thing - substantive human contribution - so a review process that exists only to claim the exemption produces content that fails on distribution even where it succeeds on compliance. The mitigation is to make one step serve both: the review must add the proprietary number, the first-hand case or the judgement call that the model could not supply, and the review log should record precisely that addition. If the log entry is empty, you have both a compliance problem and a reach problem, and the reach problem will bite first.

**human input required**

The non-substitutable contribution here IS the legal exemption, which makes this the one item in the table where the human-input requirement is written into law. Concretely, four things. (1) SUBSTANTIVE EXAMINATION OF THE CONTENT by a natural person with relevant knowledge - the Commission's wording, explicitly excluding spell-checking and superficial passes. Operationally: you must be able to say what you changed, what you verified, and what you added that the model could not have known. (2) EDITORIAL RESPONSIBILITY HELD BY A NAMED PERSON. For a solo creator this is automatic and free - you publish under your own name and you are the natural person holding ultimate responsibility - which is why this profile clears a bar that a faceless automated page cannot. (3) THE PUBLIC-INTEREST JUDGEMENT. Deciding whether a given post informs the public on politics, public health, fundamental rights, consumer safety or the other enumerated domains is a borderline call a model will make badly and over-cautiously in both directions. (4) THE DISCLOSURE DECISION ITSELF, where one is required: bare label versus process-level disclosure is a persuasion decision with evidence behind it, and it belongs to the person whose credibility is at stake. Note what this means for the vault's broader agenda: an AI writing pipeline for an EU creator has a legally load-bearing human step, and designing it out is not an efficiency gain but a change of legal position.

**detectability and disclosure**

Two mechanisms that are constantly conflated and should not be. LEGAL DISCLOSURE (this item): a human-readable statement, required only in defined cases, made clearly and distinguishably at the latest at first exposure, perceivable without special tools, and not satisfied by any embedded marking. TECHNICAL DETECTABILITY AND AUTO-LABELLING (a separate mechanism, researched in the sibling item on C2PA provenance): provider-side marking under Art 50(2) - SynthID, C2PA Content Credentials, metadata, fingerprints - plus platform-side reading of those credentials. The interaction is where creators go wrong. A platform may attach an 'AI Info' label to your image because it read a C2PA credential, regardless of whether the Act required disclosure from you; conversely, credentials stripped by a platform's re-encoding pipeline do not remove a duty you had. Neither the presence nor the absence of a platform label tells you anything about your legal position. Add a third, non-legal detection layer: platform NLP classifiers and member-facing 'seems like AI' reporting controls, which reach-limit content on quality grounds with no relationship to Article 50 at all. Three independent systems, three different triggers, three different consequences - and only one of them is the law. The practical posture: decide disclosure on the statute, expect auto-labelling on media regardless, and treat classifier risk as a writing-quality problem handled by the anti-slop gate.

**reversibility and blast radius**

Low-probability, moderate-consequence, and highly recoverable - which is a materially better risk profile than the platform-enforcement items in this table, and worth saying plainly against the alarmist framing in circulation. BLAST RADIUS: an administrative fine capped, for a micro-enterprise, at the lower of 3% of worldwide annual turnover or EUR 15M - on a small consultancy turnover that is four figures, not eight - plus Article 99(7) proportionality criteria that expressly weigh operator size. No account loss, no distribution penalty, no content removal flows from Article 50 itself. REVERSIBILITY: high and cheap. A missing disclosure is fixed by editing the post to add one; unlike an account-level integrity label there is no hidden state, no 180-day memory and no opaque appeal. The realistic downside is not the fine at all: it is the reputational cost of being publicly caught publishing an undisclosed synthetic image or avatar, which in a professional niche outweighs the administrative exposure by a wide margin and is the actual reason to get the media call right. WORST CREDIBLE CASE for the profile in scope: an AI avatar video published without disclosure, screenshotted, and circulated as evidence that the creator's other output is also synthetic - a credibility loss that no fine schedule captures and no edit fully repairs. Against that, the cost of compliance is one sentence.

#### practice

**how to apply**

- **one off setup thirty minutes**:
  - Establish deployer status in writing: 'I publish professionally and derive economic benefit, therefore I am a deployer under Art 3(4).' For almost every reader of this vault the answer is yes and settling it once removes a recurring question.
  - Write the eight public-interest domains onto the gate checklist verbatim: politics and democratic processes; public administration and services; administration of justice and law enforcement; fundamental rights; public security; public health; environmental protection; consumer safety.
  - Draft three disclosure lines and keep them ready: one for synthetic media, one for text (rarely used), one for an auto-reply agent. Write them in the language of publication.
  - Decide and record your standing position on synthetic media - the cleanest policy for a credibility-based practice is 'no AI avatars, no cloned voice, no photoreal generated imagery of real people, places or events', which removes the whole unconditional-duty branch at no cost to a text-first creator.
  - Check Poland's national implementing act and supervisory authority once, and note the date you checked.
- **per post gate sixty seconds**:
  - Q1 SYNTHETIC MEDIA: does this post contain AI-generated or AI-manipulated image, audio or video resembling a real person, object, place, entity or event that could be taken as authentic? If YES -> disclose, unconditionally. No exemption applies. Stop.
  - Q2 TOPIC: is the text published with the purpose of informing the public on one of the eight enumerated domains? If NO -> no text duty. If YES -> go to Q3.
  - Q3 REVIEW: did a named human substantively examine the content - not spelling, substance - and do you hold editorial responsibility? If YES -> exempt, no disclosure required, but log the review. If NO -> disclose, or do the review.
  - Q4 AGENT: will an AI system interact directly with readers under your name? If YES -> that system must inform them it is AI unless obvious.
  - Record the verdict with the post. A one-line record costs nothing and is the only evidence that the process existed.
- **the review log as a by product not paperwork**:
  - While editing, note the three things you would have to say anyway: what you materially changed or added, what you verified and against what, and confirmation that you hold editorial responsibility.
  - Keep it with the post - a frontmatter field, a line in the drafts file, anything durable. Retention of a couple of years is proportionate.
  - If the honest log entry is 'I changed a few words', that is your anti-slop alarm firing as much as your compliance alarm. Fix the post, not the log.
- **if disclosure is required**:
  - Place it so a reader meets it with the content - in the post body or as an on-asset label, not in a comment, not in a bio, not behind a link.
  - Write the language of publication, plainly. 'The image in this post was generated with [tool]' beats a legal formula.
  - Prefer process-level disclosure over a bare label: name the tool, name the verification you performed, name who is responsible. It is better disclosure and it demonstrably costs less trust than a bare 'AI-generated' stamp.
  - Do not apologise for it and do not hedge it.
- **what not to do**:
  - Do not add a blanket 'some content on this profile is AI-assisted' notice to your bio and treat it as compliance. It is neither clear nor distinguishable at the point of exposure, and it applies the trust cost to everything you publish including the parts you wrote yourself.
  - Do not label ordinary AI-assisted text. The Act does not ask for it and the audience penalises it.
  - Do not rely on a provider's watermark or on a platform's automatic label.
  - Do not let the gate be run by the same automated pipeline that wrote the post.

**checklist**

- **pass fail gate before publishing**:
  - Synthetic image, audio or video depicting anything real? -> if yes, disclosure present on the asset. PASS/FAIL.
  - Text on one of the eight enumerated public-interest domains? -> if yes, either disclosure present OR substantive review logged with me named as editorially responsible. PASS/FAIL.
  - Substantive human review actually performed - I can state what I changed, verified and added? PASS/FAIL. (A fail here fails the anti-slop gate too.)
  - Any AI system that will converse with readers under my name discloses that it is AI? PASS/FAIL.
  - Where disclosure is required: is it perceivable at first exposure, in the language of publication, in the post itself rather than a comment or bio? PASS/FAIL.
  - Am I disclosing something the Act does not require? -> if yes, remove it. FAIL on over-disclosure is a real fail.
- **monthly**:
  - Has my output mix changed - any new video, avatar, voice, generated imagery, or auto-reply agent? If yes, re-run the setup, not just the gate.
  - Have my topic pillars drifted toward any of the eight domains?
- **annual or on news**:
  - Re-read Article 50 and the Commission Guidelines; confirm no amendment to 50(4).
  - Confirm the status of the Digital Omnibus amendments against the Official Journal.
  - Check the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content and whether adherence is worth signalling.
  - Confirm Poland's supervisory authority and national penalty regime.

**worked example**

- **scenario**: A Poland-based independent consultant, posting professionally on LinkedIn in English, publishes three posts a week drafted with Claude and edited by hand.
- **case 1 the ordinary post**:
  - **content**: A 250-word post on retry semantics when migrating automations from Make to n8n, drafted by an LLM from the consultant's own project notes, then rewritten to add a specific June 2026 client incident and the duplicate-invoice cost it caused.
  - **q1 synthetic media**: No image beyond a screenshot of real logs. NO.
  - **q2 public interest**: Integration middleware retry semantics is not politics, public administration, justice, fundamental rights, public security, public health, environment or consumer safety. NO.
  - **q3 review**: Substantive - a real incident, a real cost and a technical correction were added. Logged. Consultant is the named natural person holding editorial responsibility.
  - **verdict**: NO DISCLOSURE REQUIRED. The duty fails at Q2 and would fail again at Q3. Adding 'written with AI' here is legally pointless and costs perceived authenticity. The compliance artefact is the one-line review log, not a label.
- **case 2 the topic drifts**:
  - **content**: The same consultant writes a 900-word post arguing that the EU AI Act's transparency regime will push small firms out of AI adoption, drafted largely by an LLM.
  - **q2 public interest**: This informs the public on politics and democratic processes and on public administration. YES - the duty is now live.
  - **q3 review**: The consultant read it properly, checked the article numbers against the Regulation, corrected two errors and added their own client evidence. Logged, and they hold editorial responsibility.
  - **verdict**: EXEMPT, no disclosure required - but only because of the review. Had the same post gone out unread from an automated pipeline, disclosure would have been mandatory. This is the case that shows the exemption doing real work, and it is exactly the case a creator would otherwise get wrong in both directions.
- **case 3 the one that actually bites**:
  - **content**: For a conference announcement the consultant generates a photoreal image of themselves on a stage they were not on, and an AI avatar video in their cloned voice.
  - **q1 synthetic media**: Image and video resembling an existing person and an existing kind of event, capable of being taken as authentic. Squarely within Art 3(60). YES.
  - **review does not help**: The human-review exemption exists only in the text limb of Art 50(4). Reviewing the video carefully changes nothing.
  - **verdict**: DISCLOSURE REQUIRED, unconditionally, clearly and distinguishably, at first exposure. A workable line: 'The stage image and the voiceover in this video were generated with [tool]. The words are mine and I verified every claim in them. I am responsible for this post.' That is process-level disclosure, it satisfies the duty, and it reads better than a bare AI stamp.
  - **better answer**: Do not make the asset. For a credibility-based consulting practice the value of a synthetic stage photo is close to zero and the downside - being screenshotted as the person who faked a conference appearance - is the one cost in this entry that no fine schedule and no edit repairs.
- **case 4 the overlooked one**:
  - **content**: The consultant deploys an agent that auto-replies to LinkedIn DMs in their voice while they are on holiday.
  - **verdict**: Article 50(1) applies: the person on the other end must be informed they are interacting with AI unless it is obvious, and it is not obvious when the agent writes in the consultant's own voice. Building and running it yourself may also make you a provider, not just a deployer. Disclose in the first message.

**cost and time to execute**

- **setup one off**: 30-45 minutes: establish deployer status, copy the eight domains onto a checklist, draft three disclosure lines, set the standing synthetic-media policy, check the Polish national position once.
- **per post**: 30-60 seconds for the four-question gate plus 1-2 minutes for the review log - and the log is largely a transcription of decisions you made while editing, so the true marginal cost is closer to a minute. Across 12 posts a month that is roughly 20-30 minutes.
- **per month**: Under an hour all-in, including a quick output-mix check. This is the cheapest item in this research table by a wide margin.
- **annual**: 1-2 hours for the review of the statute, the guidance, the Digital Omnibus status and the national position.
- **tool subscriptions**: EUR 0. There is no compliance product a solo creator needs for Article 50, and any vendor selling one to an individual professional is selling against the SME penalty rule they have not quoted.
- **cost of getting it wrong**: Over-disclosure: a persistent, unmeasured trust discount on everything you publish - the most likely cost by far, and the one nobody budgets for. Under-disclosure on synthetic media: an administrative fine capped for a micro-enterprise at the lower of 3% of turnover or EUR 15M, plus a reputational hit that is larger than the fine. Compare against the other items here: a 4-hour original-data post costs far more effort than a year of running this gate.

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

- **this is a gate not a growth lever**: Measure conformance, not performance. Targets are binary and boring, which is correct for a compliance item.
- **conformance metrics**: Percentage of published posts with a completed gate verdict (target 100%). Percentage with a substantive review log (target 100%). Count of synthetic-media assets published (a deliberate policy number, ideally zero for a credibility-based practice). Count of disclosures made, split into required versus voluntary - a rising voluntary count is a warning, not an achievement.
- **leading indicator of drift**: Share of posts whose topic falls in one of the eight public-interest domains. If this rises above roughly one in five, the exemption is doing real work every week and the review log stops being optional hygiene.
- **the indicator that connects to reach**: Median substance of the review log - can you state, in one sentence per post, the proprietary number, first-hand case or judgement you added? Empty logs predict both a compliance gap and a reach problem, and the reach problem arrives first because platform classifiers are probing for the same thing.
- **lagging and external**: Any platform AI-label applied to your content (observable on the post, and unrelated to your legal position). Any regulator communication (none expected at this scale). Whether the Code of Practice signatory list grows to include tools you depend on.
- **what not to measure**: Do not attempt to measure the reach effect of disclosing versus not disclosing on your own account. Per the sibling analytics item, detecting anything below a doubling needs hundreds of posts per arm, and the disclosure literature already gives a better-powered answer than you can generate.

**measurement feasibility**

Fully observable, which is unusual in this table and worth stating as the good news. Everything that matters here is a property of your own process rather than of a platform's hidden state: whether a gate verdict was recorded, whether a review log exists and has substance, whether a disclosure is present and placed correctly, and what fraction of your output is synthetic media or public-interest-domain text. All of it is countable from your own drafts directory with no API, no platform cooperation and no statistical inference - contrast with the analytics item, where the central quantities are structurally unobservable. Three things you cannot observe. (1) Whether a regulator or a court would agree with your public-interest classification or accept your review as substantive - no enforcement practice exists at this scale and the guidance is thinnest on exactly the term that decides it. (2) Whether a platform will auto-label your asset, which depends on credential survival through that platform's pipeline and is not announced. (3) The counterfactual trust cost of a disclosure you did make, which would require an experiment you cannot power. PRACTICAL INSTRUMENTATION: a frontmatter field on each draft with the gate verdict and the review log, greppable, auditable in minutes, retained for a couple of years. That is the entire measurement apparatus this item needs and it doubles as the evidence for the exemption.
