### Hook A/B testing loop

`hook-ab-testing-loop` · automation L1 · evidence STRONG · 7 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Hook A/B testing loop. Category: system. DEFINITION: a repeatable process for choosing which of several candidate first lines to publish, and for learning something from what happened afterwards - on a channel that provides no split-test primitive, gives you one shot per idea, and returns an outcome so noisy that the honest answer is usually 'you cannot tell'. THE REFRAME THIS ENTRY ARGUES FOR: the question is not 'how do I A/B test my hooks'. On organic social you cannot, and the arithmetic in effect_size_and_n shows why rather than asserting it. The useful question is: WHAT CAN I ACTUALLY LEARN ABOUT HOOKS AT MY VOLUME, WHAT MUST I BORROW FROM SOMEONE ELSE'S EXPERIMENT, AND WHAT MUST I SIMPLY DECIDE? MATURITY: the marketed practice is ESTABLISHED and largely unfounded - 'A/B test your hooks' appears in essentially every creator playbook and almost none of them address sample size. The honest version is EMERGING and is mostly a discipline about what NOT to conclude. WHY THIS ITEM IS UNUSUAL IN THIS RESEARCH SET: it is one of the few where the evidence is genuinely strong, and nearly all of it is negative. Two independent studies say a frontier LLM cannot rank which headline will win; a peer-reviewed registered report over 8,977 field A/B tests says the textual effects are small and direction-dependent; and the power calculation says your posting volume is two to three orders of magnitude short. Those are real findings, not an absence of evidence.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. Four clocks, and this item is dominated by the slow ones - which is good news.
(1) STABLE / permanent - the STATISTICS. Sample-size arithmetic does not rot. The power calculation in effect_size_and_n will be equally true in 2030.
(2) STABLE / peer-reviewed - the Upworthy findings. Robertson et al. (Nature Human Behaviour, 2023; N=22,743 RCTs) and Aubin Le Quere & Matias (Scientific Reports, registered report, 2025-01-06; 8,977 valid A/B tests) are field-experimental results over a public archive. They will not be overturned, though their EXTERNAL VALIDITY to 2026 professional feeds is a separate and genuinely open question.
(3) 12-24 MONTHS, possibly longer - the LLM-cannot-rank finding. arXiv:2505.03769 (2025) and LOLA / arXiv:2406.02611 (2024) both measured this on 2024-25-era models. Better models could narrow the gap. But note the finding's SHAPE: a small fine-tuned discriminator beat a frontier general model at a narrow supervised ranking task, which is the expected shape for this kind of task and is not obviously a scale problem. Re-check in 2027; do not assume it has quietly reversed.
(4) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER - the native primitives and the platform layer. YouTube's Test & Compare, Instagram's Trial Reels, and whether any platform ships an organic split-test feature (none has). Also every vendor 'hook rate benchmark' band, all of which are quarter-fresh at best.
WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE THIS ITEM: a platform shipping a genuine organic split-test primitive. There is no sign of one, and there is a structural reason - serving different content to randomised slices of an organic audience conflicts with the ranker's own objective. Do not wait for it.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

FOUR LAYERS. Layer 0 is the one that gets skipped and it invalidates everything built on top of it.

=== LAYER 0 - ACCEPT THE CONSTRAINT ===
Organic social has NO SPLIT-TEST PRIMITIVE. You publish once. The ranker decides who sees it. The impression pool is not randomised with respect to your variant - it is selected by a system that is itself reacting to early engagement with that specific variant. There is no control arm and no counterfactual.
Therefore: what creators call an organic 'A/B test' is a SEQUENTIAL COMPARISON of two different posts, shown to two different (overlapping, non-randomised) audiences, at two different times, under two different ranker states. That is a confounded observation, not an experiment. Calling it an A/B test is not pedantry - it is the error that makes every downstream conclusion unsafe, because it licenses causal language ('the question hook won') for data that cannot support it.

=== LAYER 1 - WHERE REAL PRIMITIVES DO EXIST (use these; they are the whole legitimate half of the item) ===
- PAID CREATIVE. Meta, LinkedIn and X ad platforms all provide genuine randomised A/B tests. This is THE structural insight of the item: if you have any budget at all, TEST THE HOOK ON PAID AND PUBLISH THE WINNER ORGANICALLY. A few tens of euros buys you the randomisation that organic distribution structurally cannot.
- EMAIL SUBJECT LINES. A real A/B test on a real randomised split, available on Substack, ConvertKit, Beehiiv and everything else. A newsletter mirror of your content is therefore a genuine measurement instrument - with the caveat that a subscriber base is a more committed population than a feed, so results transfer directionally at best.
- YOUTUBE TEST & COMPARE. A native, real test - for THUMBNAILS, optimising on CTR (and, per YouTube's own framing, watch time). Titles are not natively testable. Since Browse and Suggested are CTR-gated, this is the single best-instrumented hook surface that exists. [uncertain: exact eligibility rules, permitted variant count and test duration were not verified in this pass - the support page 404'd on 2026-09-11.]
- INSTAGRAM TRIAL REELS. Publish to NON-FOLLOWERS ONLY, observe, then push to followers or delete. This is a SCREENING mechanism, not a split test - there is no simultaneous control - but it is the closest organic analogue anyone offers and it is platform-sanctioned.
- NOTHING AT ALL on LinkedIn, X, TikTok organic, Threads or Reddit.

=== LAYER 2 - THE ARITHMETIC THAT SETTLES IT ===
Kohavi's standard rule of thumb for 80% power at alpha=0.05 is n = 16*sigma^2/delta^2 per arm; for a rate, sigma^2 = p(1-p). Worked, with a plausible LinkedIn baseline:
- Baseline engagement rate 5%. To detect a 10% RELATIVE lift (0.5 percentage points): n = 16 * (0.05*0.95) / 0.005^2 = 30,400 impressions PER ARM.
- To detect a 20% relative lift (1.0 pp): n = 16 * 0.0475 / 0.01^2 = 7,600 per arm.
At ~2,000 impressions per post, the first needs ~15 posts per arm (30 posts for ONE comparison) and the second ~4 per arm - and both assume randomised assignment, which you do not have, and a single comparison, not a search over 8 hook types.
Now put the effect sizes back in. The peer-reviewed textual effects are SINGLE-DIGIT PERCENT (negativity ~2.3% per word; concreteness ~+5.5% to -9.9% depending on baseline). You are equipped to detect 20% effects and the real effects are 2-10%. The gap is roughly an order of magnitude, and it does not close with patience because the posts age out of relevance.
THE VAULT'S OWN VERSION OF THIS CALCULATION, from Marketing Agent Research: at 15 posts per month, Kohavi's rule gives 79-493 YEARS PER ARM for a bandit over content formats - and formats are assigned per post, so the impressions are cluster-randomised, which makes it worse than the naive number.

=== LAYER 3 - WHAT REPLACES THE TEST (the four things that do work) ===
1. BORROW SOMEONE ELSE'S EXPERIMENT. The Upworthy Research Archive is the only clean large-N public field-experiment corpus on headlines: 27,616 tests in the archive. Use its findings as PRIORS rather than running your own underpowered version.
2. PRE-PUBLICATION SCREENING, not prediction. Cut 15 candidates to 3 on COMPREHENSION grounds (does this line communicate what I mean, does it create the gap I intend) - a task models are good at - rather than on predicted engagement, which two studies say they cannot do. Pairs directly with the sibling item 'Synthetic persona pre-testing'.
3. POST-HOC ATTRIBUTION, not prediction. Tag every published post with its hook TYPE at publication time. Monthly, compare per-type medians with empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward your overall median. Over 30-50 posts this yields a descriptive ranking of your own hook types. Not causal. Decision-useful anyway, because you are choosing between your own options, not estimating a population parameter.
4. BLOCK ROTATION WITH STRATIFICATION rather than adaptive allocation. Rotate hook types on a fixed schedule stratified by topic and day, so that type is not confounded with subject matter. This is the Marketing Agent Research recommendation and it is the correct answer at low volume: it does not buy you causal inference, but it stops your comparison being trivially confounded.

=== LAYER 4 - THE LOOP THAT ACTUALLY RUNS ===
Generate wide -> screen for comprehension -> apply borrowed priors -> decide by judgment -> TAG THE TYPE -> log the outcome -> shrink monthly -> never conclude from fewer than 8 observations per type. That is the whole loop. It is less than people want and it is what the evidence supports.

**ranking signal targeted**

TWO DIFFERENT OBJECTS, and conflating them is common. THE LOOP targets no ranking signal - it is a selection process, not a content property. THE HOOK targets the earliest signal in every platform's chain:
- LINKEDIN: the 'see more' EXPANSION, which gates DWELL TIME - the dominant LinkedIn quality signal in 2026. Nobody dwells on a post they did not expand. This is why the hook is described as gating everything: it is literally upstream of the signal that matters.
- SHORT VIDEO (Reels, TikTok, Shorts): the 3-SECOND HOLD, which gates watch time and completion rate.
- YOUTUBE BROWSE/SUGGESTED: thumbnail-plus-title CTR, which is the explicit gating factor for that surface.
- X: the detail-expand, and thereafter the downstream reaction terms in the published home-mixer scorer.
- REDDIT: the title IS the post in the feed - there is no separable hook - which makes it the one surface where hook and content cannot be optimised apart.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT THAT MAKES THE HOOK IMPORTANT AND UNMEASURABLE AT THE SAME TIME: the hook targets a GATE, and gates have a characteristic payoff shape - failing them is catastrophic and passing them well is not proportionally rewarded. A terrible hook kills the post outright; an excellent hook does not multiply a mediocre post. That shape explains both the practitioner consensus ('the hook is everything') and the measured effects ('single-digit percent'), and it should set your expectation for what any loop can deliver.

WHAT THE HOOK DOES NOT TOUCH: saves, sends, reply depth, semantic relevance, originality scoring, AI-citation. A hook cannot make a post worth saving.

**why it drives reach**

THE CASE FOR, which is real: the hook is upstream of everything. On a dwell-ranked feed, expansion gates dwell and dwell gates distribution; the first 60-90 minutes of engagement determine whether the post is escalated to a wider pool; and a post that is not expanded generates no signal at all, so its other qualities never get measured. In that sense the hook is the highest-leverage 15 words on the page and testing them is an obviously good idea.

THE CASE AGAINST THE LOOP SPECIFICALLY - four reasons, each sufficient on its own:
1. THE EFFECTS ARE SMALL. The best-measured textual effects in existence are single-digit percentages. Robertson et al. (N=22,743 RCTs, ~370M impressions) found each additional negative word moved CTR by ~2.3%. Aubin Le Quere & Matias found concreteness worth roughly +5.5% at the vague end and -9.9% at the concrete end. These are the real magnitudes, measured on a corpus built for exactly this purpose.
2. THE VARIANCE IS ENORMOUS. Post-to-post outcome variance on organic social is fat-tailed. A 3x difference between two of your own posts is unremarkable and carries no information about their hooks.
3. YOU GET ONE OBSERVATION PER POST. At 2-5 posts per week, a comparison needing 15 posts per arm takes a quarter, during which the platform, your audience and your topic all change.
4. THE ASSIGNMENT IS NOT RANDOM. The ranker chooses the audience partly in response to the variant, so the treatment affects the sampling. This is not a bias you can adjust away with more data.

THE HONEST SYNTHESIS: hook QUALITY drives reach; hook TESTING, at individual-creator volume, does not drive anything, because you cannot detect the effect you are trying to optimise. The value of this item is therefore concentrated in (a) the borrowed priors, which cost you nothing and are peer-reviewed, (b) using the real primitives where they exist (paid, email, YouTube thumbnails, Trial Reels), and (c) NOT acting on noise, which is a genuine return: the main cost of a bad hook loop is not wasted effort, it is confidently learning something false and applying it for six months.

ONE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT WORDING MOVES OUTCOMES AT ALL, at scale and outside the Upworthy corpus: arXiv:2505.03769 found that Reddit posts rewriting a YouTube video's title (rather than copying it) scored higher, p<0.001 over 86,035 controlled pairs - with the authors noting the Spearman correlation is only -0.05. Real in aggregate, negligible per post. That is the best single summary of this entire item.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

VARY, RETRIEVE, SCREEN FOR COMPREHENSION, ANNOTATE. Explicitly NOT: rank by predicted engagement.

WHAT THE MODEL IS GOOD AT HERE:
1. VARIATION. Twenty hooks in thirty seconds, across registers and structures. Genuine comparative advantage and the reason to involve a model at all.
2. RETRIEVAL AND FEW-SHOTTING ON YOUR OWN WINNERS. Feeding it your 15 highest-performing first lines and asking it to infer your hook grammar is, per the sibling 'Hook engineering' item, the single highest-leverage change available and the main defence against generic cadence.
3. COMPREHENSION SCREENING. Asking what a line communicates, what question it raises, and where a reader would stop. Models are reliable at this because it is a reading-comprehension task, not a prediction task.
4. POST-HOC ANNOTATION. Classifying published first lines into a fixed type taxonomy. Mechanical, consistent, and the thing that makes the monthly loop possible.

WHAT THE MODEL DEMONSTRABLY CANNOT DO - and this is the best-evidenced negative claim in the whole research set, from two independent studies:
- arXiv:2505.03769 (Hu, Jin, Ye, Divakaran & Kumar), pairwise ranking of which of two cross-posted titles gets more engagement, over 86,035 controlled pairs: a FINE-TUNED BERT reached 76.5% accuracy on the mixed dataset under a date-based split (the abstract quotes 74% for the headline figure), GPT-4o reached 58.3%, and the random baseline was 50.9%. A frontier LLM scored roughly 8 points above chance on a task a small supervised discriminator handled 26 points above chance.
- LOLA (Ye, Yoganarasimhan & Zheng, arXiv:2406.02611), over 17,681 Upworthy headline A/B tests: 'prompt-based approaches perform poorly, while both OpenAI-embedding-based models and the fine-tuned Llama-3-8B achieve marginally higher accuracy than random predictions.'
Two different corpora, two different tasks, two different research groups, same conclusion: ASKING AN LLM WHICH HOOK WILL WIN PRODUCES SOMETHING BARELY DISTINGUISHABLE FROM A COIN FLIP. Every product feature that scores or ranks your hooks for predicted engagement is built on a capability these papers say is not there.

THE DISTINCTION THAT RESOLVES THE APPARENT CONTRADICTION WITH OTHER EVIDENCE: models are competitive at WRITING engaging copy and poor at JUDGING which copy is more engaging. Generation and discrimination are different capabilities here, and the whole design of this loop follows from keeping them apart - let the model write the candidates, never let it pick the winner.

ONE MORE MODEL FAILURE, from the sibling synthetic-persona item: an LLM panel converges on the SAFEST, most generic variant, and the bias is SYSTEMATIC rather than random - so sampling more personas does not fix it. That is a second, independent reason not to delegate selection.

**automation level**

L1 for generation. L2 for the ledger. L0 for the selection decision, on evidentiary rather than philosophical grounds.

L1 AI-ASSISTED: hook generation, few-shot variation, comprehension screening, draft annotation.
L2 AUTONOMOUS-WITH-GUARDRAILS, legitimately: the LEDGER MECHANICS - auto-tagging published posts by hook type against a fixed taxonomy, pulling per-post metrics, computing shrinkage-adjusted per-type medians, and refusing to report a type with fewer than 8 observations. This is deterministic bookkeeping with checkable outputs and it is the part worth automating, because it is the part humans reliably abandon.
L0, MANDATORY: choosing which hook to publish. Not because judgment is sacred but because the two studies above measured the alternative and found it near-chance.
NOTHING AT L3, and here the vendor gap is unusually stark: 'AI picks your best-performing hook' is a shipped feature in several products and is, on the available evidence, a capability claim without support. Opus Clip's 'virality scoring' sits in the same category - useful as a rough ordering hint for which SEGMENT of a video to clip, not as a prediction of outcome. Treat any numeric virality score as an interface convention, not a measurement.

THE ONE PLACE GENUINE AUTOMATION IS AVAILABLE AND UNDERUSED: paid A/B testing, which is real randomisation, fully automated by the ad platform, and cheap. If you want an automated hook optimiser, that is the one that exists.

**prompt patterns**

Six patterns. Note that the third is the one doing the real work, and that none of them asks the model to predict engagement.

1. FEW-SHOT ON YOUR OWN WINNERS (the highest-leverage prompt in the item).
'Here are the first lines of my 15 highest-performing posts from the last year, each with its impressions-per-follower ratio. Infer my hook grammar: sentence length, punctuation habits, how I use numbers, where I put the turn. Do not describe it in the abstract - state it as five rules. Now write 12 hooks for today's post that follow those rules.'
This grounds the variants in your own voice rather than the model's default cadence, which is both the quality move and the anti-slop move.

2. HAND-FIRST RULE (a procedure, not a prompt). Write one candidate yourself BEFORE you read the model's list. Once you have seen twelve fluent options, anchoring makes it nearly impossible to produce a thirteenth that is genuinely yours. Track how often your hand-written candidate wins; if it wins often, the model is adding variety rather than quality, which is useful to know.

3. COMPREHENSION SCREEN, NOT PREFERENCE SCREEN (run per variant, in SEPARATE contexts).
'You will see only a first line, nothing else. Answer four questions: (a) What do you expect this post to be about? (b) What question do you now have that would make you keep reading? (c) At what point would you stop reading and why? (d) What is this line promising, in plain words?'
Then compare (d) against what the post actually delivers. This is the task models perform reliably, and it catches the two failure modes that matter: a line that communicates something other than what you meant, and a line that promises what the post does not deliver.
HYGIENE, from the sibling synthetic-persona item: randomise variant order and never label variants ordinally (A/B/C, v1/v2). Model behaviour is sensitive to order and labelling, and those labels inject systematic bias.

4. CONCRETENESS CALIBRATION (applying the peer-reviewed prior directly).
'Rate this hook 1-5 for concreteness, where 1 is fully abstract and 5 is a specific named instance with numbers. Return only the number.' TARGET 3. This encodes Aubin Le Quere & Matias's inverted-U: only 8.7% of Upworthy headlines benefited from MORE concreteness while 50.9% were HURT by it. Specific enough to be believable, vague enough to leave a gap.

5. TYPE ANNOTATION (what makes the monthly loop possible).
'Classify this first line into exactly one of: QUESTION / NUMBER / CONTRADICTION / CONFESSION / DIRECT-CLAIM / SCENE / NAMED-ARTIFACT / STAKES. Return the label only, no explanation.'
Fix the taxonomy once and never change it mid-year, or your historical comparisons become meaningless.

6. TRUTH CONDITION (the check no statistical loop performs).
'Here is the hook and here is the full post. Does the post deliver what the hook promises? Name the gap if there is one.' A hook that over-promises buys the expansion and loses the reader, and on platforms whose scorers penalise negative downstream reactions it is actively measured against you.

THE ANTI-PATTERN, stated plainly because it is what everyone does: 'Which of these 10 hooks will get the most engagement? Rank them.' This is precisely the task arXiv:2505.03769 and LOLA measured and found near-chance. The output will be confident, well-reasoned and uninformative.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

STRONG - and unusually so for this research set, because the strong evidence is all about LIMITS.
STRONG / peer-reviewed field experiments: the Upworthy results. Robertson et al. (Nature Human Behaviour 2023, N=22,743 randomised trials, ~105,000 headline variations, ~5.7M clicks, ~370M impressions) and Aubin Le Quere & Matias (Scientific Reports 2025, REGISTERED REPORT, 8,977 valid A/B tests, 35,910 headline instances). Registered-report status is worth noting - the hypotheses were pre-committed.
STRONG / independent academic preprints with large N and controlled designs: arXiv:2505.03769 (86,035 controlled pairs) and arXiv:2406.02611 / LOLA (17,681 A/B tests). Two independent confirmations of the same negative result about LLM ranking.
STRONG / arithmetic: the sample-size calculation. Not evidence in the empirical sense; it is a proof that the empirical question cannot be answered at your volume.
MODERATE, with a serious external-validity problem: whether ANY of the Upworthy findings transfer. That corpus is 2013-2015 NEWS HEADLINES on a content aggregator, optimised for CLICK, where the publisher bore no personal reputational cost. Your case is 2026 professional-identity posts optimised for DWELL where you personally own the consequence. The best evidence in the field is from a different field. This should be stated every time the numbers are quoted.
PRELIMINARY / EXPLICITLY FLAGGED BY ITS AUTHORS: Banerjee & Urminsky (SSRN 3770366) on numerals in headlines - the circulating version is stamped 'PRELIMINARY RESULTS FROM AN EXPLORATORY DATASET' with a warning that confirmatory results are likely to differ. Direction only, no point estimate.
VENDOR-CLAIM: every 'hook rate' benchmark band in circulation. No independent large-N study of hook types versus social reach exists.
NON-EXISTENT: any measured benefit of running a hook-testing loop.

**evidence provenance**

PEER-REVIEWED: Robertson, Pretus, Rathje, Harris & Van Bavel (Nature Human Behaviour, 2023) - negativity and headline click-through over the Upworthy corpus. Aubin Le Quere & Matias (Scientific Reports, 2025-01-06) - a REGISTERED REPORT on headline concreteness, i.e. pre-committed hypotheses and analysis plan, which is the strongest design class present anywhere in this research set.
INDEPENDENT ACADEMIC PREPRINTS: Hu, Jin, Ye, Divakaran & Kumar (arXiv:2505.03769, 2025-04-26), Georgia Tech / SRI-affiliated; Ye, Yoganarasimhan & Zheng (arXiv:2406.02611, LOLA, 2024, rev. 2024-11-26), University of Washington. Neither peer-reviewed at time of writing; both with large N and disclosed method.
PUBLIC RESEARCH DATA: the Upworthy Research Archive itself - 27,616 field A/B tests released for research use. An unusual and valuable asset: a real publisher's real experiments, published rather than summarised.
WORKING PAPER, SELF-FLAGGED PRELIMINARY: Banerjee & Urminsky (SSRN 3770366, Chicago Booth).
PLATFORM-OFFICIAL: YouTube Test & Compare; Instagram Trial Reels; the ad platforms' A/B features.
VENDOR-WITH-PRODUCT-TO-SELL: hook-rate benchmark bands, AuthoredUp-class corpora, synthetic-panel accuracy claims.
OWN PRIOR WORK, NOT INDEPENDENT: content/PROJECTS/AGENTIC-SYSTEMS/Marketing Agent Research.md - the 79-493-years-per-arm Kohavi computation, the block-rotation recommendation, the empirical-Bayes shrinkage proposal, the PersonalBench note on LLM judges, and the 'do not build engagement prediction' verdict grounded in Martin et al. (WWW 2016) on the fundamental unpredictability of social outcomes.
NOTE ON WHAT IS MISSING: there is no peer-reviewed study of hook types on 2026 professional social feeds. Nobody has run it. That absence is itself the most important provenance fact in the item.

**sources**

- Hu, Jin, Ye, Divakaran & Kumar, 'The Influence of Text Variation on User Engagement in Cross-Platform Content Sharing', arXiv:2505.03769 (2025-04-26) - fine-tuned BERT 76.5% vs GPT-4o 58.3% vs 50.9% random on pairwise engagement ranking; 86,035 controlled pairs; abstract quotes 74% - https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03769 - [independent academic preprint, large-N, controlled design]
- Ye, Yoganarasimhan & Zheng, 'LOLA: LLM-Assisted Online Learning Algorithm for Content Experiments', arXiv:2406.02611 (2024) - over 17,681 Upworthy headline A/B tests, prompt-based LLM approaches 'perform poorly'; embedding-based and fine-tuned Llama-3-8B only 'marginally higher accuracy than random predictions' - https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02611 - [independent academic preprint]
- Robertson, Pretus, Rathje, Harris & Van Bavel, 'Negativity drives online news consumption', Nature Human Behaviour (2023) - N=22,743 RCTs, ~105,000 headline variations, ~5.7M clicks over ~370M impressions; ~2.3% CTR per additional negative word - https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-023-01538-4 - [peer-reviewed]
- Aubin Le Quere & Matias, headline concreteness registered report, Scientific Reports (2025-01-06) - 8,977 valid Upworthy A/B tests, 35,910 headline instances; interaction coefficient -0.058, p<0.001; 8.7% helped by more concreteness vs 50.9% hurt - [peer-reviewed REGISTERED REPORT; strongest design class in this research set]
- Banerjee & Urminsky, 'The Language That Drives Engagement: A Systematic Large-scale Analysis of Headline Experiments', SSRN 3770366 (Chicago Booth) - numerals raise CTR; most other fluency cues do not. STAMPED 'PRELIMINARY RESULTS FROM AN EXPLORATORY DATASET' by its authors - https://home.uchicago.edu/ourminsky/Banerjee_Urminsky_Headlines.pdf - [working paper, self-flagged preliminary, direction only]
- Upworthy Research Archive - 27,616 public field A/B tests on live headlines; the only clean large-N public headline-experiment corpus in existence - [public research dataset]
- Martin, Hofman, Sharma, Anderson & Watts, 'Exploring Limits to Prediction in Complex Social Systems', WWW 2016 - the fundamental-unpredictability result underpinning the 'do not build engagement prediction' verdict - [peer-reviewed]
- VAULT: content/PROJECTS/AGENTIC-SYSTEMS/Marketing Agent Research.md (2026-08-25) - the Kohavi computation giving 79-493 years per arm at 15 posts/month; the cluster-randomisation problem for per-post format assignment; block rotation with stratification plus monthly empirical-Bayes shrinkage as the recommended alternative; PersonalBench on LLM judges rating texts as varied where stylometry showed they were not; and the explicit instruction not to build engagement prediction but post-hoc attribution instead - [own prior work, NOT independent]
- VAULT: content/BUSINESS/KNOWLEDGE/INFO/Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026.md - which signal the hook gates per surface; Instagram Trial Reels as sanctioned cold-start testing; YouTube Test & Compare for thumbnails on a CTR-gated surface - [vault compilation]
- VAULT SIBLING: results/Synthetic_persona_pre-testing.json - the pre-publication screening layer this item pairs with, including the finding that an LLM panel's convergence on the safest variant is SYSTEMATIC rather than random - [sibling research item]
- VAULT SIBLING: results/Hook_engineering.json - the hook craft this loop selects among, including the concreteness inverted-U and the few-shot-on-your-own-winners recommendation - [sibling research item]
- Kohavi, Tang & Xu, 'Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments' - the n = 16*sigma^2/delta^2 per-arm rule of thumb used for the power arithmetic here - [standard reference text]

#### fit

**platform and format fit**

Cross-referencing 'Social Media Algorithms - Maximizing Reach in 2026'. The decisive variable is not the platform's audience - it is whether the platform gives you a primitive and whether it exposes the metric the hook targets.

WHERE THE LOOP GENUINELY WORKS:
- PAID CREATIVE (any platform). Real randomisation, real control arm, automated. The highest-value structural move in the item: test on paid, publish the winner organically.
- EMAIL. Real subject-line A/B on a real split, and the open rate is directly observable. A newsletter mirror of your social content is a measurement instrument, not just a distribution channel.
- YOUTUBE. Test & Compare on thumbnails, on a surface (Browse/Suggested) where thumbnail-plus-title CTR is the explicit gate. The best-instrumented hook surface in existence. Titles remain untestable.
- SHORT VIDEO GENERALLY. Not because of a primitive but because of the METRIC: 3-second retention and view duration are directly reported. This is the only place where the thing the hook targets is actually visible to you. If you want a working hook loop, run it on video.

WHERE IT PARTIALLY WORKS:
- INSTAGRAM. Trial Reels gives you a sanctioned non-follower screening pass before committing to your followers. Not a split test; still the best organic screening mechanism anyone offers.

WHERE IT DOES NOT WORK AND IS MOST DISCUSSED:
- LINKEDIN. No primitive, and - the deeper problem - the metric the hook targets ('see more' expansion) is NOT EXPOSED. You end up measuring impressions, which the ranker determined, as a proxy for expansion, which you cannot see. The platform where hook testing is discussed most is the one where it is least possible.
- X, TIKTOK ORGANIC, THREADS, BLUESKY, SUBSTACK NOTES. No primitive.
- REDDIT. Structurally different: the title IS the post in the feed, so hook and content are not separable, and community fit dominates wording. Note that arXiv:2505.03769 is a Reddit study - and its finding is that adapting the title to community norms is what matters, which is a fit question rather than an optimisation one.

BY FORMAT: hooks matter most where there is a HARD FOLD - LinkedIn's 'see more', the 3-second video threshold, the YouTube thumbnail. They matter least in carousels (slide 1 is a visual decision, not a textual one) and in formats where the whole post is visible at once. For document posts, the 'hook' to test is slide 1's design, and that belongs to the sibling carousel item.

**audience fit**

B2B / TECHNICAL - the worst case for the loop and the best case for the discipline. Audiences are small, so the sample-size problem is at its most severe (a 1,500-impression post needs ~20 posts per arm to detect a 10% effect). At the same time, this is the audience where a bad hook costs the most: an over-promising line in front of people who might hire you damages standing in a way no engagement metric records. Practical consequence: run the TRUTH CONDITION check rigorously and skip the statistics.

B2C / HIGH-VOLUME CREATORS - the only population where a within-account loop can converge. At 20+ posts per month with five-figure impressions, per-type medians become estimable over a quarter. Even then, 30-50 posts is the floor before any type ranking means anything.

TECHNICAL vs GENERAL - a real difference in what a hook can be. Technical audiences respond to specificity and version numbers and are actively repelled by curiosity-gap phrasing, which reads as marketing. General audiences are the population the Upworthy findings were measured on, so the borrowed priors transfer better there and worse to technical feeds. Another reason to treat the Upworthy numbers as priors rather than parameters.

PL vs EN - two specific points. (1) YOU CANNOT A/B LANGUAGE, per the sibling multilingual item: the same post in two languages reaches two overlapping-but-different audiences at two different times, confounding language with audience, timing and novelty. A PL hook and an EN hook are not two arms of anything. (2) TEMPLATE FATIGUE IS ASYMMETRIC: PL-language professional feeds run roughly 12-24 months behind EN on formula saturation, so a clean, conventional hook still reads as competent in Polish where the same structure reads as canned in English. The practical effect is that the borrowed EN priors are more useful on the PL track than on the EN one - and that window is closing.

ACROSS ALL AUDIENCES: the single most transferable instrument is not a metric, it is the COMMENTS. Comments quoting the body prove the hook did its job; comments reacting only to the hook prove it did not.

**scales with**

THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS POSTS PER MONTH, and it is arithmetic rather than effort - which is why working harder does not help.

WHAT CAPS IT:
1. POSTING VOLUME. Every arm needs observations and you produce 2-20 per month. This is the constraint and everything else is secondary.
2. IMPRESSIONS PER POST. Directly sets how many posts a comparison needs. A 10,000-impression account needs a fifth as many posts as a 2,000-impression one for the same comparison - so the loop scales with audience size in the ordinary direction.
3. YOUR OWN OUTCOME VARIANCE. Fat-tailed performance inflates the required n. Creators with occasional breakout posts - which is most creators worth reading - have the worst signal-to-noise.
4. THE EFFECT SIZE YOU ARE CHASING. And the honest effects are 2-10%, which is below the detection threshold at essentially any individual-creator volume.
5. THE NUMBER OF HOOK TYPES. Every type you add splits the same data further. Six types is already ambitious; ten is a guarantee of noise.

THE PERVERSE SCALING, worth stating because it is the item's central irony: THE ONLY ACCOUNTS WITH ENOUGH VOLUME TO RUN THE LOOP ARE THE ONES THAT NEED IT LEAST. A creator posting 25 times a month to 50,000 impressions each has both the data and, already, the working hooks. A creator posting four times a month to 1,500 impressions has neither, and is the one reading the advice.

WHAT DOES NOT CAP IT: budget (the loop is nearly free), tooling, or team size. And note that PAID A/B TESTING BREAKS THE SCALING ENTIRELY - a few tens of euros of ad spend buys the randomisation and the sample size that years of organic posting cannot. If you have any budget, the volume constraint is not binding on you and you should stop treating it as though it were.

CEILING BY OBJECTIVE: for VIRALITY the loop's ceiling is low (small effects, high variance). For NOT PUBLISHING A BAD HOOK the ceiling is high and reachable immediately, because that is a comprehension check rather than a measurement. For AI CITATION the loop is irrelevant and can be mildly counterproductive (see ai_search_citability).

**decay and saturation**

THE CLEANEST DECAY PROFILE IN THIS RESEARCH SET, because the durable parts and the rotting parts are cleanly separable.

DOES NOT DECAY: the statistics; the Upworthy field-experimental findings; the discipline of not concluding from n=2; the comprehension screen; the truth condition. These are permanent.

DECAYS IN 12-24 MONTHS: every specific HOOK TEMPLATE. This is well-attested rather than speculative - broetry is the canonical case, a hook form that went from high-performing to actively cringe-inducing inside about two years and is now a named anti-pattern. 'I did X for 30 days'; 'Unpopular opinion:'; 'Nobody talks about this, but'; the one-line-paragraph ladder. Each had a window and each closed. Any loop that learns a template will learn one that is already partly decayed, because by the time you have enough observations to detect it, it has been visible long enough to saturate. THIS IS A STRUCTURAL PROBLEM WITH THE LOOP, not an accident: the measurement lag and the decay rate are the same order of magnitude.

DECAYS QUARTERLY: native primitives and platform behaviour.

MAY DECAY, WATCH IT: the LLM-cannot-rank finding. Measured on 2024-25 models. A frontier model fine-tuned on your own outcome data would be a different proposition from a prompted general model - and is, in effect, what the BERT result already demonstrates. If someone ships that as a product with real validation, revisit.

SATURATION: hook fatigue is real, platform-specific, and asymmetric by language (EN feeds are more saturated than PL by roughly 12-24 months). The counter-move is not a better template but a shift in KIND - a hook made of a specific you own (a number, a version string, a dated incident) cannot saturate, because nobody else has it. This is the same conclusion the rest of this research keeps arriving at from different directions.

THE ONE CHANGE THAT WOULD TRANSFORM THE ITEM: a platform shipping an organic split-test primitive. None has, there is a structural reason (randomised delivery conflicts with the ranker's objective), and planning around it would be planning around something that has not happened in fifteen years of social feeds.

#### risk

**failure modes**

Ten. The first three are the ones that make a loop actively worse than no loop - because they manufacture confident false beliefs.

1. CALLING A SEQUENTIAL COMPARISON AN A/B TEST. Two posts, two audiences, two times, one ranker reacting to each. This is the definitional error and it licenses causal language for data that cannot bear it.
2. STOPPING ON A WIN. Comparing two posts, seeing a 40% difference, and concluding the question hook works. At n=2 per arm with fat-tailed variance, a 3x gap is unremarkable. This is the single most common failure and it feels exactly like learning.
3. TRUSTING AN LLM PANEL'S RANKING. The failure this item exists to name. GPT-4o at 58.3% against a 50.9% baseline; prompt-based approaches 'perform poorly' over 17,681 real tests. The ranking will arrive confident and well-argued and will be near-noise.
4. OPTIMISING A CONFOUNDED METRIC. On text surfaces you measure impressions - which the ranker determined, partly in response to the hook, partly for reasons unrelated to it - as a proxy for expansion, which you cannot see. You are optimising the ranker's decision, not the reader's.
5. VARIANCE BLINDNESS. Not looking at your own historical spread before declaring a difference. Ten minutes with your own data will show you that your posts already differ by 3-5x for no reason you can name.
6. CHANGING MORE THAN ONE THING. The hook AND the topic AND the day AND the format. Every real post is a different post; this is not fixable, only acknowledgeable, and it is another reason to stratify rather than to compare pairs.
7. WINNER'S CURSE AND REGRESSION TO THE MEAN. Last month's best-performing type was partly lucky; next month it regresses; you conclude the audience changed or the algorithm shifted. Empirical-Bayes shrinkage exists precisely to damp this and is the reason the monthly step is not a plain average.
8. SURVIVORSHIP IN THE LEDGER. You only have outcomes for hooks you published. The eleven you rejected have no data, so the ledger can only tell you about the region of hook-space you already favour. It cannot discover a type you never try.
9. RUNNING A BANDIT. Explicitly warned against in Marketing Agent Research: 79-493 years per arm at 15 posts/month, and per-post assignment means cluster-randomised impressions. A bandit at this volume does not merely fail to converge - it will confidently allocate to a lucky arm and stay there.
10. BUILDING ENGAGEMENT PREDICTION. Marketing Agent Research's verdict, grounded in Martin et al. (WWW 2016) on fundamental unpredictability and in LOLA's result over 17,681 real tests. The outcome is unpredictable in principle, not for want of data. Build post-hoc attribution instead.

THE META-FAILURE: treating the absence of a result as a reason to try harder. In this item, 'no detectable difference' is usually the TRUE answer, and accepting it is the skill.

**ai slop risk**

MODERATE, with a specific and well-documented mechanism.

THE MECHANISM: generating twenty hooks is free, so the binding step becomes selection - and if selection is delegated to a model, it converges on the SAFEST, most legible, most generic variant. The sibling synthetic-persona item is explicit that this bias is SYSTEMATIC rather than random, which means sampling more variants or more personas does not average it out. You get a well-formed, unobjectionable, forgettable first line, reliably.

THE TELLS:
1. EVERY POST OPENS WITH THE SAME KIND OF LINE. Not the same words - the same move. Always a contradiction, always a number, always a confession. This is a cross-post tell, which is exactly the unit LinkedIn says its detection operates on.
2. HOOKS THAT ARE PERFECTLY CALIBRATED AND SAY NOTHING. 'Most people get this wrong.' 'Here is what nobody tells you about X.' Structurally correct, contentless, and instantly recognisable in 2026.
3. A DECAYED TEMPLATE APPLIED AT SCALE - the loop found a pattern, the pattern was already saturating, and now every post carries it.
4. UNIFORM HOOK LENGTH. A parameter, not a choice.
5. CURIOSITY GAPS THE POST DOES NOT CLOSE. The most damaging tell, because it trains your own audience to distrust your first lines - and readers punish this far faster than any classifier does.

THE COUNTERS, in order of effectiveness:
- FEW-SHOT ON YOUR OWN WINNERS rather than generating cold. Grounds the batch in your grammar instead of the model's.
- THE HAND-FIRST RULE: write one candidate before you see the model's list. Track how often it wins; a high win rate tells you the model is contributing variety rather than quality, which is worth knowing.
- ROTATE HOOK TYPES DELIBERATELY across posts, which the ledger makes visible.
- THE TRUTH CONDITION, which is the only check that catches tell #5.

A NOTE ON WHERE THE SLOP RISK IS LOW: the hook is the shortest and most heavily-edited text in any post. If any part of a post gets human attention, it is this one. The risk here is real but it is smaller than in the body, and smaller than in the repurposing pipeline.

**human input required**

FIVE THINGS, and the first is non-substitutable on evidentiary grounds rather than on principle.

1. THE SELECTION DECISION. Irreducibly human, because two independent studies measured the alternative: a frontier LLM ranks which headline wins at 58.3% against a 50.9% baseline, and prompt-based approaches over 17,681 real A/B tests perform 'poorly'. This is not a preference for human judgment - it is the only option with evidence behind it, and even human judgment here is weak. The honest framing is: the decision is yours because nothing better exists, not because you are good at it.

2. THE HAND-WRITTEN CANDIDATE, produced BEFORE reading the model's list. Anchoring is severe: after twelve fluent options you will not produce a thirteenth that is genuinely different. This costs ninety seconds and is the main source of hooks that do not sound like everyone else's.

3. THE TRUTH CONDITION - does the post deliver what the hook promised? No statistical loop performs this check, and it determines whether a 'winning' hook is actually winning or is clickbaiting your own audience into a dwell-then-bounce. It is also the one that compounds: readers remember whether your first lines are honest, and a reputation for over-promising is not recoverable by optimisation.

4. THE ANNOTATION JUDGMENT. Classifying your own hook by type requires knowing what you were trying to do, which a classifier reading the output cannot recover. Model-assisted annotation is fine; blind annotation corrupts the ledger slowly and invisibly.

5. READING THE COMMENTS. The only qualitative read on whether the hook attracted the right PEOPLE rather than the most people. Comments quoting the body prove expansion; comments reacting only to the hook prove the opposite; comments from an audience you did not want are the signal that a hook is working against you on an interest-graph platform, where it also teaches the recommender to show you to the wrong cluster.

WHAT THIS ITEM DOES NOT REQUIRE, in contrast to most others here: a proprietary number, a first-hand story or a named client. Those belong to the post's SUBSTANCE and are the sibling HITL item's domain. A hook is a craft decision on top of substance that must already exist - which means a great hook on an empty post is the most efficient way to waste the one shot you get.

**detectability and disclosure**

THE LOOP ITSELF IS NOT DETECTABLE AND TRIGGERS NO DISCLOSURE. Choosing between your own candidate first lines is editorial work and leaves no artifact. Nothing here is machine-detectable, auto-labelled, or within the scope of C2PA or SynthID, which cover synthetic media rather than text.

BUT THREE REAL DETECTION-ADJACENT POINTS:
1. THE OUTPUT OF A BADLY-RUN LOOP IS DETECTABLE even though the loop is not. If the loop converges on one hook shape, every post opens the same way - and cross-post pattern uniformity is precisely what LinkedIn describes its classifiers as looking at (patterns across a member's content, not individual posts). A loop that 'works' in the naive sense is therefore a route INTO a genericness signal.
2. THE PLATFORM CAN RUN THE EXPERIMENT YOU CANNOT - and this asymmetry is worth sitting with. X's published home-mixer scorer penalises the downstream consequences of a post heavily: mutes, blocks, negative reactions, 'show less often'. Meta demotes engagement bait explicitly. A hook that over-promises produces exactly those downstream signals, and the platform observes them across millions of impressions with proper randomisation. So the effect you cannot measure is being measured - against you. The practical implication: optimise for the post being worth having opened, because that is the quantity the platform is actually scoring.
3. ENGAGEMENT BAIT IS A NAMED, ENFORCED CATEGORY. An unconstrained hook optimiser converges toward it by construction, because bait is what maximises a proxy metric. This is the clearest case in the research of a metric-optimisation loop walking into a policy category.

DISCLOSURE: none triggered by hook selection. The EU AI Act analysis is inherited from the drafting step and is set out in the sibling 'Human-in-the-loop editorial protocol' item. One small consequence worth noting: if a model generated the first line and a human selected it, that selection is a substantive editorial act on the most load-bearing sentence of the post - which strengthens rather than weakens the Article 50(4) carve-out position.

**reversibility and blast radius**

THE LOWEST BLAST RADIUS IN THIS RESEARCH SET for any single action, and a genuine slow-burn risk underneath it.

PER POST: a bad hook costs you one post's reach. Fully recoverable, no account-level consequence, no record. You can and should experiment freely at this level - the asymmetry strongly favours trying unusual hooks, because the downside is bounded at one post and the upside is fat-tailed.

THE THREE DURABLE RISKS, in ascending order of how much they actually matter:
1. ENGAGEMENT-BAIT DEMOTION. Real, named in policy, and per-post or per-pattern rather than catastrophic. Recoverable by stopping.
2. LEARNING A FALSE LESSON AND APPLYING IT FOR MONTHS. The characteristic cost of this item, and it is invisible by construction: you concluded from n=2 that question hooks work, you have written question hooks for six months, and there is no signal that will tell you otherwise because the thing you would need to detect the error is the experiment you could not run. This is why the ledger's refusal-to-report-below-8-observations rule is the most important line in the whole system - it is a guard against your own conclusions, not against the data.
3. AUDIENCE MIS-SELECTION - the sleeper, and the one worth actually worrying about. A hook that attracts the wrong readers does three things at once: it degrades your comment quality, it teaches the recommender which cluster to show you to on interest-graph platforms, and it shifts who follows you. The last two compound and are slow to reverse, because you are now optimising for an audience you did not want and receiving positive feedback from it. Recovery takes months of deliberately narrower content and looks, from the metrics, like decline.

ACCOUNT SUSPENSION: not a realistic outcome. Shadowban: not from hooks alone.

THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: be bold per post (low cost, fat upside), be conservative per conclusion (high cost, invisible), and watch WHO shows up in the comments rather than how many.

#### practice

**how to apply**

SETUP, once, 1-2 hours.
1. DEFINE 6-8 HOOK TYPES AND FIX THE TAXONOMY. Suggested: QUESTION / NUMBER / CONTRADICTION / CONFESSION / DIRECT-CLAIM / SCENE / NAMED-ARTIFACT / STAKES. Fixed means fixed - changing it mid-year destroys your historical comparisons.
2. CREATE hooks.csv: post id, date, surface, hook text, type, topic, the metric, and whether your hand-written candidate won.
3. CHOOSE YOUR METRIC PER SURFACE, and choose the least confounded one available: VIDEO - 3-second retention (directly reported; use this if you have it). YOUTUBE - CTR via Test & Compare (a real experiment). EMAIL - open rate (a real A/B). TEXT - first-90-minute engagement rate per impression, acknowledged as a weak proxy for the expansion you cannot see.
4. WRITE DOWN THE STOPPING RULE BEFORE YOU HAVE ANY DATA: 'I will not conclude anything about a hook type from fewer than 8 observations.' Writing it down in advance is the point; it is a pre-commitment against your future self's pattern-matching.
5. COMPUTE YOUR OWN VARIANCE from your last 20 posts. Look at the spread. This ten-minute exercise does more to calibrate you than anything else in the item.

PER POST, 10-20 minutes.
6. WRITE ONE HOOK BY HAND, before opening a model.
7. GENERATE 12-15 with few-shot on your own winners (pattern 1).
8. RUN THE COMPREHENSION SCREEN (pattern 3) on the strongest 5-6, each in a SEPARATE context, order randomised, no ordinal labels. You are asking what each line communicates, never which will perform.
9. APPLY THE BORROWED PRIORS: target concreteness ~3 of 5 (the inverted-U); a numeral helps; negativity raises click and risks the mute on professional surfaces - use it deliberately or not at all.
10. RUN THE TRUTH CONDITION (pattern 6). Kill any hook the post does not pay off, however good it is. This is the only hard stop in the loop.
11. CHOOSE BY JUDGMENT among the survivors. Prefer the one that only you could have written. If two are equivalent, pick the type you have fewest observations of.
12. TAG THE TYPE IN THE LEDGER AT PUBLICATION TIME. Retrospective tagging is contaminated by knowing the outcome.

MONTHLY, 20-30 minutes.
13. PULL THE METRIC for each post.
14. COMPUTE per-type medians with EMPIRICAL-BAYES SHRINKAGE toward your overall median. Report nothing for a type with fewer than 8 observations - not even provisionally.
15. READ THE COMMENTS PER TYPE, not just the numbers. Which types brought people who engaged with the substance?
16. ROTATE TYPES IN BLOCKS, stratified by topic, so type is not confounded with subject matter.

WHERE YOU HAVE A REAL PRIMITIVE - do this instead of all of the above, it is strictly better:
17. PAID: run the hook as an ad A/B for a few tens of euros; publish the winner organically. Real randomisation, real control, days not quarters.
18. YOUTUBE: Test & Compare on thumbnails.
19. INSTAGRAM: Trial Reels to non-followers, promote the winner.
20. EMAIL: A/B the subject line on the newsletter version of the same idea.

NEVER: run a bandit; ask a model which hook will win; stop on a win; conclude from n=2; build an engagement predictor; change the taxonomy mid-year.

**checklist**

- PASS/FAIL - Did I write one hook by hand BEFORE seeing the model's list?
- PASS/FAIL - Does the post actually deliver what this hook promises? (Hard stop. Kill the hook, not the post.)
- PASS/FAIL - Did I screen the candidates on COMPREHENSION (what does this line communicate?) rather than on predicted engagement?
- PASS/FAIL - Were variants presented to the model in randomised order with no ordinal labels (no A/B/C, no v1/v2)?
- PASS/FAIL - Is the hook's concreteness around 3 of 5 - specific enough to be believable, vague enough to leave a gap?
- PASS/FAIL - Is there something in this hook only I could have written (a number, a version, a dated specific)?
- PASS/FAIL - Is this hook a DIFFERENT TYPE from my last two posts? (Cross-post uniformity is what pattern detection sees.)
- PASS/FAIL - Have I tagged the hook type in the ledger AT PUBLICATION, not retrospectively?
- PASS/FAIL - Would this hook be rejected as engagement bait by a strict reading of LinkedIn's or Meta's policy? (If borderline: rewrite.)
- PASS/FAIL - Does this hook put a client detail or a number I have not cleared in the most-read sentence of the post?
- PASS/FAIL - Before drawing ANY conclusion from the ledger: do I have at least 8 observations for this type?
- PASS/FAIL - Have I compared against my OWN median for this surface, rather than against another post or another platform?
- PASS/FAIL - Am I about to conclude something causal from a sequential comparison? (If yes: stop. It is not an A/B test.)
- PASS/FAIL - If I have any ad budget: am I testing on paid, where the randomisation is real, instead of theorising about organic?

#### measurement

**kpis and leading indicators**

LOOP-HEALTH METRICS (primary, fully observable, and the ones that tell you whether the loop is honest):
1. OBSERVATIONS PER HOOK TYPE - the gating number. Until a type reaches 8, it has no reportable median. Track this before tracking anything else; it is what stops the loop lying to you.
2. TYPE DIVERSITY OVER THE LAST TEN POSTS - a falling count means the loop has converged, which on current evidence means it has converged on noise and is building a cross-post pattern.
3. HAND-WRITTEN-CANDIDATE WIN RATE - how often your pre-model hook is the one you publish. A useful and slightly humbling number: it tells you whether the model is contributing quality or only variety.
4. TRUTH-CONDITION FAILURES - how often a hook gets killed for over-promising. Zero means you are not checking.

OUTCOME PROXIES, ranked by how confounded they are (least first):
- VIDEO 3-SECOND RETENTION. Directly reported, directly the thing the hook targets. The only clean hook metric that exists on any surface. If you make video, this is your instrument.
- YOUTUBE CTR via Test & Compare. A real experiment.
- EMAIL OPEN RATE. A real A/B.
- FIRST-90-MINUTE ENGAGEMENT RATE PER IMPRESSION on text surfaces. Confounded by ranker behaviour; use it as a weak proxy and never as evidence.
- Raw impressions. Do not use. This is the ranker's decision, not the reader's.

LEADING INDICATORS, in order of usefulness - and on text surfaces these are better than the numbers:
- COMMENTS QUOTING THE BODY. Direct proof the hook did its job and the reader expanded. The single best available signal on LinkedIn.
- Comments reacting ONLY to the hook. Proof it did not - the reader engaged with the promise and not the payoff.
- WHO is commenting. A hook that brings the wrong audience is working against you even while the numbers rise, and on interest-graph platforms it is also retraining the recommender.
- Unprompted DMs about the specific in the post.

WHAT NOT TO TRACK: a 'hook score'; predicted engagement from any model; type rankings below n=8; and any comparison of one post to another post rather than to a surface median.

**measurement feasibility**

THE CORE PROBLEM OF THE ITEM, and it is worse than the sample-size problem because no amount of volume fixes it: THE METRIC THE HOOK TARGETS IS NOT EXPOSED ON THE SURFACE WHERE HOOKS ARE MOST DISCUSSED.

NOT OBSERVABLE:
- LINKEDIN 'SEE MORE' EXPANSION RATE. This is precisely what a text hook does and it is not reported to creators. You are forced to measure impressions - a ranker decision made partly in response to the variant - as a proxy for expansion, which is unobserved. That substitution is not a minor imprecision; it means the measured quantity and the target quantity are causally entangled.
- DWELL TIME. Not exposed anywhere, despite being the dominant LinkedIn ranking input in 2026.
- THE COUNTERFACTUAL. You cannot publish the same post with two hooks. There is no control arm, ever, on organic.
- Whether a post was demoted for engagement bait.

FULLY OBSERVABLE, AND THIS IS WHERE THE LOOP ACTUALLY WORKS:
- VIDEO 3-SECOND RETENTION AND VIEW DURATION. Directly reported on every video surface, directly measures the hook's job. If you want a working hook loop, run it on video - this is the single most actionable sentence in the field.
- YOUTUBE CTR through Test & Compare - a genuine randomised test.
- EMAIL OPEN RATE through a genuine subject-line A/B.
- PAID CREATIVE performance through a genuine ad A/B.
- All loop-health metrics, because you own the ledger.

PARTLY OBSERVABLE: first-90-minute engagement per impression (weak proxy); X detail-expands over impressions (the closest text-surface analogue to an expansion rate, and genuinely useful); Instagram sends per reach.

THE HONEST POSITION, stated as a rule: MEASURE WHERE THE METRIC EXISTS (video, email, YouTube, paid) AND BORROW PRIORS WHERE IT DOES NOT (LinkedIn, X, Threads). On text surfaces, maintain a hook LIBRARY with post-hoc annotation and treat it as descriptive, never causal. A creator who runs a rigorous hook loop on their video output and applies the learnings to their text output is doing the only version of this that is methodologically defensible - and it is better than what almost anyone is doing.

**ai search citability**

LOW DIRECT RELEVANCE, and one genuine conflict that is worth knowing about because almost nobody names it.

WHY MOSTLY IRRELEVANT: citation is indifferent to hook performance. The median AI-cited LinkedIn post carries only 15-25 reactions and at most one comment (Semrush, 89,000 cited URLs across 325,000 prompts, Jan-Feb 2026). Engines cite for authority, clarity and extractability, not for engagement, and there is effectively no follower floor. A great hook does not make a post citable and a mediocre one does not prevent it.

THE GENUINE CONFLICT: A CURIOSITY-GAP HOOK IS AN ACTIVELY BAD FIRST SENTENCE FOR EXTRACTION. The whole mechanism of a good hook - on the Loewenstein information-gap account the sibling hook item rests on - is to WITHHOLD the claim so the reader opens the post. The whole mechanism of a citable passage is to STATE the claim, self-contained, with its evidence in the same sentence, so a retrieval system can lift it without context. 'Most people get human-in-the-loop wrong' is a functional hook and a worthless retrieval target. 'The European Commission's July 2026 guidance states that a spell-check does not constitute human review under AI Act Article 50' is a weak hook and an excellent retrieval target.
These are different objective functions pulling on the same fifteen words, and you cannot fully satisfy both.

THE PRACTICAL RESOLUTION: decide per post which objective the FIRST LINE serves, and make sure the OTHER objective is served elsewhere in the post. A curiosity hook is fine provided the claim-plus-evidence sentence appears in the body in extractable form. What fails both is a post whose hook withholds and whose body never states the claim cleanly anywhere.

ONE INDIRECT BENEFIT: the TRUTH CONDITION check - does the post deliver what the hook promised - forces the claim to exist somewhere in the post in a checkable form, which is a precondition for extraction. So the one part of this loop that helps citability is the honesty check, not the optimisation.

#### omitted as uncertain

- conflicting evidence
- cost and time to execute
