### Human-in-the-loop editorial protocol

`human-in-the-loop-protocol` · automation L1 · evidence SPLIT · 7 field(s) omitted as uncertain

#### identity

**basics**

Name: Human-in-the-loop editorial protocol. Category: system. DEFINITION: a written, named, auditable gate that (a) declares in advance which parts of a post the model may produce and which parts a human MUST supply, (b) requires the human contribution to be non-substitutable - something that could not have been generated - and (c) leaves a record proving who approved what and when. It is the production-side control layer for every other item in this research: the copy tactics say what to write, this says what must be true before it ships. WHAT IT IS NOT: 'read the draft before you post it'. That sentence is the slogan this item exists to replace. Two authorities now agree it is insufficient. The European Commission's Article 50 guidance says superficial, solely formal or procedural checks - spell-checking, grammatical correction - do not constitute human review. LinkedIn's May 2026 position says the same thing from the other side: AI may help you write, but the post must represent your voice and your perspectives, and content that appears AI-generated and lacks clear perspective gets its reach restricted. MATURITY: the CONCEPT is established (editorial workflows predate AI by a century). The legally-defined and platform-enforced version is EMERGING and became concrete in a six-week window: Commission guidelines 2026-07-20, Commission Article 50 FAQ 2026-07-24, Article 50 applicable from 2026-08-02, LinkedIn's 'seems like AI slop' report button 2026-07-30. What is NOT established is any operational standard for individual creators - the guidance is written for publishers with editors-in-chief, and nobody has translated it into a one-person workflow. That translation is what this entry attempts.

**as of date and volatility**

As of 2026-09-11. Four clocks, and they run at very different speeds - conflating them is the main way this item decays invisibly. (1) STABLE / years - the EU AI Act itself. Article 50 is primary legislation, applicable since 2026-08-02; the text of the 50(4) second-subparagraph carve-out will not change without a legislative amendment. Article 99(4) sets fines for Article 50 infringement at up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is HIGHER, with Article 99(6) making it whichever is LOWER for SMEs and start-ups. (2) SLOW / 12-24 months - the Commission's interpretive layer. The guidelines (2026-07-20) and the transparency FAQ (2026-07-24) are soft law and can be revised, but the 'spell-checking and grammatical correction do not suffice' line is a clarification of the statutory word 'review', not a policy choice, and is very unlikely to reverse. The associated Code of Practice references an interoperability solution for detection mechanisms by 2027-02-02 - a dated milestone worth watching. (3) QUARTER-TO-QUARTER - the platform layer, which is what actually determines your reach. LinkedIn announced reach restriction for AI-appearing content on 2026-05-21, shipped a user-facing 'seems like AI slop' report on 2026-07-30, began privately flagging to authors when their content reads as inauthentic, and retired its own 'enhance your post' AI writer in favour of a proofreading tool in the same move. Meta formalised original-creator rules in March 2026 with account-wide consequences. Every one of these can change again this quarter. (4) APPRECIATING, not decaying - the competitive value. Pangram measured 13.8% of 1,002,627 posts as AI-generated across platforms in April-June 2026, rising to 41% for LinkedIn long-form; Originality.ai classified 81.2% of 5,000 sampled LinkedIn long-form posts as likely-AI in July 2026. The scarcer genuinely human writing becomes, the more a gate that guarantees it is worth. This is the only clock pointing your way and it is the reason to build the gate at all. PRACTICAL RULE: rebuild the platform assumptions quarterly; re-read the Commission guidance annually or on any amendment; never restate a 2026 detector-prevalence figure as a current fact after mid-2027.

#### mechanism

**how it works**

THE SHAPE OF THE GATE. Two columns and four gates. COLUMN A - what the model may produce: structure, variants, compression, critique, retrieval from your own corpus, mechanical checks, translation drafts, and the tedious parts of formatting. COLUMN B - what a human must supply: the claim being made, the evidence behind it, at least one non-substitutable specific, the judgment about what to leave out, and the decision to publish. The protocol is the written statement of which column each element of a post belongs to, plus four gates that a draft must clear.

GATE 1 - PROVENANCE. Every factual claim in the draft is traced to a named source you can produce on demand. The model outputs a claim ledger alongside the post: claim, source, and source class (mine / public / ABSENT). Any row marked ABSENT is either sourced or the claim is deleted. This gate is the single highest-value one: it catches the failure mode - confidently specific invented numbers - that has the largest blast radius.

GATE 2 - NON-SUBSTITUTABLE INPUT. The post must contain at least one element that could only come from you (see human_input_required for the enumerated list). The operational test is the SUBSTITUTION AUDIT: swap your name for a competitor's and your numbers for different plausible ones. If the post still works unchanged, it contains nothing only you could have written and it fails. This is the checkable version of 'do not post slop', and - crucially - it is a close proxy for what LinkedIn's classifiers are described as probing for: perspective, and patterns across a member's content.

GATE 3 - SUBSTANTIVE EDIT. The human must change meaning, not surface. A useful forcing function: require the human edit to be expressible as a diff in which at least one change alters a claim, a hedge, an ordering, or a deletion - not only word choice. This is the gate the Commission's language maps onto directly: deliberate examination of the substance by a person with relevant knowledge, including fact-checking, as opposed to a formal or procedural check.

GATE 4 - RECORDED APPROVAL. An artifact exists proving a named person approved this specific text at a specific time. Without it, you have a habit, not a protocol - and under Article 50 you have no evidence of the carve-out you are relying on.

THE APPROVAL MECHANISM - reuse, do not re-derive. The vault note 'Marketing Agent Research' (2026-08-25) settled this for the sibling agent project and its conclusions transfer intact:
- APPROVAL = MERGING A PULL REQUEST. A PR gives you an unbounded pause (no timeout, no idle cost), approval from a phone, and - the property no agent-runtime primitive offers - NATIVE EDIT-BEFORE-APPROVE via suggested changes. Neither a `defer` nor an `always_ask` permission mode lets a human change the tool input; they only let you say yes or no to what the agent already chose. The git commit is simultaneously the publication trigger and the evidentiary record of editorial review.
- EDITORIAL STATE LIVES IN THE REPO, not at a vendor: calendar, dedup index and approval history in a SQLite/Turso file next to git.
- REFERENCE CORPORA MOUNT READ-ONLY. A social agent ingests hostile internet text by design; writable memory turns one successful prompt injection into trusted memory for every later session.
- AUTONOMY CEILING L2/L3 in that note's numbering: the agent plans and waits; full autonomy is treated as unavailable.

THE SILENT-FAILURE TRAPS - the part that makes this an engineering item rather than a policy item. Each of these produces a gate that LOOKS installed and is not, with no error and no warning:
- Kestra's `Pause` task defaults to `behavior: RESUME`. When the timeout expires the flow continues as if approved. Silent auto-publication.
- Cloudflare Workflows' `waitForEvent` has a default 24-hour timeout - squarely inside the window you are waiting on a human - and the vendor's own human-in-the-loop example catches the expiry and 'proceeds with default action'.
- GitHub Actions required reviewers only work on PUBLIC repositories for Free/Pro/Team plans. Merging the PR sidesteps this entirely, which is one more reason to put the gate on the merge rather than on a workflow environment.
- English-only anti-slop linters (sloptrim's 71 patterns, content-quality-scorer.py) return clean on Polish text. A false pass in the gate that exists to protect you.
- faststylometry's default `tok_match_pattern = r'^[a-z][a-z]+$'` strips every Polish word containing a diacritic and returns confident numbers while broken.

THE NO-TOUCH-AFTER-REVIEW RULE. Once the human has reviewed, no model touches the text again. This is not fastidiousness: the Orrick analysis of the Commission guidelines states that substantive AI intervention occurring AFTER human review can void the exception. A final 'polish pass' is the most natural thing in the world to do and it is the move that undoes the whole protocol - and re-introduces the cadence tells you just edited out.

**ranking signal targeted**

HONEST ANSWER: none directly. This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL, not a booster - it does not move a signal upward, it keeps you out of a demotion bucket. Treating it as a reach tactic will make you disappointed and then make you abandon it.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY TOUCHES, in descending order of confidence:
1. THE LOW-QUALITY / GENERICNESS CLASSIFIER (platform-stated, magnitude unknown). LinkedIn's stated position is that content which appears AI-generated and lacks clear perspective has its reach restricted, that it runs classifiers for this, and - since 2026-07-30 - that a user-facing 'seems like AI slop' report tunes those classifiers. LinkedIn's chief product officer described the button as 'a source of signal that will allow LinkedIn to tune its AI models to better identify slop'. Gate 2 (non-substitutable input) is the direct counter-signal. Note the detection unit: LinkedIn's described approach looks at PATTERNS ACROSS A MEMBER'S CONTENT, so the relevant object is your corpus, not your post.
2. ORIGINALITY / AUTHENTICITY SCORING (platform-stated across LinkedIn, Meta, Instagram, TikTok). Every major platform in 2026 scores originality at the account level, not just the post level.
3. DWELL TIME (indirect, second-order). A post carrying a real number with a method line, or a real incident with a date, is read more slowly than an assertion. But the gate does not target dwell - dwell is a side effect of the substance the gate forces in. See the sibling item 'Dwell-time copy architecture' for the direct version.
4. SEMANTIC RELEVANCE / TOPIC AUTHORITY (indirect). A gate that demands first-hand specifics tends to keep you on the one topic where you actually have them, which is what LinkedIn's 360Brew-era topic-authority signal rewards.

WHAT IT DOES NOT TOUCH: first-hour comments, sends, saves, completion rate, reply depth. None of these respond to a gate. If your reach problem is distribution velocity, this is the wrong item - see 'Comment-driven CTA design' and 'Narrowcast share-to-DM trigger design'.

**why it drives reach**

THE CAUSAL STORY HAS THREE LINKS, and the second is the one people miss.

LINK 1 - the penalty is account-scoped, not post-scoped. This is the structural fact that makes a gate rational. Meta's March 2026 original-creator rules make a Page with a repost history non-recommendable AND demonetisable ACCOUNT-WIDE - the reach cut applies to that account's original posts too, not only to the offending clip. Instagram's rule that 10+ reposts in 30 days can exclude an account from recommendations has the same shape. LinkedIn's approach is described as pattern-based across a member's content and, as of July 2026, includes privately flagging to a member that their content reads as inauthentic. Consequence: the expected cost of publishing one ungated post is NOT bounded by that post's performance. It is a small probability of a persistent, invisible, account-level tax on everything you publish afterwards. A gate converts an unbounded tail risk into a bounded, known, per-post time cost. That trade is favourable at almost any plausible parameterisation, which is why the argument for the gate survives even though nobody can quote you a reach lift for it.

LINK 2 - the gate's OUTPUT is what the ranker is looking for, not the gate itself. No platform can see your workflow. What it sees is a post containing a number with a sample size, a dated incident, a named tool version, a stated trade-off. The gate is simply the most reliable way to make sure that object exists. This is why 'add a HITL step' with no substance requirement buys nothing - a human clicking approve on a generic draft produces a generic post, and the classifier sees the post.

LINK 3 - scarcity. Pangram, N=1,002,627 posts, April-June 2026: 13.8% AI overall; LinkedIn 30% short-form and 41% long-form; LinkedIn accounted for 62% of ALL flagged AI content while being 35% of scanned posts. Originality.ai put 81.2% of 5,000 sampled LinkedIn long-form posts in the likely-AI bucket in July 2026 (against 53.7% of 3,368 posts in 2025). Whatever the true rate - both figures come from vendors selling detection - the direction is unambiguous and the denominator is what matters: a post that visibly could not have been generated is competing in a thinner field every quarter. The gate's return is rising for reasons entirely outside your control.

THE HONEST CAVEAT. There is no measured reach delta for editorial gating. Nobody has run the experiment, and you cannot run it either (see measurement_feasibility). The case rests on the asymmetry in Link 1 and the platform-official statements in Link 2, not on an effect size. Anyone selling you a percentage here is selling you a vendor number.

#### ai angle

**ai role**

DRAFT, CRITIQUE, RETRIEVE, VARY, CHECK. Never approve, never self-grade, never touch the text after review.

1. DRAFT - from a human-written brief, not from a topic. The inversion matters: the default workflow is 'human gives topic, model writes, human edits', which puts the human in the weakest position (reacting to a finished artifact, which triggers anchoring and makes rubber-stamping almost inevitable). The protocol reverses it: the human writes five lines - the claim, the evidence, the non-substitutable specific, the audience, the one action - before the model is invoked at all.
2. CRITIQUE - adversarially, in a named role. Hostile editor, skeptical methodologist, the competitor who would quote this against you. This is the highest-value model task in the whole workflow because it is the one where the model's lack of ego is an advantage.
3. RETRIEVE - from your own corpus. See the sibling item 'RAG-grounded post generation'; the retrieval step is what makes Gate 2 cheap rather than expensive, because the non-substitutable specifics are already written down somewhere in the vault.
4. VARY - hooks, orderings, compressions. Cheap, safe, and the model's genuine comparative advantage.
5. CHECK, mechanically only - does every number have a source token attached? is there a first-person specific? is there a date? does any sentence contain a statistic with no referent? These are string-level questions with right answers and can be automated (L2).

WHAT THE MODEL MUST NOT DO, and why each is a real failure and not a purity rule:
- APPROVE. Beyond the legal point, the approval decision is where the human's accountability attaches; delegating it deletes the thing the protocol exists to create.
- SELF-GRADE. A model asked to critique its own draft passes almost everything. Marketing Agent Research names this explicitly as a mine.
- GATE THE VOICE AS A JUDGE. PersonalBench found LLM judges rating texts as varied where stylometry showed they were not. Use a stylometric metric, not a judge, for voice - and if the text is Polish, check first that your stylometry library is not silently deleting every diacritic word (faststylometry's default token pattern does exactly this).
- TOUCH THE TEXT AFTER HUMAN REVIEW. Substantive AI intervention after review can void the Article 50 carve-out, per the Orrick reading of the Commission guidelines. This is a hard sequencing constraint, not a style preference.

**automation level**

L1 for drafting. L2 for the mechanical checks. L0 BY CONSTRUCTION for the approval decision - the gate is definitionally the step that is not automated, so an 'automated HITL' is a contradiction and, in practice, the most common way this item fails.

Mapped onto the taxonomy: the DRAFT is L1 AI-assisted. The CLAIM-LEDGER, string-level checks and variant generation can run L2 autonomous-with-guardrails behind a fixed rubric. The APPROVE step is L0 and must stay there. Nothing here is L3, and in this item L3 is not merely unwise - it is the failure state with a name.

THE VENDOR-LABEL WARNING, sharpened for this item. Most tools marketed as 'AI agents' for social are L1 schedulers with an approve button. That is fine. The dangerous subclass is the tool whose approve button has a TIMEOUT THAT DEFAULTS TO PROCEED - Kestra's `Pause` with `behavior: RESUME`, Cloudflare Workflows' `waitForEvent` with its 24-hour default and a reference HITL example that proceeds with a default action on expiry. A gate that publishes when you fail to answer is L3 wearing an L2 costume, and it will pass every demo. AUDIT ACTION, do it once and write down the answer: for every tool in your publishing path, what happens when the human never responds? If the answer is 'it publishes', change it or replace the tool.

The corollary, from Marketing Agent Research: putting the gate OUTSIDE the agent runtime (merge a PR) rather than inside it (a permission prompt) is what makes L0 actually hold, because a PR has no timeout and an unanswered PR simply stays open forever.

**prompt patterns**

Six patterns, in workflow order. All of them are written to make the human do work the model cannot, which is the opposite of how post-generation prompts are usually written.

1. BRIEF-FIRST REFUSAL (run before any drafting).
'Here is my brief: CLAIM / EVIDENCE / THE THING ONLY I KNOW / AUDIENCE / ONE ACTION. Do not write the post yet. List the three things you would need from me that you cannot invent or infer. Then ask me for them, one question at a time.'
Why it works: it forces the missing-input problem to surface BEFORE a plausible draft exists. Once a finished draft is on screen, the human's job silently changes from 'supply what is missing' to 'approve what is there'.

2. CLAIM LEDGER (run with the draft, every time).
'Output the post. Then output a table with one row per factual claim: CLAIM | SOURCE | CLASS (mine / public / ABSENT). Every number, date, name and comparative counts as a claim. Do not silently drop a claim to avoid marking it ABSENT. If a claim came from your training data rather than from something I gave you, class it ABSENT.'
This is the single most load-bearing prompt in the protocol. It converts fact-checking from a vigilance task (which humans fail at) into a list-processing task (which humans are fine at).

3. SUBSTITUTION AUDIT (the Gate 2 test).
'Rewrite this post replacing my name with a competitor's and every number with a different plausible number. Now compare the two versions. Which sentences changed meaning, and which survived intact? If more than 80% survived intact, tell me the post contains nothing only I could have written.'
Why it works: it makes non-substitutability MEASURABLE instead of a matter of taste.

4. HOSTILE EDITOR (adversarial pass).
'You are an editor who will be personally and legally liable for this publication. Name: (a) the three claims you would refuse to publish without a source; (b) the one sentence a competitor could screenshot and quote against me; (c) the one place a knowledgeable reader would say <that is not how it works>. Be specific and do not soften.'
Deliberately phrased in the Commission's own vocabulary - liability, substantive grounds, fact-checking - because that is the standard the carve-out is written against.

5. DIFF-FORCING EDIT (keeps the human's edit substantive).
'I am going to edit this. Return the post as plain text with no formatting so I can diff it. After I return my edited version, classify each of my changes as SURFACE (word choice, punctuation, length) or SUBSTANTIVE (changed a claim, added a hedge, reordered an argument, deleted something). If all my changes are SURFACE, say so plainly.'
This one is uncomfortable by design. It is the prompt that tells you your gate has degraded into a spell-check - exactly the thing the guidance says does not count.

6. POST-REVIEW LOCK (a rule, not a prompt). After the human edit, the text is frozen. If something must change, the human changes it by hand. Never paste the reviewed text back into a model for a final polish.

ANTI-PATTERNS: 'make this sound more human' (produces a different generic register and adds detectable rewriting artefacts); 'rate this post 1-10' (self-grading, passes everything); 'check this for AI patterns' (the model that wrote it is the worst possible detector of it); and any prompt that asks the model whether the post is ready to publish.

**tool examples**

- **approval path recommended**:
  - GitHub / GitLab pull request as the approval gate - unlimited pause, zero idle cost, mobile approval, native edit-before-approve via suggested changes, and the merge commit doubles as the Article 50 evidence record. This is the Marketing Agent Research verdict and it transfers unchanged.
  - Claude Agent SDK with process-exit-and-resume - the runtime half of the same design; the agent exits rather than idling while a human decides.
- **approval tools with known traps**:
  - Kestra `Pause` task - DEFAULT `behavior: RESUME`. Times out into auto-publication. Must be explicitly reconfigured.
  - Cloudflare Workflows `waitForEvent` - default 24h timeout; the vendor's own HITL example proceeds with a default action on expiry.
  - GitHub Actions required reviewers - public repositories only on Free/Pro/Team plans; not a usable gate on a private content repo.
  - Agent permission modes (`defer`, `always_ask`) - allow yes/no but NOT editing the tool input, so they cannot host an editorial gate.
- **quality and detection side**:
  - Vale (free, open source) - prose linter; enforces house-style rules deterministically. Good for the surface half; explicitly NOT the substance half.
  - Pangram - AI text classifier; vendor claims 0.01% false-positive rate on its 3.3 model. Useful as an occasional spot-check on your own output, not as a gate.
  - Originality.ai - detector vendor; source of the LinkedIn prevalence figures. Same caveat.
  - sloptrim (71 patterns) and ericosiu's content-quality-scorer.py - ENGLISH ONLY. Return clean on Polish text. Do not wire these into a PL track.
  - faststylometry - default `tok_match_pattern = r'^[a-z][a-z]+$'` deletes every Polish diacritic word; patch the pattern before trusting any number it produces.
  - Langfuse - trace store; attach the approval event and the T+7 metric pull to the same trace so the gate's decisions are auditable after the fact.
- **platform side 2026**:
  - LinkedIn 'seems like AI slop' report button - shipped 2026-07-30; feeds LinkedIn's own classifier tuning.
  - LinkedIn proofreading tool - replaced the 'enhance your post' AI writer in July 2026. Note what this signals: the platform moved its own first-party tool from generation to correction.
  - LinkedIn private inauthenticity flag - the platform tells the author, privately, when their content reads as heavily AI-assisted.
- **polish track**: Bielik (Apache-2.0) for post-correction of Polish text - commercially safe. PLLuM is CC-BY-NC-4.0 and is NOT commercially usable. Both per Marketing Agent Research.

#### evidence

**evidence strength**

SPLIT, and the split is the point.
STRONG (legal): the conditions of the Article 50(4) carve-out and the exclusion of spell-checking from 'human review'. Primary legislation plus the Commission's own published guidance and FAQ. This is as close to fact as anything in this research gets.
MODERATE (platform-official, direction only): that LinkedIn restricts reach of content appearing AI-generated and lacking perspective, runs classifiers, accepts user reports as a tuning signal, and privately flags authors. All directly attributed to named LinkedIn staff in contemporaneous trade reporting. The DIRECTION is solid; no magnitude has ever been published.
MODERATE (vendor, large-N, disclosed method): the AI-prevalence denominators - Pangram N=1,002,627, Originality.ai N=5,000. Large samples, stated methods, and both vendors sell detection. Treat as a range, not a point.
ANECDOTAL / INTERNAL: the approval-mechanics conclusions (PR-as-gate, timeout traps). These come from the vault's own 'Marketing Agent Research' - a 31-item two-phase research pass, i.e. your own prior work, not an independent source. The tool-behaviour claims within it are verifiable against vendor documentation and should be re-verified before you depend on them.
UNVERIFIED / NON-EXISTENT: any reach effect for the gate. There is no study, no vendor number, and no plausible way to produce one.
OVERALL: strong on 'what the rule is', moderate on 'what the platform does', and absent on 'what it buys you in reach'. Build the gate for the asymmetry and the legal position, not for a promised lift.

**evidence provenance**

REGULATOR-OFFICIAL: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Articles 50 and 99; European Commission 'Transparency obligations under Article 50 AI Act' FAQ (24 July 2026); Commission guidelines on AI transparency obligations (20 July 2026). Highest class available for the legal content of this item.
PROFESSIONAL LEGAL ANALYSIS: Orrick, 'EU AI Act: Transparency Obligations for AI-Generated Content' (August 2026). A law firm interpreting the guidelines - authoritative on reading, not on outcome. Source of the post-review-intervention point.
PLATFORM-OFFICIAL (via trade-press reporting of named executives): LinkedIn VP Laura Lorenzetti on the May 2026 reach restriction; LinkedIn's chief product officer on the July 2026 report button. The statements are official; the reporting is secondary.
VENDOR-WITH-PRODUCT-TO-SELL, LARGE-N, DISCLOSED METHOD: Pangram (detector vendor; 1,002,627 posts; opt-in extension users, which is NOT a random sample of the feed); Originality.ai (detector vendor; 5,000 posts sampled; 3,368 posts from 99 profiles in the 2025 comparison); Semrush (SEO vendor; 325,000 prompts / 89,000 LinkedIn URLs, for the citability half).
PEER-REVIEWED: none directly on editorial gating. The adjacent peer-reviewed material (PersonalBench on LLM-judge unreliability, cited via Marketing Agent Research) supports a design choice inside the gate, not the gate itself.
OWN PRIOR WORK, NOT INDEPENDENT: content/PROJECTS/AGENTIC-SYSTEMS/Marketing Agent Research.md. Flagged deliberately - it is the source of most of the mechanics here and it is not an external authority. Its factual claims about tool defaults are re-verifiable and should be re-verified.
ABSENT ENTIRELY: any independent evaluation of whether editorial gating changes distribution.
